title: Validating the Single Item Kawaii Measure
summary: Kawaii is the Japanese instantiation of cuteness. As a multimodal percept theoretically derived from the notion of baby schema, kawaii can be a property of voice and sound, visual appearance and form factor, and movement and expression. However, measuring user perceptions of kawaii remains an open question. In the absence of a validated instrument, a one-item self-report measure has been used extensively, but has not been validated. Here, we report on three types of validity -- convergent, known groups, and cross-context -- and reliability for the single item measure across nine data sets featuring responses to video game character voices and visual appearances and computer-generated voice assistant voices from N=967 unique participants. Our results demonstrate initial evidence of the validity of the one-item measure for voice and visual kawaii perceptions. Further rigour can be pursued with novel stimuli, test-retest validation, and concurrent validity against the upcoming multi-item measure of kawaii.

AI.tldr: The paper validates a single-item self-report measure for assessing perceptions of kawaii (Japanese cuteness) across voice, visual, and multimodal stimuli, using nine datasets (N=967). Results show initial convergent, known-groups, and cross-context validity, supporting its use pending further validation against a forthcoming multi-item instrument.
AI.motivation: Kawaii is a multimodal percept rooted in baby schema, manifesting in voice, appearance, and movement. Despite extensive use of a one-item self-report measure in prior research, no formal validation of this instrument exists, leaving a gap in the empirical measurement of kawaii perceptions.
AI.method: The authors assessed three validity types (convergent, known-groups, cross-context) and reliability for the single-item kawaii measure across nine datasets comprising 967 unique participants. Stimuli included video game character voices, visual appearances, and computer-generated voice assistant voices.
AI.result: The single-item measure demonstrated initial evidence of validity for both voice and visual kawaii perceptions across all three validity types tested, along with acceptable reliability.
AI.conclusion: The one-item kawaii measure shows promising validity as a practical tool, though further rigor is recommended through novel stimuli, test-retest reliability assessment, and concurrent validation against an upcoming multi-item kawaii scale.

title: How Far Can Wearable-Compatible Signals Go? A Controlled Decomposition of Non-EEG Sleep Staging
summary: Consumer wearables increasingly infer sleep stages from signals including heart rate, accelerometry, and photoplethysmography. However, existing studies often report end-to-end performance under a fixed signal setting, making it difficult to determine whether the observed performance comes from genuine physiological decoding, temporal priors, or dataset-specific confounds. To address this limitation, we introduce a four-layer controlled decomposition framework for non-EEG sleep staging, covering signal source, physiological representation, temporal prior, and decision layers. The framework is evaluated across a signal-quality ladder spanning Apple Watch Sleep-Accel ($N=31$), the Sleep Heart Health Study ($N=195$, laboratory ECG, respiratory, and SpO$_2$ signals), and Sleep-EDF-20 as an EEG+EOG reference, using the same compact Mamba2 model throughout. Laboratory cardiorespiratory signals reach $κ=0.492$, while EEG+EOG reaches $κ=0.796$, leaving a residual gap of $Δκ=+0.304$ that reflects missing cortical information rather than temporal modeling alone. Consumer HR/ACC reaches only $κ=0.255$, quantifying the additional penalty of derived wearable signals and real-world sensing constraints. Confidence-based abstention provides a calibrated operating mode: removing the 20% lowest-confidence epochs increases $κ$ from $0.452$ to $0.512$, while a label-shuffled control collapses to $κ=-0.003$. These results support non-EEG sleep staging as coarse, confidence-aware sleep-structure monitoring rather than EEG-equivalent five-class clinical staging.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a controlled decomposition framework for non-EEG sleep staging that isolates contributions from signal source, physiological representation, temporal priors, and decision layers. Evaluated across a signal-quality ladder (Apple Watch, SHHS laboratory signals, Sleep-EDF-20 EEG+EOG), results show cardiorespiratory signals reach κ=0.492 vs. EEG κ=0.796, while consumer wearables achieve only κ=0.255. Confidence-based abstention improves performance, and label-shuffled controls confirm genuine physiological decoding rather than dataset confounds.
AI.motivation: Existing non-EEG sleep staging studies report end-to-end performance under fixed signal settings, making it impossible to disentangle whether observed accuracy stems from genuine physiological decoding, temporal priors, or dataset-specific confounds. There is a need for a principled decomposition framework that isolates these factors across varying signal quality tiers.
AI.method: A four-layer controlled decomposition framework covering (1) signal source, (2) physiological representation, (3) temporal prior, and (4) decision layers. Evaluated using a single compact Mamba2 model across a signal-quality ladder: Apple Watch Sleep-Accel (N=31, consumer HR/ACC), Sleep Heart Health Study (N=195, laboratory ECG/respiratory/SpO₂), and Sleep-EDF-20 (EEG+EOG reference). Includes confidence-based abstention and label-shuffled controls.
AI.result: Laboratory cardiorespiratory signals: κ=0.492; EEG+EOG: κ=0.796 (Δκ=+0.304 gap reflecting missing cortical information). Consumer HR/ACC: κ=0.255 (additional penalty from derived wearable signals and real-world constraints). Confidence-based abstention removing 20% lowest-confidence epochs raises κ from 0.452 to 0.512. Label-shuffled control collapses to κ=−0.003, confirming genuine physiological decoding.
AI.conclusion: Non-EEG sleep staging should be framed as coarse, confidence-aware sleep-structure monitoring rather than EEG-equivalent five-class clinical staging. The decomposition framework provides a principled way to attribute performance across the processing pipeline.

title: Associations Between Support-Seekers' Cross-Community Interactions and Their Engagement with Received Comments in Online Health Communities
summary: Support-seeker' active engagement with received comments, e.g., showing positive sentiment and willingness to improve in the replies, can indicate the success of online health communities (OHCs). Their participation in other communities may correlate with their engagement in OHCs but remains under-explored. This paper analyzes 26, 725 seekers' behaviors in the other 40, 479 communities and their associations with seekers' engagement with received comments under their 78, 501 posts in 30 Baidu Tieba OHCs. We found that seekers primarily posted in other communities that are also health-related (25.3%), followed by those about games and entertainment (e.g., Dota, 20.8%). Seekers who posted in other communities about health (26.3%) or personal issues (e.g., saving money, 20.7%) before had relatively higher probabilities of subsequently posting in the 30 OHCs we identified, but this posting experience was associated with fewer replies and less expressed willingness to improve based on received comments. We provide insights into fostering seekers' engagement in OHCs based on cross-community interactions.

AI.tldr: This study examines how support-seekers' participation in non-OHC communities on Baidu Tieba relates to their engagement with received comments in online health communities, finding that prior posting experience in health or personal-issue communities correlates with lower engagement levels.
AI.motivation: Understanding what drives support-seekers' active engagement with received comments (e.g., positive sentiment, willingness to improve) is critical for measuring OHC success. However, the role of seekers' cross-community participation—their activity in other, non-health communities—remains largely unexplored as a potential correlate of their engagement within OHCs.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 26,725 support-seekers' behavioral data across 40,479 other communities and their engagement with comments on 78,501 posts within 30 Baidu Tieba OHCs. They categorized the other communities seekers posted in and examined associations between prior cross-community posting experience and subsequent engagement indicators (reply count, expressed willingness to improve) within the OHCs.
AI.result: Seekers posted most frequently in other health-related communities (25.3%), followed by games/entertainment (e.g., Dota, 20.8%). Those with prior posting experience in health-related (26.3%) or personal-issue communities (e.g., saving money, 20.7%) showed higher probabilities of later posting in the 30 target OHCs. However, this cross-community experience was paradoxically associated with fewer replies and lower expressed willingness to improve based on received comments.
AI.conclusion: Cross-community interactions are meaningfully associated with support-seekers' engagement patterns in OHCs, revealing a tension: prior experience in similar communities facilitates entry into OHCs but may dampen active engagement once there. The findings offer actionable insights for designing interventions to foster deeper engagement in OHCs.

title: Mammal: Supporting Breastfeeding Monitoring Through Computational Garments with Inter-Body Sensing
summary: Breastfeeding provides critical insight into infant feeding competence and physiological health, yet objective monitoring remains difficult due to the intimate and internal nature of feeding. We present Mammal, a caregiver-worn computational garment that unobtrusively monitors breastfeeding without attaching sensors to the infant. Mammal leverages inter-body signal transmission through natural mouth-to-breast contact to capture infant cardiac and feeding-related acoustic signals on the caregiver's body. Using novel algorithms to detect latch onset, infer infant electrocardiogram (ECG), and identify suck and swallow events from inter-body signals, Mammal estimates latch duration, in-feeding heart rate, suck-swallow-breathe (SSB) ratio, and milk intake. In a user study with 10 caregiver-infant dyads, Mammal achieves a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 5.56% for latch duration, a mean absolute error (MAE) of 3.61 bpm for infant heart rate estimation, a mean absolute error of 0.12 for SSB ratio estimation, and a mean relative error of 15.76% for milk intake, with participants reporting high comfort and wearability.

AI.tldr: Mammal is a caregiver-worn smart garment that monitors breastfeeding by capturing infant cardiac and acoustic signals through mouth-to-breast inter-body transmission, enabling estimation of latch duration, heart rate, suck-swallow-breathe ratio, and milk intake without sensors on the infant.
AI.motivation: Objective breastfeeding monitoring is clinically important for assessing infant feeding competence and physiological health, but remains challenging due to the intimate, internal nature of feeding. Existing methods either attach sensors directly to the infant (intrusive) or lack quantitative precision.
AI.method: The Mammal computational garment is worn by the caregiver and exploits inter-body signal transmission: when the infant latches, cardiac (ECG) and feeding-related acoustic signals propagate through mouth-to-breast contact to sensors embedded in the garment. Novel algorithms detect latch onset, infer infant ECG, and identify suck/swallow events from these inter-body signals to compute feeding metrics.
AI.result: In a 10-dyad user study, Mammal achieved: 5.56% MAPE for latch duration, 3.61 bpm MAE for infant heart rate, 0.12 MAE for SSB ratio, and 15.76% mean relative error for milk intake. Participants reported high comfort and wearability.
AI.conclusion: Mammal demonstrates that caregiver-worn sensing via inter-body signal transmission is a viable, unobtrusive approach for objective breastfeeding monitoring, providing clinically relevant metrics without instrumenting the infant.

title: Understanding Developer Pain Points in Federated Learning: Insights from Stack Overflow and GitHub
summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without centralizing raw data, but building and operating FL systems remains difficult due to distributed execution, rapidly evolving frameworks, and privacy and governance requirements. In this paper, we present an empirical study of FL developer challenges by independently analyzing 495 Stack Overflow posts and 9,116 GitHub issues and pull requests from 92 FL-related projects. Using BERTopic-based topic modeling and difficulty indicators such as unresolved rates and median resolution time, we characterize recurring problem areas and compare how they manifest across the two support platforms, Stack Overflow and GitHub. Our analysis surfaces nine dominant Stack Overflow topics and thirteen GitHub topics, with persistent difficulties concentrated in environment setup and dependency compatibility, API breakages and migration, training instability under non-IID data, evaluation and metric correctness, and the integration of privacy-preserving mechanisms. We also categorize posts by question intent to understand the kinds of help developers seek; this intent analysis shows that "How"-type questions dominate, reflecting strong demand for procedural guidance. Several topics, such as "TFF Installation and Environment Compatibility" and "Federated Feature Engineering and SecureBoost Issues," exhibit high unresolved rates and long resolution times, suggesting shortcomings in tooling, documentation, and debugging support. Based on these findings, we provide actionable implications for FL framework designers, documentation authors, and educators. Although our results are constrained to public discussions and a subset of widely discussed frameworks, the study offers a scalable method for continuously monitoring developer pain points and improving the usability, reliability, and deployability of FL systems.

AI.tldr: An empirical study analyzing 495 Stack Overflow posts and 9,116 GitHub issues/PRs across 92 FL projects using BERTopic modeling, revealing nine Stack Overflow and thirteen GitHub dominant topics. Key pain points include environment setup, API instability, non-IID training issues, evaluation correctness, and privacy mechanism integration, with actionable implications for FL tooling and documentation.
AI.motivation: Federated Learning systems are difficult to build and operate due to distributed execution, rapidly evolving frameworks, and privacy/governance requirements. There is a lack of systematic, empirical understanding of the specific challenges FL developers face in practice.
AI.method: The authors collected 495 Stack Overflow posts and 9,116 GitHub issues/pull requests from 92 FL-related projects. They applied BERTopic-based topic modeling to surface dominant problem areas and used difficulty indicators (unresolved rates, median resolution time) to quantify topic severity. They also categorized posts by question intent (e.g., "How"-type) to understand the nature of developer help-seeking behavior.
AI.result: Nine dominant topics emerged from Stack Overflow and thirteen from GitHub. Persistent difficulties concentrate in: environment setup/dependency compatibility, API breakages and migration, training instability under non-IID data, evaluation and metric correctness, and integration of privacy-preserving mechanisms. "How"-type questions dominate, indicating strong demand for procedural guidance. Topics like "TFF Installation and Environment Compatibility" and "Federated Feature Engineering and SecureBoost Issues" show high unresolved rates and long resolution times.
AI.conclusion: The study provides actionable implications for FL framework designers, documentation authors, and educators to address recurring developer pain points. While limited to public discussions and a subset of widely discussed frameworks, the method offers a scalable approach for continuously monitoring developer challenges and improving FL system usability, reliability, and deployability.

title: CHMAS: A Coupled Hierarchical Framework for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: Presented at the 2026 American Control Conference (ACC 2026). This version corrects the author names in Reference 1. The technical content, results, and conclusions are unchanged
summary:
Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) systems face fundamental
  challenges in balancing global coordination with local execution
  across different temporal scales. This paper introduces the Coupled
  Hierarchical Multi-Agent System (CHMAS), a novel framework that
  decomposes multi-agent decision-making into centralized strategic
  planning and distributed tactical execution with bidirectional
  information flow. The strategic layer integrates all agents' states
  with an exclusive global environmental state to generate guidance
  actions every $T$ timesteps, while tactical agents execute
  distributed policies augmented by strategic guidance and local
  neighborhood observations. Unlike existing hierarchical approaches
  with unidirectional control, CHMAS establishes a feedback mechanism
  where accumulated tactical rewards influence strategic objectives
  through a coupling coefficient $λ$, ensuring strategic plans
  remain grounded in tactical feasibility. To address the
  non-stationarity inherent in hierarchical learning, we propose an
  asynchronous update protocol where strategic parameters update every
  $N_f$ tactical episodes, allowing tactical policies to converge to
  quasi-stationary points between strategic changes. We present both a
  general bi-level formulation capturing full system dynamics and a
  tractable additive approximation enabling rigorous analysis.
  Theoretical analysis proves that this asynchronous scheme achieves
  $\mathcal{O}(\log K/\sqrt{K})$ convergence for the strategic layer
  after $K$ strategic updates under standard assumptions. Experimental
  validation in a multi-agent foraging domain demonstrates successful
  learning of spatially partitioned exploration strategies, with both
  layers converging stably despite hierarchical coupling.

AI.tldr: CHMAS introduces a hierarchical MARL framework with a bidirectional coupling between centralized strategic planning (updated every T timesteps) and distributed tactical execution. An asynchronous update protocol (strategic updates every N_f tactical episodes) addresses non-stationarity, achieving O(log K/√K) convergence for the strategic layer. Validated in multi-agent foraging with stable convergence and learned spatial partitioning.
AI.motivation: MARL systems struggle to balance global coordination with local execution across different temporal scales. Existing hierarchical approaches use unidirectional control (top-down only), causing strategic plans to become detached from tactical realities. Additionally, hierarchical learning suffers from non-stationarity as tactical policies must adapt to changing strategic guidance.
AI.method: CHMAS decomposes decision-making into two layers: (1) a centralized strategic layer that aggregates all agent states plus a global environmental state to produce guidance actions every T timesteps; (2) distributed tactical agents executing policies augmented by strategic guidance and local neighborhood observations. A coupling coefficient λ enables bottom-up feedback where accumulated tactical rewards influence strategic objectives. An asynchronous update protocol freezes strategic parameters for N_f tactical episodes, letting tactical policies converge to quasi-stationary points. Both a general bi-level formulation and a tractable additive approximation are provided.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis proves O(log K/√K) convergence for the strategic layer after K strategic updates under standard assumptions. Experimental validation in multi-agent foraging demonstrates stable convergence of both layers and successful emergence of spatially partitioned exploration strategies.
AI.conclusion: CHMAS effectively balances centralized coordination with distributed execution through bidirectional coupling and asynchronous updates, with formal convergence guarantees and empirical success in foraging tasks. The framework addresses both the temporal-scale mismatch and non-stationarity challenges in hierarchical MARL.

title: Personalized Recommendation Tool Learning via Autonomous Language Agents
summary: Although large language models (LLMs) have recently gained traction in recommender systems due to their strong reasoning capabilities and extensive world knowledge, previous LLM-based agents suffer from hallucination and context-length limitations, and thus are not suitable for full-ranking recommendation tasks. To circumvent these limitations through architectural design rather than modifying the LLM itself, we propose an agent-based recommendation framework, memory-based $\textbf{P}$ersonalized $\textbf{R}$ecommendation $\textbf{T}$ool learning via autonomous language $\textbf{A}$gents (PRTA), in which an LLM acts as a central planner interacting with multiple recommendation models as tools. The LLM-based agent is responsible for high-level reasoning and personalized tool selection, while traditional recommendation models perform full-ranking scoring, leveraging their scalability in modeling behavioral patterns. To support personalized tool selection, we design reflection mechanisms that enable the agent to evaluate and compare tools for each user based on user profiles and candidate ranked lists. Extensive experiments across three public datasets demonstrate the superiority of \modelname over traditional recommendation and LLM-based baselines in improving full-ranking recommendation performance.

AI.tldr: PRTA is an agent-based recommendation framework where an LLM serves as a central planner that selects and coordinates multiple traditional recommendation models as tools, using reflection mechanisms for personalized tool selection, thereby overcoming LLM hallucination and context-length limitations in full-ranking recommendation.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based recommender agents suffer from hallucination and context-length limitations, making them unsuitable for full-ranking recommendation tasks. The authors aim to address these limitations through architectural design (rather than modifying the LLM itself) by combining the reasoning strengths of LLMs with the scalability of traditional recommendation models.
AI.method: The PRTA framework features an LLM-based central planner agent that performs high-level reasoning and personalized tool selection, while traditional recommendation models handle full-ranking scoring. A key innovation is the reflection mechanism, which enables the agent to evaluate and compare different tools for each user based on user profiles and candidate ranked lists, facilitating personalized tool selection.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three public datasets show that PRTA outperforms both traditional recommendation methods and LLM-based baselines in full-ranking recommendation performance.
AI.conclusion: PRTA demonstrates that a hybrid architecture—pairing an LLM as a reasoning orchestrator with specialized recommendation models as tools—effectively mitigates LLM limitations while leveraging their complementary strengths, offering a superior approach to full-ranking recommendation.

title: JailMeter: An Evidence-Based Evaluation Framework for Jailbreak Attacks on Large Language Models
summary: The assessment of jailbreak attacks against large language models currently suffers from inconsistent evaluation criteria and methods, leading to unreliable estimates of attack success rates. We propose JailMeter, an evidence-based evaluation framework designed to more faithfully measure jailbreak effectiveness. Inspired by the Information Bottleneck theory, JailMeter applies dual-feedback optimization to filter jailbreak noise from model responses while preserving content relevant to the original malicious question. This process produces concise evidence for a rigorous assessment under which an attack is validated only when the response captures the malicious intent and delivers a complete answer, thereby signaling a substantive bypass of model safety alignment. We evaluate JailMeter on JailMeter-Eva, a challenging benchmark containing 330 human-labeled, non-rejected jailbreak instances. JailMeter achieves an accuracy of 97.27%, substantially outperforming existing evaluation methods. To support large-scale evaluation, we further distill JailMeter into a small language model, JailMeter\textsubscript{SLM}, which maintains comparable reliability with significantly reduced computational costs. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Magi2B0y/JailMeter.

AI.tldr: JailMeter proposes an evidence-based evaluation framework for jailbreak attacks on LLMs, using dual-feedback optimization inspired by Information Bottleneck theory to filter noise and assess whether responses truly bypass safety alignment. It achieves 97.27% accuracy on a human-labeled benchmark and is distilled into a smaller model for scalable evaluation.
AI.motivation: Current jailbreak attack assessment suffers from inconsistent evaluation criteria and methods, producing unreliable attack success rate estimates. There is a need for a rigorous, faithful evaluation framework that reliably determines whether a jailbreak has substantively bypassed model safety alignment.
AI.method: JailMeter is an evidence-based evaluation framework leveraging dual-feedback optimization grounded in Information Bottleneck theory. It filters jailbreak-induced noise from model responses while preserving content relevant to the original malicious question, producing concise evidence. An attack is validated only when the response captures malicious intent and delivers a complete answer. For scalability, JailMeter is distilled into a small language model (JailMeter_SLM) with comparable reliability at reduced cost.
AI.result: On the JailMeter-Eva benchmark (330 human-labeled, non-rejected jailbreak instances), JailMeter achieves 97.27% accuracy, substantially outperforming existing evaluation methods. The distilled JailMeter_SLM maintains comparable reliability with significantly lower computational cost.
AI.conclusion: JailMeter provides a more faithful and evidence-driven alternative for jailbreak evaluation, addressing the inconsistency problem in current methods. Its high accuracy and distilled, cost-efficient variant make it suitable for both rigorous and large-scale assessments. Code and dataset are publicly available.

title: Stateful Guardrails for Multi-Turn LLM Systems: A Conversational Risk Accumulation Framework
summary: Most safety guardrails for large language models (LLMs) evaluate each prompt-response pair in isolation, which misses failures that arise only over a dialogue as benign turns compose into harm. We term this Conversational Risk Accumulation (CRA): gradual intent drift, fragmented assembly of prohibited instructions, and sensitivity build-up from repeated disclosures. We propose a session-layer CRA Framework that tracks three trajectory signals: semantic drift from a session anchor, a sensitivity-weighted information accumulation graph over extracted entities, and a compliance-gradient signal capturing increasing willingness to comply. For scoring, we provide (i) an unsupervised convex fusion for attribution and ablations, and (ii) CRA-Net DA, a compact learned trajectory model trained with family-adversarial objectives to reduce length and topic-coverage confounds. To benchmark CRA, we release CRA-Bench v0.1 (1,200 eight-turn sessions across three threat families with topic-matched benign twins), CRA-Bench v0.2 (LLM-paraphrased variants to reduce template artifacts), and an extended 5-family set (2,000 sessions adding persona priming and context stuffing). We introduce a trajectory-native evaluation protocol with session-level splits, mixed-set threshold calibration, Trajectory AUROC, turns-to-detection, calibrated false-positive metrics, bootstrap confidence intervals, leave-one-family-out diagnostic stress tests, and synthetic-to-human transfer checks. Claims focus on within-distribution session scoring on CRA-Bench and human-transfer subsets.

AI.tldr: Existing LLM safety guardrails evaluate individual prompt-response pairs in isolation, missing harms that emerge gradually across multi-turn dialogues through conversational risk accumulation (CRA). The authors propose a session-layer framework tracking semantic drift, sensitivity-weighted information accumulation, and compliance gradients, along with scoring methods and a new benchmark (CRA-Bench) for evaluating dialogue-level safety.
AI.motivation: Current LLM safety evaluations are predominantly turn-level, assessing each prompt-response pair independently. This misses a critical failure mode: conversational risk accumulation (CRA), where benign individual turns compose into harmful outcomes through gradual intent drift, fragmented assembly of prohibited instructions, and sensitivity build-up from repeated disclosures. No existing benchmark or framework systematically addresses session-level safety degradation.
AI.method: The authors propose a CRA Framework operating at the session layer with three trajectory signals: (1) semantic drift from a session anchor, (2) a sensitivity-weighted information accumulation graph over extracted entities, and (3) a compliance-gradient signal capturing increasing willingness to comply. For scoring, they provide an unsupervised convex fusion method for attribution/ablation and CRA-Net DA, a compact learned trajectory model trained with family-adversarial objectives to mitigate length and topic-coverage confounds. They release CRA-Bench v0.1 (1,200 eight-turn sessions across three threat families with topic-matched benign twins), v0.2 (LLM-paraphrased variants), and an extended five-family set (2,000 sessions with persona priming and context stuffing). A trajectory-native evaluation protocol is introduced with session-level splits, mixed-set threshold calibration, Trajectory AUROC, turns-to-detection, and various diagnostic stress tests.
AI.result: The paper reports within-distribution session scoring results on CRA-Bench and human-transfer subsets, demonstrating that the proposed trajectory-level detection methods can identify conversational risk accumulation that turn-level guardrails miss. The evaluation protocol provides calibrated false-positive metrics, bootstrap confidence intervals, leave-one-family-out diagnostic stress tests, and synthetic-to-human transfer checks.
AI.conclusion: Session-layer monitoring of conversational risk accumulation addresses a critical blind spot in LLM safety. Tracking semantic drift, information accumulation, and compliance gradients across dialogue turns enables detection of harms that are invisible to per-turn evaluation. The CRA-Bench benchmark and trajectory-native evaluation protocol provide a foundation for future work on multi-turn LLM safety.

title: FineServe: A Fine-Grained Dataset and Characterization of Global LLM Serving Workloads
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as always-on online services, making efficient LLM serving a critical systems challenge. Achieving low latency and high throughput under volatile demand requires deep understanding of real-world serving workloads, yet existing studies often rely on proxy traces or coarse-grained characterizations that fail to capture the heterogeneity of modern multi-model LLM platforms. We present FineServe, an in-the-wild, multi-model LLM serving workload dataset collected from a global commercial marketplace, enabling fine-grained characterization of real-world serving dynamics across heterogeneous models and tasks. Leveraging FineServe, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of arrival dynamics and token behavior, revealing fundamentally different fluctuation regimes across model architectures, scales and task intents. Building on these insights, we develop the FineServe workload generator, which composes fine-grained model-aware workloads into configurable mixtures tailored for benchmarking multi-model serving platforms. By exposing these fine-grained workload dynamics, FineServe provides a realistic foundation for evaluating routing, scheduling, and capacity-planning strategies in LLM serving systems. FineServe is available at https://github.com/hihiztc1/FineServe.

AI.tldr: FineServe introduces a real-world, multi-model LLM serving workload dataset collected from a commercial marketplace, enabling fine-grained characterization of arrival dynamics and token behavior across heterogeneous models. The authors reveal distinct fluctuation regimes across model architectures, scales, and task intents, and provide a configurable workload generator for benchmarking LLM serving systems.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM serving workload studies rely on proxy traces or coarse-grained characterizations that fail to capture the heterogeneity of real-world multi-model platforms. There is a critical need for realistic, fine-grained workload data to inform routing, scheduling, and capacity-planning in production LLM serving systems.
AI.method: The authors collect an in-the-wild dataset (FineServe) from a global commercial LLM marketplace, capturing serving dynamics across diverse models and tasks. They conduct comprehensive analysis of arrival dynamics and token behavior to characterize fluctuation regimes. Based on these insights, they develop a configurable workload generator that composes fine-grained, model-aware workloads for multi-model serving benchmarks.
AI.result: The analysis reveals fundamentally different fluctuation regimes across model architectures, scales, and task intents — demonstrating that real-world multi-model workloads exhibit heterogeneity not captured by prior proxy-based or coarse-grained studies.
AI.conclusion: FineServe provides a realistic foundation for evaluating routing, scheduling, and capacity-planning strategies in LLM serving systems. The dataset and workload generator are publicly available to facilitate future systems research.

title: Native Multi-Dimensional Subquadratic Operators via Input Dependent Long Convolutions
summary: Subquadratic alternatives to attention require compromises when applied to multi-dimensional data: standard convolutions lack global receptive fields and input dependency, while recurrent models require rasterizing data such as images, volumes, and partial differential equation (PDE) into an ad-hoc $1\rm D$ scan order that violates their spatial structure. We introduce \textit{HyenaND}, a subquadratic, global, input-dependent operator that acts directly on the native geometry of multidimensional data through convolutions with implicitly parametrized global, input-dependent multi-dimensional convolutional kernels. Our CUDA implementation, \texttt{nSubQ}, fuses the FFT-convolution path to turn HyenaND's $\mathcal{O}(L \log L)$ scaling into wall-clock speedups. Across long-context genomics, computer vision, medical imaging, and PDE modeling, pure HyenaND stacks match the accuracy of strong attention baselines, while hybrid configurations that interleave HyenaND and attention layers outperform both pure attention and strong recurrence-based hybrids.

AI.tldr: HyenaND introduces a subquadratic, global, input-dependent operator for multi-dimensional data that uses implicitly parametrized global convolutions, avoiding the need to rasterize data into 1D sequences. It matches attention accuracy and can outperform attention and recurrence-based hybrids.
AI.motivation: Subquadratic attention alternatives like standard convolutions lack global receptive fields and input dependency, while recurrent models require flattening multi-dimensional data (images, volumes, PDE grids) into 1D scan orders that destroy native spatial structure. There is a need for an efficient operator that operates directly on multi-dimensional data while preserving these properties.
AI.method: HyenaND generalizes the Hyena operator to N dimensions by performing convolutions with implicitly parametrized global, input-dependent multi-dimensional convolutional kernels. It operates directly on the native geometry of multi-dimensional data without rasterization. A CUDA implementation called nSubQ fuses the FFT-convolution path to achieve wall-clock speedups from the O(L log L) theoretical scaling.
AI.result: Pure HyenaND stacks match the accuracy of strong attention baselines across long-context genomics, computer vision, medical imaging, and PDE modeling. Hybrid configurations interleaving HyenaND and attention layers outperform both pure attention and strong recurrence-based hybrids.
AI.conclusion: HyenaND demonstrates that subquadratic, input-dependent, global operators can be effectively designed for native multi-dimensional data, eliminating the rasterization compromise. It offers a practical and performant alternative to attention for a broad range of multi-dimensional domains.

title: TargetFinder: Detecting Widgets from Pixels on Desktop Interfaces
summary: ''Target-aware'' pointing techniques, like Bubble Cursor or Semantic Pointing, outperform traditional pointing by leveraging knowledge of target locations. Yet the lack of application-agnostic widget geometry information limits their adoption across the desktop. We present TargetFinder, a computer vision-based system for real-time detection of GUI widgets. TargetFinder leverages several fine-tuned YOLO networks trained on a new dataset of 520 annotated desktop screenshots (~38,000 annotations) spanning Windows, macOS, Ubuntu, and web interfaces. TargetFinder uses lightweight screen monitoring and low-latency detection, achieving millisecond responsiveness suitable for interactive use. Evaluations show that TargetFinder outperforms the baseline methods (OmniParser and REMAUI), while system-wide implementations of Bubble Cursor and Semantic Pointing demonstrate the feasibility of deploying universal target-aware techniques that work across applications. We release the dataset, models, annotation tool, and an open-source library for research and applications.

AI.tldr: TargetFinder is a CV-based system using fine-tuned YOLO networks to detect GUI widgets across operating systems in real time, enabling universal deployment of target-aware pointing techniques like Bubble Cursor and Semantic Pointing.
AI.motivation: Target-aware pointing techniques (e.g., Bubble Cursor, Semantic Pointing) improve pointing performance but are hindered by the lack of application-agnostic widget geometry information, limiting their adoption across diverse desktop environments.
AI.method: The authors built a dataset of 520 annotated desktop screenshots (~38,000 annotations) spanning Windows, macOS, Ubuntu, and web interfaces. They fine-tuned multiple YOLO networks on this dataset for real-time widget detection, combined with lightweight screen monitoring and low-latency inference to achieve millisecond responsiveness.
AI.result: TargetFinder outperformed baseline methods (OmniParser and REMAUI). System-wide implementations of Bubble Cursor and Semantic Pointing demonstrated feasibility of cross-application, universal target-aware pointing.
AI.conclusion: TargetFinder enables practical deployment of target-aware pointing across arbitrary desktop applications. The authors release the dataset, models, annotation tool, and open-source library to support further research.

title: PerfAgent: Profiler-Guided Iterative Refinement for Repository-Level Code Optimization
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents now perform well on correctness-oriented repository-level tasks, including SWE-Bench issue resolution and feature implementation in real codebases. However, they still struggle with repository-level code optimization, which requires preserving behavior while improving runtime performance. Passing tests is not enough in this setting; a patch must preserve behavior, implement code optimization, and approach expert speedups. Current agents often miss bottlenecks hidden behind abstraction layers and native extensions, stop after shallow speedups, or insufficiently test the code patches that thus may silently break edge cases. We present PerfAgent, a profiler-guided, verifier-in-the-loop workflow that gives an off-the-shelf coding agent the feedback needed to find real hotspots, improve beyond the first passing patch, and use profiler evidence rather than timing alone to decide what to optimize next. On two challenging optimization benchmarks, GSO and SWE-fficiency-Lite, PerfAgent more than doubles the rate of expert-matching patches over OpenHands with GPT-5.1, improving from 19.6% to 39.2% on GSO and from 26% to 74% on SWE-fficiency-Lite. It also surpasses an oracle best-of-five baseline at substantially lower cost, showing that the gains come from better feedback rather than additional test-time sampling.

AI.tldr: PerfAgent is a profiler-guided, verifier-in-the-loop workflow that helps LLM coding agents tackle repository-level code optimization by identifying real performance hotspots, iterating beyond shallow speedups, and using profiler evidence to guide decisions. It more than doubles expert-matching patch rates over baseline OpenHands with GPT-5.1 on two benchmarks (GSO: 19.6%→39.2%; SWE-fficiency-Lite: 26%→74%) while costing less than an oracle best-of-five baseline.
AI.motivation: LLM agents excel at correctness-oriented repository tasks (e.g., SWE-Bench) but struggle with code optimization, where merely passing tests is insufficient — patches must preserve behavior, meaningfully improve runtime, and approach expert-level speedups. Current agents fail because they miss bottlenecks hidden behind abstraction layers and native extensions, settle for superficial speedups, and inadequately test patches, risking silent breakage of edge cases.
AI.method: PerfAgent introduces a profiler-guided, verifier-in-the-loop workflow. Rather than relying solely on timing, it uses profiler evidence to locate real hotspots and decide what to optimize next. The system provides an off-the-shelf coding agent with iterative feedback, enabling it to improve beyond the first passing patch. A verifier component ensures behavioral correctness throughout the optimization process.
AI.result: On GSO, PerfAgent raises the rate of expert-matching patches from 19.6% to 39.2% (OpenHands with GPT-5.1 baseline). On SWE-fficiency-Lite, it improves from 26% to 74%. It also surpasses an oracle best-of-five baseline at substantially lower cost, demonstrating that gains derive from superior feedback rather than increased test-time sampling.
AI.conclusion: Profiler-guided feedback with verifier-in-the-loop is a highly effective strategy for repository-level code optimization by LLM agents, substantially outperforming both standard agent workflows and naive sampling-based approaches. The approach addresses key failure modes — hidden bottlenecks, shallow speedups, and insufficient testing — yielding significant gains across benchmarks.

title: Same Game, Different Story: A Minimal Conservative Strategic Robustness Benchmark for Large Language Model Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in strategic settings where outcomes depend on the actions of other agents. This raises a reliability question: will a model choose consistently when the same incentives are presented through different narratives? We introduce Same Game, Different Story, a benchmark that defines strategic robustness as invariance of model-induced action distributions under payoff-preserving changes in framing. We illustrate the framework through a secondary analysis of published aggregate cooperation rates for GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and LLaMa-2 across four social-dilemma games. The retained comparison covers business and friend-sharing framings, representing 24 model-game-context cells and 7,200 decisions in the source study. Because trial-level data were unavailable, approximate counts were reconstructed from published figures; the resulting estimates are therefore illustrative rather than an exact replication. Under the paper's conservative transformation, pooled strategic robustness is 0.783, and friend-sharing framing increases cooperation by 0.307 relative to business framing. The results indicate that social-relational framing can substantially alter LLM behavior even when the underlying action sets and payoffs remain fixed. Strategic robustness should therefore be evaluated separately from strategic competence, using families of payoff-equivalent prompts rather than a single presentation of a game.

AI.tldr: Introduces "Same Game, Different Story," a benchmark assessing whether LLMs maintain consistent action distributions when identical payoff structures are presented through different narrative framings. A secondary analysis of GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and LLaMa-2 across social-dilemma games reveals pooled strategic robustness of 0.783 and that friend-sharing framing increases cooperation by 0.307 over business framing, demonstrating that framing alone significantly alters LLM behavior.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in strategic multi-agent settings, yet no systematic framework exists to evaluate whether models respond consistently to identical incentives when the narrative framing varies. This raises a reliability concern: strategic behavior should be invariant under payoff-preserving transformations of game descriptions, but LLMs may be sensitive to superficial framing differences.
AI.method: The paper proposes the "Same Game, Different Story" benchmark defining strategic robustness as invariance of model-induced action distributions under payoff-preserving framing changes. It illustrates the framework through secondary analysis of published aggregate cooperation rates for GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and LLaMa-2 across four social-dilemma games, comparing business vs. friend-sharing framings. Approximate trial-level counts were reconstructed from published figures, covering 24 model-game-context cells and approximately 7,200 decisions. A conservative transformation was applied.
AI.result: Pooled strategic robustness is 0.783 under the conservative transformation. Friend-sharing framing increases cooperation by 0.307 relative to business framing. Results demonstrate that social-relational framing can substantially alter LLM behavior even when action sets and payoffs remain fixed.
AI.conclusion: Strategic robustness must be evaluated separately from strategic competence. Reliable assessment requires families of payoff-equivalent prompts rather than a single presentation of a game, as narrative framing alone can produce materially different behavioral outcomes.

title: CIR at iKAT SCAI 2026: Exploring Clarification Need Prediction in Agentic Conversational Search
summary: This paper presents the participation of the Cologne Information Retrieval group in the iKAT SCAI 2026 shared task. We use an agentic conversational search system, equipped with tools for query rewriting, retrieval and reranking, answer generation, and clarification need prediction and clarification question generation. We experiment with two different neural clarification need prediction models.

AI.tldr: The Cologne Information Retrieval group participated in the iKAT SCAI 2026 shared task using an agentic conversational search system with modular tools for query rewriting, retrieval, reranking, answer generation, clarification prediction, and clarification question generation, experimenting with two neural clarification need prediction models.
AI.motivation: To participate in the iKAT SCAI 2026 shared task and explore agentic conversational search architectures capable of identifying when clarification is needed and generating appropriate clarification questions.
AI.method: An agentic conversational search system composed of modular tools: query rewriting, retrieval and reranking, answer generation, clarification need prediction, and clarification question generation. Two different neural models were experimented with for the clarification need prediction component.
AI.result: The abstract does not report specific quantitative results; only the experimental setup with two neural clarification need prediction models is mentioned.
AI.conclusion: The abstract does not provide explicit conclusions, as it appears to be a system description paper outlining the architecture and experimental configuration submitted to the shared task.

title: ChannelGuard: Safe Models Do Not Compose into Safe Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent LLM applications chain a planner, worker agents, a verifier, and a synthesizer, and every hop between agents is an unmonitored channel through which an adversary can smuggle instructions. Existing defenses guard only the input boundary (IBProtector, Llama Guard, perplexity filters, SmoothLLM) or run outside the application as opaque, stochastic provider-side filters. We show this gap carries a consequence rarely measured: on a 2,100-trace evaluation across eight attack families, five defenses, and three model backends, an undefended pipeline that appears fully safe under standard reporting (attack success 0.000 on tool- and memory-poisoning) owes that safety almost entirely to the cloud provider's server-side filter (54 of 60 blocks on Azure GPT-5), and silently shifts to the agent model's own alignment on a backend without such a filter. Outcome-only reporting hides this dependence. We present ChannelGuard, a training-free defense-in-depth framework placing information-bottleneck gates on every inter-agent channel; each scores channel text against an adversarial phrase bank by embedding similarity and deterministically passes, compresses, or blocks it, adding no LLM call, while an attribution method records which layer stopped each attack. ChannelGuard's tool-output gate blocks Tool Poisoning 30 of 30 at the application layer, identically across Azure GPT-5, Anthropic Sonnet 4.5, and Anthropic Haiku 4.5, whereas the undefended pipeline shifts entirely across backends; it also lowers Prompt Injection attack success by half (0.333 to 0.167) and preserves GSM8K accuracy exactly (0.867). White-box adaptive paraphrase evades every embedding gate, where a perturb-and-vote baseline does better. An extended appendix adds baselines, ablations, sweeps, a benign-preservation analysis, and a judge audit (kappa = 0.900), at a total cost of 47.36 USD.

AI.tldr: ChannelGuard is a training-free defense-in-depth framework that places information-bottleneck gates on every inter-agent channel in multi-agent LLM applications, using embedding similarity against an adversarial phrase bank to deterministically pass, compress, or block messages. It operates at the application layer, blocking tool poisoning entirely across backends and reducing prompt injection success by half, while preserving task accuracy.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM pipelines contain unmonitored inter-agent channels that adversaries can exploit. Existing defenses only guard the input boundary or run as opaque provider-side filters, creating a hidden dependence on cloud-provider filtering that outcome-only reporting obscures. The authors demonstrate this gap empirically: an undefended pipeline appearing safe under standard metrics owes its safety almost entirely to server-side filtering, and silently fails on backends without such filters.
AI.method: ChannelGuard places information-bottleneck gates on every inter-agent channel. Each gate scores channel text against an adversarial phrase bank using embedding similarity and deterministically passes, compresses, or blocks content — requiring no additional LLM calls. An attribution method records which layer stopped each attack. The system is evaluated on a 2,100-trace benchmark across eight attack families, five defenses, three model backends (Azure GPT-5, Anthropic Sonnet 4.5, Anthropic Haiku 4.5), with baselines including IBProtector, Llama Guard, perplexity filters, and SmoothLLM.
AI.result: ChannelGuard's tool-output gate blocks Tool Poisoning 30/30 at the application layer identically across all three backends, while the undefended pipeline shifts entirely across backends. It lowers Prompt Injection attack success from 0.333 to 0.167 and preserves GSM8K accuracy exactly (0.867). White-box adaptive paraphrase attacks evade every embedding gate, where a perturb-and-vote baseline performs better. A judge audit yields kappa = 0.900, and the total experiment cost is $47.36.
AI.conclusion: Defense-in-depth at the application layer is necessary because provider-side filtering is backend-dependent and invisible to standard reporting. Deterministic, embedding-based gating on every inter-agent channel provides backend-agnostic protection against tool poisoning and partial protection against prompt injection without sacrificing task performance, though adaptive paraphrase attacks remain a vulnerability for embedding-based gates.

title: When Reasoning Narrows the Move: Diversity Collapse in LLM Game Play
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is widely used to adapt large language models to downstream tasks, but its effect on behavioral diversity in sequential decision-making remains under-explored. We study this question in a controlled suite of deterministic board games based on tic-tac-toe variants, where optimal actions are exactly computable and diversity can be measured directly. Across state-level evaluation, arena gameplay, and training trajectories, we find that reasoning-mode generation frequently suppresses action diversity without uniformly improving action accuracy. Furthermore, standard SFT improves accuracy but often induces premature diversity collapse, which exceeds what is minimally required by the accuracy-diversity tradeoff. We then show that action augmentation, which trains on all optimal actions per state rather than a single demonstrated action, would partially mitigates this effect. Our results identify narrow-support imitation as a source of policy collapse in LLM decision-making and suggest that preserving action support during SFT is important for maintaining exploratory behavior.

AI.tldr: SFT on LLMs for sequential decision-making suppresses action diversity and induces premature diversity collapse, even when accuracy improves. Training on all optimal actions (action augmentation) partially mitigates this narrowing effect.
AI.motivation: SFT is widely used to adapt LLMs to downstream tasks, but its impact on behavioral diversity in sequential decision-making is not well understood. The authors aim to systematically characterize how SFT affects action diversity, beyond just accuracy.
AI.method: The authors use a controlled suite of deterministic board games based on tic-tac-toe variants, where optimal actions are exactly computable and diversity can be directly measured. They evaluate across state-level accuracy, arena gameplay, and training trajectories, and test an intervention called action augmentation (training on all optimal actions rather than a single demonstrated action).
AI.result: Reasoning-mode generation frequently suppresses action diversity without uniformly improving accuracy. Standard SFT improves accuracy but induces premature diversity collapse exceeding what is minimally required by the accuracy-diversity tradeoff. Action augmentation partially mitigates this diversity collapse.
AI.conclusion: Narrow-support imitation is a key source of policy collapse in LLM decision-making. Preserving action support during SFT is important for maintaining exploratory behavior in sequential tasks.

title: Hybrid LSTM-Graph Neural Framework for Robust Financial Fraud Detection and Adversarial Resilience
summary: Financial institutions face significant challenges in detecting sophisticated money laundering patterns, such as smurfing and layering, due to extreme data imbalance (0.13% fraud rate) and evolving adversarial evasion tactics. This paper proposes FraudShield AI, a hybrid framework that integrates Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks with hand-crafted Graph Topological Features to capture both temporal sequences and structural relational context. By engineering network-centric features including PageRank Centrality, In-Degree dynamics, and a custom Flow Ratio, the system shifts the detection paradigm from isolated transaction analysis to network-level forensics. A Focal Loss objective is used to address class imbalance, and a dynamic thresholding mechanism is introduced to improve resilience against low-value smurfing attacks. Experimental evaluation on the PaySim dataset shows that the proposed hybrid model substantially outperforms Logistic Regression and XGBoost baselines in Precision, Recall, and F1-Score, particularly on hard-to-detect micro-transaction fraud patterns. An ablation study confirms the complementary contribution of both the temporal and topological components.

AI.tldr: FraudShield AI combines LSTM networks with graph topological features (PageRank, In-Degree, Flow Ratio) and Focal Loss to detect money laundering in highly imbalanced transaction data, significantly outperforming baseline models on the PaySim dataset.
AI.motivation: Money laundering detection is hindered by extreme class imbalance (~0.13% fraud rate) and adversarial evasion tactics like smurfing and layering. Traditional methods analyzing transactions in isolation fail to capture the relational structure exploited by sophisticated criminals, motivating a shift toward network-level forensic analysis.
AI.method: FraudShield AI is a hybrid framework with three key components: (1) LSTM networks to model temporal transaction sequences; (2) hand-crafted graph topological features (PageRank Centrality, In-Degree dynamics, custom Flow Ratio) to capture structural relational context; (3) Focal Loss to address class imbalance by down-weighting easy negatives, plus a dynamic thresholding mechanism to counter low-value smurfing attacks. The framework operates at the network forensics level rather than analyzing isolated transactions.
AI.result: On the PaySim dataset, FraudShield AI substantially outperformed Logistic Regression and XGBoost baselines in Precision, Recall, and F1-Score, with particularly strong gains on hard-to-detect micro-transaction fraud patterns. An ablation study confirmed that both temporal (LSTM) and topological (graph feature) components contribute complementary value.
AI.conclusion: Integrating temporal deep learning with graph-based topological features provides a robust solution for financial fraud detection under severe class imbalance. The complementary nature of both components is validated, and the dynamic thresholding mechanism proves effective against adversarial smurfing tactics.

title: Bayesian Wind Tunnels for Model Selection
summary:
Prior work has shown that transformers can perform exact Bayesian filtering within a fixed
  hypothesis class. Can they also perform Bayesian model selection -- identifying the correct
  hypothesis class from data? We introduce model-selection Bayesian wind tunnels: controlled
  environments where ground-truth posteriors over hypothesis classes are available in closed
  form. Using fixed-point-free involutions -- whose defining property f(f(x))=x is purely
  relational -- a 2.8M-parameter transformer achieves 0.01-bit entropy agreement with the
  Bayesian optimum (3 seeds), with both integer tokens and opaque symbols whose meanings
  change every episode. This extends to non-nested comparisons: involutions vs. 3-cycles
  (where neither class is a subset of the other) achieve class-posterior MAE under 0.001,
  demonstrating genuine model selection beyond simplicity/subset bias. We then identify a
  sharp perceptual access condition: when the discriminative statistic requires arithmetic --
  modular addition (rotations) or multiplication (f(x)=cx mod p) -- model selection succeeds
  with integer tokens but fails completely with opaque symbols, and this boundary persists
  under 112x scaling (2.8M to 316M parameters). A stationarity control confirms the operative
  factor: opaque tokens with a fixed relabeling succeed (0.009-bit MAE), showing that stable
  semantics, not integer identity, enable circuit compilation. Header subtask diagnostics
  localize the failure to the composition of header inversion with arithmetic rather than
  header parsing itself. Probing frontier LLMs on the same tasks shows qualitative Bayesian
  behavior but a large calibration gap (~55x), measured through lossy probes and therefore
  directional rather than exact.

AI.tldr: Transformers can perform exact Bayesian model selection (identifying the correct hypothesis class from data), not just filtering within a fixed class. Success depends on "perceptual access" — whether the discriminative statistic can be compiled into circuits from stable token semantics. With transparent integer tokens, transformers achieve near-optimal Bayesian posteriors for both nested and non-nested hypothesis classes, but fail completely with opaque symbols when the statistic requires arithmetic.
AI.motivation: While prior work established that transformers can do Bayesian filtering within a fixed hypothesis class, it was unknown whether they can perform Bayesian model selection — identifying which hypothesis class generated the data. This paper investigates this question systematically, since model selection is a fundamentally harder meta-inference problem that requires comparing across different structural assumptions rather than just updating within one.
AI.method: The authors introduce "model-selection Bayesian wind tunnels" — controlled environments with closed-form ground-truth posteriors over hypothesis classes. They use fixed-point-free involutions (f(f(x))=x) and 3-cycles as hypothesis classes, allowing both nested and non-nested comparisons. They train transformers on sequences of (x, f(x)) pairs and evaluate agreement with the Bayesian posterior. Two key manipulations are compared: integer tokens (where arithmetic structure is perceptible) versus opaque symbols (randomly reassigned each episode). They also probe frontier LLMs using lossy probes for directional comparison. Scaling experiments go from 2.8M to 316M parameters.
AI.result: A 2.8M-parameter transformer achieves 0.01-bit entropy agreement with the Bayesian optimum for involution detection. For non-nested comparisons (involutions vs. 3-cycles), class-posterior MAE is under 0.001, ruling out simplicity/subset bias. A sharp perceptual access boundary emerges: model selection succeeds with integer tokens but fails completely with opaque symbols when the discriminative statistic requires arithmetic (modular addition/multiplication). This boundary persists under 112× scaling. However, opaque tokens with a fixed relabeling succeed (0.009-bit MAE), indicating stable semantics — not integer identity — enable circuit compilation. Header subtask diagnostics localize the failure to composing header inversion with arithmetic. Frontier LLMs show qualitative Bayesian behavior but with a ~55× calibration gap.
AI.conclusion: Transformers can perform Bayesian model selection when the discriminative statistic is perceptually accessible to their circuit-building mechanisms. The critical factor is stable token semantics enabling circuit compilation, not parameter count or integer representations per se. This reveals a fundamental architectural constraint: transformers cannot discover latent arithmetic structure from opaque symbols, regardless of scale, pointing to an important limitation in their inductive biases for relational reasoning.

title: A Framework of User Experience Principles for Human-AI Agent Interaction in the Workplace
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 1 table, to be published in the proceedings of Mensch und Computer 2026
summary: As AI agents become integral to business workflows, establishing guiding user experience (UX) principles is crucial for ensuring user trust and successful adoption. To address this, our study uses a multi-method approach - combining participatory design workshop, paper-and-pencil, expert review, meta-analysis, and in-depth interviews - to identify and validate a design framework of eight core UX principles for human-AI agent interaction in the workplace. Together with their underlying criteria, these principles provide actionable guardrails for designers and software engineers, creating a foundation for developing effective and human-centered AI agent interactions. This study contributes to a structured foundation for future empirical studies on agentic AI in enterprise settings.

AI.tldr: A multi-method study identifies and validates eight core UX design principles for human-AI agent interaction in workplace settings, providing actionable guardrails for designers and engineers.
AI.motivation: As AI agents become increasingly embedded in business workflows, there is a lack of established, validated UX principles to guide the design of human-AI agent interactions, risking erosion of user trust and hindering successful adoption.
AI.method: A multi-method approach combining five techniques: participatory design workshops, paper-and-pencil exercises, expert review, meta-analysis of existing research, and in-depth interviews. These were used to both identify and validate the proposed design framework.
AI.result: A validated design framework comprising eight core UX principles with associated underlying criteria, serving as actionable guardrails for designers and software engineers building human-centered AI agent interactions.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a structured foundation for future empirical research on agentic AI in enterprise settings and offers practical guidance for developing effective, human-centered AI agent interactions in the workplace.

title: Context Matters: Improving the Practical Reliability of LLM-Based Unit Test Generation
summary: Automated unit test generation has recently benefited from advances in large language models (LLMs), yet our industrial deployments reveal a persistent gap between promising research results and practical usability. In real-world projects with complex frameworks and cross-file dependencies, LLM-generated tests frequently fail to compile, require costly manual repair, or provide unstable coverage improvements. This paper reports our experience in designing, deploying, and evaluating CATGen, a context-aware workflow for LLM-based unit test generation, informed by repeated industrial failures and refinements. Rather than relying on LLMs to infer incomplete project context, we found that compilation robustness critically depends on making project-level dependencies explicit, stabilizing test class scaffolding, and replacing iterative LLM-based repair with lightweight static analysis. These experience-driven insights shaped CATGen's multi-stage design, which combines structured context retrieval, deterministic test skeleton construction, and program analysis-based post-processing. We evaluate CATGen on real-world complex focal methods from proprietary industrial projects and additionally on the Defects4J benchmark to assess generalizability. Across both settings, CATGen substantially improves compilation success and structural coverage while significantly reducing generation time and token consumption compared to existing LLM-based approaches. Our results demonstrate that reliable LLM-based unit test generation in practice depends less on prompt engineering alone and more on systematic engineering support grounded in real-world development constraints.

AI.tldr: CATGen is a context-aware, multi-stage workflow for LLM-based unit test generation that prioritizes compilation robustness through deterministic scaffolding, explicit project-level dependency injection, and static analysis-based post-processing over iterative LLM repair, demonstrating significant improvements in compilation success, coverage, and efficiency in both industrial and benchmark settings.
AI.motivation: Despite recent advances in LLM-based test generation, industrial deployments suffer from a persistent gap between research results and practical usability: generated tests frequently fail to compile, require costly manual repair, or yield unstable coverage in complex real-world projects with frameworks and cross-file dependencies.
AI.method: CATGen employs a multi-stage design informed by industrial failure analysis: (1) structured context retrieval that makes project-level dependencies explicit, (2) deterministic test skeleton construction for stable scaffolding, and (3) program analysis-based post-processing that replaces iterative LLM-based repair with lightweight static analysis. Evaluated on proprietary industrial projects and the Defects4J benchmark.
AI.result: CATGen substantially improves compilation success rates and structural coverage while significantly reducing both generation time and token consumption compared to existing LLM-based approaches, across both industrial and Defects4J settings.
AI.conclusion: Reliable LLM-based unit test generation in practice depends less on prompt engineering alone and more on systematic engineering support — specifically, making project context explicit, stabilizing scaffolding, and applying lightweight static analysis — grounded in real-world development constraints.

title: Not Birds of a Feather: Personality-Based Partner Selection in LLM Agents
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly let one agent choose which other agents to work with, and agents are increasingly given personalities through personas. We test whether Big Five personality alone influences partner selection when capability is explicitly held constant. Host agents chose among six validated candidate archetypes -- five marked high on one trait (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism) plus a balanced control -- presented with randomized names and ordering across five task categories (375 trials). With neutral hosts (Study 1, n=150), selection departed drastically from chance ($χ^2(5)=325.8$, $p<.001$), following a task-stereotype map: the open archetype won 100% of creative trials, the conscientious archetype 90-97% of strategic, synthesis, and problem-solving trials, and the neurotic archetype 37% of analytical trials (Cramer's V=.74); the extraverted, agreeable, and balanced archetypes were almost never chosen, although human meta-analyses identify team agreeableness as among the strongest personality predictors of team performance. With personality-assigned hosts (Study 2, n=225), and contrary to human similarity-attraction, self-similar partners were selected below chance (11.1% vs. 16.7%, p=.025) and at greater-than-chance trait distance (p<.0001); conscientious hosts diversified away from their own archetype, recruiting vigilant and open partners. Personality-based selection in LLM agents is real, strong, task-stereotyped, non-homophilous, and miscalibrated against human team-performance evidence -- with direct implications for bias auditing in agent marketplaces.

AI.tldr: LLM agents exhibit strong, task-stereotyped personality-based partner selection that contradicts human similarity-attraction patterns and is miscalibrated against evidence on human team performance.
AI.motivation: As multi-agent LLM systems increasingly employ personas and autonomous partner selection, it is critical to understand whether and how Big Five personality traits influence agent choices — and whether those choices align with human social patterns or team-performance evidence.
AI.method: Two-study design: Host agents selected among six validated candidate archetypes (high openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism, plus balanced control) across five task categories, with randomized names and ordering. Study 1 (n=150) used neutral hosts; Study 2 (n=225) used personality-assigned hosts. Selection patterns were analyzed via chi-square, Cramér's V, and distance-based measures.
AI.result: Study 1: selection departed drastically from chance (χ²(5)=325.8, p<.001), following a task-stereotype map — open archetype won 100% of creative trials, conscientious 90-97% of strategic/synthesis/problem-solving trials, neurotic 37% of analytical trials. Extraverted, agreeable, and balanced archetypes were almost never chosen. Study 2: self-similar selection occurred below chance (11.1% vs. 16.7%, p=.025), with greater-than-chance trait distance (p<.0001); conscientious hosts diversified away from their own archetype. Cramér's V=.74 overall.
AI.conclusion: Personality-based selection in LLM agents is real, strong, task-stereotyped, non-homophilous, and miscalibrated against human team-performance evidence — particularly the neglect of agreeableness — with direct implications for bias auditing in agent marketplaces.

title: Zero-Observation User Reactivation with Gap-Driven Dimensional Gating
comment: Accepted at the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys 2026)
summary:
Sequential recommendation (SR) models capture continuously observed behavior, but a returning user may have no interactions for months or years. We define this setting as Zero-Observation Reactivation: the user has a pre-gap history, while the platform observes no behavioral signals during a macro-gap Delta t. Under a chronologically aligned Gap-Synthesize Protocol on three Amazon datasets (Video Games, CDs & Vinyl, and Movies & TV), Hit@10 decreases monotonically across the evaluated gap buckets and reaches its lowest level beyond one year. The pattern appears across recurrent, unidirectional, and bidirectional SR backbones.
  We propose DeltaGate, a lightweight output-layer plugin that keeps the backbone frozen and routes each representation dimension between the personalized history and a learned, zero-initialized global prior. The gate is conditioned jointly on Delta t and the personalized representation. In a controlled diagnostic, we hold the personalized representation fixed and vary Delta t to isolate the trained gate's response to the gap input. In the >365d Video Games bucket, DG-SASRec reaches 0.047 Hit@10 versus 0.031 for SASRec, while DG-BERT4Rec reaches 0.046 versus 0.025 for BERT4Rec, with 66K trainable parameters (2--4% overhead). End-to-end retraining attains higher absolute accuracy but changes the backbone embeddings; the frozen plugin preserves zero backbone drift, uses about 40x fewer trainable parameters, and retains observable dimension-wise routing. The source code is available at https://github.com/jdding/DeltaGate.

AI.tldr: DeltaGate is a lightweight, frozen-backbone plugin for sequential recommendation that addresses the "Zero-Observation Reactivation" problem — where users return after long gaps (months to years) with no behavioral signals. It uses a gating mechanism conditioned on gap duration (Δt) and personalized representations to route between history-based and learned global priors, achieving significant Hit@10 gains over baselines (e.g., 0.047 vs 0.031 for SASRec) with only 66K added parameters (2–4% overhead).
AI.motivation: Sequential recommendation models assume continuous observation, but in reality, users often return after extended macro-gaps (months to years) during which no behavioral signals are observed. This "Zero-Observation Reactivation" setting causes severe performance degradation — Hit@10 drops monotonically with increasing gap duration across all major SR backbones (recurrent, unidirectional, bidirectional). Existing models lack a principled mechanism to handle uncertainty from prolonged absence.
AI.method: The authors propose DeltaGate, an output-layer plugin that freezes the backbone SR model and routes each representation dimension between two sources: (1) the personalized history representation from the frozen backbone, and (2) a learned, zero-initialized global prior. The gate is conditioned jointly on the macro-gap duration Δt and the personalized representation itself. A Gap-Synthesize Protocol is introduced to evaluate under chronologically aligned gap buckets on three Amazon datasets. A controlled diagnostic fixes the personalized representation while varying Δt to isolate the gate's response.
AI.result: Hit@10 decreases monotonically across all evaluated gap buckets, reaching its lowest beyond one year. In the >365-day Video Games bucket, DG-SASRec achieves 0.047 Hit@10 (vs. 0.031 for SASRec) and DG-BERT4Rec achieves 0.046 (vs. 0.025 for BERT4Rec). DeltaGate uses only 66K trainable parameters (2–4% overhead). Compared to end-to-end retraining, the frozen plugin preserves zero backbone drift, uses ~40× fewer trainable parameters, and retains interpretable dimension-wise routing.
AI.conclusion: DeltaGate effectively mitigates the Zero-Observation Reactivation problem with minimal overhead, demonstrating that conditioning on gap duration and dynamically routing between personalized and global signals is a parameter-efficient strategy. The frozen-plugin approach preserves the backbone's learned representations while providing interpretable dimension-wise routing, making it a practical solution for real-world recommendation systems where users exhibit long inactivity periods.

title: ChainWatch: A Kill Chain-Aligned Sequential Detection Framework for Multi-Step Attacks in MCP-Based AI Agent Systems
summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open-source standard that allows AI agents to connect to external tools, databases, and services. While this connectivity enables powerful agent capabilities, it also introduces multi-step attacks that existing per-call defenses cannot reliably detect. Attackers can compose individually benign tool invocations into malicious sequences that evade isolated inspection. This paper presents ChainWatch, a sequential detection framework for identifying multi-step attacks in MCP-based AI agent systems. ChainWatch models attack progression using a six-stage kill chain and applies a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to classify tool-call sequences. Detection rules are triggered when a session exhibits suspicious progression across multiple stages. The framework is supported by a structured threat model covering direct sequential attacks, indirect prompt injection chains, and hybrid multi-stage attacks. A 20-dimensional feature extraction schema captures behavioral signals from tool interactions. We demonstrate the approach using five representative attack scenarios from the security literature, showing how ChainWatch detects attack chains that evade traditional per-call security mechanisms.

AI.tldr: ChainWatch is an HMM-based sequential detection framework for MCP-based AI agent systems that identifies multi-step attacks by modeling attack progression through a six-stage kill chain, detecting malicious sequences that evade per-call inspection.
AI.motivation: MCP enables AI agents to connect to external tools, but existing per-call defenses fail to detect multi-step attacks where individually benign tool invocations compose into malicious sequences. A gap exists in detecting sequential attack patterns that span multiple calls.
AI.method: ChainWatch employs a six-stage kill chain model of attack progression and uses a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to classify tool-call sequences.
