A 20-dimensional feature extraction schema captures behavioral signals from tool interactions. Detection rules trigger when sessions exhibit suspicious cross-stage progression. The threat model covers direct sequential attacks, indirect prompt injection chains, and hybrid multi-stage attacks.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated on five representative attack scenarios from the security literature, showing effective detection of attack chains that bypass traditional per-call security mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Sequential detection via HMM-based kill chain modeling provides a viable approach for securing MCP-based AI agent systems against multi-step attacks that per-call defenses cannot catch.

title: On the Computational Complexity of Structural Generalization
summary: Structural generalization has been measured repeatedly by several benchmarks, yet it has never been formally defined. We give a definition that translates the two premises (compositional structure and unbounded generalization) into mathematical language. The definition itself is neutral: a compiler that hard-codes the rules satisfies it just as well. But structural generalization becomes a scientific question only insofar as the capacity can autonomously emerge from finite data. This question pits the computational lower bound $\mathrm{NC}^1$ against the learnable ceiling $\mathrm{TC}^0$ of pure Transformers. Under a Montagovian instantiation, each compositional rule splits into two projections: a syntactic face ($F_γ$) and a semantic face ($G_γ$). Tree evaluation on the $G_γ$ side is an instantiation of BFVP, which is $\mathrm{NC}^1$-complete (Buss, 1987). A pure Transformer must learn both faces at once, but Kraus et al. (2026) prove that its learnable class $\subseteq \mathrm{TC}^0$. Under the standard assumption $\mathrm{TC}^0 \neq \mathrm{NC}^1$, a pure Transformer cannot learn structural generalization. Neuro-symbolic systems achieve the best benchmark scores precisely because they inject $G_γ$, sidestepping the genuinely hard half. Benchmark scores cannot distinguish "learned" from "given." This is what this paper sets out to make clear.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a formal mathematical definition of structural generalization and proves that pure Transformers cannot learn it (as their learnable class ⊆ TC⁰, while structural generalization requires NC¹-completeness), explaining why neuro-symbolic systems outperform on benchmarks by circumventing the genuinely hard semantic component.
AI.motivation: Structural generalization is widely measured by benchmarks but has never been formally defined. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a rigorous definition and investigating whether the capacity for structural generalization can autonomously emerge from finite data in neural architectures, specifically pure Transformers.
AI.method: The authors define structural generalization mathematically, decomposing each compositional rule into syntactic (F_γ) and semantic (G_γ) faces under a Montagovian framework. They map tree evaluation on G_γ to the Boolean Formula Value Problem (BFVP), which is NC¹-complete, then leverage Kraus et al. (2026)'s result that pure Transformer learnability is bounded by TC⁰ to establish a complexity-class separation argument.
AI.result: Under the standard assumption that TC⁰ ≠ NC¹, pure Transformers provably cannot learn structural generalization. Neuro-symbolic systems achieve superior benchmark performance precisely because they inject G_γ directly (i.e., the semantic face is given rather than learned), meaning benchmark scores cannot distinguish learned from pre-supplied structure.
AI.conclusion: Structural generalization, formally defined, presents a fundamental computational barrier for pure Transformers due to the TC⁰ vs. NC¹ gap. The strong benchmark performance of neuro-symbolic systems is attributable to architectural privilege rather than genuine learning, and the field must recognize that current evaluations fail to differentiate learned structural capacity from externally supplied structure.

title: OpenEvoShield: Dual Non-Stationary Continual Defense for Open-World Multi-Agent System Attacks
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, where adversaries inject malicious instructions through inter-agent communication to propagate harmful behaviors. Unlike static threats, these attacks are doubly dynamic: adversaries refine injection strategies against deployed defenses while normal-agent behavior drifts with system expansion. Existing defenses treat deployment as a closed-world problem and degrade rapidly once either distribution shifts beyond training coverage. We propose OpenEvoShield, a co-evolutionary continual defense framework for LLM-MAS. An asymmetric rate controller (M1) decouples fast attack-side and slow normal-side learning rates from dual drift signals. A normal-boundary updater (M2) maintains a dynamic behavioral boundary at the slow rate, while an EWC-regularized policy ensemble (M3) fast-adapts without catastrophic forgetting. An energy-based multi-granularity detector (M4) fuses node-, subgraph-, and graph-level evidence to classify novel attacks as out-of-distribution. Experiments over 100 deployment rounds across five benchmarks and four MAS topologies show that OpenEvoShield outperforms static and continual baselines, detecting most previously unseen attacks while keeping false positive rates low.

AI.tldr: OpenEvoShield is a co-evolutionary defense framework for LLM-based multi-agent systems that addresses doubly dynamic adversarial injection attacks by decoupling fast attack adaptation from slow normal-behavior drift, using four integrated mechanisms: an asymmetric rate controller, a normal-boundary updater, an EWC-regularized policy ensemble, and an energy-based multi-granularity detector.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems face adversarial injection attacks through inter-agent communication, characterized by a doubly dynamic threat landscape: adversaries continuously refine injection strategies while normal-agent behavior drifts as systems scale. Existing defenses assume a closed-world, static deployment and fail catastrophically when either distribution shifts beyond their training coverage. There is a need for a defense that continually adapts to both shifting attack and normal distributions without forgetting previously learned patterns.
AI.method: OpenEvoShield proposes four co-evolutionary modules: (M1) an asymmetric rate controller that decouples fast adaptation to attack-side changes from slow adaptation to normal-side behavioral drift using dual drift signals; (M2) a normal-boundary updater that maintains a dynamic behavioral boundary at the slow rate; (M3) an EWC-regularized policy ensemble that enables fast adaptation while preventing catastrophic forgetting via Elastic Weight Consolidation; and (M4) an energy-based multi-granularity detector that fuses evidence at node, subgraph, and graph levels to classify novel attacks as out-of-distribution samples.
AI.result: Experiments conducted over 100 deployment rounds across five benchmarks and four MAS topologies demonstrate that OpenEvoShield outperforms both static and continual learning baselines, successfully detecting most previously unseen attacks while maintaining low false positive rates.
AI.conclusion: OpenEvoShield provides an effective continual defense for LLM-MAS against evolving adversarial injection attacks by co-evolving with both attack and normal distribution shifts. The decoupled learning rates and multi-granularity OOD detection prove critical for sustained performance in open-world deployments.

title: CruiseBench: A Real-Flight-Aligned N-CMAPSS Benchmark for Engine RUL Prediction
summary: Remaining useful life (RUL) prediction estimates how long an engine can continue safe operation and is central to maintenance planning. N-CMAPSS extends C-MAPSS by simulating run-to-failure aero-engine trajectories using recorded real-flight profiles and retaining complete within-flight time series rather than cycle-level snapshots. However, this added realism reduces evaluation control because full-flight records increase data volume and entangle degradation cues with operating-regime variation, complicating preprocessing choices and direct comparisons of RUL modeling performance. To mitigate this issue, this paper proposes CruiseBench, a cruise-stage RUL benchmark derived from N-CMAPSS. It introduces CPM-N-CMAPSS (Cruising-Period Mask for N-CMAPSS), a mask artifact that stores cycle-local cruising intervals identified by the common-altitude method for the nine accessible subdatasets. CruiseBench applies a fixed protocol to the masked rows, using scenario descriptors and measured sensors as inputs while excluding virtual sensors, health parameters, and auxiliary metadata from the feature tensor, preserving native-resolution windows, and applying dataset-wise RUL caps. Experiments with LSTM, GRU, TCN, and TSMixer provide baseline results for this setting. Under CruiseBench-eta5-W256-S10, TSMixer obtains the lowest average RMSE, $3.4\pm1.71$, and Saxena score, $(2.50\pm2.99)\times 10^{4}$. Ablation studies show that flight-stage selection, temporal downscaling method, and RUL-cap threshold affect reported results. With its fixed cruise-stage protocol, CruiseBench provides a reproducible sub-benchmark for controlled RUL model comparison and CPM-N-CMAPSS provides a stage-specific data foundation for future transfer-learning and domain-adaptation studies.

AI.tldr: CruiseBench, derived from N-CMAPSS, isolates cruise-stage data using CPM-N-CMAPSS masks and a fixed protocol to enable controlled, reproducible RUL prediction benchmarking. TSMixer achieves the best baseline results (RMSE: 3.4±1.71).
AI.motivation: N-CMAPSS adds realism by retaining full-flight time series from real flight profiles, but this entangles degradation cues with operating-regime variation, inflates data volume, and complicates preprocessing and fair model comparison. A controlled benchmark is needed to isolate degradation signals from operational variation.
AI.method: The authors propose CPM-N-CMAPSS, a mask artifact that identifies cruise-stage intervals via a common-altitude method across nine N-CMAPSS subdatasets. CruiseBench then applies a fixed protocol: using only scenario descriptors and measured sensors (excluding virtual sensors, health parameters, and metadata), preserving native-resolution windows, and enforcing dataset-wise RUL caps. Baselines are established with LSTM, GRU, TCN, and TSMixer under settings like CruiseBench-eta5-W256-S10.
AI.result: Under CruiseBench-eta5-W256-S10, TSMixer yields the lowest average RMSE (3.4±1.71) and Saxena score (2.50±2.99)×10⁴. Ablation studies confirm that flight-stage selection, temporal downscaling method, and RUL-cap threshold significantly influence reported performance.
AI.conclusion: CruiseBench offers a reproducible, stage-specific sub-benchmark for controlled RUL model comparison, while CPM-N-CMAPSS provides a foundation for future transfer-learning and domain-adaptation research on aero-engine prognostics.

title: Visual Indicators to Increase the Detection of Linguistic Media Bias
comment: Conditionally accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
summary: The influence of linguistic bias in online news articles is a growing concern, particularly in the context of shaping public opinion and rising political polarization. While there is a growing body of literature on indicators for misinformation, none have been sufficiently tested to counteract the influence of media bias. Hence, we design six indicators (Bias Bar, Bias Gauge, Bias Highlights, Political Scale, Sentiment Scale, and Trust Score) and test their impact on linguistic bias detection and perception in a two-phased experiment (n = 214). First, we expose participants to short, social-media-like statements along with one indicator and query bias perception. Second, we evaluate bias detection by removing the indicator and asking participants to mark biased words. In addition, we examine how trust, sharing discernment, and sentiment relate to bias perception and detection. Our results show that highlighting biased phrases and showing total bias with contextual information in a gauge significantly improve bias detection skills. However, the strongest predictor for reduced bias detection was political congruency between the statement and the participant. We conclude with design recommendations for linguistic media bias indicators in online news environments.

AI.tldr: This paper designs and tests six UI indicators (Bias Bar, Bias Gauge, Bias Highlights, Political Scale, Sentiment Scale, Trust Score) through a two-phase experiment (n=214) to assess their impact on linguistic bias detection and perception. Results show that highlighting biased phrases and contextual gauge displays significantly improve bias detection, though political congruency remains the strongest predictor of reduced detection. Design recommendations for bias indicators in online news are provided.
AI.motivation: Growing concern over linguistic bias in online news and its role in shaping public opinion and political polarization. Existing misinformation indicators are insufficiently tested for counteracting media bias, creating a gap that this study aims to fill by empirically evaluating indicator efficacy.
AI.method: Two-phased experimental design with 214 participants. Phase 1: participants viewed short social-media-like statements accompanied by one of six bias indicators and reported bias perception. Phase 2: indicators were removed and participants marked biased words to evaluate detection skills. Additional measures examined relationships among trust, sharing discernment, sentiment, and bias perception/detection.
AI.result: Bias Highlights (phrase-level annotation) and Bias Gauge (total bias with contextual information) significantly improved bias detection. Political congruency between statement stance and participant ideology was the strongest predictor of reduced bias detection, outweighing indicator effects.
AI.conclusion: Linguistic bias indicators can improve detection when designed to highlight specific biased phrases and provide contextualized bias scores. However, political identity remains a dominant moderating factor. The paper offers concrete design recommendations for implementing bias indicators in online news platforms.

title: Bridging Behavior and Implementation: Automated Java Glue Code Generation for Behavior-Driven Development
summary: Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) helps technical and non-technical stakeholders share a common understanding of software requirements through natural-language scenarios. Glue code makes these scenarios executable by mapping each step to the corresponding project code. However, developing and maintaining glue code requires knowledge of both the intended behavior and the underlying codebase, making it a labor-intensive part of BDD as requirements evolve. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong code generation capabilities, their use for automated glue code generation remains unexplored. This task requires reasoning over underspecified behavior, related BDD artifacts, and large project codebases. We present AutoGlue, a hierarchical multi-agent framework for automated Java glue code generation. AutoGlue follows a behavior-first workflow that separates behavior interpretation, context retrieval, and code generation. A Behavior Interpreter derives the intent of a step from its scenario context, while a Developer agent retrieves relevant BDD artifacts and project code before generating the final glue code. We evaluate AutoGlue on 1,307 steps from eight open-source Java projects. Compared with few-shot prompting, AutoGlue improves API F1 by 58.7% and CodeBLEU by 43.7%. It produces directly usable glue code for 46.1% of the evaluated steps, while most partially correct outputs require only minor revisions, such as adding missing actions or refining parameters. Ablation results show that behavior interpretation and project-aware context retrieval both contribute substantially to generation quality. These findings demonstrate that LLMs can effectively connect natural-language behavior specifications with project code and support specification-driven software development.

AI.tldr: AutoGlue is a hierarchical multi-agent LLM framework that automates glue code generation for Behavior-Driven Development (BDD). It separates behavior interpretation, context retrieval, and code generation, achieving 58.7% improvement in API F1 and 43.7% in CodeBLEU over few-shot prompting. It produces directly usable glue code for 46.1% of 1,307 evaluated steps across eight Java projects.
AI.motivation: BDD glue code development is labor-intensive, requiring knowledge of both intended behavior and the project codebase. As requirements evolve, maintaining this mapping between natural-language scenarios and code becomes a bottleneck. While LLMs excel at code generation, automated glue code generation is unexplored because it demands reasoning over underspecified behavior, related BDD artifacts, and large codebases simultaneously.
AI.method: AutoGlue employs a hierarchical multi-agent architecture with a behavior-first workflow: (1) A Behavior Interpreter agent derives step intent from surrounding scenario context; (2) a Developer agent retrieves relevant BDD artifacts (feature files, existing step definitions) and project code via context retrieval; (3) the Developer agent then generates the final glue code. This separation decouples behavior understanding from code generation, enabling each agent to focus on its specialized subtask.
AI.result: Evaluated on 1,307 steps from eight open-source Java projects, AutoGlue improved API F1 by 58.7% and CodeBLEU by 43.7% over few-shot prompting. It generated directly usable glue code for 46.1% of steps; partially correct outputs typically required only minor revisions (adding missing actions, refining parameters). Ablation studies confirmed that both behavior interpretation and project-aware context retrieval contributed substantially to generation quality.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively bridge natural-language behavior specifications with project code, supporting specification-driven software development. AutoGlue demonstrates that a behavior-first, multi-agent decomposition significantly outperforms monolithic prompting approaches for this complex, context-dependent code generation task.

title: Dreamer-CPC: Message Learning with World Models for Decentralized Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures. Under review at ICONIP 2026
summary: In multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), inter-agent communication is effective for improving performance under partial observability. Representation learning-based approaches enable decentralized agents to learn messages grounded in their own observations, but they rely only on current observations and cannot convey information accumulated over time. We propose Dreamer-CPC, a decentralized model-based MARL method that integrates message learning based on Collective Predictive Coding (CPC) into the world model of DreamerV3. Each agent independently maintains a world model and a message module, and infers and exchanges messages from the latent states of the world model that reflect the history of past observations and actions. We evaluated Dreamer-CPC in two environments: Observer, a non-cooperative information-sharing task, and CatchApple, a newly introduced task in which task-relevant observations are temporarily missing. In both environments, Dreamer-CPC outperformed IPPO-CPC, an existing CPC-based method that generates messages from current observations, as well as no-communication baselines. In particular, in CatchApple, Dreamer-CPC achieved 4 to 5 times the episode return of IPPO-CPC, demonstrating effective coordination where other methods fail due to missing observations. These results suggest that communication grounded in the latent dynamics of world models can support decentralized decision-making when current observations alone are insufficient.

AI.tldr: Dreamer-CPC integrates Collective Predictive Coding (CPC) into DreamerV3's world model, enabling decentralized MARL agents to communicate using messages derived from latent states that encode historical context, outperforming observation-only CPC methods in partially observable and observation-missing scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing representation learning-based communication methods in MARL generate messages solely from current observations, failing to convey temporal information accumulated over time. This is especially problematic when task-relevant observations are temporarily missing, requiring agents to coordinate using past experiences.
AI.method: Dreamer-CPC is a decentralized model-based MARL method that integrates CPC-based message learning into DreamerV3's world model. Each agent independently maintains a world model and a message module, inferring and exchanging messages from latent states that encode the full history of past observations and actions, rather than from raw current observations alone.
AI.result: Evaluated on two environments: (1) Observer, a non-cooperative information-sharing task, and (2) CatchApple, a novel task with temporarily missing task-relevant observations. Dreamer-CPC outperformed IPPO-CPC (observation-based CPC) and no-communication baselines. In CatchApple, Dreamer-CPC achieved 4–5× the episode return of IPPO-CPC, demonstrating effective coordination where other methods fail.
AI.conclusion: Communication grounded in the latent dynamics of world models supports robust decentralized decision-making when current observations alone are insufficient, suggesting that history-informed message generation is critical for coordination under severe partial observability.

title: Using Hierarchical Controlled Vocabularies to Understand CLIP Retrieval Failures in Historical Photo Collections
summary: GLAM institutions (Galleries, Libraries, Archives, and Museums) organise image access using controlled vocabularies such as the Art and Architecture Thesaurus (AAT). For content-based image retrieval in these settings, vision-language models like CLIP are increasingly used, but their performance varies. This variation is known to relate to measures like concept abstraction and concept frequency. However, no prior work explains this variation in terms of the structural properties of vocabularies like the AAT that GLAM professionals already use. The AAT groups concepts into broad facets (Objects, Activities, Agents, etc.) and arranges terms hierarchically within them. In this paper, we ask whether two structural properties (root facet type and hierarchy depth) explain where CLIP retrieval succeeds and fails, and where fine-tuning helps. Across three historical photographic collections annotated with AAT terms, we examine visual coherence (whether a term's photographs cluster in CLIP's embedding space), text-image alignment (whether its label is near that cluster), and standard retrieval measures, which conflate the two. We find that visual coherence and text-image alignment are nearly uncorrelated across terms and jointly separate distinct failure modes. Terms whose photographs cluster tightly but whose label is distant from the cluster retrieve poorly in every collection, in two of three collections even worse than terms that fail on both metrics. We also show that while retrieval metrics do not correlate significantly with either structural property, root facet type does significantly separate categories with varying visual coherence. Finally, we find that fine-tuning improves retrieval overall, but its gains favour shallower terms in the hierarchy, where text-image alignment improves most, beyond what concept frequency explains.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how two structural properties of the AAT—root facet type and hierarchy depth—explain where CLIP-based image retrieval succeeds or fails in GLAM collections. The authors separate visual coherence from text-image alignment, finding them nearly uncorrelated and jointly diagnostic of distinct failure modes. Root facet type significantly differentiates visual coherence, and fine-tuning disproportionately benefits shallower hierarchy terms.
AI.motivation: Prior work explains CLIP's variable retrieval performance using measures like concept abstraction and frequency, but no work connects this variation to the structural properties of controlled vocabularies (e.g., AAT) that GLAM professionals already employ. Bridging this gap could make performance diagnosis more actionable for practitioners.
AI.method: The authors decompose retrieval quality into two uncorrelated components—visual coherence (whether a term's images cluster in CLIP embedding space) and text-image alignment (whether the term's label is near that cluster)—alongside standard retrieval metrics. They then analyze how these relate to AAT root facet type and hierarchy depth across three historical photographic collections annotated with AAT terms. They also assess fine-tuning effects through this lens.
AI.result: Visual coherence and text-image alignment are nearly uncorrelated and reveal distinct failure modes: terms with tight clusters but distant labels perform worst. Root facet type significantly separates categories by visual coherence level, though retrieval metrics alone show no significant correlation with either structural property. Fine-tuning improves retrieval overall but especially benefits shallower hierarchy terms by improving text-image alignment, beyond what concept frequency predicts.
AI.conclusion: Structural properties of controlled vocabularies—particularly root facet type and hierarchy depth—offer meaningful signals for diagnosing and anticipating CLIP retrieval failures in GLAM settings, and fine-tuning strategies should account for these structural dimensions rather than relying solely on frequency-based heuristics.

title: Building Trust in Autonomous Commerce: A Verifiable Global Event Timeline and AI-Ready Fraud Intelligence Layer
comment: 18 pages, 4 tables, 1 figure. Preprint also available on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19060285
summary: Agentic commerce protocols such as AP2 and ACP define mechanisms for secure agent-initiated transactions but do not provide interoperable, tamper-evident auditability or verifiable temporal ordering of events across heterogeneous domains. This paper addresses these gaps by proposing a verifiable global event timeline for agentic commerce, constructed from four core components: canonical event schemas that enforce deterministic serialization, deterministic batch formation ensuring reproducible ordering without reliance on synchronized clocks, Merkle-based append-only commitments providing logarithmic-cost inclusion proofs, and blockchain anchoring establishing a tamper-evident temporal backbone. Building on this infrastructure, we introduce a cryptographically signed fraud marker that binds risk labels to anchored evidence through an unforgeable provenance chain, and a dataset lineage model enabling reproducible, tamper-evident AI training pipelines. Empirical results from a prototype implementation demonstrate: Merkle tree construction processes 50,000 events in 47 milliseconds; end-to-end verification completes in under 0.013 milliseconds regardless of batch size; inclusion proof sizes grow logarithmically from 320 bytes at 1,000 events to 512 bytes at 50,000 events; and Merkle-based verification outperforms linear scan by 14.4x at 50,000 events.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a verifiable global event timeline for agentic commerce using canonical schemas, deterministic batch formation, Merkle-based commitments, and blockchain anchoring, enabling tamper-evident auditability, cryptographically signed fraud markers, and reproducible AI dataset lineage. A prototype shows Merkle tree construction at 50K events in 47ms, sub-0.013ms verification, and 14.4x speedup over linear scan.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic commerce protocols (AP2, ACP) lack interoperable, tamper-evident auditability and verifiable temporal ordering across heterogeneous domains. This gap prevents reliable fraud detection, cross-domain provenance tracking, and trustworthy AI training pipelines.
AI.method: Four-layer architecture: (1) canonical event schemas for deterministic serialization; (2) deterministic batch formation for reproducible ordering without synchronized clocks; (3) Merkle-based append-only commitments for O(log n) inclusion proofs; (4) blockchain anchoring as a tamper-evident temporal backbone. Additionally, a cryptographically signed fraud marker binds risk labels via unforgeable provenance chains, and a dataset lineage model supports reproducible AI training.
AI.result: Prototype benchmarks: Merkle tree construction of 50,000 events in 47ms; end-to-end verification under 0.013ms regardless of batch size; inclusion proof sizes scale logarithmically (320 bytes at 1K events, 512 bytes at 50K events); Merkle verification outperforms linear scan by 14.4x at 50K events.
AI.conclusion: The proposed verifiable event timeline successfully bridges auditability gaps in agentic commerce, providing efficient, scalable, and cryptographically sound mechanisms for temporal ordering, fraud marking, and dataset lineage, with strong empirical performance supporting practical deployment.

title: Scaling Laws for Hypernetwork-Based Knowledge Injection in Large Language Models
comment: Preprint, 22 pages, 14 figures. Dataset collection available at https://huggingface.co/collections/nace-ai/hypernetwork-datasets
summary: Injecting factual knowledge into large language models (LLMs) reliably and at scale remains an open challenge. Hypernetworks provide a promising solution to large-scale knowledge injection. Although hypernetworks are typically applied for test-time adaptation, we explore their use in train-time knowledge injection, where, given a large corpus of facts, we train a hypernetwork to generate a fixed LoRA adapter that, when inserted into the target model, enable the model to answer questions about those facts. In this work, we investigate whether hypernetworks can be used to perform train-time knowledge injection and how this ability varies with scale. The scaling behavior of hypernetworks remains largely unstudied. Our design decouples the hypernetwork's injection capacity from the target model's general capability, enabling, for the first time, a rigorous study of scaling laws for hypernetwork architectures. We characterize how loss, reasoning accuracy, and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization vary with hypernetwork depth, width, and target network size. We construct a large-scale dataset, called MegaWikiQA, containing tens of millions of multi-hop question-answer examples across 39 domains constructed from examples in Wikidata5M. Our results reveal: (i) hypernetwork-based injection exhibits broadly predictive power law scaling along all architecture axes; and (ii) hypernetworks are capable of reliable OOD generalization at increasing scales, suggesting that hypernetwork provides a promising alternative to other train-time adaptation methods such as LoRA finetuning and full fine-tuning, exhibiting steeper scaling exponents in all OOD evaluations. Together, these results establish hypernetworks as a principled and scalable substrate for train-time adaptation, and provide the first empirically grounded scaling laws to guide hypernetworks for factual reasoning in large language models.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates hypernetworks for train-time factual knowledge injection into LLMs, establishing the first scaling laws for hypernetwork architectures and showing they exhibit power-law scaling with steeper OOD generalization exponents compared to LoRA and full fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Injecting factual knowledge into LLMs reliably and at scale remains an open challenge. Hypernetworks offer a promising approach, but their scaling behavior is largely unstudied, and prior work focuses on test-time adaptation rather than train-time knowledge injection.
AI.method: The authors train a hypernetwork to generate fixed LoRA adapters from a large fact corpus. The hypernetwork's injection capacity is decoupled from the target model's general capability, enabling rigorous scaling law analysis. Experiments use MegaWikiQA, a newly constructed dataset with tens of millions of multi-hop QA examples across 39 domains from Wikidata5M. Scaling is characterized along hypernetwork depth, width, and target network size.
AI.result: Hypernetwork-based injection exhibits predictive power-law scaling along all architectural axes. Hypernetworks achieve reliable OOD generalization at increasing scales and demonstrate steeper scaling exponents than LoRA fine-tuning and full fine-tuning across all OOD evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Hypernetworks are a principled and scalable substrate for train-time adaptation, with empirically grounded scaling laws that can guide future work on factual reasoning in LLMs.

title: Benchmarking Confidential GPU Inference on NVIDIA H100 under Intel TDX
summary: Confidential computing is becoming a practical deployment requirement for AI inference workloads that process sensitive inputs or protect proprietary model assets. However, the performance cost of enabling confidential execution for GPU-accelerated large language model serving remains workload dependent and operationally important. This paper presents a benchmark study comparing standard non-confidential execution with confidential computing mode on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU hosted in an Intel TDX confidential instance. The evaluation uses two representative language models, Mistral-7B v0.1 and Qwen3-30B-A3B, and measures time to first token, end-to-end request latency, per-request token generation throughput, global token throughput, and closed-loop request throughput under increasing concurrency. In fixed request-rate experiments, confidential mode increases average TTFT by 21.8% for Mistral-7B and 27.8% for Qwen3-30B-A3B, while global token throughput drops by 17.7% and 21.1%, respectively. In closed-loop concurrency experiments, throughput gaps remain in the 11.5-20.2% range, but the larger model reaches its saturation knee earlier under confidential mode. The results suggest that confidential GPU inference can retain usable throughput under load, but capacity planning must account for both the steady throughput penalty and the earlier saturation behavior observed for larger models.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks the performance overhead of confidential computing for LLM inference on an NVIDIA H100 GPU in an Intel TDX environment. Using Mistral-7B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it finds confidential mode increases TTFT by 22–28%, reduces global token throughput by 18–21%, and causes earlier saturation for the larger model, yet retains usable throughput under load.
AI.motivation: Confidential computing is increasingly required for AI inference to protect sensitive inputs and proprietary models, but its performance cost on GPU-accelerated LLM serving is workload-dependent and not well-characterized. The study aims to quantify this overhead to inform operational capacity planning.
AI.method: The authors conduct a benchmark study comparing standard (non-confidential) vs. confidential execution on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU within an Intel TDX confidential instance. Two models — Mistral-7B v0.1 (7B parameters) and Qwen3-30B-A3B (30B parameters with mixture-of-experts) — are evaluated across metrics including time-to-first-token (TTFT), end-to-end request latency, per-request token generation throughput, global token throughput, and closed-loop request throughput under increasing concurrency, using both fixed request-rate and closed-loop concurrency experiments.
AI.result: Under fixed request-rate experiments, confidential mode increases average TTFT by 21.8% (Mistral-7B) and 27.8% (Qwen3-30B-A3B), while global token throughput drops by 17.7% and 21.1% respectively. In closed-loop concurrency experiments, throughput gaps range from 11.5% to 20.2%, with the larger Qwen model reaching its saturation knee earlier under confidential mode.
AI.conclusion: Confidential GPU inference can retain usable throughput under load, but capacity planning must account for both the steady throughput penalty and the earlier saturation behavior observed for larger models, which may require provisioning additional resources to meet latency targets under confidential execution.

title: Air Quality Arena: A Large-Scale Multi-Region Ground Monitoring Dataset and Benchmark for Air Quality Forecasting with Time-Series Foundation Models
summary: Air pollution causes an estimated 7.9 million premature deaths annually, making accurate forecasting a critical public health priority. Machine learning is increasingly being applied to forecast air pollution levels, yet existing benchmarks remain narrow in both geographic scope and pollutant coverage, and fail to evaluate the latest generation of time series foundation models (TSFMs) on real world, large scale data. We present Air Quality Arena (AQA), a large scale multi-country and multi-pollutant dataset (AQA-Data) and benchmark (AQA-Bench) to address this gap. AQA covers 6 major pollutants over a three year period across 7 diverse countries and 4 continents, with more than 14,000 station-pollutant series, aiming to provide a comprehensive benchmark for air quality tasks. We benchmark this dataset across 11 leading time series foundation models and classical baselines to assess performance on short-term air quality forecasting. Our results demonstrate that TSFMs are effective zero-shot forecasters and consistently outperform classical baselines, with our top-performing model employing a cross-modal architecture that leverages a vision foundation model for time series forecasting. AQA is publicly released at AirQualityArena.github.io

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Air Quality Arena (AQA), a large-scale, multi-country, multi-pollutant dataset and benchmark for air quality forecasting. Covering 6 pollutants across 7 countries and 4 continents with over 14,000 station-pollutant series, AQA evaluates 11 time series foundation models (TSFMs) and classical baselines. Results show TSFMs excel as zero-shot forecasters, with a cross-modal vision foundation model achieving top performance.
AI.motivation: Air pollution causes ~7.9M premature deaths annually, making accurate forecasting critical. Existing benchmarks are limited in geographic scope and pollutant coverage, and fail to evaluate modern time series foundation models on real-world, large-scale data. AQA fills this gap with a comprehensive, publicly available resource.
AI.method: The authors construct AQA-Data — a dataset spanning 6 major pollutants, 7 countries across 4 continents, 3 years of data, and more than 14,000 station-pollutant series. They establish AQA-Bench, evaluating 11 leading TSFMs alongside classical baselines on short-term air quality forecasting. The best model uses a cross-modal architecture leveraging a vision foundation model for time series prediction.
AI.result: TSFMs prove effective as zero-shot forecasters, consistently outperforming classical baselines. The top-performing approach employs a cross-modal architecture that repurposes a vision foundation model for time series forecasting, achieving superior accuracy on short-term air quality prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: AQA provides the first large-scale, geographically diverse benchmark for air quality forecasting that rigorously tests modern TSFMs. The strong zero-shot performance of TSFMs — particularly cross-modal models — highlights their promise for real-world air quality applications. The dataset and benchmark are publicly released to spur further research.

title: Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study
summary: With generative AI (GenAI) entering classrooms the question to which teaching approach best supports metacognitive skill acquisition in AI-assisted learning becomes pressing. In this short-term longitudinal study we investigate two contrasting approaches: experiential learning encompassing hands-on approaches and instructional learning such as classical lectures. We conducted a quasi-experiment with 126 university students from a first-year engineering course which were distributed across the two conditions and completed a two hour session on learning with GenAI in the corresponding learning style. Metacognitive awareness which encompasses both knowledge of cognition (understanding effective AI-use strategies) and regulation of cognition (applying that knowledge in practice) was measured before and after the session. Additionally, students longitudinal metacognitive awareness was tracked over the trimester and assessed again five weeks after the initial intervention. Results reveal that experiential methods outperform instructional approaches in engagement and knowledge of cognition immediately after the intervention. By five weeks, the two groups converged on these measures, while the experiential group showed a delayed, continuous within-group increase in regulation of cognition that was not observed in the instructional group. This suggests that the benefits of experiential approaches extend beyond conventional educational settings to AI-assisted learning, and that knowledge and regulation may develop on different timescales under experiential learning.

AI.tldr: A quasi-experiment with 126 engineering students compared experiential vs. instructional learning approaches for acquiring metacognitive skills in GenAI-assisted learning. Experiential methods yielded immediate gains in engagement and knowledge of cognition; both groups converged by week 5, but only the experiential group showed a sustained, delayed increase in regulation of cognition.
AI.motivation: With generative AI entering classrooms, it is pressing to determine which teaching approach best supports metacognitive skill acquisition in AI-assisted learning contexts. The authors aim to fill the gap in understanding how different pedagogical methods—experiential (hands-on) versus instructional (lecture-based)—differentially affect the development of metacognitive awareness over time.
AI.method: A short-term longitudinal quasi-experiment with 126 first-year engineering students, distributed across two conditions: experiential learning (hands-on) and instructional learning (classical lectures). Both groups completed a two-hour session on learning with GenAI. Metacognitive awareness (knowledge of cognition and regulation of cognition) was measured pre- and post-session, with a follow-up assessment five weeks later to track longitudinal change over the trimester.
AI.result: Experiential methods outperformed instructional approaches in engagement and knowledge of cognition immediately after the intervention. By five weeks, the two groups converged on these measures. Notably, the experiential group exhibited a delayed, continuous within-group increase in regulation of cognition that was absent in the instructional group, suggesting distinct developmental timescales for knowledge and regulation under experiential learning.
AI.conclusion: The benefits of experiential approaches extend to AI-assisted learning beyond conventional educational settings. Knowledge of cognition and regulation of cognition appear to develop on different timescales under experiential learning, with regulation gains emerging only after a delay, highlighting the importance of longitudinal assessment in metacognitive training research.

title: Towards Automated Formal Verification of zkEVMs Using LLM-Guided Constraint Synthesis
summary: Zero-Knowledge Ethereum Virtual Machines (zkEVMs) secure Ethereum rollups by generating zero-knowledge proofs that guarantee off-chain execution correctness. However, subtle implementation bugs (e.g., incorrect gas accounting) can lead to valid proofs certifying semantically faulty states, thereby silently defeating cryptographic guarantees. Formal verification via SMT solvers can prevent this, but is bottlenecked by specification: current zkEVM development practice lacks automated methods to translate Rust opcode handlers into verification models. Current practices rely on unsustainable manual specifications, while LLM-based approaches suffer from hallucination and lack formal guarantees. To address this, we propose VeriSynth, a framework that synthesizes executable Python/Z3 verification models from Rust zkEVM code. VeriSynth enforces a hybrid paradigm: an LLM acts strictly as a formalization frontend to translate code into symbolic constraints, while an SMT solver serves as the correctness arbiter. To handle complex multi-component state transitions, VeriSynth integrates semantic decomposition, retrieval-grounded prompting, and verification-guided auto-repair into a closed-loop pipeline. We evaluate VeriSynth on the first source-level zkEVM verification benchmark, encompassing both correct and faulty opcode implementations. VeriSynth achieves a bug detection rate of over 90%, substantially outperforming direct and conversational LLM baselines, as well as a production-grade handwritten mutation-testing suite. Ablation studies confirm that each pipeline component is critical to the framework's overall effectiveness.

AI.tldr: VeriSynth is a framework that synthesizes executable Python/Z3 verification models from Rust zkEVM code using a hybrid LLM+SMT pipeline, incorporating semantic decomposition, retrieval-grounded prompting, and verification-guided auto-repair to achieve over 90% bug detection on a new zkEVM verification benchmark.
AI.motivation: zkEVM implementations in Rust are vulnerable to subtle bugs (e.g., incorrect gas accounting) that can produce valid zero-knowledge proofs for semantically invalid states, undermining the security guarantees of Ethereum rollups. Formal verification via SMT solvers could prevent this, but the bottleneck is specification: there is no automated method to translate Rust opcode handlers into verifiable models. Manual specification is unsustainable, and LLM-based approaches are unreliable due to hallucination and lack of formal correctness guarantees.
AI.method: VeriSynth employs a closed-loop hybrid pipeline: (1) an LLM serves strictly as a formalization frontend to translate Rust code into symbolic Z3 constraints; (2) semantic decomposition breaks complex multi-component state transitions into manageable units; (3) retrieval-grounded prompting supplies relevant context to improve translation accuracy; (4) an SMT solver acts as the correctness arbiter, checking generated models; (5) verification-guided auto-repair iteratively refines failed models based on counterexample feedback.
AI.result: Evaluated on the first source-level zkEVM verification benchmark (covering both correct and buggy opcode implementations), VeriSynth achieves over 90% bug detection rate, significantly outperforming direct LLM baselines, conversational LLM baselines, and a production-grade handwritten mutation-testing suite. Ablation studies confirm that semantic decomposition, retrieval-grounded prompting, and auto-repair are each critical to overall effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: VeriSynth demonstrates that a disciplined hybrid architecture—LLM for formalization translation, SMT for correctness arbitration, with retrieval and auto-repair in the loop—can automate zkEVM verification model synthesis with high accuracy, overcoming the limitations of both purely manual and purely LLM-based approaches.

title: Harnessing Disagreement: Detecting Correlated Agreement Blindness in Multi-Agent Triage
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at PAAMS 2026; this is the author's pre-review submitted version
summary: Disagreement-triggered escalation can create a structural blind spot in multi-agent arbitration: as base learners improve, they tend to converge, weakening safety monitoring where correlated failures concentrate. We term this correlated agreement blindness and present ARAT (Arbitrated Reasoning Agents for Alarm Triage), a directed-star system combining an inductive Random Forest (RF) agent, an analogical case-based k-nearest neighbour (k-NN) agent, and a calibrated meta-model to mitigate this effect. On 82,332 holdout samples from the UNSW-NB15 network intrusion detection dataset, 57.2% of errors occur under agreement and 90.6% of dangerous under-predictions evade disagreement-based monitoring even after conservative override; ablation shows that strengthening base learners increases error correlation while reducing disagreement. ARAT reduces under-prediction relative to soft voting from 4.80% to 1.70% via conservative override (-2.6pp) and a safety-flag gate (-0.5pp), demonstrating architectural gains. Cross-dataset validation on clinical readmission supports these indicators, suggesting that diversification improves safety only when it generates productive disagreement rather than convergence. These results indicate that disagreement-triggered escalation can be blind to correlated failure, a risk that may intensify as agentic pipelines deploy increasingly capable, correlated models.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent systems that escalate on disagreement suffer from "correlated agreement blindness," where improving base learners converge and fail together silently. The authors propose ARAT, a directed-star architecture with diverse agents and a calibrated meta-model, achieving significant reduction in dangerous under-predictions on network intrusion detection and clinical readmission tasks.
AI.motivation: Disagreement-based escalation mechanisms in multi-agent systems assume that disagreement signals uncertainty or error. However, as base learners improve, they tend to converge in their predictions, creating correlated failures that occur under agreement — precisely where monitoring is weakest. This structural blind spot, which the authors term "correlated agreement blindness," means that the most dangerous errors (e.g., missed network intrusions) systematically evade escalation and remain undetected.
AI.method: ARAT (Arbitrated Reasoning Agents for Alarm Triage) employs a directed-star architecture with three components: (1) an inductive Random Forest agent, (2) an analogical case-based k-NN agent, and (3) a calibrated meta-model serving as arbitrator. The system applies a conservative override mechanism that biases toward the safety-critical class when confidence is low, plus a safety-flag gate for residual high-risk cases. Diversity is architecturally enforced through complementary reasoning paradigms (inductive vs. analogical) rather than relying solely on statistical ensembling. Evaluation uses 82,332 holdout samples from UNSW-NB15 with cross-dataset validation on clinical readmission.
AI.result: On UNSW-NB15, 57.2% of all errors occurred under base-learner agreement, and 90.6% of dangerous under-predictions evaded disagreement-based monitoring even with conservative override. Ablation confirmed that strengthening base learners increases error correlation while reducing disagreement signals. ARAT reduced under-prediction from 4.80% (soft voting baseline) to 1.70% — a 3.1 percentage point improvement via conservative override (-2.6pp) and safety-flag gate (-0.5pp). Cross-dataset validation on clinical readmission confirmed the pattern, showing that diversification improves safety only when it yields productive disagreement.
AI.conclusion: Disagreement-triggered escalation carries an inherent structural risk: as agents become more capable and correlated, their failures concentrate under agreement, creating a monitoring blind spot precisely where it is most needed. Architectural diversification across reasoning paradigms, combined with calibrated meta-arbitration, can partially mitigate this effect. The problem is likely to intensify as agentic pipelines deploy increasingly capable but correlated models.

title: UniRank: Benchmarking Ranking Models for Unified Sequential Modeling and Feature Interaction
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures, and 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/salmon1802/UniRank
summary: Ranking is a core stage in online advertising and recommender systems. Modern ranking models increasingly unify sequential modeling and feature interaction, yet many advances rely on proprietary data, closed implementations, and large-scale industrial infrastructure. This setting limits reproducible comparison and hinders academic study of scaling laws, long-sequence modeling, and multi-task ranking. To address these limitations, this paper proposes UniRank, an open benchmark for ranking models that unify sequential modeling and feature interaction. UniRank uses chronological pointwise autoregressive supervision, standardizes evaluation across feedback tasks, and provides a PyTorch toolkit with Distributed Data Parallel training, operator optimization, mixed-precision training, attention optimization, and other efficiency techniques that reduce hardware requirements. We benchmark 15 representative unified ranking models on five large-scale public datasets from short-video, advertising, and e-commerce platforms, with the largest dataset containing over 700 million instances and the longest behavior sequence exceeding 10^5 interactions. UniRank provides a reproducible basis for comparing unified ranking models, studying scaling laws under limited compute, and narrowing the gap between academic and industrial ranking research. We believe UniRank benefits researchers, practitioners, and beginners through reproducible experiments, production-oriented evaluation, and accessible implementations. Code and data are available at https://github.com/salmon1802/UniRank.

AI.tldr: UniRank is an open benchmark for unified ranking models that combines sequential modeling and feature interaction, featuring 15 models evaluated on 5 large-scale public datasets (up to 700M instances, 10^5-length sequences) with an optimized PyTorch toolkit to enable reproducible academic research on par with industrial systems.
AI.motivation: Current advances in ranking models that unify sequential modeling and feature interaction are hindered by proprietary data, closed implementations, and industrial-scale infrastructure requirements, limiting reproducible comparison, scaling law studies, long-sequence modeling research, and multi-task ranking exploration in academic settings.
AI.method: UniRank employs chronological pointwise autoregressive supervision for training, standardizes evaluation across multiple feedback tasks, and provides a PyTorch toolkit with Distributed Data Parallel training, operator optimization, mixed-precision training, and attention optimization to reduce hardware requirements. Fifteen representative unified ranking models are benchmarked on five public datasets from short-video, advertising, and e-commerce domains.
AI.result: The benchmark enables reproducible comparison across 15 unified ranking models on datasets up to 700 million instances with behavior sequences exceeding 100,000 interactions, facilitating systematic study of scaling laws under limited computational budgets.
AI.conclusion: UniRank narrows the gap between academic and industrial ranking research by providing reproducible experiments, production-oriented evaluation, and accessible implementations, benefiting researchers, practitioners, and beginners alike.

title: Intelligent Disruption: Undetectable Attacks on Wireless Autoencoders
summary: Adversarial attacks can degrade the legitimate decision performance in wireless autoencoder communications. However, in complex scenarios with multiple adversaries, the cumulative leakage interference (CLI) caused by the multiple parallel attacks increases the chance of detecting the attacks, while dynamical environments also make the fixed attack strategies difficult to have stable effectiveness. To jointly enhance the undetectability, aggressivity and adaptability of adversarial attacks, we propose a deep learning based intelligent attack framework. Specifically, considering the CLI caused by the multiple parallel attacks, a deep neural network based transmit power control is established to reduce the interference leakage by regulating the transmit power of these adversaries, thereby improving the undetectability. Furthermore, to enhance the attack effectiveness and stability in the dynamic environment, the conditional generative adversarial attack is further developed. The generator takes the attack channel information as the conditional input to produce the perturbating signals to mislead the discriminator by making the attacked received signals resemble the clean received signals, while the discriminator distinguishes between the two under the same condition. Through the adversarial training, the generator can learn to create adaptive perturbating signals with enhanced attack performance. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms benchmarks in terms of attack undetectability, aggressivity and adaptability.

AI.tldr: A deep learning framework combining DNN-based power control and conditional GAN-based attack generation is proposed to jointly improve undetectability, aggressivity, and adaptability of adversarial attacks in wireless autoencoder communications under multi-adversary scenarios.
AI.motivation: In multi-adversary wireless autoencoder communication scenarios, cumulative leakage interference (CLI) from parallel attacks increases detection risk, and dynamic environments render fixed attack strategies ineffective. Existing approaches fail to jointly address undetectability, aggressivity, and adaptability.
AI.method: The framework has two components: (1) a DNN-based transmit power control mechanism that regulates adversarial transmit power to reduce CLI and improve undetectability; (2) a conditional generative adversarial attack where the generator uses attack channel information as conditional input to produce perturbating signals that mimic clean received signals, while the discriminator distinguishes them under the same condition. Adversarial training enables adaptive perturbation generation.
AI.result: Simulation results show the proposed framework outperforms benchmarks in attack undetectability, aggressivity, and adaptability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed intelligent attack framework effectively enhances adversarial attack performance in wireless autoencoder communications by jointly optimizing power control and conditional adversarial perturbation generation, achieving superior undetectability, aggressivity, and adaptability in multi-adversary dynamic environments.

title: Task Competence Is Not Instruction Following: Evaluating Instruction-Conflicting Behavior in Small Language Models
summary: Instruction tuning is meant to make language models follow user requests, yet it is unclear whether small models comply when an instruction conflicts with their usual task behavior. We study this across three tasks - multiple-choice question answering (MCQA), sentiment classification, and mathematical question answering - by pairing a standard instruction with a conflicting non-standard one (select an incorrect option, output the opposite sentiment, or return twice the answer). This cross-task design allows us to test whether resistance to conflicting instructions is tied to specific task characteristics or reflects a broader behavioral tendency. As all predictions are scored against the original ground truth, a model that ignores the non-standard instruction still appears accurate. Using standard accuracy, non-standard accuracy, and an Instruction-Following Failure Rate (IFFR), we evaluate instruction-tuned Qwen models across sizes. Both standard accuracy and instruction following generally improve with scale, although the pattern is not consistent across all tasks and datasets. Small models stay competent yet routinely ignore the non-standard instruction, while larger models show a clear gap between the two settings. These findings suggest that gains in task capability do not automatically provide reliable control over model behavior. Task competence and instruction following are therefore distinct abilities, and reporting only standard accuracy hides instruction-following failures.

AI.tldr: Small instruction-tuned models often ignore conflicting instructions despite remaining task-competent, while larger models better follow non-standard instructions. Task capability and instruction following are distinct abilities, and standard accuracy metrics mask instruction-following failures.
AI.motivation: Instruction tuning aims to make language models follow user requests, but it is unclear whether small models comply when an instruction conflicts with their default task behavior. The authors seek to disentangle task competence from instruction-following ability and expose the limitations of standard evaluation metrics.
AI.method: The authors design a cross-task evaluation across three tasks (MCQA, sentiment classification, mathematical QA) where each task pairs a standard instruction with a conflicting non-standard one (e.g., select the wrong option, output opposite sentiment, return twice the answer). They evaluate instruction-tuned Qwen models of varying sizes using three metrics: standard accuracy, non-standard accuracy, and Instruction-Following Failure Rate (IFFR). All predictions are scored against the original ground truth, so ignoring the non-standard instruction still yields high standard accuracy.
AI.result: Standard accuracy and instruction following generally improve with model scale, though inconsistently across tasks and datasets. Small models remain task-competent but routinely ignore conflicting instructions. Larger models show a clear gap between standard and non-standard settings, indicating better compliance. The findings reveal that gains in task capability do not automatically confer reliable control over model behavior.
AI.conclusion: Task competence and instruction following are distinct abilities that do not co-evolve neatly with scale. Reporting only standard accuracy conceals instruction-following failures, warranting complementary metrics like IFFR to properly assess model controllability and alignment.

title: FormulaSPIN: Self-Play Fine-Tuning for Natural Language to Spreadsheet Formula Generation
comment: 15 pages,7 figures, 14 tables. Accepted to ACL 2026 Main Conference Oral
summary: Spreadsheet applications are used by hundreds of millions worldwide, yet writing formulas remains a significant barrier. Existing approaches rely on static supervised data, which quickly saturates on limited annotations. In this paper, we introduce FORMULASPIN, a self-play framework that breaks the ceiling of supervised fine-tuning by enabling iterative self-improvement without any additional data. Vanilla SPIN fails on this task: it uniformly penalizes every non-matching output, so execution-equivalent alternatives are punished as negatives in one example while serving as ground truth in another, producing contradictory gradients. Our framework resolves this by exploiting formula generation's unique advantage: binary executability provides implicit supervision that separates semantic errors from valid stylistic variants. We frame training as a two-player game in which the main player learns to prefer ground-truth formulas over those from its previous version, while execution feedback sorts outputs into distinct granularities-enabling an adaptive curriculum that shifts from semantic correctness to stylistic refinement. To further increase accuracy, we incorporate ExecVote, a semantic-level voting mechanism that naturally handles multiple valid formulations. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FORMULASPIN achieves state-of-the-art performance, with 74.9% exact match and 87.1% execution accuracy on NL2FORMULA, matching models trained with additional preference annotations while outperforming both traditional SFT and frontier proprietary models. These findings underscore self-play's potential to tackle scarce data tasks and open the door to extending it beyond executable domains.

AI.tldr: FORMULASPIN is a self-play framework for spreadsheet formula generation that overcomes supervised fine-tuning data limitations. It resolves Vanilla SPIN's failure (punishing execution-equivalent alternatives) by leveraging binary executability as implicit supervision, framing training as a two-player game with an adaptive curriculum, and using ExecVote for semantic-level voting. It achieves SOTA (74.9% EM, 87.1% exec accuracy) without additional annotations.
AI.motivation: Spreadsheet formula writing remains a barrier for millions of users. Supervised fine-tuning saturates on limited annotations, and existing self-play methods (Vanilla SPIN) fail because they uniformly penalize all non-matching outputs, treating execution-equivalent stylistic variants as negatives — producing contradictory gradients that harm learning.
AI.method: FORMULASPIN frames training as a two-player game where: (1) the main player learns to prefer ground-truth formulas over its previous-version outputs; (2) binary execution feedback sorts outputs into distinct granularities, enabling an adaptive curriculum that progresses from semantic correctness to stylistic refinement; and (3) ExecVote, a semantic-level voting mechanism, handles multiple valid formulations during inference to boost accuracy.
AI.result: FORMULASPIN achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks: 74.9% exact match and 87.1% execution accuracy on NL2FORMULA, matching models trained with additional preference annotations while outperforming traditional SFT and frontier proprietary models.
AI.conclusion: Self-play via FORMULASPIN effectively breaks the data ceiling for formula generation by exploiting executability as free implicit supervision. This demonstrates self-play's potential for scarce-data tasks and suggests extensibility beyond executable domains.

title: Challenges of Explainability in Continual Learning for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Deep learning models have shown strong potential for time series forecasting, yet their deployment in real-world environmental monitoring remains challenging due to non-stationary dynamics and limited explainability. In this work, we investigate explainability as a central tool for understanding continual learning in adaptive time series forecasting, with Experience Replay strategies. We study neural forecasting architectures such as PatchMixer, PatchTST and DLinear, augmented with attention-based sampling mechanisms to support model adaptation over time. Explainability is leveraged through attention rollout and gradient-based attribution methods (Grad-CAM) to analyze both predictive behavior and sampling strategies within a continual learning framework. Experiments conducted on real-world piezometric time series exhibiting heterogeneous patterns and regime shifts show that analyzing model and sampling behaviors provides valuable insights into the dynamics of the continual learning framework. Beyond predictive performance, our results highlight the challenges and opportunities of using explainability to understand continual learning behaviors, revealing how attribution patterns evolve over time and how they can inform data selection and adaptation strategies in non-stationary forecasting scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper explores using explainability techniques (attention rollout, Grad-CAM) to understand and improve continual learning with Experience Replay for adaptive time series forecasting. Experiments on piezometric data with regime shifts demonstrate that analyzing attribution patterns reveals how models adapt over time and can inform better data selection strategies in non-stationary environments.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for time series forecasting face two key deployment challenges: (1) non-stationary dynamics that cause model degradation over time, and (2) limited explainability of model behavior. The authors argue that explainability can serve as a diagnostic tool to understand how continual learning frameworks adapt, particularly how Experience Replay sampling strategies influence model behavior under distribution shifts.
AI.method: The authors study three neural forecasting architectures — PatchMixer, PatchTST, and DLinear — augmented with attention-based sampling mechanisms within a continual learning framework using Experience Replay. Explainability is assessed via two post-hoc methods: attention rollout (tracing attention flow across layers) and gradient-based attribution (Grad-CAM), applied to both the predictive behavior of the models and the sampling strategies themselves. Experiments use real-world piezometric time series exhibiting heterogeneous patterns and regime shifts.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that attribution patterns evolve over time as the model continually adapts, providing insights into how the continual learning framework responds to regime shifts. The explainability analysis of sampling strategies uncovers which historical exemplars are prioritized during replay, offering a window into the model's adaptation dynamics that goes beyond standard predictive performance metrics.
AI.conclusion: Explainability is a valuable tool for understanding continual learning behavior in non-stationary time series forecasting. Attribution evolution over time can inform data selection and adaptation strategies, though significant challenges remain in effectively leveraging these insights for robust deployment in real-world environmental monitoring.

title: A Task Taxonomy for Edge and Trail Bundling
comment: Accepted for presentation at IEEE VIS (Short Paper)
summary: Edge bundling reduces visual clutter by aggregating similar edges, yet practitioners lack a structured vocabulary for reasoning about the tasks that bundled visualizations support. Such a vocabulary is needed both to evaluate the general utility of bundling and to compare different bundling approaches. We address this gap by assembling a corpus of 102 papers, 49 of which contain explicit bundling tasks, spanning node-link diagrams, geographic trail sets, and parallel coordinate plots. From this corpus, we derive a task taxonomy organized as a matrix of scope (Element, Bundle, Global, Multi-view) crossed with action (Verify, Identify, Characterize, Quantify, Compare, Assess), instantiated across the three representation types. We show that bundling simultaneously enables tasks (bundle-level and global reasoning) and disables others (element-level precision), a duality not captured by existing task frameworks. Our coded corpus and taxonomy are released as supplemental material on OSF (osf.io/23r67).

AI.tldr: The paper presents a task taxonomy for edge bundling visualizations derived from a corpus of 102 papers, organized as a matrix of scope (Element, Bundle, Global, Multi-view) × action (Verify, Identify, Characterize, Quantify, Compare, Assess), revealing that bundling simultaneously enables bundle-level/global reasoning while disabling element-level precision.
AI.motivation: Practitioners lack a structured vocabulary for reasoning about tasks supported by bundled visualizations. Such a vocabulary is essential for evaluating the general utility of bundling and for comparing different bundling approaches.
AI.method: The authors assembled a corpus of 102 papers (49 containing explicit bundling tasks) spanning node-link diagrams, geographic trail sets, and parallel coordinate plots. From this corpus, they derived a task taxonomy organized as a matrix of scope (Element, Bundle, Global, Multi-view) crossed with action (Verify, Identify, Characterize, Quantify, Compare, Assess), instantiated across the three representation types.
AI.result: A structured task taxonomy was produced. The analysis revealed a duality: bundling simultaneously enables certain tasks (bundle-level and global reasoning) while disabling others (element-level precision), a phenomenon not captured by existing task frameworks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed taxonomy fills a critical gap by providing a structured vocabulary for bundling tasks, enabling more rigorous evaluation and comparison of bundling techniques. The coded corpus and taxonomy are publicly released on OSF.

title: Beyond Fail-to-Pass: Iterative Hardening of Co-Generated Bug Reproduction Tests and Fixes
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have made automated program repair (APR) increasingly practical for real-world bugs, but repairing directly from bug reports remains underconstrained. Bug reproduction tests (BRTs) help close this gap by turning a bug report into an executable, bug-specific signal that can guide repair and validate candidate patches. Existing work has therefore studied BRT generation as a core subproblem in APR and mainly evaluates a generated BRT using the fail-to-pass (F->P) criterion, which requires the test to fail on the buggy code but pass on the golden fix. We show that F->P alone is insufficient when the goal of a BRT is to improve downstream repair. In particular, some F->P BRTs are lax, reproducing the observed symptom yet still admitting plausible-but-incorrect patches. We formalize this missing quality dimension by separating F->P BRTs into rigorous and lax ones, and show empirically that only the former consistently improve repair success. We further find that co-generation introduces test--fix error coupling, where the in-trajectory fail-to-pass (F->P) check can pass even when both the generated patch and generated test are wrong. Based on these findings, we propose CoHarden, a co-generation framework that uses the Lax signal as an in-loop convergence criterion. CoHarden first generates a test before any fix, then iteratively hardens the test and fix against surviving mutation patches until the generated test no longer admits Lax regressions. Experiments show that CoHarden reaches 69.4% Resolved and 78.9% F->P on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming the strongest fix-only and cogeneration baselines by +9.6 and +7.9 percentage points in Resolved, respectively, with consistent gains across LLM backbones and benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CoHarden, a co-generation framework for automated program repair that iteratively hardens both bug reproduction tests and fixes. It identifies that the standard fail-to-pass (F→P) criterion is insufficient for evaluating BRT quality, distinguishes between rigorous and lax BRTs, and demonstrates that hardening against lax tests significantly improves downstream repair success (69.4% Resolved on SWE-bench Verified).
AI.motivation: Existing BRT generation for APR relies on the fail-to-pass (F→P) criterion, but the authors demonstrate that F→P alone is insufficient: some BRTs are "lax" — they reproduce the symptom yet still admit plausible-but-incorrect patches. Additionally, in co-generation settings, test-fix error coupling can cause the F→P check to pass even when both the generated patch and test are wrong. These gaps motivate a more rigorous approach to BRT quality assessment and co-generation.
AI.method: CoHarden operates in three phases: (1) test-first generation — a BRT is generated before any fix; (2) iterative hardening — the test and fix are jointly hardened against surviving mutation patches (plausible-but-incorrect patches that pass the current test); (3) convergence — the loop terminates when the test no longer admits lax regressions. The framework uses the Lax signal as an in-loop convergence criterion and is LLM-agnostic, tested across multiple backbones.
AI.result: CoHarden achieves 69.4% Resolved and 78.9% F→P on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming the strongest fix-only baselines by +9.6pp and co-generation baselines by +7.9pp in Resolved. Gains are consistent across different LLM backbones and benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: The F→P criterion alone is inadequate for assessing BRT quality in APR; distinguishing rigorous from lax BRTs is critical. CoHarden demonstrates that using lax-test hardening as an in-loop convergence signal during co-generation substantially improves repair outcomes, setting a new state-of-the-art on SWE-bench Verified.

title: Knowledge-Centric Self-Improvement
summary: Self-improving AI systems typically treat the agent as the object that improves, by optimizing prompts, workflows, harnesses, or even the agent's own code. This agent-centric view can make improvements expensive to maintain and difficult to transfer, because gains become tied to a particular agent design, task distribution, or adaptation run. We study a complementary paradigm: knowledge-centric self-improvement, in which agents remain generic and disposable while the persistent object is a curated knowledge base that agents can leverage for future tasks. We conduct controlled case studies to operationalize this idea via a simple protocol. Agents attempt one task, then contribute evidence-grounded insights to a shared knowledge base via task-level and cross-task forums, followed by knowledge distillation. Because self-improvement is contained in the knowledge rather than the agent, improvement can be more inspectable, transferable, and portable. Across abstract reasoning, coding, and terminal benchmarks, this protocol improves solve rates while reducing dollar cost relative to agent-centric baselines. The resulting distilled knowledge also transfers to held-out tasks and across LLM families, indicating that the improvement is not merely an LLM- or run-specific behavior. These results support a new view of self-improving agentic systems: progress can be driven primarily by the curated persistent knowledge. Code is available at https://github.com/recursive-knowledge/KSI.

AI.tldr: A knowledge-centric self-improvement paradigm where generic agents contribute curated insights to a persistent shared knowledge base, yielding more inspectable, transferable, and cost-efficient improvements compared to traditional agent-centric approaches.
AI.motivation: Traditional self-improving AI systems are agent-centric—improvements are embedded in prompts, workflows, or code tied to a specific agent design, making gains expensive to maintain and hard to transfer across agents, tasks, or runs. The authors propose a complementary paradigm focused on the knowledge base as the persistent object of improvement.
AI.method: Agents attempt tasks and contribute evidence-grounded insights to a shared knowledge base through task-level and cross-task forums, followed by a knowledge distillation step. The agents themselves remain generic and disposable; all improvement resides in the curated knowledge. Controlled case studies evaluate this protocol against agent-centric baselines on abstract reasoning, coding, and terminal benchmarks.
AI.result: The protocol improves solve rates while reducing dollar cost relative to agent-centric baselines. Distilled knowledge transfers to held-out tasks and across LLM families, demonstrating that improvements are not confined to a specific model or run.
AI.conclusion: Progress in self-improving agentic systems can be driven primarily by curated persistent knowledge rather than agent-specific modifications. This knowledge-centric view offers greater inspectability, transferability, and portability, supporting a new design philosophy for AI systems.
