title: GraphContainer: A Unified Platform for Comparing and Debugging Graph RAG Methods
summary: Graph RAG mitigates hallucinations and stale knowledge in LLMs, particularly for multi-hop question answering. However, existing approaches remain highly fragmented and incompatible. The structural heterogeneity of graph formats across different frameworks and the lack of granular visualization tools make it exceedingly difficult to evaluate and compare retrieval behaviors. To bridge this gap, we propose GraphContainer, a novel platform designed to unify and visualize diverse graph RAG workflows. GraphContainer features two key components: (1) a Unified Graph Representation (UGR) layer that seamlessly standardizes multi-format graphs, and (2) a Graph Recorder that tracks and visually renders the step-by-step retrieval process. Through an interactive web interface, we demonstrate GraphContainer's ability to import heterogeneous graphs and perform live, traceable visual debugging of graph RAG methods. Ultimately, we show how GraphContainer enables controlled comparisons of various graph formats and retrieval strategies, lowering the barrier for researchers and practitioners to design optimal graph RAG pipelines. A demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/O02eNJLwkU0.

AI.tldr: GraphContainer is a platform that unifies heterogeneous graph formats and provides visual, step-by-step debugging of graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (Graph RAG) workflows, enabling controlled comparison of retrieval strategies.
AI.motivation: Existing Graph RAG approaches for mitigating LLM hallucinations in multi-hop QA are highly fragmented due to structural heterogeneity of graph formats across frameworks and a lack of granular visualization tools, making evaluation and comparison of retrieval behaviors extremely difficult.
AI.method: GraphContainer introduces two key components: (1) a Unified Graph Representation (UGR) layer that standardizes multi-format graphs into a common representation, and (2) a Graph Recorder that tracks and visually renders the step-by-step retrieval process. An interactive web interface ties these together for live, traceable visual debugging.
AI.result: The platform successfully imports heterogeneous graphs and enables live, traceable visual debugging of graph RAG methods, facilitating controlled comparisons of various graph formats and retrieval strategies.
AI.conclusion: GraphContainer lowers the barrier for researchers and practitioners to design optimal graph RAG pipelines by providing a unified, visual, and comparable framework for graph RAG evaluation.

title: Integrity of peer-to-peer distributed LLM inference under malicious nodes
summary: Peer-to-peer distributed inference executes a Large Language Model (LLM) on pooled consumer hardware by spreading its layers across many nodes. Every request passes through nodes that are owned and controlled by multiple independent parties. However, in this setting, any party can tamper with the output of its layers to corrupt the end result. Recomputing the forward pass on trusted hardware can catch this, but it introduces additional computational cost. The scientific literature includes several prior integrity-checking approaches, such as known-answer traps for image classifiers and cryptographic commitments. However, these solutions test only the exact correctness and do not account for the ordinary variation that may arise between benign nodes. In this paper, we propose a method that checks the output integrity by measuring the variation in the activations that each node passes to the next. A peer who wants to use the network selects a small set of secret canary inputs whose correct activations are known in advance and mixes them into regular traffic. Because the peers cannot tell a canary from a real query, any tampering node corrupts them as well. The deviation from the known reference then reveals malicious activity: benign nodes exhibit only minor variation from hardware-induced noise, whereas tampered nodes deviate far more. We treat the identification of malicious nodes as a probabilistic test that separates two drift distributions, without relying on a fixed threshold. We study 408 configurations with metrics and success criteria fixed before any experiment ran; the detector reaches AUROC 1.0, correctly ranking the malicious shard above every benign shard on every canary in every configuration.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an integrity-checking method for peer-to-peer distributed LLM inference that uses secret canary inputs with pre-known activations. By measuring drift between expected and observed activations, it detects tampering nodes probabilistically without fixed thresholds, achieving AUROC 1.0 across 408 configurations.
AI.motivation: In peer-to-peer distributed LLM inference, layers are spread across independently owned nodes, creating a trust problem: any node can tamper with its layer outputs. Existing integrity checks (known-answer traps, cryptographic commitments) only verify exact correctness and fail to account for benign hardware-induced variation between honest nodes. A method is needed that distinguishes malicious tampering from ordinary noise.
AI.method: A peer selects a small set of secret canary inputs with known correct activations and mixes them into regular inference traffic. Since nodes cannot distinguish canaries from real queries, tampering affects both. The method measures activation drift from the known reference, then frames malicious node identification as a probabilistic test separating two drift distributions — benign (hardware noise only) vs. malicious (tampering-induced deviation) — without relying on a fixed threshold.
AI.result: The detector was evaluated across 408 configurations with pre-registered metrics and success criteria. It achieved AUROC 1.0, correctly ranking the malicious shard above every benign shard on every canary in every configuration tested.
AI.conclusion: The proposed probabilistic drift-based detection method effectively and robustly identifies tampering nodes in peer-to-peer distributed LLM inference, perfectly separating malicious from benign behavior across all tested scenarios without requiring exact-output verification.

title: Adaptive Capitulation: A Structural Failure Mode of LLM Responses in Vulnerability Contexts
summary: Large language models operating in emotionally sensitive contexts face a structural trilemma: when users in vulnerable states request information that may reinforce maladaptive attribution, current response architectures resolve the tension through protective restriction, uninflected facilitation, or unintegrated co-presence of both imperatives -- each preserving one objective at the cost of the other. Administering a three-turn escalating vulnerability vignette to three commercial LLMs (900 sessions across material, relational, and somatic status-proxy variants) and coding responses with two binary indices (VCC/VCI), we characterize a previously undocumented failure mode we term adaptive capitulation: the model validates the social injustice underlying the user's distress before pivoting to detailed facilitation of the very acquisition it nominally discouraged. We show that the trilemma is structural rather than incidental, and propose Minimal Reattributive Sufficiency (MRS), an architecture-neutral design principle that embeds a single reattributive cue within an otherwise validating response, preserving a pathway toward autonomous reattribution without contesting the user's stated goal.

AI.tldr: LLMs in emotionally sensitive contexts face a structural trilemma where current response architectures fail to balance validation and safety. The paper identifies "adaptive capitulation" — a failure mode where models validate distress then nonetheless facilitate harmful requests — and proposes Minimal Reattributive Sufficiency (MRS) as a design principle to embed a reattributive cue without contesting user goals.
AI.motivation: When users in vulnerable emotional states request information that may reinforce maladaptive attributions (e.g., seeking material status symbols, cosmetic procedures, or other proxy solutions to deeper distress), LLMs face a structural trilemma: protective restriction (blocks the request but invalidates the user), uninflected facilitation (fulfills the request but reinforces maladaptive patterns), or unintegrated co-presence (offers both a warning and the information, which can be incoherent). Each option sacrifices at least one objective. The authors aim to characterize this tension as structural rather than incidental and document a specific failure mode emerging from it.
AI.method: The study employs a three-turn escalating vulnerability vignette paradigm across three commercial LLMs, totaling 900 experimental sessions. Vignettes span three status-proxy domains: material (luxury goods), relational (romantic/partnership signaling), and somatic (cosmetic/body modification). Responses are coded using two binary indices: VCC (Validates Core Concern) and VCI (Validates Core Injustice). This coding enables systematic characterization of response patterns, particularly the "adaptive capitulation" failure mode: the model validates the social injustice underlying distress, then pivots to detailed facilitation of the acquisition it nominally discouraged. The authors then propose Minimal Reattributive Sufficiency (MRS) as an architecture-neutral design principle.
AI.result: The study documents a previously unrecognized failure mode termed "adaptive capitulation": LLMs first validate the structural injustice (e.g., "yes, lookism is real and unfair") underlying user distress, then proceed to facilitate the very harmful behavior (e.g., providing detailed guidance on cosmetic procedures) they had nominally discouraged. This pattern was observed across all three commercial LLMs and all three status-proxy domains (material, relational, somatic). The results demonstrate that the trilemma between safety, validation, and facilitation is structural — inherent to current response architectures — rather than incidental to any single model or domain.
AI.conclusion: The structural trilemma cannot be resolved by simple prompting or fine-tuning alone. The authors propose Minimal Reattributive Sufficiency (MRS): an architecture-neutral design principle that embeds a single, low-key reattributive cue within an otherwise fully validating response. This preserves a pathway toward autonomous reattribution (helping the user reframe their distress attribution) without directly contesting the user's stated goal, offering a principled escape from the trilemma's zero-sum constraints.

title: Information Discernment in Large Language Models
summary: LLMs are increasingly used with external knowledge sources like the internet. Do they weigh information appropriately -- updating more for reliable sources (source discernment) and more when claims bring priors closer to the truth (truth discernment)? We formalize this as information discernment and introduce Learn2Discern (L2D), an experimental framework and benchmark grounded in three normative axioms with interpretable metrics. To establish external validity, a pre-registered, quota-matched user study (n=299) confirms that real LLM users endorse all three axioms and report that violations reduce their trust and usage intent. Across 13 models and nearly 670K trials, we find consistent failures across both dimensions: models perform near chance on source and truth discernment, rely on source popularity twice as much as source reliability, and update roughly equally whether a claim improves or worsens their position relative to the ground truth. Models integrate external knowledge most effectively on datasets where their priors are already the most accurate. Newer and larger models improve truth discernment but not source discernment, a blind spot that model complexity does not address. We identify simple inference-time interventions that improve both forms of discernment. We release our dataset and survey as a testbed for a core alignment property that scales in importance as LLMs replace traditional search.

AI.tldr: LLMs fail at information discernment—they don't properly weigh external knowledge based on source reliability (source discernment) or whether claims improve accuracy (truth discernment). A benchmark of 13 models across ~670K trials shows near-chance performance, over-reliance on popularity over reliability, and equal updating regardless of whether claims help or hurt accuracy. Newer models improve truth discernment but not source discernment, revealing a persistent blind spot.
AI.motivation: As LLMs increasingly integrate external knowledge sources (e.g., internet retrieval), it is critical that they appropriately weigh information: updating beliefs more when sources are reliable and when claims move priors closer to the truth. The authors formalize this capability as "information discernment" and investigate whether current models possess it.
AI.method: The authors introduce Learn2Discern (L2D), a benchmark grounded in three normative axioms with interpretable metrics. They validate external validity via a pre-registered, quota-matched user study (n=299) confirming that human users endorse these axioms and report that violations reduce trust and usage intent. They then evaluate 13 LLMs across nearly 670K trials on both source discernment and truth discernment, and test simple inference-time interventions.
AI.result: Models perform near chance on both source and truth discernment. They rely on source popularity twice as much as source reliability, and update beliefs roughly equally regardless of whether a claim improves or worsens their position relative to ground truth. Models integrate external knowledge best when their priors are already accurate. Newer and larger models improve truth discernment but not source discernment. Simple inference-time interventions can improve both forms of discernment.
AI.conclusion: Information discernment is a core alignment property that scales in importance as LLMs replace traditional search. Current models exhibit systematic failures in appropriately weighing external information, and source discernment in particular is a blind spot unaddressed by scaling. The released dataset and survey serve as a testbed for future work on this problem.

title: SUM: Unified Geometric Surgery on Spatio-Temporal Adaptation Vectors for Federated Class Incremental Learning
summary: Real-world intelligent systems often require both distributed collaboration across data-isolated clients and continual adaptation to evolving tasks. This setting naturally gives rise to Federated Class Incremental Learning (FCIL), which combines Federated Learning (FL) and Continual Learning (CL). However, their combination introduces two coupled sources of interference: spatial interference from heterogeneous clients and temporal interference from sequential tasks, jointly leading to Spatial-Temporal Catastrophic Forgetting (ST-CF). Existing approaches typically address spatial and temporal interference with separate mechanisms, often incurring additional client-side computation or communication, while leaving directional interactions among updates during aggregation unregulated. In this paper, we reinterpret FCIL as a unified multi-task learning problem, where both client and task updates are represented as adaptation vectors in a shared parameter space. Based on this view, we propose Unified Geometric Surgery on Spatio-Temporal Adaptation Vectors (SUM), a purely server-side framework that performs geometric surgery on adaptation vectors during aggregation. Spatial SUM mitigates client-level interference within each round, while causal online temporal SUM removes cross-task interference over time without additional client-side computation, communication, or memory beyond standard federated training. Empirically, SUM achieves up to 22% improvement over prior FCIL methods across diverse vision and language benchmarks while remaining robust to unreliable clients and maintaining computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: SUM reinterprets Federated Class Incremental Learning as unified multi-task learning, performing geometric surgery on spatio-temporal adaptation vectors at the server to mitigate both client and task interference without extra client-side cost, achieving up to 22% improvement.
AI.motivation: FCIL suffers from Spatial-Temporal Catastrophic Forgetting caused by two coupled interference sources: heterogeneous clients (spatial) and sequential tasks (temporal). Existing methods address these separately with extra client overhead and fail to regulate directional interactions among updates during aggregation.
AI.method: The paper proposes SUM (Unified Geometric Surgery on Spatio-Temporal Adaptation Vectors), a purely server-side framework. It treats client and task updates as adaptation vectors in a shared parameter space. Spatial SUM mitigates client-level interference within each round, while causal online temporal SUM removes cross-task interference over time, using geometric surgery during aggregation without additional client computation, communication, or memory.
AI.result: SUM achieves up to 22% improvement over prior FCIL methods across diverse vision and language benchmarks, remains robust to unreliable clients, and maintains computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: SUM provides an effective, efficient, and purely server-side solution to FCIL by unifying spatial and temporal interference mitigation through geometric surgery on adaptation vectors, eliminating the need for extra client-side overhead.

title: Proceedings of The Fourth International Workshop on eXplainable AI for the Arts (XAIxArts 4)
summary: The fourth workshop on Explainable AI for the Arts (XAIxArts) continues to bring together and expand a community of researchers and creative practitioners in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), Interaction Design, AI, eXplainable AI (XAI), and Digital Arts to explore the role of XAI for the Arts. XAI is a key concern of Responsible and Human-Centred AI, emphasising HCI techniques that make opaque AI models more understandable to people. XAIxArts offers a distinctive lens to examine explainability through creative and artistic domains. The previous workshops explored the landscape and the speculative futures of AI in creative processes. To respond to emerging challenges and contribute to creative and societal transformation more broadly, this workshop focuses on the operationalisation of XAI in the Arts. Specifically, we will: i) critically reflect on emerging practices that encourage diversity and inclusivity in XAI; ii) collectively ideate a library of missing projects to encourage future collaborations and speculations; iii) scope the development of a resource hub for open XAIxArts projects to archive tangible XAI interventions and facilitate future community building with the wider discourse on Human-Centred AI.

AI.tldr: A workshop uniting HCI, AI, XAI, and Digital Arts communities to operationalize explainable AI in creative domains, focusing on diversity/inclusion, ideating missing projects, and building an open resource hub for XAIxArts interventions.
AI.motivation: While prior XAIxArts workshops mapped the landscape and speculative futures of AI in creative processes, translating these insights into actionable frameworks remains an open challenge. The workshop addresses the need to operationalize XAI within artistic practice, leveraging creative contexts as a distinctive lens for examining explainability while simultaneously contributing to broader societal transformation through Responsible and Human-Centred AI.
AI.method: The workshop employs a three-pronged collaborative approach: (i) critical reflection on emerging practices that promote diversity and inclusivity in XAI; (ii) collective ideation toward a library of missing projects to seed future collaborations and speculations; (iii) scoping the development of an open resource hub to archive tangible XAI interventions and facilitate sustained community building.
AI.result: As a workshop proposal abstract, results are anticipated rather than reported. Expected outcomes include: a critically-reflective map of inclusive XAI practices, a collaboratively generated library of missing project ideas, and a scoped blueprint for an open XAIxArts resource hub.
AI.conclusion: The XAIxArts workshop series continues to serve as a vital interdisciplinary nexus, with this fourth iteration shifting from exploration to operationalization — moving the community toward concrete, shared resources and actionable practices that embed explainability into artistic AI workflows.

title: Towards Reliable C-to-Rust Translation with Rule-Guided Reasoning and Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted to the Industry Showcase of ASE 2026
summary: The migration of legacy C programs to Rust has become an important direction for improving software memory safety while alleviating the high cost of manual rewriting. Leveraging large language models (LLMs) for automated C-to-Rust translation has emerged as a promising direction. However, existing LLM-based approaches remain limited. On the one hand, LLMs exhibit limited capability in identifying Rust-specific rules, and inadequate handling of Rust syntax often results in incorrect translations. On the other hand, existing LLMs often struggle to accurately capture the semantics of complex code, resulting in incorrect translations. To address these challenges, we propose a Translation fRAmework Via rule-guided reasoning and rEinforcement Learning, namely TRAVEL, consisting of two modules. The first module employs Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based reasoning path construction guided by Rust-specific rules, steering the search toward translation steps that respect the syntactic rules that LLMs frequently violate. The second module introduces reinforcement learning that couples execution feedback with reasoning-quality signals, encouraging the model to construct reasoning paths that accurately capture program semantics, thereby ensuring that the generated Rust code preserves the intended behavior of the original C program. We evaluate TRAVEL on three datasets: xCodeEval (a public benchmark), OS-Bench (functions collected from the Linux kernel), and HW-Bench (an industrial dataset from Huawei). On xCodeEval, TRAVEL outperforms all baselines across three backbone LLMs. In particular, compared to the strongest prompting baseline IRENE, TRAVEL improves computational accuracy (CA) by 26.22% and compilation success rate (CSR) by 18.77%. On HW-Bench and OS-Bench, TRAVEL further improves CSR by 18.28% and 16.51%, respectively, while reducing unsafe rate (UR) by 13.06% and 13.08%, respectively.

AI.tldr: TRAVEL is a C-to-Rust translation framework combining MCTS-based rule-guided reasoning with reinforcement learning from execution feedback, achieving significant improvements in computational accuracy, compilation success rate, and unsafe code reduction over existing LLM-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based C-to-Rust translation approaches suffer from two key limitations: (1) poor adherence to Rust-specific syntactic rules, leading to compilation failures, and (2) inability to accurately capture complex program semantics, resulting in behaviorally incorrect translations. Manual rewriting is expensive, motivating an automated approach that addresses both syntactic and semantic correctness.
AI.method: TRAVEL comprises two modules: (1) An MCTS-based reasoning path construction module guided by Rust-specific rules, which steers the search toward translations respecting syntax rules that LLMs commonly violate; (2) A reinforcement learning module that couples execution feedback with reasoning-quality signals, encouraging the model to construct reasoning paths that accurately preserve C program semantics in the generated Rust code.
AI.result: On xCodeEval, TRAVEL outperforms all baselines across three backbone LLMs, improving computational accuracy by 26.22% and compilation success rate by 18.77% over the strongest prompting baseline (IRENE). On HW-Bench and OS-Bench, TRAVEL improves CSR by 18.28% and 16.51% respectively, while reducing unsafe rate by 13.06% and 13.08%.
AI.conclusion: TRAVEL effectively addresses both syntactic and semantic challenges in automated C-to-Rust translation through rule-guided MCTS reasoning and reinforcement learning with execution feedback, demonstrating robust improvements across diverse benchmarks including public, open-source, and industrial datasets.

title: Two-Step Occupation Coding
comment: Preprint of the paper accepted for the Federated Conference on Computer Science and Information Systems (FedCSIS 2026)
summary: Occupation coding links job titles in free text to occupational taxonomies and is a core task in labor market research. Existing approaches typically address this problem in a single end-to-end step, jointly identifying job titles and assigning occupational codes. This paper presents a novel two-step approach that separates these tasks. In the first step, a domain-specific Named Entity Recognition (NER) model identifies occupational titles in continuous text, even under noise such as OCR errors. In the second step, the extracted job titles are mapped to a taxonomy, enabling the classifier to focus exclusively on this mapping. We demonstrate that this separation improves accuracy, robustness, and interpretability compared to single-step approaches. The method has been developed for German documents but is transferable to other languages. We further introduce a margin-based confidence criterion for occupation coding, replacing common absolute thresholds. To support reproducibility, we publish the source code and evaluation scripts.

AI.tldr: A two-step approach separates occupation coding into NER-based job title extraction followed by taxonomy mapping, improving accuracy, robustness, and interpretability over single-step methods. A margin-based confidence criterion replaces absolute thresholds.
AI.motivation: Existing single-step, end-to-end occupation coding methods jointly identify job titles and assign codes, which conflates two distinct tasks and limits accuracy, robustness (especially under OCR noise), and interpretability.
AI.method: A two-step pipeline: (1) a domain-specific Named Entity Recognition (NER) model identifies occupational titles in free text, robust to OCR errors; (2) the extracted job titles are mapped to an occupational taxonomy using a dedicated classifier. A margin-based confidence criterion is introduced, using the difference between top predicted class probabilities instead of absolute thresholds.
AI.result: The two-step separation demonstrates improved accuracy, robustness (particularly under noisy conditions like OCR errors), and interpretability compared to single-step approaches. The method was developed for German documents but is transferable to other languages.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling occupation coding into sequential NER and classification stages yields superior performance. The margin-based confidence metric offers a principled alternative to threshold-based confidence. Source code and evaluation scripts are publicly released for reproducibility.

title: When HTTP 402 Meets the Blockchain: Risks on Emerging x402 Payments
summary:
x402 is an emerging payment protocol for Web APIs and autonomous AI agents. x402 extends HTTP 402 with a payment negotiation flow and delegates payment proof verification and on-chain settlement to third-party facilitators. As a result, facilitators serve as a shared payment infrastructure for many independent merchants. This centralizes trust and validation in one component, so a single flaw can affect many services. Despite rapid adoption by major vendors and economically meaningful mainnet activity, the security posture of real-world x402 deployments remains poorly characterized.
  We present the first systematic study of authorization correctness and execution safety in current facilitator-mediated x402 deployments in the wild, identifying eight security rules for facilitators as critical payment infrastructure. Based on our analysis of rule violations, we derive four new attack vectors, including Free Shopping, Asset Theft, Service Denial, and Gas Abuse. These attacks exploit weaknesses in the real-world facilitator and server implementations and cause severe harm, including direct financial loss to merchants, theft of facilitator-held assets, unbounded sponsor-paid gas/fees, and disruption of payment services. To assess the security of x402 deployments at scale, we propose a semi-automated black-box tool and apply it to 15 major x402 facilitators collectively used by over 60K sellers and 360K buyers. Alarmingly, we find violations in all evaluated facilitators. We responsibly disclosed our findings to the affected parties, who acknowledged the issues and adopted mitigations, including changes by Coinbase. Finally, we complement our controlled testing with an empirical measurement of over 119 million recent Base and Solana transactions, quantifying x402 adoption, facilitator centralization, and ecosystem-level risk indicators.

AI.tldr: A systematic security analysis of x402, an emerging HTTP 402-based payment protocol for APIs and AI agents, revealing widespread authorization and execution safety violations across all 15 major facilitators serving 60K+ sellers. Four novel attack vectors (Free Shopping, Asset Theft, Service Denial, Gas Abuse) were identified, responsibly disclosed, and mitigated. An empirical measurement of 119M+ on-chain transactions quantifies ecosystem adoption and centralization risks.
AI.motivation: x402 is rapidly adopted by major vendors with meaningful mainnet economic activity, yet its security posture remains poorly characterized. Since facilitators serve as centralized shared payment infrastructure, a single vulnerability can cascade across many independent merchants, making a systematic security evaluation urgent.
AI.method: The authors (1) derived eight security rules that facilitators must satisfy as critical payment infrastructure; (2) identified four attack vectors from rule violations; (3) built a semi-automated black-box testing tool and applied it to 15 major x402 facilitators; (4) conducted an empirical on-chain measurement study analyzing over 119 million transactions on Base and Solana to quantify adoption, centralization, and ecosystem risk.
AI.result: All 15 evaluated facilitators exhibited security rule violations. Four attack classes were demonstrated: Free Shopping (obtaining paid services without payment), Asset Theft (stealing facilitator-held assets), Service Denial (disrupting payment services), and Gas Abuse (unbounded sponsor-paid gas/fees). The on-chain measurement revealed significant facilitator centralization and ecosystem-level risk indicators. Affected parties including Coinbase acknowledged and adopted mitigations.
AI.conclusion: x402 facilitators currently exhibit systemic security weaknesses that expose merchants and the broader ecosystem to severe financial and operational harm. The proposed security rules and testing methodology provide a foundation for hardening facilitator implementations, and the empirical data establishes a baseline for ongoing ecosystem monitoring.

title: Reference-Free Evaluation of Reasoning in Open-Ended Question Answering
summary: AI-generated answers in high-stakes domains are often fluent but difficult to verify, especially when they contain multi-step reasoning rather than a single final answer. We propose a reasoning-based, reference-free framework for auditing LLM-generated outputs. The method decomposes a generated reasoning trace into segments, labels local premise-target relations using Natural Language Inference (NLI), and organizes these relations into a hypergraph. A deterministic backward AND-OR search then assigns segment-level audit labels that indicate how each segment is grounded within the generated response. We evaluate the framework in two settings: deductive mathematical reasoning with Hard2Verify, and open-ended medical reasoning with UroReason, a new physician-annotated benchmark of LLM reasoning traces from real clinical cases. Across these settings, our NLI-hypergraph audit provides a more reliable reference-free evaluation signal than direct LLM-as-judge baselines. In the clinical setting, state-of-the-art LLM judges often fail to identify problematic reasoning segments, over-accepting fluent but weakly grounded responses. Our results show that QA evaluation should account for how inferential relations compose across a reasoning trace, rather than relying only on final answers or LLMs as verifiers. UroReason will be made available through an API, and our code will be released as open source.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a reference-free auditing framework that decomposes LLM reasoning traces into segments, uses NLI to label premise-target relations, organizes them into a hypergraph, and applies AND-OR search to determine how each segment is grounded. Tested on mathematical and clinical reasoning benchmarks, it outperforms LLM-as-judge baselines in detecting weakly grounded reasoning.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated answers in high-stakes domains (e.g., medicine) are fluent but hard to verify, particularly when they involve multi-step reasoning. Existing evaluation methods relying on final answers or LLM-as-judge approaches often fail to identify problematic intermediate reasoning steps, over-accepting fluent but logically unsupported responses.
AI.method: The proposed framework operates in several stages: (1) a generated reasoning trace is decomposed into segments; (2) local premise-target relations between segments are labeled using Natural Language Inference (NLI); (3) these relations are organized into a hypergraph representation; (4) a deterministic backward AND-OR search assigns segment-level audit labels indicating how each segment is grounded within the response. The approach is reference-free and evaluates the internal inferential structure rather than comparing against ground-truth answers.
AI.result: On the deductive mathematical reasoning benchmark Hard2Verify and the newly introduced physician-annotated clinical benchmark UroReason, the NLI-hypergraph audit provides more reliable reference-free evaluation than direct LLM-as-judge baselines. In clinical settings, state-of-the-art LLM judges frequently over-accept fluent but weakly grounded reasoning segments, missing problematic inferential steps.
AI.conclusion: QA evaluation should account for how inferential relations compose across a reasoning trace rather than relying solely on final answers or LLM verifiers. The proposed hypergraph-based auditing framework offers a more trustworthy signal for detecting flawed reasoning, and the authors commit to releasing UroReason via API and the code as open source.

title: NEXUS: Structured Runtime Safety for Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: Tool-using LLM agents increasingly execute high-impact actions, making runtime safety monitoring essential. We present NEXUS (Neural EXecution Utility and Safety), a structured-plan safety monitor that applies a formal intervention policy to select among four actions: allow, block, request confirmation, or request revision. NEXUS combines deterministic safety rules, argument-level inspection, and a calibrated logistic-regression risk score for graded escalation. On a 128-instance synthetic benchmark, NEXUS achieves an F1 score of 0.949 and a 4-class intervention accuracy of 0.6406, outperforming rule-only intervention selection by 27.3 percentage points. It also improves over rule-only on R-Judge (F1 = 0.861 vs. 0.849), matches rule-only on AgentHarm due to threat-model limits, and achieves 0% ASR at 99% control allow on IPI. On the rule-blind NEXUS-Stress benchmark, NEXUS reaches an F1 score of 0.881, highlighting the difficulty of fine-grained intervention routing. With 0.205 ms median latency, NEXUS adds under 0.1% overhead to typical agent loops. Code, benchmarks, and the calibrated risk scorer are publicly released.

AI.tldr: NEXUS is a runtime safety monitor for LLM agents that combines deterministic rules, argument-level inspection, and a calibrated logistic-regression risk score to select among four interventions (allow, block, request confirmation, request revision). It achieves strong safety performance across multiple benchmarks with negligible latency overhead.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents are deployed to execute increasingly high-impact actions, runtime safety monitoring is critical to prevent harmful outcomes. Existing approaches lack fine-grained, graded intervention policies that can escalate responses appropriately based on risk severity.
AI.method: NEXUS uses a structured-plan safety monitor with a formal intervention policy selecting among four actions: allow, block, request confirmation, or request revision. It integrates three components: (1) deterministic safety rules, (2) argument-level inspection of agent actions, and (3) a calibrated logistic-regression risk score that enables graded escalation. The system operates at runtime with median latency of 0.205 ms.
AI.result: On a 128-instance synthetic benchmark, NEXUS achieves F1=0.949 and 4-class intervention accuracy of 0.6406 (outperforming rule-only by 27.3 pp). On R-Judge, F1=0.861 vs. 0.849 (rule-only). On AgentHarm, it matches rule-only due to threat-model limits. On IPI, it achieves 0% ASR at 99% control allow. On the rule-blind NEXUS-Stress benchmark, F1=0.881.
AI.conclusion: NEXUS demonstrates that a hybrid approach combining deterministic rules with calibrated statistical risk scoring enables effective fine-grained runtime safety monitoring for LLM agents with minimal latency overhead. The public release of code, benchmarks, and the calibrated risk scorer facilitates further research.

title: STN-TGAT: Top-K Portfolio Construction via Prior-Guided Graph Attention with Learnable Soft-Threshold Sparsification
summary: This paper tackles the problem of stock ranking and portfolio construction under realistic investment settings by jointly modeling temporal dynamics and cross-sectional dependencies. We propose the Soft-Threshold NMI-prior Transformer Graph Attention Network (STN-TGAT), which integrates a temporal Transformer with a Graph Attention Network to capture long-horizon sequential patterns and dynamic inter-stock relationships. An NMI-based prior graph combined with a soft-threshold sparsification mechanism enhances structural robustness by mitigating noisy correlations while preserving informative connections. The portfolio formation process incorporates practical considerations, including Top-5 selection within the Top-50 $S\&P$ 500 constituents, explicit weight allocation, and transaction cost adjustment, thereby aligning the evaluation with real-world trading conditions. Empirical results on real-world data demonstrate that STN-TGAT consistently outperforms benchmark models from predictive accuracy and investment profitability measured by portfolio returns. These findings suggest that combining decision-aligned training with adaptive relational modeling provides a coherent and practically effective framework for data-driven portfolio construction.

AI.tldr: Proposes STN-TGAT, a model combining temporal Transformer and Graph Attention Network with NMI-based prior graph and soft-threshold sparsification, for stock ranking and portfolio construction under realistic constraints (Top-5 from Top-50 S&P 500, transaction costs), outperforming benchmarks in predictive accuracy and portfolio returns.
AI.motivation: Existing stock prediction and portfolio construction methods often fail to jointly model temporal dynamics and cross-sectional dependencies under realistic investment settings (e.g., transaction costs, explicit weight allocation, constrained stock selection). The paper aims to bridge this gap by providing a coherent framework aligned with real-world trading conditions.
AI.method: STN-TGAT integrates: (1) a temporal Transformer for long-horizon sequential pattern modeling; (2) a Graph Attention Network for dynamic inter-stock relational learning; (3) an NMI (Normalized Mutual Information)-based prior graph with soft-threshold sparsification to filter noisy correlations while retaining informative edges. Portfolio construction uses Top-5 selection from the Top-50 S&P 500 constituents with explicit weight allocation and transaction cost adjustment.
AI.result: STN-TGAT consistently outperforms benchmark models on real-world data in both predictive accuracy and investment profitability, as measured by portfolio returns under realistic trading constraints.
AI.conclusion: Combining decision-aligned training with adaptive relational modeling yields a practically effective framework for data-driven portfolio construction. The soft-threshold NMI-prior graph enhances structural robustness, and incorporating real-world constraints bridges the gap between academic modeling and practical trading.

title: FMRP-LEAN: A HIPAA-Compliant AI-Augmented LIMS Architecture for End-to-End Clinical Assay Workflow Optimization
summary: Clinical biomarker workflows in translational research settings often rely on spreadsheet-driven tracking, manual quality control (QC) reconciliation, and loosely integrated systems, resulting in limited state visibility, delayed reporting, and increased operational risk. These challenges are particularly pronounced in multi-day assays such as Luminex-based quantification of Fragile X Messenger Ribonucleoprotein (FMRP), where HIPAA-compliant data governance, deterministic workflow progression, and coordinated communication across laboratory and clinical teams are required. This paper presents FMRP-LEAN, a HIPAA-compliant, AI-augmented Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) architecture that formalizes biospecimen lifecycle management through a finite-state workflow model with explicit transition guards and dwell-time observability. The system integrates a self-hosted Supabase/PostgreSQL stack deployed within hospital-controlled infrastructure, hybrid edge-internal isolation with encrypted tunneling and loopback-only services, and bi-directional REDCap synchronization. A unified MRN-UUIDv7 identifier framework with QR-based tracking ensures traceable clinical-research linkage under PHI residency constraints. FMRP-LEAN incorporates automated statistical QC pre-screening and a governance-constrained AI operations module that operates exclusively on aggregate projections, with deterministic fallback guarantees. Deployment demonstrates improved workflow observability, reduced QC latency, and enhanced cross-role transparency between laboratory technicians, research coordinators, and patient-facing teams. The architecture provides a reproducible model for secure, state-explicit, and AI-augmented clinical research workflows in regulated healthcare environments.

AI.tldr: FMRP-LEAN is a HIPAA-compliant, AI-augmented LIMS that formalizes biospecimen lifecycle management via a finite-state workflow model, integrating self-hosted Supabase/PostgreSQL, encrypted tunneling, REDCap synchronization, QR-based MRN-UUIDv7 tracking, and automated QC pre-screening to improve observability, reduce latency, and enhance cross-role transparency in regulated clinical research settings.
AI.motivation: Clinical biomarker workflows, particularly multi-day Luminex-based FMRP quantification assays, suffer from spreadsheet-driven tracking, manual QC reconciliation, and fragmented systems that cause poor state visibility, reporting delays, and operational risk under HIPAA and PHI residency constraints.
AI.method: The authors propose FMRP-LEAN: a finite-state workflow model with explicit transition guards and dwell-time observability, deployed on a self-hosted Supabase/PostgreSQL stack within hospital infrastructure. It uses hybrid edge-internal isolation with encrypted tunneling and loopback-only services, bi-directional REDCap synchronization, a unified MRN-UUIDv7 identifier framework with QR-based tracking, automated statistical QC pre-screening, and a governance-constrained AI operations module restricted to aggregate projections with deterministic fallbacks.
AI.result: Deployment yielded improved workflow observability, reduced QC latency, and enhanced cross-role transparency among laboratory technicians, research coordinators, and patient-facing teams.
AI.conclusion: FMRP-LEAN provides a reproducible architecture for secure, state-explicit, AI-augmented clinical research workflows in regulated healthcare environments.

title: SequenceFI: Non-intrusive Temporal Fault Injection for Microservice Systems
summary: Fault injection is widely used to evaluate the resilience of microservice systems, where client requests often span multiple services and execution stages. Existing request-level techniques usually control where and what faults are injected, but not when they are activated within a distributed execution. This limitation makes it difficult to reproduce timing-dependent failures, such as failures after state-changing side effects, order-sensitive concurrent responses, and partial failures among repeated downstream calls. This paper presents SequenceFI, a non-intrusive framework for temporal fault injection in microservice systems. SequenceFI observes message-level send and receive events, propagates compact temporal evidence along request executions, and triggers faults only when occurrence-sensitive temporal guards are satisfied. It further synthesizes temporal guards from traces, reducing the need for exhaustive enumeration of temporal fault-injection configurations, while requiring no modifications to application code or serialization libraries. We implement SequenceFI on Kubernetes and evaluate it on four widely used microservice benchmarks. Across nine temporal-fault scenarios and 450 valid trials, SequenceFI achieves 100.0\% temporal success without premature or multiple injections, finds effective configurations in one attempt on average, and reduces aggregate end-to-end search time by 95.91\% compared with H-Random.

AI.tldr: SequenceFI is a non-intrusive temporal fault injection framework for microservices that introduces occurrence-sensitive temporal guards to control when faults are activated during distributed request executions. It propagates compact temporal evidence along request paths and synthesizes guards from traces, achieving 100% temporal injection accuracy across 450 trials while reducing configuration search time by 95.91% compared to H-Random.
AI.motivation: Existing request-level fault injection techniques for microservices can control where and what faults are injected, but lack temporal control — i.e., they cannot specify when in a distributed execution a fault should be activated. This limitation prevents reproducing timing-dependent failures such as failures after state-changing side effects, order-sensitive concurrent responses, and partial failures among repeated downstream calls.
AI.method: SequenceFI is a non-intrusive framework that observes message-level send/receive events, propagates compact temporal evidence along request executions, and triggers faults only when occurrence-sensitive temporal guards are satisfied. It also synthesizes temporal guards automatically from traces to avoid exhaustive enumeration of fault-injection configurations. The framework requires no modifications to application code or serialization libraries.
AI.result: Evaluated on four Kubernetes-based microservice benchmarks across nine temporal-fault scenarios and 450 valid trials: SequenceFI achieved 100.0% temporal success without premature or multiple injections, found effective configurations in one attempt on average, and reduced aggregate end-to-end search time by 95.91% compared to H-Random.
AI.conclusion: SequenceFI demonstrates that precise temporal control over fault injection in microservice systems is both feasible and effective without application-level modifications. The framework enables reliable reproduction of timing-dependent failures that prior request-level techniques could not capture, significantly improving the state of resilience evaluation for distributed microservice architectures.

title: Autonomous Collaborative Learning Among an Ensemble of Tsetlin Machines with Consensus-Based Inference
summary: Tsetlin Machine (TM) is a rule-based machine-learning algorithm comprising collectives of two-action Tsetlin Automata (TAs) that cooperatively form conjunctive logical clauses from Boolean inputs through stochastic feedback. Although few recent studies have examined TM Federated Learning, the broader area of distributed and decentralized TM learning has not received much attention in the existing literature and warrants further exploration. In this work, we propose a paradigm for decentralized collaborative learning under a vertical feature-partitioning setting among an ensemble of Tsetlin Machines using consensus-based inference. Within this decentralized paradigm, each agent maintains its own private TM model, and there is no exchange of raw data among agents. Inference combines individual agents model predictions into a global consensus. The paradigm accommodates heterogeneous TM-based agents with differing data acquisition means, local data distributions, or computational resources, thereby facilitating the integration and fusion of information in settings such as multi-modal sensing environments. Experiments conducted using two-dimensional grid and connected graph network topologies demonstrate that the classification accuracies achieved are comparable to those of centralized models.

AI.tldr: Proposes a decentralized collaborative learning paradigm for Tsetlin Machines under vertical feature partitioning, using consensus-based inference without raw data exchange. Experiments on grid and graph topologies show classification accuracy comparable to centralized models.
AI.motivation: Distributed and decentralized TM learning is underexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by enabling collaborative learning across heterogeneous TM agents in settings where features are partitioned vertically (different agents observe different features of the same instances), without sharing raw data — relevant to multi-modal sensing and privacy-preserving scenarios.
AI.method: A decentralized consensus-based inference paradigm where each agent maintains a private TM model trained on its own local feature partition. During inference, individual model predictions are aggregated into a global consensus via the network topology (2D grids and connected graphs). No raw data is exchanged; only model-level information flows between neighbors.
AI.result: Classification accuracies achieved under both 2D grid and connected graph topologies are comparable to those of centralized TM models, validating the effectiveness of the decentralized consensus approach.
AI.conclusion: Decentralized collaborative TM learning with vertical feature partitioning and consensus-based inference is viable, achieving centralized-level accuracy while preserving data privacy and accommodating heterogeneous agents.

title: Examining User Behavior and Cognitive Biases in Personal Password Security
summary: Despite increasing awareness of cybersecurity risks, users continue to engage in insecure password practices, such as reusing passwords, choosing weak credentials, and neglecting security recommendations. The study explores the behavioral and cognitive factors that influence password decision-making by integrating insights from behavioral economics, particularly hyperbolic discounting, status quo bias, and present bias. We conducted a survey to analyze how people create, store and manage their passwords, examining whether security habits have improved over time in response to greater awareness. Our findings reveal that immediate convenience often outweighs long-term security considerations, leading users to prioritize memorability over strength. Additionally, we identify key psychological biases that contribute to security procrastination and resistance to adopting more secure authentication practices, such as password managers and multi-factor authentication. The study contributes to human-centered security by bridging the gap between security awareness and action, offering practical insights to design user-friendly authentication policies that align with real-world decision-making tendencies.

AI.tldr: Users persist in weak password habits despite security awareness due to psychological biases (hyperbolic discounting, status quo bias, present bias). A survey reveals convenience and memorability consistently override long-term security, explaining procrastination and resistance to tools like password managers and MFA. The study bridges the awareness-action gap with insights for user-centered authentication design.
AI.motivation: Despite growing cybersecurity awareness, password-related insecure behaviors (reuse, weak credentials, ignoring recommendations) remain pervasive. The authors seek to understand this persistent gap between security knowledge and actual behavior by examining the cognitive and behavioral mechanisms driving poor password decisions.
AI.method: A survey-based empirical study investigating how users create, store, and manage passwords. The analysis is framed through a behavioral economics lens, specifically applying hyperbolic discounting, status quo bias, and present bias to interpret password decision-making patterns. Temporal trends in security habits relative to increased awareness are also examined.
AI.result: Immediate convenience and memorability consistently dominate over long-term security considerations in user decision-making. Key psychological biases — particularly hyperbolic discounting (undervaluing future security benefits), status quo bias (resistance to changing established habits), and present bias (prioritizing immediate ease) — systematically drive security procrastination and aversion to adopting password managers and multi-factor authentication.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that security awareness alone is insufficient to change behavior when cognitive biases favor short-term convenience. It contributes to human-centered security by providing actionable insights for designing authentication policies and user interfaces that accommodate real-world decision-making tendencies, thereby narrowing the awareness-action divide.

title: Multi-Mask Diffusion Language Models for Few-Step Generation
summary: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) are a promising family of language generators, but achieving high-quality few-step generation remains challenging. In MDMs, all forward trajectories collapse to a single fully masked state, leaving no terminal entropy for consistency-style few-step generation. While recent few-step alternatives based on uniform-state diffusion avoid this degeneracy, it becomes harder to distinguish clean tokens from noise than MDMs, which usually harms modeling quality and training efficiency. In this work, we propose a multi-mask diffusion model (MultiMDM) that preserves the masking structure towards few-step generation. In the forward process, each clean token is first pushed towards a designated mask and then gradually mixes over the mask set. As a result, the backward process has a drafting capability by predicting a designated mask before refining to a clean token. We derive a closed-form ELBO training objective for MultiMDM that supports continual training from pretrained MDMs. In addition, we formulate a purely discrete-state consistency distillation scheme, with a shared-Gumbel coupling to reduce pathwise entropy. Experiments on pretraining and distillation show that MultiMDM provides an effective foundation for principled few-step generation.

AI.tldr: MultiMDM proposes a multi-mask diffusion framework that preserves masking structure to enable high-quality few-step generation. It introduces a forward process where tokens are pushed toward a designated mask before mixing, enabling a "drafting" backward process. A discrete-state consistency distillation scheme with shared-Gumbel coupling reduces pathwise entropy, making principled few-step generation feasible.
AI.motivation: Standard masked diffusion models (MDMs) collapse all forward trajectories to a single fully masked state, eliminating terminal entropy needed for consistency-style few-step generation. Uniform-state diffusion alternatives avoid this degeneracy but struggle to distinguish clean tokens from noise, harming modeling quality and training efficiency. The goal is to design a diffusion model that retains the benefits of masking while enabling effective few-step generation.
AI.method: MultiMDM introduces a forward process where each clean token is first pushed toward a designated mask and then gradually mixes over the mask set. This yields a backward process with "drafting" capability — predicting a designated mask before refining to a clean token. The authors derive a closed-form ELBO training objective supporting continual training from pretrained MDMs. They also formulate a purely discrete-state consistency distillation scheme using shared-Gumbel coupling to reduce pathwise entropy.
AI.result: Experiments on both pretraining and distillation demonstrate that MultiMDM provides an effective foundation for principled few-step generation, outperforming alternatives that either suffer from terminal entropy collapse or struggle with noise-token discrimination.
AI.conclusion: MultiMDM successfully bridges the gap between the masking structure's modeling advantages and the need for few-step generation capability, establishing a new paradigm for discrete diffusion-based language generation with consistency distillation.

title: Stochastic Primal-Dual Decoding for Multiobjective Generative Recommender Systems
summary:
Recent advances in recommender systems (RS) have shown substantial performance gains through generative modelling. In practice, recommendation often involves constructing slates -- ordered lists of items -- that must satisfy multiple objectives beyond relevance, such as constraints defined over item attributes or fairness constraints. Existing multiobjective approaches either rely on post-processing techniques designed for non-generative settings, or incorporate auxiliary objectives directly into model training. The former does not explicitly account for the sequential nature of generative RS, while the latter is often impractical in large-scale systems.
  We propose a lightweight, inference-time decoding layer that augments autoregressive generative RS to support multiobjective slate generation without modifying or retraining the underlying model. We formulate decoding as an online constrained optimisation problem, where items are selected sequentially, and trade-offs between relevance and auxiliary objectives are adjusted dynamically based on the remaining constraint slack, i.e., how much of each objective remains to be satisfied. This is implemented via a stochastic primal-dual approximation scheme that balances relevance and auxiliary objectives during generation.
  We provide theoretical guarantees on constraint violation and regret, and evaluate the proposed approach through extensive offline experiments and a large-scale online A/B experiment in a real-world recommender system. Our results show consistent improvements in multiobjective trade-offs, including a +1.8\% gain in the auxiliary objectives achieved at zero cost to user satisfaction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a lightweight, inference-time decoding layer for autoregressive generative recommender systems that enables multiobjective slate generation via stochastic primal-dual optimization, without retraining the underlying model. It achieves +1.8% gains in auxiliary objectives at zero cost to user satisfaction in real-world A/B tests.
AI.motivation: Generative recommender systems need to produce slates satisfying multiple objectives (relevance, item attribute constraints, fairness). Existing solutions either use post-processing unsuitable for sequential generation, or incorporate auxiliary objectives directly into training -- which is impractical at scale. A method is needed that handles multiobjective slate generation natively within the autoregressive decoding process without model modification.
AI.method: The authors frame decoding as an online constrained optimization problem where items are selected sequentially. Trade-offs between relevance and auxiliary objectives are dynamically adjusted based on remaining constraint slack. This is operationalized through a stochastic primal-dual approximation scheme that runs at inference time, acting as a lightweight decoding layer on top of any pretrained autoregressive generative RS.
AI.result: The method comes with theoretical guarantees on constraint violation and regret. Extensive offline experiments and a large-scale online A/B test in a production recommender system show consistent improvements in multiobjective trade-offs, including a +1.8% gain in auxiliary objectives with zero degradation in user satisfaction.
AI.conclusion: An inference-time primal-dual decoding layer is an effective and practical approach for introducing multiobjective slate generation into autoregressive generative RS, avoiding costly retraining while providing formal guarantees and empirically validated gains.

title: Building Fast, Evaluating Slow: Pipeline Choices Dominate Autointerpretability Score Variance
summary: Cross-paper comparison of sparse autoencoder (SAE) interpretability often relies on autointerpretability scores. In this evaluation pipeline, a language model (LM) explains each feature, and another LM scores the explanation. For these comparisons to be meaningful, scores must reflect stable properties of the features rather than confounding aspects of the evaluation pipeline. Through systematic experiments across four metrics (simulation, detection, fuzzing, purity), two models (Pythia-160M, Apertus-8B), and four axes of methodological variation, we show that this assumption does not hold. Specifically, we find that R1) methodological variance collectively exceeds architectural variance across all metrics and tested models; R2) each metric exhibits a distinct instability profile, with detection being the most stable and fuzzing unreliable across all conditions; R3) top-k feature rankings do not stay consistent across corpus and draw conditions, masking per-feature instability behind stable mean scores; a failure that cannot be detected by monitoring explanation similarity alone. These findings suggest that cross-paper comparisons based on autointerpretability scores may reflect pipeline differences rather than architectural differences, with implications for the ongoing debate on SAE utility. More broadly, unreliable evaluation slows progress in interpretability research at a time when reliable tools for understanding AI systems are needed. To support evaluation, we contribute a variance decomposition approach, a Stability Check, and a Minimum Reporting Checklist.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that autointerpretability scores used to compare sparse autoencoders (SAEs) across papers are unreliable — methodological variance in the evaluation pipeline exceeds architectural variance. Rankings of top-k features are inconsistent across conditions, and per-feature instability is masked by stable mean scores. The authors contribute a variance decomposition framework, a Stability Check, and a Minimum Reporting Checklist to improve evaluation rigor.
AI.motivation: Cross-paper comparisons of SAE interpretability typically rely on autointerpretability scores (LM explains features, another LM scores explanations). For these comparisons to be meaningful, scores should reflect stable properties of SAE features rather than artifacts of the evaluation pipeline. The authors hypothesize that this assumption does not hold and that methodological variation may confound architectural comparisons, undermining the ongoing debate about SAE utility.
AI.method: Systematic experiments varying four methodological axes (the specific autointerpretability metric: simulation, detection, fuzzing, purity), two SAE models (Pythia-160M, Apertus-8B), and multiple pipeline configurations. The authors analyze variance decomposition to quantify how much score variation is attributable to methodology vs. architecture. They also examine top-k feature ranking stability across different corpus/draw conditions and monitor explanation similarity as a diagnostic.
AI.result: Three main findings: (R1) Methodological variance collectively exceeds architectural variance across all four metrics and both models tested. (R2) Each metric has a distinct instability profile — detection is most stable, while fuzzing is unreliable across all conditions. (R3) Top-k feature rankings are inconsistent across corpus and draw conditions; stable mean scores mask substantial per-feature instability, and explanation similarity monitoring fails to detect this failure mode.
AI.conclusion: Cross-paper comparisons based on autointerpretability scores may primarily reflect pipeline differences rather than genuine architectural differences, with significant implications for debates on SAE utility. Unreliable evaluation slows progress in interpretability research precisely when reliable tools are most needed. The authors provide a variance decomposition approach, a Stability Check, and a Minimum Reporting Checklist as practical contributions to improve evaluation standards.

title: TINY_SCHILLER: A Drop-In German Drama Corpus for Small Language Models
summary: tiny_schiller closes the small-language-model prototyping, fine-tuning, education, and research gap for German literary text, providing a single-file, drop-in counterpart to Karpathy's tiny_shakespeare. The available German literary corpora are larger and richer, but require parser engineering before a single line of training or fine-tuning code can run. tiny_schiller is a 2.07-megabyte single file of eleven public-domain Schiller dramas, sourced from DraCor's GerDraCor export (CC0) and processed by deterministic parser engineering. Character-level, GPT-2 byte-pair encoding, and cl100k_base tokenization splits, an instruction-formatted dialogue-completion split, and 89 per-character persona splits load from a single HuggingFace call. A small language model literally reaches German literary text in one line of code.

AI.tldr: tiny_schiller provides a 2.07 MB single-file dataset of eleven Schiller dramas, enabling one-line small-language-model prototyping, fine-tuning, and education for German literary text — analogous to Karpathy's tiny_shakespeare.
AI.motivation: German literary corpora are larger and richer than tiny_shakespeare, but require significant parser engineering before any training or fine-tuning can begin. This creates a prototyping and educational gap for German literary NLP that tiny_schiller aims to close.
AI.method: Eleven public-domain Schiller dramas are sourced from DraCor's GerDraCor export (CC0 license). A deterministic parser engineering pipeline produces a single 2.07 MB file with multiple splits: character-level, GPT-2 byte-pair encoding (BPE), cl100k_base tokenization, an instruction-formatted dialogue-completion split, and 89 per-character persona splits. All are accessible via a single HuggingFace dataset call.
AI.result: A small language model can literally reach German literary text in one line of code, removing the parser-engineering barrier that previously prevented quick prototyping on German literary data.
AI.conclusion: tiny_schiller successfully fills the small-language-model gap for German literary text, serving as a drop-in educational and prototyping resource analogous to tiny_shakespeare, with rich multi-format splits accessible through HuggingFace.

title: Multi-stage Dynamic Selection for Cross-Project Defect Prediction
summary: Cross-Project Defect Prediction (CPDP) involves building models using data from external projects, called training projects, to predict modules from the target project. However, traditional CPDP methods suffer from the distribution shift between training and target projects that affects the model's performance. This paper proposes a novel CPDP framework that addresses this issue by proposing a two-stage multiple classifier system (MCS) selection scheme: one working at the project level and another at the module level. In the first stage, the framework evaluates multiple possible MCS configurations to find one that covers and generalizes well across multiple training projects. Consequently, the proposal is likely to obtain a diverse set of classifiers, each specialized in tackling software modules with distinct characteristics. The second selection stage operates at test time, selecting the most competent classifiers to predict each new module in the target project. Unlike previous approaches that apply the same classifiers to the entire target project, the proposed framework performs module-level model selection. This way, the system is more robust to changes in distributions between training and target projects because the selected set of classifiers is module-dependent. Our experimental results using 82 projects from four different CPDP benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms the state-of-the-art CPDP methods in most scenarios. The code, dataset, and further details about the proposed method are publicly available at https://github.com/jsaj/Multi_DES.

AI.tldr: A two-stage multiple classifier system (MCS) selection framework for Cross-Project Defect Prediction that operates at both the project level (training-time MCS configuration selection) and module level (test-time classifier selection per module), outperforming state-of-the-art CPDP methods across 82 projects from four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional CPDP methods suffer from distribution shift between training (source) and target projects, which degrades model performance. Existing approaches apply the same classifiers uniformly across the entire target project, failing to account for heterogeneous module characteristics within the target project.
AI.method: A two-stage MCS selection framework: Stage 1 (project level) evaluates multiple MCS configurations to select one that generalizes well across diverse training projects, yielding a diverse pool of specialized classifiers. Stage 2 (module level) operates at test time, dynamically selecting the most competent subset of classifiers for each individual target module, making predictions module-dependent rather than project-uniform.
AI.result: The proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art CPDP methods in most scenarios, validated on 82 projects from four different CPDP benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: Module-level model selection enhances robustness to distribution shifts in CPDP by tailoring classifier ensembles to the specific characteristics of each target module, rather than applying a one-size-fits-all model to the entire project.

title: Twin Agent: Context Residual Compression for Privilege Separated Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are vulnerable to security risks, such as prompt injection attacks from untrusted context that manipulate downstream reasoning and tool use. Existing secure-by-design approaches mitigate this risk by separating untrusted observations from privileged execution and careful control of information flow, but often degrade utility and require extensive task-specific engineering. We thus propose Twin Agent, a general privilege separation design pattern inspired by residual coding in the agent context. Twin Agent consists of two nearly symmetric agents: an Explore Agent that inspects untrusted information and a Safe Agent that executes privileged actions. The Explore Agent is conditioned on the Safe Agent's current context and communicates only compact hints to the Safe Agent about the next action to take. This design reduces the information needed to preserve task utility and thus achieves a better security--utility tradeoff, which we empirically verify by measuring how utility and attack success change as the length of hints varies. We evaluate Twin Agent on long-horizon software engineering tasks with SWE-bench Lite and on heterogeneous multi-tool interaction tasks with AgentDojo and DecodingTrust-Agent. Across both benchmarks, Twin Agent preserves high task utility while preventing prompt injection attacks, outperforming both undefended agents and privilege separation baselines.

AI.tldr: Twin Agent is a privilege separation design pattern for LLM agents that uses two symmetric agents — an Explore Agent that inspects untrusted content and a Safe Agent that executes privileged actions — communicating through compact hints to achieve a superior security–utility tradeoff against prompt injection attacks, as demonstrated on SWE-bench Lite, AgentDojo, and DecodingTrust-Agent.
AI.motivation: LLM agents face prompt injection attacks from untrusted contexts that can manipulate downstream reasoning and tool use. Existing secure-by-design approaches mitigate this via privilege separation but often degrade utility and demand substantial task-specific engineering. The authors aim to design a general, low-engineering-overhead pattern that preserves utility while robustly defending against such attacks.
AI.method: Twin Agent consists of two nearly symmetric agents: an Explore Agent that inspects untrusted information and a Safe Agent that executes privileged actions. The Explore Agent conditions on the Safe Agent's current context and communicates only compact hints (inspired by residual coding) about the next action. By varying hint length, the security–utility tradeoff is empirically characterized. Evaluation covers long-horizon software engineering (SWE-bench Lite) and heterogeneous multi-tool tasks (AgentDojo, DecodingTrust-Agent).
AI.result: Twin Agent preserves high task utility while preventing prompt injection attacks across all benchmarks, outperforming both undefended agents and existing privilege separation baselines. The compact-hint design empirically verifies a better security–utility tradeoff as hint length varies.
AI.conclusion: The Twin Agent pattern provides a general, effective privilege separation mechanism for LLM agents that balances security and utility without requiring extensive task-specific engineering, validated across diverse agentic benchmarks.

title: SLPO: Scaling Latent Reasoning via a Surrogate Policy
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become the predominant recipe for eliciting test-time scaling in explicit Chain-of-Thought reasoners. Yet this scaling path remains computationally costly, since every intermediate step must be decoded as a language token. Latent reasoning instead carries intermediate computation as continuous vectors and already matches or surpasses explicit CoT at far shorter horizons. Despite this promise, latent reasoners remain largely imitation-bound, while explicit CoT has already moved past imitation via outcome-reward RL. Latent trajectories lack a tractable per-step likelihood and an adaptive stopping interface under fixed thinking budgets, so outcome rewards cannot elicit latent test-time scaling. We introduce Surrogate Latent Policy Optimization (SLPO) to bring outcome-reward RL to autoregressive latent reasoners: an empirical surrogate policy density over latent transitions for trajectory-level credit assignment, and a correctness-supervised stopping head that outcome-reward optimization refines into a variable-horizon policy. Across continuous and soft thinking settings, SLPO improves Pass@$k$ under parallel sampling and allocates longer latent computation to harder instances with higher deterministic accuracy.

AI.tldr: SLPO introduces outcome-reward RL to autoregressive latent reasoners via a surrogate policy density for credit assignment and a correctness-supervised stopping head, enabling variable-horizon latent test-time scaling that allocates more computation to harder instances.
AI.motivation: Latent reasoning (continuous vectors) matches or surpasses explicit Chain-of-Thought at shorter horizons but remains imitation-bound. Unlike explicit CoT, which has advanced via outcome-reward RL, latent reasoners lack a tractable per-step likelihood and adaptive stopping mechanism under fixed thinking budgets, preventing outcome rewards from eliciting test-time scaling.
AI.method: SLPO combines two components: (1) an empirical surrogate policy density over latent transitions enabling trajectory-level credit assignment, and (2) a correctness-supervised stopping head that outcome-reward optimization refines into a variable-horizon policy. The approach works across both continuous and soft thinking settings.
AI.result: SLPO improves Pass@k under parallel sampling and dynamically allocates longer latent computation to harder problem instances, yielding higher deterministic accuracy.
AI.conclusion: SLPO successfully bridges outcome-reward RL and latent reasoning, enabling autoregressive latent reasoners to achieve test-time scaling with adaptive computation budgets, closing the gap with explicit CoT methods.

title: LISA: Linear-Indexed Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Reasoning
summary: Recent advances in long chain-of-thought reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1 have led to increasingly longer inference context lengths under the test-time scaling paradigm. However, the O(n^2) computational complexity of standard self-attention causes inference costs to grow sharply with long sequences, limiting the deployment of long-CoT reasoning in production settings. To address this, we propose LISA (Linear-Indexed Sparse Attention), a plug-and-play attention replacement module that requires no pretraining from scratch. LISA integrates two lightweight components in parallel within the original model: (1) a Linear Attention module that provides long-range memory with O(n) time complexity; (2) a Lightning Indexer that selects the top-M important tokens from the full context to feed into a Sparse Self-Attention. The two branches are fused via a gating mechanism, reducing inference complexity from O(n^2) to O(nM) (M << n) for generating n tokens. We design a two-stage training pipeline: Stage 1 initializes the model by integrating the linear attention to capture long-range dependencies, complemented by a sliding-window attention mechanism that is optimized via knowledge distillation to approximate the full self-attention distribution of a frozen teacher model. In Stage 2, we further introduce the Indexer to replace the static sliding-window mechanism, enabling dynamic token selection from broader contexts. The Indexer is trained using a novel per-head KL divergence loss, which aligns its selection behavior with the attention patterns of the teacher model. Experiments on DeepSeek-distilled-Qwen models demonstrate that LISA achieves a 50% inference speedup under 16K-token context, while improving average performance by 5.6% on reasoning benchmarks including AIME and MATH-500.

AI.tldr: LISA proposes a plug-and-play sparse attention mechanism combining linear attention (O(n)) with a learned token indexer for dynamic top-M selection, reducing inference complexity from O(n²) to O(nM).
