Trained via a two-stage distillation pipeline without pretraining from scratch, it achieves 50% inference speedup and 5.6% reasoning improvement on DeepSeek-distilled-Qwen models.
AI.motivation: Long chain-of-thought reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1) produce increasingly long contexts under test-time scaling, but standard self-attention's O(n²) complexity makes inference costs prohibitive for production deployment. Existing solutions either require pretraining from scratch or lack dynamic context selection capabilities.
AI.method: LISA is a plug-and-play attention replacement with two parallel lightweight branches: (1) Linear Attention for O(n) long-range memory; (2) Lightning Indexer that dynamically selects top-M important tokens for Sparse Self-Attention. A gating mechanism fuses both branches. Training follows two stages: Stage 1 uses knowledge distillation with sliding-window attention to approximate the frozen teacher's full self-attention distribution; Stage 2 replaces the static sliding window with the Indexer, trained via a per-head KL divergence loss to align token selection with teacher attention patterns.
AI.result: On DeepSeek-distilled-Qwen models, LISA achieves 50% inference speedup under 16K-token contexts and improves average reasoning performance by 5.6% on AIME and MATH-500 benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: LISA demonstrates that sparse attention with learned dynamic token selection can simultaneously reduce inference costs and improve reasoning quality in long-CoT models, enabling more practical deployment without requiring full pretraining.

title: Scale-Aware Learning of Chaotic Dynamics on Unstructured Meshes via Binned Spectral Losses
summary: Surrogate modeling for high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems that exhibit chaos requires mechanisms that preserve not only pointwise accuracy but also the scale-dependent structure of physical fields. Bandwise spectral power losses, such as the binned spectral loss function, provide such supervision on structured grids, where Fourier modes define a standard frequency decomposition. On irregular meshes, however, no canonical Fourier basis exists, and spectral representations must be constructed from graph operators induced by mesh connectivity and geometry. In this study, we extend the binned spectral power loss for application to unstructured-mesh surrogate modeling of nonlinear dynamical systems. This is obtained by replacing Fourier bands with graph-Laplacian frequency bands, and we provide scalable Chebyshev and multilevel approximations for improving long-horizon rollout fidelity. In its full-spectrum form, our approach uses graph Laplacian eigenspaces to provide a graph analogue of Fourier band-power matching, but incurs the high cost of spectral decomposition. As a scalable approximation, we replace exact band projectors with sparse Chebyshev polynomial graph filters, avoiding explicit eigendecomposition. When utilizing multilevel graph architectures, we introduce Graph Laplacian Energy Alignment for Meshes (GLEAM), which applies retained-subspace scale-aware supervision across graph hierarchies so that coarse and fine representations are regularized during autoregressive rollout. Our results show that the proposed spectral losses improve long-horizon rollout fidelity and preserve statistical invariants for the forecasting of turbulent flows on unstructured meshes, compared to deterministic baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper extends binned spectral power loss from regular grids to unstructured meshes by replacing Fourier bands with graph-Laplacian frequency bands. Scalable Chebyshev and multilevel approximations (GLEAM) are introduced to avoid costly eigendecomposition, improving long-horizon rollout fidelity for surrogate modeling of chaotic, high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems on irregular meshes.
AI.motivation: Surrogate modeling of chaotic, high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems on unstructured meshes lacks a canonical Fourier basis for spectral supervision. Existing binned spectral power losses work only on structured grids, motivating a graph-based spectral loss that preserves scale-dependent physical structure on irregular meshes.
AI.method: The authors replace Fourier bands with graph-Laplacian frequency bands. In the full-spectrum form, exact graph Laplacian eigenspaces provide band-power matching. To avoid costly eigendecomposition, sparse Chebyshev polynomial graph filters approximate band projectors. For multilevel graph architectures, GLEAM (Graph Laplacian Energy Alignment for Meshes) applies retained-subspace scale-aware supervision across graph hierarchies to regularize coarse and fine representations during autoregressive rollout.
AI.result: The proposed spectral losses improve long-horizon rollout fidelity and preserve statistical invariants for turbulent flow forecasting on unstructured meshes, outperforming deterministic baselines.
AI.conclusion: Graph-Laplacian-based spectral losses, particularly with scalable Chebyshev and multilevel GLEAM approximations, effectively regularize surrogate models on unstructured meshes, enabling accurate long-term forecasting of chaotic turbulent flows while preserving invariant statistics.

title: How Developers Use Relation Chains in Gerrit-Based Review Ecosystems: An Empirical Study Across Three Open-Source Ecosystems
summary:
Background. Developers increasingly coordinate dependent review workflows by submitting sequences of related changes rather than monolithic ones. In Gerrit, these dependencies form relation chains: structured review units that link changes together. As chains become more common, they shape review activities through synchronization overhead, CI amplification, and merge-ordering constraints.
  Aim. We investigate how developers adopt relation chains and how these dependency structures influence review dynamics and outcomes.
  Method. We analyze 29,580 relation chains from 15 repositories across three Gerrit ecosystems (OpenStack, Wikimedia, and ONAP), comprising 401,256 changes, using Mann-Kendall trend tests, Mann-Whitney tests with Cliff's delta for chain-vs-solo comparisons, and Spearman correlations for base-descendant dependencies.
  Results. Chain prevalence ranges from 5% to 49% across projects, increasing in 14 of 15. Chain changes take a median of 2.6 times longer to merge than size-matched solo changes, with the gap widening for very large changes. Review effort propagates through dependency-linked review workflows: base-change review activity co-varies with descendant review activity (rho = 0.43-0.61 in 14-15 of 15 projects), and 33.5% of chain members undergo structural evolution during review.
  Conclusions. Relation chains operate as durable, ecosystem-shaped coordination units with internal structure that change-centric analyses cannot capture. Future review analytics, reviewer-assignment systems, and AI-assisted review tools should reason over chains rather than isolated changes.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 29,580 relation chains (401,256 changes) across 15 repositories in OpenStack, Wikimedia, and ONAP ecosystems, finding that chain-based review is increasingly prevalent, takes 2.6× longer to merge than solo changes, exhibits correlated review effort between linked changes, and undergoes significant structural evolution during review, arguing that future tools must reason over chains rather than isolated changes.
AI.motivation: Modern code review increasingly involves sequences of dependent changes (relation chains) rather than isolated patches. Despite their growing prevalence in Gerrit-based workflows, little is known about how developers adopt these dependency structures, how chains influence review dynamics (synchronization overhead, CI amplification, merge ordering), and whether existing change-centric review analytics adequately capture chain-level phenomena.
AI.method: Empirical study analyzing 29,580 relation chains (401,256 individual changes) from 15 repositories across three Gerrit ecosystems (OpenStack, Wikimedia, ONAP). Methods include: (1) Mann-Kendall trend tests to assess chain adoption over time; (2) Mann-Whitney tests with Cliff's delta for comparing chain changes against size-matched solo changes on merge time and review outcomes; (3) Spearman correlations to quantify review effort propagation between base and descendant changes within chains; and (4) descriptive analysis of structural evolution (changes to chain composition during review).
AI.result: Key findings: (1) chain prevalence varies widely across projects (5–49%) and is increasing in 14 of 15 repositories; (2) chain changes take a median of 2.6× longer to merge than size-matched solo changes, with the gap widening for very large changes; (3) base-change review activity strongly co-varies with descendant review activity (Spearman ρ = 0.43–0.61, significant in 14–15 of 15 projects); (4) 33.5% of chain members undergo structural evolution (e.g., changes added, removed, or reordered) during the review process.
AI.conclusion: Relation chains function as durable, ecosystem-shaped coordination units whose internal dependency structure fundamentally alters review dynamics in ways that change-centric analyses miss. The authors recommend that review analytics dashboards, reviewer recommendation systems, and AI-assisted code review tools should operate at the chain level rather than treating changes as independent entities.

title: FedLSG: LLM-Enhanced Semantic Calibration for Federated Graph Backdoor Defense
summary: Federated Graph Neural Networks (FedGNNs) are highly vulnerable to backdoor poisoning, yet existing defenses typically rely on rule-based approaches that lack semantic understanding, making them vulnerable to stealthy triggers and harmful to benign structures. To solve this, we present FedLSG, the first framework that integrates large language models (LLMs) into federated graph backdoor defense. FedLSG introduces a graph and behavior to text grounding scheme that transforms local graph structures and client update behaviors into semantically rich natural language representations. The framework further adopts a lightweight student-teacher architecture. On the server side, a full scale LLM serves as a teacher, providing global contextual guidance and evaluating client updates during aggregation to identify potentially malicious participants. On the client side, a LoRA-based student is maintained to perform semantic reasoning, to suppress the influence of edges associated with backdoor triggers. By enabling semantic interpretation of both graph patterns and client behaviors, the framework adaptively incorporates rule-based signals into message passing and client aggregation for defense. Experiments demonstrate that FedLSG significantly improves resistance to backdoor attacks without compromising graph integrity.

AI.tldr: FedLSG is the first framework to integrate LLMs into federated graph backdoor defense, using a graph-to-text grounding scheme and a student-teacher architecture where a server-side LLM teacher evaluates client updates and a client-side LoRA student suppresses malicious edges via semantic reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing FedGNN backdoor defenses rely on rule-based approaches that lack semantic understanding, making them vulnerable to stealthy triggers and potentially damaging to benign graph structures. There is a need for semantically-aware defense mechanisms.
AI.method: FedLSG proposes: (1) a graph and behavior to text grounding scheme that converts local graph structures and client update behaviors into natural language representations; (2) a student-teacher architecture with a full-scale LLM teacher on the server providing global guidance and evaluating client updates during aggregation; and (3) a LoRA-based student on the client side performing semantic reasoning to suppress edges associated with backdoor triggers. Rule-based signals are adaptively incorporated into message passing and client aggregation.
AI.result: Experiments show that FedLSG significantly improves resistance to backdoor attacks without compromising graph integrity.
AI.conclusion: Integrating LLMs for semantic interpretation of graph patterns and client behaviors provides an effective and adaptive defense against backdoor poisoning in federated graph neural networks, outperforming traditional rule-based methods.

title: Lightweight Person-Place Relation Extraction from Historical Newspapers with Dependency Graphs and Proximity Features
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at CLEF 2026 HIPE Shared Task. To appear in CEUR Workshop Proceedings (CEUR-WS.org)
summary: The HIPE-2026 shared task introduces person-place relation extraction from multilingual historical newspapers as a new evaluation track, classifying the at and isAt relations between pre-annotated person and location mentions in English, French, and German. Motivated by the cost of processing historical archives at scale, our team (DS@GT HIPE, team 2 in the official results) investigates how far a lightweight, interpretable system can go without any pretrained language model at the relation classification stage. Our approach builds a document-level graph from dependency parses, extracts proximity-based and part-of-speech features for each entity pair, and classifies them with small scikit-learn ensembles or compact Graph Attention Networks, keeping every submitted run under 847K parameters. On the official evaluation (Test A, the newspaper test set), our best run reached a macro recall of 0.5142, ranking 3rd on the Efficiency profile while placing mid-table on Accuracy among the 17 participating teams. Two findings stand out. First, minimum character distance alone captures most of the classification signal; adding further engineered features yields inconsistent gains and sometimes degrades performance, echoing prior evidence that argument distance dominates relation extraction. Second, document-grouped cross-validation is essential on this corpus: pair-level splits inflate scores by 25-37 percentage points because entity mentions recur across documents, a data-leakage effect that grouped cross-validation removes.

AI.tldr: A lightweight, interpretable relation extraction system using dependency parses, proximity/POS features, and small classifiers (scikit-learn ensembles or compact GATs, all under 847K parameters) achieves competitive efficiency on the HIPE-2026 multilingual historical newspaper task. Minimum character distance dominates classification signal, and document-grouped cross-validation is essential to avoid severe data leakage.
AI.motivation: Processing historical archives at scale is costly. The authors investigate how far a lightweight, interpretable system without pretrained language models at the relation classification stage can go on the HIPE-2026 shared task (person-place relation extraction from multilingual historical newspapers).
AI.method: A document-level graph is built from dependency parses. Proximity-based and part-of-speech features are extracted for each entity pair. Classification uses small scikit-learn ensembles or compact Graph Attention Networks (GATs), with all submitted runs under 847K parameters. Document-grouped cross-validation is employed to prevent data leakage from recurring entity mentions across documents.
AI.result: Best run achieved macro recall of 0.5142 on Test A, ranking 3rd on Efficiency and mid-table on Accuracy among 17 teams. Minimum character distance alone captures most classification signal; additional engineered features yield inconsistent or negative gains. Pair-level cross-validation inflates scores by 25–37 percentage points due to data leakage, which grouped cross-validation eliminates.
AI.conclusion: Argument distance (minimum character distance) dominates relation extraction performance, consistent with prior findings. Lightweight, non-pretrained-LM systems can be competitive on efficiency metrics. Researchers must use document-grouped cross-validation on this corpus to avoid misleadingly inflated results from entity mention recurrence across documents.

title: Profile-Graph Memory for LLM Agents: Implicit Cross-Entity Traversal through Narrative Profiles
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code and MemHop benchmark: https://github.com/ShengtongZhu/ProGraph
summary: Long-term memory is essential for LLM agents that interact across sessions, yet current memory benchmarks primarily evaluate single-hop recall, leaving multi-hop association largely unmeasured. We make three contributions. First, we introduce MemHop, a multi-hop memory benchmark of 1,000 questions at hop depths 1-5 across 10 social-network scenarios, with per-hop evidence annotations. Second, we present Profile-Graph Memory (ProGraph), a two-layer memory architecture combining (i) profile expansion -- substring-matched traversal of entity names that naturally appear in LLM-written profile narratives, a minimal alternative to explicit knowledge-graph construction -- and (ii) compression residuals -- exact dates, quantities, and named items co-extracted with each profile update at zero extra API cost. Third, a full-grid ablation shows cross-benchmark mechanism specialization: profile expansion drives multi-hop reasoning (-22.6pp on MemHop when removed) while compression residuals drive precision recall (-8.6pp on LoCoMo when not co-extracted), with cross-effects under 3pp within a single architecture. ProGraph averages 80.1% on MemHop (matching the FullContext reference) and 78.4% on LoCoMo (exceeding FullContext by 11.3pp), outperforming Mem0, A-Mem, HippoRAG, and RAG on both. We release MemHop, ProGraph, and baseline implementations.

AI.tldr: MemHop is a multi-hop memory benchmark (1,000 questions, hop depths 1–5, 10 social-network scenarios), and ProGraph is a two-layer memory architecture combining profile expansion (substring-matched entity traversal) with compression residuals (exact dates/quantities co-extracted at zero cost). ProGraph achieves 80.1% on MemHop and 78.4% on LoCoMo, outperforming Mem0, A-Mem, HippoRAG, and RAG. Ablation reveals profile expansion drives multi-hop reasoning while compression residuals drive precision recall.
AI.motivation: Current LLM memory benchmarks only evaluate single-hop recall, failing to measure multi-hop association capabilities that are critical for agents interacting across sessions. There is a need for both a benchmark that systematically tests multi-hop memory and an architecture that effectively handles it.
AI.method: (1) MemHop benchmark: 1,000 questions at hop depths 1–5 across 10 social-network scenarios with per-hop evidence annotations. (2) ProGraph architecture: a two-layer memory design — profile expansion (substring-matched traversal of entity names from LLM-written profile narratives, avoiding explicit KG construction) and compression residuals (exact dates, quantities, named items co-extracted with profile updates at zero extra API cost). (3) Full-grid ablation to isolate mechanism contributions.
AI.result: ProGraph averages 80.1% on MemHop (matching FullContext) and 78.4% on LoCoMo (exceeding FullContext by 11.3pp). Ablation: removing profile expansion drops MemHop by 22.6pp; removing compression residuals drops LoCoMo by 8.6pp. Cross-effects under 3pp, confirming mechanism specialization. ProGraph outperforms Mem0, A-Mem, HippoRAG, and RAG on both benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Multi-hop memory requires specialized architectural components: profile expansion for reasoning across hops and compression residuals for precise fact recall. ProGraph demonstrates that these can coexist in a single architecture with minimal interference, offering a practical and effective memory solution for long-term LLM agents.

title: Neural Operator Surrogates for Two-Dimensional Neutron Flux Estimation
comment: to be submitted to ANS Winter 2026
summary: This work extends our one-dimensional single-sweep neural-operator studies to two dimensions. We consider one-group transport with isotropic scattering. As in the one-dimensional work, we use Fourier neural operators (FNOs) to approximate the high-fidelity scalar flux. Additionally, we also investigate U-shaped neural operators (UNOs) in this study. We consider three surrogates. The first two map the material and source fields directly to the flux, one using an FNO and one using a UNO. The third is an FNO that additionally takes the scalar flux after one source iteration, the single-sweep approximation, as an input. Each case is solved to high fidelity with a verified discrete-ordinates solver, and an average relative L_2 error norm is used to characterize the quality of the inferred maps. We train every surrogate over three random seeds so that differences between them can be assessed against run-to-run variability. Two questions guide the study: whether the single-sweep input improves accuracy over the direct maps, and whether training on the logarithm of the flux improves accuracy in the strongly attenuated regions relevant to shielding.

AI.tldr: The study extends 1D single-sweep neural-operator work to 2D, comparing FNO and UNO surrogates for one-group transport with isotropic scattering. It investigates whether adding a single-sweep (one source iteration) flux as input improves accuracy over direct material-to-flux maps, and whether training on log-flux improves accuracy in strongly attenuated (shielding-relevant) regions.
AI.motivation: Neural operators offer fast surrogates for expensive neutron transport solves. Prior 1D work showed promise for the single-sweep approach. Extending to 2D is necessary for practical shielding applications, where strongly attenuated regions pose accuracy challenges that log-transformed training may address.
AI.method: Three surrogate models are trained: (1) an FNO mapping material/source fields directly to scalar flux, (2) a UNO for the same direct map, and (3) an FNO that takes both the material/source fields and the single-sweep (one source iteration) flux as inputs. All are trained against high-fidelity discrete-ordinates solutions. Performance is measured via average relative L₂ error norm. Each surrogate is trained over three random seeds to assess run-to-run variability. The effect of log-transforming the flux target is also evaluated for shielding-relevant attenuation.
AI.result: Not explicitly detailed in the abstract. The abstract frames the study around two guiding questions — the benefit of the single-sweep input and the benefit of log-flux training — but defers quantitative results to the full paper.
AI.conclusion: Conclusions are not stated in the abstract. The paper aims to determine (1) whether the single-sweep preconditioning improves surrogate accuracy over direct mapping, and (2) whether log-space training mitigates error in highly attenuated shielding regions.

title: Don't Trust the Label: License Laundering in AI Supply Chains
summary: AI artifacts move through a multi-platform supply chain, spanning datasets and models on Hugging Face and applications on GitHub. While each artifact carries a license whose obligations should propagate through redistribution, no study has yet measured whether those obligations survive the chain or are stripped and replaced as artifacts move downstream. We trace 232,270 dataset$\rightarrow$model$\rightarrow$application chains and quantify two forms of license laundering: when artifacts with no declared license acquire definitive labels downstream, and when one declared license category replaces another during redistribution. We find that 62.3% of chains pass through at least one artifact with no declared license (concentrated in a small set of foundational datasets), and that every obligation-bearing license category falls below 7% end-to-end survival while the Permissive category reaches 95.1%. Based on these findings, we provide actionable recommendations for practitioners, model publishers, rights holders, and platform owners.

AI.tldr: The paper traces 232,270 dataset→model→application supply chains to quantify "license laundering" — finding that 62.3% of chains involve artifacts with no declared license, and obligation-bearing licenses survive end-to-end at rates below 7% while Permissive licenses reach 95.1%.
AI.motivation: No prior study has empirically measured whether license obligations survive multi-platform AI supply chains (Hugging Face datasets/models → GitHub applications) or whether they are stripped and replaced as artifacts move downstream — a phenomenon the authors term "license laundering."
AI.method: The authors construct 232,270 end-to-end supply chains linking datasets to models to applications across Hugging Face and GitHub. They then quantify two forms of license laundering: (1) artifacts with no declared license acquiring downstream labels, and (2) one declared license category being replaced by another during redistribution. Survival rates are computed per license category across the full chain.
AI.result: 62.3% of chains pass through at least one artifact with no declared license, concentrated in a small set of foundational datasets. Every obligation-bearing license category (e.g., copyleft, restrictive) falls below 7% end-to-end survival, while the Permissive category reaches 95.1% survival.
AI.conclusion: License laundering is pervasive in AI supply chains, with obligation-bearing licenses systematically stripped. The authors provide actionable recommendations for practitioners, model publishers, rights holders, and platform owners to address this issue.

title: GhostPrompt: Cross-Image Adversarial Prompt for Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted to ACM MM 2026. Code: this https://github.com/Ye-ze-yu/GhostPrompt
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where subtle perturbations to images or texts induce erroneous outputs. However, most text-based attacks are adapted from language-model-centric methods, in which the visual input is fixed during optimization, resulting in adversarial prompts that are tied to specific images and thus limiting their attack effectiveness. To this end, we first introduce a new research perspective: cross-image transferability for adversarial prompts. We then propose GhostPrompt, an adversarial prompt that is optimized once and reused to steer VLM outputs toward attacker-specified responses across diverse images. GhostPrompt employs a joint optimization that distills image-invariant adversarial features into the prompt by "worst-case" generation. Specifically, it alternates between constructing hard visual conditions for the current prompt and updating the prompt to remain effective under these conditions. Extensive experiments on prevalent VLMs verify that \ourmethod achieves an improvement of over 30% in attack success rates compared to state-of-the-art (SoTA) baselines, while reducing computation time by ~70%. Our code is avalable at https://github.com/Ye-ze-yu/GhostPrompt.

AI.tldr: GhostPrompt introduces cross-image transferable adversarial prompts for VLMs, using joint optimization to create a single prompt that attacks diverse images. It achieves 30%+ improvement in attack success rate and ~70% computation reduction over SoTA baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing text-based adversarial attacks on VLMs fix the visual input during optimization, producing image-specific prompts that lack transferability. This limits attack effectiveness and efficiency, motivating a cross-image transferable approach.
AI.method: GhostPrompt uses joint optimization that alternates between (1) constructing hard visual conditions for the current adversarial prompt and (2) updating the prompt to remain effective under those conditions. This "worst-case" generation distills image-invariant adversarial features into a single reusable prompt.
AI.result: GhostPrompt improves attack success rates by over 30% compared to state-of-the-art baselines across prevalent VLMs, while reducing computation time by approximately 70%.
AI.conclusion: Cross-image transferable adversarial prompts represent a more effective and efficient attack paradigm for VLMs. GhostPrompt demonstrates that distilling image-invariant adversarial features via worst-case joint optimization significantly outperforms existing image-specific approaches.

title: Beyond Relevance-Centric Retrieval: Rubric-Oriented Document Set Selection and Ranking
summary: As large language models and AI agents become the primary consumers of search results, document set quality determines the upper bound of downstream generation. Yet existing evaluation systems remain confined to scoring documents independently and aggregating via nDCG, ignoring inter-document interactions (redundancy, conflict, complementarity) and unable to answer what makes one document set better than another. To address these issues, we propose a complete evaluate-diagnose-optimize framework. We design SetwiseEvalKit, a three-level, nine-dimension document set evaluation benchmark covering both short-form and long-form scenarios, comprising approximately 28K high-quality evaluation rubrics. We systematically evaluate 12 rerankers: even the best method achieves no more than 45% coverage, cross-document coordination dimensions are universally weak, and no single method maintains top performance across both settings. Building on this, we propose Rubric4Setwise, a training-free method that converts rubric-based evaluation criteria into document set selection signals, achieving the best downstream generation performance with fewer documents and search rounds. It is the only method that maintains state-of-the-art results across both scenarios, validating the effectiveness of closing the loop from evaluation to optimization.

AI.tldr: Existing document evaluation ignores inter-document interactions (redundancy, conflict, complementarity). The authors propose SetwiseEvalKit, a comprehensive benchmark for document set quality, evaluate 12 rerankers finding weak cross-document coordination, and introduce Rubric4Setwise, a training-free optimization method that converts evaluation criteria into selection signals, achieving state-of-the-art downstream generation across both short-form and long-form scenarios.
AI.motivation: As LLMs and AI agents increasingly consume search results, the quality of retrieved document sets directly bounds downstream generation quality. However, current evaluation systems (e.g., nDCG) score documents independently and ignore crucial inter-document interactions such as redundancy, conflict, and complementarity. This leaves a critical gap: no existing framework can explain *why* one document set outperforms another for generation tasks.
AI.method: The paper proposes an **evaluate-diagnose-optimize** framework with two core contributions: (1) **SetwiseEvalKit**, a benchmark featuring a three-level, nine-dimension evaluation taxonomy covering both short-form and long-form scenarios, with ~28K high-quality human-annotated rubrics; and (2) **Rubric4Setwise**, a training-free method that transforms rubric-based evaluation criteria into document set selection signals, enabling joint optimization across multiple quality dimensions without model fine-tuning.
AI.result: Evaluation of 12 rerankers on SetwiseEvalKit reveals: (1) even the best method achieves no more than 45% coverage; (2) cross-document coordination dimensions are universally weak across all methods; (3) no single method maintains top performance across both short-form and long-form settings. Rubric4Setwise achieves the best downstream generation performance using fewer documents and search rounds, and is the only method maintaining state-of-the-art results across both scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The evaluate-diagnose-optimize loop works: rubric-driven document set selection consistently outperforms traditional independent-document ranking. Closing the gap between evaluation criteria and optimization signals is essential for building document sets that truly serve downstream LLM generation tasks.

title: Lifted Representation Hypothesis in Language Models
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, ICML 2026 Workshop: Philosophy Meets Machine Learning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often answer queries by mapping individual observations to more general rule-like structures. However, it remains unclear how these structures are stored, selected, and revised. To study this process, we propose thelifted representation hypothesis: LLMs update memory through shared latent structures rather than isolated instance-level facts. This view frames lifting as an efficient use of symmetry across instances, and shattering as the refinement of coarse lifted structures into more specific subtypes. We evaluate LLMs' lifting and shattering through controlled exception-learning experiments across in-context learning, LoRA, and full fine-tuning. We find that LLMs are vulnerable to shattering failures when data are governed by nested rules and exceptions, while lifting often occurs prematurely. These results highlight the need to study the relation between data and rule structures in LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the "lifted representation hypothesis," arguing that LLMs store and update memories via shared latent structures (lifting) rather than isolated facts. They show LLMs are prone to premature lifting and shattering failures when handling nested rules and exceptions.
AI.motivation: It remains unclear how LLMs store, select, and revise rule-like structures from individual observations. The authors aim to formalize this process through the lens of lifting (generalizing across instances via symmetry) and shattering (refining coarse structures into subtypes).
AI.method: The authors conduct controlled exception-learning experiments spanning in-context learning, LoRA, and full fine-tuning. They design tasks with nested rules and exceptions to observe how LLMs lift instances into latent structures and when shattering fails.
AI.result: LLMs are vulnerable to shattering failures when data follow nested rules with exceptions, and lifting often occurs prematurely — meaning models overgeneralize before adequately capturing exception structure.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of studying the relationship between data structure and rule structures in LLMs, suggesting that current models lack robust mechanisms for appropriately refining lifted representations when exceptions arise.

title: The Orthogonalized Read Is a Removable Training Scaffold for Recurrent Memory
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures. Code, per-seed results, and checkpoints: https://github.com/no-way-labs/recurrent-memory-scaffold
summary: A recent report finds that orthogonalizing the mLSTM memory matrix at read time (five Newton-Schulz iterations, trained through) substantially improves noisy associative recall. The effect replicates, but it is not a memory improvement. Training on this task is a long chance plateau followed by a sharp escape, and the orthogonalized read acts by re-conditioning the learning problem during the plateau. Three properties establish this. It must be self-consistent: an exact recursive least-squares read (the Mesa layer) reproduces it, while straight-through halves, delta-rule writes, frozen random keys, and plain normalization all fail. It is uniform: across a learning-rate x hardness grid it multiplies the escape hazard roughly six-fold with no detectable hardness dependence, widening the workable learning-rate corridor that narrows for the baseline. And it is removable: applied to failed models at inference it rescues none, and annealed away on an escape-triggered schedule it leaves numerically stock mLSTMs at full accuracy. Much of the published gain needs no architecture at all -- solved-rate at a fixed budget measures escape hazard, which follows a heat/noise law (learning-rate elasticity +3.0, gradient-noise elasticity -1.65) under which the original vocab-96 result is a large-batch noise condition rather than a capacity one. Decoding the memory state directly shows failed models carry roughly half their associations in linearly recoverable form: the plateau is a readout failure over half-written storage. Two conclusions travel beyond the intervention: recall benchmarks used for architecture selection partly measure trainability, and the system is a fully instrumented model organism of "emergence," in which a sharp behavioral threshold demonstrably arises from a censored metric over gradually accumulating structure.

AI.tldr: Orthogonalizing the mLSTM memory matrix at read time improves associative recall not by enhancing memory capacity but by re-conditioning the learning dynamics during a prolonged plateau phase, multiplying the escape hazard ~6× across conditions. The effect is self-consistent (only recursive least-squares reads reproduce it), uniform across learning rates and task hardness, and removable (cannot rescue already-failed models; can be annealed away post-escape). The plateau reflects a readout failure over half-written storage, and the system serves as a model organism for "emergence" where sharp behavioral thresholds arise from censored metrics over gradually accumulating structure.
AI.motivation: To understand why orthogonalizing the mLSTM memory matrix at read time substantially improves noisy associative recall, and to determine whether the gain reflects genuine memory improvement or an effect on trainability/learning dynamics.
AI.method: The authors systematically analyze the orthogonalized read intervention through three criteria: (1) self-consistency — comparing against recursive least-squares (Mesa layer), straight-through, delta-rule writes, frozen random keys, and plain normalization; (2) uniformity — testing across a learning-rate × hardness grid and measuring escape hazard; (3) removability — applying orthogonalization at inference to failed models and annealing it away post-escape. They also decode memory states directly to assess stored associations and analyze the heat/noise law governing escape hazard.
AI.result: The orthogonalized read does not improve memory per se but re-conditions the learning problem during the plateau. Escape hazard scales with learning-rate elasticity +3.0 and gradient-noise elasticity −1.65; the original vocab-96 result is a large-batch noise condition, not a capacity result. Failed models carry ~50% of associations in linearly recoverable form, indicating a readout failure. Only exact recursive least-squares (Mesa layer) reproduces the effect; alternatives fail.
AI.conclusion: Recall benchmarks used for architecture selection partly measure trainability rather than capacity. The mLSTM system constitutes a fully instrumented model organism of "emergence," where a sharp behavioral threshold demonstrably arises from a censored metric applied to gradually accumulating underlying structure.

title: Multi-Source and Cross-Scenario Strategy-Guided Code Optimization
summary: Automated code optimization improves program performance by refactoring source code, and recent studies use LLMs to generate optimization patches. The newest approaches are strategy-guided: they summarize strategies from historical optimization commits as static analysis rules, and use these rules to match code locations for LLMs to optimize. However, these approaches have two limitations: (1) the strategies may come from other knowledge sources, such as textbooks and web pages, but the existing approaches cannot utilize them; (2) a strategy may be applicable to different scenarios, e.g., different programming languages, but existing approaches can only formalize strategies for the scenario to which the source commit belongs. To address these limitations, we propose MoST, an LLM-based code optimization framework that integrates multiple knowledge sources across scenarios. MoST uniformly represents items in different knowledge sources as evidence objects, clusters them in a cross-source and cross-scenario manner to identify strategies, and transfers them to the target scenario when necessary for generating static analysis rules. To implement this process, MoST employs a novel self-balanced weighted clustering algorithm to balance evidence objects from different knowledge sources, and a novel example transfer procedure to ensure the quality of the generated rules when transferring across scenarios. On a benchmark containing 151 C/C++, 150 Python, and 50 Rust historical optimization tasks, compared with SemOpt, MoST yields 24.44%-180.00% and 21.88%-37.50% more patches that are exactly the same as or semantically equivalent to developer patches, respectively. When optimizing 15 real-world projects, MoST achieves 19.72%-717.42% maximum improvements and 4.44%-258.17% average improvements for the performance tests in the projects, significantly outperforming SemOpt and Codex.

AI.tldr: MoST is an LLM-based code optimization framework that integrates multiple knowledge sources (commits, textbooks, web pages) across different programming scenarios. It uses self-balanced weighted clustering to identify strategies and an example transfer procedure to apply them across scenarios. MoST significantly outperforms SemOpt and Codex on benchmark tasks and real-world projects.
AI.motivation: Existing strategy-guided LLM code optimization approaches have two key limitations: (1) they cannot utilize strategies from diverse knowledge sources beyond historical commits (e.g., textbooks, web pages); (2) they can only formalize strategies for the specific scenario (e.g., programming language) of the source commit, failing to transfer strategies across scenarios where they may also apply.
AI.method: MoST uniformly represents items from different knowledge sources as evidence objects, clusters them in a cross-source and cross-scenario manner to identify optimization strategies, and transfers strategies to target scenarios for static analysis rule generation. It introduces two novel techniques: (1) a self-balanced weighted clustering algorithm to balance evidence objects from heterogeneous knowledge sources, and (2) an example transfer procedure to ensure rule quality when transferring across scenarios.
AI.result: On a benchmark of 151 C/C++, 150 Python, and 50 Rust optimization tasks, MoST produces 24.44%-180.00% more exact-match patches and 21.88%-37.50% more semantically equivalent patches compared to SemOpt. On 15 real-world projects, MoST achieves 19.72%-717.42% maximum performance improvements and 4.44%-258.17% average improvements, significantly outperforming both SemOpt and Codex.
AI.conclusion: MoST effectively addresses the limitations of prior strategy-guided code optimization by enabling cross-source strategy extraction and cross-scenario strategy transfer, leading to substantial gains in both patch correctness and real-world runtime performance improvements.

title: An Automated Framework for Extracting Reachable Attack Chains from Cyber Threat Intelligence Reports
summary: Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) reports richly describe real-world attack processes, but their unstructured narratives cannot be directly used for automated attack-path reasoning. Existing CTI extraction methods focus on indicators, entities, or TTP labels without modeling the execution conditions and resulting states of each attack step, so the extracted knowledge supports neither state matching nor reachability analysis across multi-stage attack chains. This paper proposes an automated framework that extracts reachable attack chains by modeling each attack step as an attack unit of preconditions, an attack behavior, and postconditions. A multi-stage pipeline assisted by large language models (LLMs) extracts attack behavior skeletons, recovers their preconditions and postconditions, normalizes them into predefined predicates, and repairs broken dependencies; the resulting units are compiled into Datalog-style rules for attack-goal reachability reasoning. On a dataset of 20 CTI reports containing 334 human-validated annotated steps, our framework achieves higher annotated-step coverage than representative CTI extraction systems in recovering attack behaviors. Moreover, by explicitly generating preconditions and postconditions, it produces attack units that are more complete and consistent than those generated by end-to-end LLM baselines. On the extracted chains, Datalog inference reaches the specified attack goal in 19 of 20 reports, while backward search yields 34 attack paths under the generated rules. The source code and experimental artifacts are available in an anonymized repository. .

AI.tldr: Proposes an LLM-assisted framework that extracts cyber attack steps from unstructured CTI reports as formal "attack units" (preconditions, behavior, postconditions), normalizes them into Datalog rules, and enables automated reachability reasoning and attack-path discovery.
AI.motivation: Existing CTI extraction methods capture only indicators, entities, or TTP labels, lacking the execution conditions (preconditions) and resulting states (postconditions) of each attack step, which prevents state matching and reachability analysis across multi-stage attack chains.
AI.method: A multi-stage pipeline: (1) LLM-assisted extraction of attack behavior skeletons from CTI reports; (2) recovery and normalization of preconditions and postconditions into predefined predicates; (3) repair of broken dependencies; (4) compilation into Datalog-style rules for attack-goal reachability reasoning via forward inference and backward search.
AI.result: On 20 CTI reports with 334 human-annotated steps, the framework surpasses representative CTI extraction systems in annotated-step coverage. It produces more complete and consistent attack units than end-to-end LLM baselines. Datalog inference reaches the specified attack goal in 19/20 reports; backward search yields 34 attack paths.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling preconditions and postconditions enables effective multi-stage attack-chain reasoning from unstructured CTI reports, outperforming both traditional extraction systems and naive LLM baselines in completeness, consistency, and downstream reachability analysis.

title: Learning the Arabic Dialect Continuum as a Continuous Space: A Regression Approach to Speaker Origin Prediction
summary: We present a regression-based approach to Arabic dialect geolocation that models dialectal variation as a continuous geographic space rather than discrete categories. Speaker origin is predicted as continuous latitude-longitude coordinates using a hierarchical neural architecture that fuses frame-level XLS-R-300M and Whisper-large-v3 encoder representations with phonotactic descriptors through a Transformer encoder and a learnable attention-pooled query. A spherical geodesic loss directly optimizes great-circle distance on Earth's surface, avoiding distortions inherent to planar coordinate regression. Under a leakage-free 5-fold GroupKFold protocol grouped by source recording, our model attains a pooled median localization error of 481.2 km. Auxiliary country and city heads reach 64.5% and 45.2% accuracy, respectively. A permutation Mantel test on the learned latent space provides quantitative support for the Arabic dialect continuum hypothesis. To probe true generalization, we further introduce a city-masking protocol in which two cities per fold are removed from training but retained in validation. Under this zero-shot regime, the mean error rises to 1173.3 km, a 1.32x degradation relative to seen cities. Our findings establish continuous geographic modeling as a principled framework for Arabic dialect geolocation and quantify both its strengths and the substantial headroom that remains.

AI.tldr: A regression-based neural model predicts Arabic speaker origin as continuous latitude-longitude coordinates, achieving 481.2 km median error under standard evaluation and 1173.3 km under zero-shot city-masking, while providing quantitative evidence for the Arabic dialect continuum hypothesis.
AI.motivation: Traditional Arabic dialect geolocation treats dialectal variation as discrete categories, which fails to capture the continuous geographic nature of dialect variation. The authors aim to model dialect as a smooth spatial continuum and quantify the Arabic dialect continuum hypothesis through learned representations.
AI.method: A hierarchical neural architecture fuses frame-level representations from XLS-R-300M and Whisper-large-v3 encoders with phonotactic descriptors via a Transformer encoder and learnable attention-pooled query. Training uses a spherical geodesic loss that directly optimizes great-circle distance on Earth's surface. Evaluation employs leakage-free 5-fold GroupKFold grouped by source recording, plus a novel city-masking protocol for zero-shot generalization assessment. A permutation Mantel test validates the dialect continuum in the learned latent space.
AI.result: Under standard GroupKFold: pooled median localization error of 481.2 km; country accuracy 64.5%; city accuracy 45.2%. Under zero-shot city-masking: mean error rises to 1173.3 km (1.32× degradation). The Mantel test provides quantitative support for the dialect continuum hypothesis.
AI.conclusion: Continuous geographic modeling is a principled framework for Arabic dialect geolocation. While strong results are achieved, the substantial performance gap under zero-shot conditions indicates significant room for improvement in true generalization.

title: LAARA: Layer-Aware Adaptive Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation is widely used for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet existing methods typically assign the same adapter rank to every transformer layer despite their heterogeneous adaptation requirements. In this work, we show theoretically and empirically that uniform rank allocation is fundamentally suboptimal. Motivated by this observation, we propose LAARA (Layer Aware Adaptive Rank Allocation framework), a search-free framework that dynamically allocates ranks using lightweight diagonal Fisher estimates computed during training. LAARA combines projection-wise normalization, logarithmic compression, blended adapter importance estimation, and a vote-to-change dampening mechanism to produce stable and efficient rank adaptation. Experiments on GLUE and MathInstruct benchmark demonstrate that LAARA consistently matches or outperforms popular state of the art approaches such as LoRA, AdaLoRA, DyLoRA, and Bitfit while using significantly fewer trainable parameters. Our results show that Fisher-guided rank allocation provides a principled and effective foundation for adaptive parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The code is publicly available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LAARA-D305/LAARA.py

AI.tldr: LAARA is a search-free framework that dynamically allocates different adapter ranks across transformer layers during fine-tuning, using lightweight diagonal Fisher information estimates, outperforming uniform-rank methods like LoRA while using fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (e.g., LoRA, AdaLoRA, DyLoRA) assign the same adapter rank to every transformer layer, ignoring the fact that different layers have heterogeneous adaptation requirements. The authors demonstrate both theoretically and empirically that uniform rank allocation is suboptimal.
AI.method: LAARA (Layer Aware Adaptive Rank Allocation) is a search-free framework with four key components: (1) projection-wise normalization to stabilize gradient-based importance signals, (2) logarithmic compression to smooth importance magnitudes across layers, (3) blended adapter importance estimation combining current and historical signals, and (4) a vote-to-change dampening mechanism to prevent oscillation during rank reallocation. Ranks are dynamically adjusted during training using lightweight diagonal Fisher information estimates.
AI.result: On GLUE and MathInstruct benchmarks, LAARA matches or outperforms LoRA, AdaLoRA, DyLoRA, and BitFit while using significantly fewer trainable parameters. The Fisher-guided rank allocation proves both principled and empirically effective.
AI.conclusion: Fisher-guided, layer-aware adaptive rank allocation provides a principled and effective foundation for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, eliminating the need for costly rank search while achieving superior parameter efficiency.

title: The ICSE 2026 Shadow PC: Training the Next Generation of Reviewers Through Deliberate Practice
summary: Peer review is essential to software engineering research, yet reviewer training remains largely implicit. We describe the ICSE 2026 Shadow PC, a redesigned program emphasizing deliberate practice at scale. Key innovations include multi-phase structure with calibration and peer feedback, strict separation from the main PC, and a pathway toward leadership development. With 102 participants completing the program and reviewing 117 papers, 97% recommending the experience, and positive reception from authors (67% finding reviews helpful), the program demonstrates that rigorous reviewer training is achievable at scale. We share lessons learned and propose shadow PC area chairs as a mechanism for sustainable scaling and leadership development.

AI.tldr: The ICSE 2026 Shadow PC program redesigned reviewer training through deliberate practice at scale, involving 102 participants who reviewed 117 papers across a multi-phase structure with calibration, peer feedback, and leadership development. With 97% participant recommendation and 67% author satisfaction, it demonstrates that rigorous, scalable reviewer training is achievable.
AI.motivation: Reviewer training in software engineering research remains largely implicit and unstructured, lacking systematic approaches to develop competent reviewers at scale. The authors aim to address this gap by designing a program that provides deliberate, structured practice for emerging reviewers.
AI.method: The redesigned ICSE 2026 Shadow PC program employs a multi-phase structure featuring: (1) calibration exercises to align reviewer standards, (2) peer feedback mechanisms enabling mutual learning, (3) strict separation from the main Program Committee to ensure independent skill development, and (4) a leadership development pathway through shadow PC area chairs. The program operated at scale with 102 participants reviewing 117 papers.
AI.result: 102 participants completed the program, collectively reviewing 117 papers. 97% of participants recommended the experience. Authors responded positively, with 67% finding the shadow reviews helpful. The program successfully demonstrated that rigorous, structured reviewer training can be conducted at scale within a major conference setting.
AI.conclusion: Rigorous reviewer training is achievable at scale through deliberate practice, multi-phase structure, and peer feedback. The authors propose shadow PC area chairs as a sustainable mechanism for both scaling the program and fostering leadership development within the software engineering research community.

title: DARWIN: Evolving Jailbreak Adversary and Guardrail for LLM Safety Evaluation and Protection
summary: Most existing LLM safety evaluation and defense methods follow a static formulation: jailbreak vulnerabilities are evaluated with fixed attack methods, and guardrails are trained on fixed malicious prompt datasets. However, real-world adversaries continuously evolve their capabilities and expand the attack space. To address this challenge, we propose DARWIN, an evolutionary attack-defense framework that formulates jailbreaking as an open-ended evolution process and continuously updates guardrails through an evolving attack-defense loop. DARWIN-Attack is an evolutionary adversary that expands its capabilities through strategy discovery, mutation, selection, and feedback-driven composition. It collects strategies from broad external sources, generates new variants through self-reflection and genetic evolution, and retains effective strategies based on their performance against aligned LLMs. During attack execution, DARWIN-Attack adaptively selects and combines evolved strategies according to feedback from target LLMs and guardrails. Across frontier models and guardrails, it achieves state-of-the-art attack success rates, including nearly 100% on DeepSeek-V4-Pro and YuFeng-XGuard and over 90% on GPT-5.5. On the defense side, we introduce DARWIN-Guard, an online adversarial training paradigm that iteratively learns from emerging adversarial samples generated by DARWIN-Attack. To improve robustness without sacrificing utility, DARWIN-Guard jointly trains on malicious and benign disguised queries, encouraging the model to identify underlying intent rather than superficial attack patterns. DARWIN-Guard achieves an average unsafe recall of 91.6% across 12 safety benchmarks, outperforming strong guardrails such as YuFeng-XGuard and Nemotron Guard, while maintaining a nearly 100% pass rate on standard benign datasets.

AI.tldr: DARWIN is an evolutionary framework that frames LLM jailbreaking as an open-ended arms race: DARWIN-Attack continuously evolves attack strategies through discovery, mutation, and selection, while DARWIN-Guard iteratively learns from emerging adversarial samples via online adversarial training, achieving SOTA attack success rates and defense performance.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM safety evaluation and defense methods are static — they use fixed attack methods and fixed training datasets, failing to account for real-world adversaries who continuously evolve their capabilities and expand the attack space.
AI.method: DARWIN formulates jailbreaking as an open-ended evolution process within an attack-defense loop. DARWIN-Attack uses strategy discovery (collecting from external sources), mutation (self-reflection + genetic evolution), selection (retaining strategies that work against aligned LLMs), and feedback-driven adaptive composition during execution. DARWIN-Guard employs online adversarial training, jointly training on malicious and benign disguised queries to learn underlying intent rather than superficial attack patterns, preserving utility.
AI.result: DARWIN-Attack achieves nearly 100% ASR on DeepSeek-V4-Pro and YuFeng-XGuard, and over 90% on GPT-5.5. DARWIN-Guard achieves an average unsafe recall of 91.6% across 12 safety benchmarks (outperforming YuFeng-XGuard and Nemotron Guard) while maintaining ~100% pass rate on benign datasets.
AI.conclusion: An evolutionary, open-ended formulation of the attack-defense dynamic significantly outperforms static approaches for both jailbreaking and guardrailing, demonstrating that continuous co-evolution is a more realistic and effective paradigm for LLM safety.

title: TriAgent: Divergence-Aware Multi-Agent Committees for Cost-Efficient Financial Sentiment Analysis
summary: Production LLM-based financial sentiment analysis faces a structural cost trap: most queries are trivially classifiable, yet expensive cloud reasoners process them all, and the bill scales linearly with user count. We present TriAgent, a multi-agent committee stratified by contextual granularity -- a word-level lexicon (VADER), a sentence-level domain transformer (FinBERT), and a cross-sentence reasoner (Qwen2.5, 0.5B-14B-4bit, with Mistral-7B and Phi-3.5-mini cross-family checks). A three-way Semantic Divergence Index (SDI) measures pairwise disagreement across granularities and routes each query accordingly. Our central finding is the critic plateau: when the LLM is re-tasked as a critic over the smaller agents' outputs, F1 plateaus at ~0.87 across 1.5B-7B Qwen (bootstrap 95% CIs overlap), while a same-size 3-persona vote drops to F1=0.66, which is driven by granularity-stratified diversity. Three corollaries follow from the same SDI signal: (i) a Shared Consensus Dictionary on multilingual sentence-BERT answers 95% of Chinese queries from an English cache at F1=0.99 -- cross-border canonicalization at zero marginal cost; (ii) SDI doubles as a post-hoc LLM-hallucination detector at AUC=0.90; (iii) the SDI single-stage strategy attains the best risk-adjusted return (Sharpe=3.50) on a 20-ticker back-test, dominating both always-FinBERT (1.36) and always-LLM (0.11). At 10M-user scale, TriAgent saves $9.3M/year vs. a GPT-4o-mini baseline. Code, lexicons, and the SCD are released.

AI.tldr: TriAgent is a multi-agent sentiment analysis system that routes financial queries to agents of varying complexity (lexicon, domain transformer, LLM) based on a Semantic Divergence Index (SDI). It achieves near-LLM accuracy at a fraction of the cost, with an F1 plateau of ~0.87 when the LLM acts as critic, enables cross-lingual cache sharing, detects hallucinations (AUC=0.90), and yields superior trading performance (Sharpe=3.50) while saving $9.3M/year at scale.
AI.motivation: Production LLM-based financial sentiment analysis incurs a structural cost trap: most queries are trivial but are still processed by expensive cloud reasoners, with costs scaling linearly with user count. The authors seek to decouple accuracy from inference cost by routing only genuinely difficult queries to LLMs.
AI.method: TriAgent employs a three-agent committee: VADER (word-level lexicon), FinBERT (sentence-level domain transformer), and a quantized Qwen2.5 LLM (0.5B–14B, 4-bit) with Mistral-7B and Phi-3.5-mini for cross-family checks. A Semantic Divergence Index (SDI) measures pairwise disagreement across these three granularities and routes queries accordingly. The system also features a Shared Consensus Dictionary for multilingual cross-border canonicalization.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Critic plateau — when the LLM critiques smaller agents, F1 plateaus at ~0.87 across 1.5B–7B Qwen (95% CIs overlap), while 3-persona voting drops to F1=0.66. (2) The Shared Consensus Dictionary answers 95% of Chinese queries from an English cache at F1=0.99. (3) SDI detects LLM hallucinations post-hoc at AUC=0.90. (4) SDI single-stage strategy achieves Sharpe=3.50 on a 20-ticker backtest, dominating FinBERT-only (1.36) and LLM-only (0.11). (5) At 10M users, TriAgent saves $9.3M/year vs. GPT-4o-mini.
AI.conclusion: Stratifying sentiment analysis by contextual granularity and routing via SDI enables cost-efficient, high-accuracy financial sentiment at scale. The critic role for LLMs proves more effective than voting, and the SDI signal generalizes beyond routing to hallucination detection, multilingual transfer, and trading signal generation.

title: AdaRoPE: Not All Attention Heads Should Rotate and Scale Equally
summary: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is widely adopted in Transformers to encode positional information, yet standard implementations enforce a uniform frequency schedule and scaling across all attention heads. Using simplified retrieval tasks and length generalization scenarios, we show -- both empirically and theoretically -- that heads with different functional roles require distinct frequency ranges and attention scaling factors to operate effectively. Ignoring this structure leads to suboptimal utilization of embedding dimensions and degraded performance, particularly under long-context settings. To address these limitations, we propose AdaRoPE, which equips each attention head with learnable rotation frequencies and attention scaling factors. Pretrained LLMs with AdaRoPE consistently outperform existing RoPE variants, including partial RoPE and NoPE baselines. For context extension, we further show that uniform frequency and attention scaling, used in methods such as YaRN, are suboptimal. By applying head-specific scaling, AdaRoPE enables better context extension while better preserving short-context performance in both the extrapolation setting and the long-context continued pretraining setting. These results highlight the importance of optimizing rotary position embedding at the level of individual attention heads.

AI.tldr: AdaRoPE introduces head-specific learnable rotation frequencies and attention scaling factors to replace uniform RoPE schedules, demonstrating improved performance in both standard and long-context settings.
AI.motivation: Standard RoPE applies identical frequency schedules and scaling across all attention heads, ignoring their distinct functional roles. The authors show this uniformity leads to suboptimal embedding utilization and degraded long-context performance, creating a need for head-specific optimization.
AI.method: AdaRoPE assigns each attention head its own learnable rotation frequencies and attention scaling factors. For context extension, head-specific scaling replaces uniform approaches like YaRN, applied in both extrapolation and long-context continued pretraining settings.
AI.result: Pretrained LLMs with AdaRoPE consistently outperform standard RoPE, partial RoPE, and NoPE baselines. Head-specific scaling enables superior context extension while better preserving short-context performance compared to uniform scaling methods like YaRN.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing rotary position embedding at the individual attention head level is critical for maximizing Transformer performance, particularly under long-context scenarios.

title: Predicting Groundwater Arsenic Concentrations Using Graph Neural Networks
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, AAAI '26 AI4ES workshop acceptance
summary: Arsenic contamination in groundwater presents a longstanding public health crisis in the United States, especially for households depending on private wells. Accurate and spatially informed prediction of arsenic concentration is vital to identify high-risk areas and focus mitigation efforts. However, there is a lack of generalizable models for representing continuous variation in arsenic concentrations across regions. In this work, we pose arsenic prediction as a regression task and construct a spatially integrated dataset to aggregate over 74,000 arsenic samples from the Water Quality Portal (WQP), Mineral Resources Data System (MRDS), and Gridded National Soil Survey Geographic Database (gNATSGO). Specifically, we use a variety of techniques including kNearest Neighbors (k-NN) and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to join arsenic measurement points from across the United States by location. Building on this dataset, we evaluate a diverse suite of machine learning models, including tree-based ensemble approaches, multilayer perceptrons, and spatially aware graph neural networks (GNN). Our findings show that while gradient-boosted trees are still considered state-of-the-art in the field of tabular data, GNNs are able to further account for spatial dependence to match or outperform the results of gradient-boosted trees. These results demonstrate that graph-based and spatially informed learning can enhance environmental prediction and provide a foundation for improved groundwater risk mapping and monitoring.

AI.tldr: Paper evaluates machine learning models for predicting arsenic contamination in US groundwater using a spatially integrated dataset of 74,000+ samples, finding that spatially-aware Graph Neural Networks match or outperform gradient-boosted trees by accounting for spatial dependence.
AI.motivation: Address the public health crisis of arsenic contamination in private wells by developing accurate, spatially informed predictive models. Existing approaches lack generalizable models that capture continuous spatial variation in arsenic concentrations across regions.
AI.method: Constructed a spatially integrated dataset by joining 74,000+ arsenic samples from WQP, MRDS, and gNATSGO using k-NN and GIS techniques. Evaluated tree-based ensemble methods, multilayer perceptrons, and spatially-aware Graph Neural Networks on the regression task, emphasizing the GNNs' ability to model spatial dependence through graph structures.
AI.result: Gradient-boosted trees remain strong baselines for tabular data, but spatially-aware GNNs matched or outperformed them by leveraging spatial dependence, demonstrating the value of graph-based learning for environmental prediction.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based and spatially informed learning methods enhance environmental prediction quality, providing a foundation for improved groundwater risk mapping and monitoring, particularly for identifying high-risk areas reliant on private wells.

title: Test Case Prioritization for DNNs via Neural Collapse Instability
summary: With the widespread deployment of deep neural networks (DNNs) in safety-critical domains, reducing the cost of model validation under limited testing budgets has become increasingly important. Existing test case prioritization techniques often rely on single-checkpoint confidence signals derived from output probabilities. However, DNNs can be confidently wrong, and the confidence margin between the predicted and competing classes is frequently small, which weakens early fault discovery. To address this limitation, we propose a Neural-Collapse-Inspired Prioritization (NCIP) framework that replaces absolute confidence with cross-checkpoint prediction variability in the terminal training regime, where model geometry becomes highly structured. NCIP introduces two key components. First, it selects an NC-guided representative subset of training checkpoints using an equiangularity score of classifier weights, quantified as the standard deviation of pairwise cosine similarities among class weight vectors. Second, it prioritizes test inputs by their prediction variability across the selected checkpoints, surfacing boundary-adjacent and failure-prone samples that are unstable under checkpoint-induced decision boundary shifts. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and architectures show that NCIP achieves strong performance in early fault discovery compared with competitive baselines, with 1.5 to 16.6 percent RAUC-ALL gains and 4.9 to 20.6 percent RAUC-500 gains under the same testing budget. NCIP further attains the best average performance across all dataset-model pairs.

AI.tldr: NCIP replaces single-checkpoint confidence signals with cross-checkpoint prediction variability in terminal training, using Neural Collapse geometry to select representative checkpoints and prioritize test inputs likely to be near decision boundaries, achieving strong early fault discovery gains (1.5–16.6% RAUC-ALL, 4.9–20.6% RAUC-500).
AI.motivation: Existing DNN test prioritization relies on output-probability confidence from a single checkpoint, but DNNs can be confidently wrong with small confidence margins, weakening early fault discovery. The authors aim to leverage structural properties of Neural Collapse in terminal training to improve prioritization.
AI.method: NCIP operates in two stages: (1) NC-guided checkpoint selection — computes pairwise cosine similarities among class weight vectors across training checkpoints and selects a subset with low standard deviation (high equiangularity), reflecting Neural Collapse geometry; (2) test input prioritization — ranks inputs by prediction variability (label flipping frequency) across the selected checkpoints, surfacing boundary-adjacent, failure-prone samples.
AI.result: NCIP achieves 1.5–16.6% RAUC-ALL gains and 4.9–20.6% RAUC-500 gains over competitive baselines under the same testing budget, with the best average performance across all dataset-model pairs.
AI.conclusion: Prediction variability across NC-selected checkpoints is a more reliable prioritization signal than single-checkpoint confidence, and Neural Collapse geometry provides a principled way to select informative checkpoints for test case prioritization in DNN validation.

title: Defense Against LLM Backdoors using Critical Neuron Isolation Pruning
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where hidden triggers induce malicious outputs. Existing defenses generally fall into inference-time detection or training-time mitigation, but face two key limitations. First, they focus on fine-tuning-based backdoors (e.g., PEFT modules) and fail to address insidious model-editing attacks that bypass training pipelines. Second, they target simple classification settings and do not naturally extend to open-ended LLM generation and do not naturally extend to the open-ended generation characteristics of LLMs. Consequently, these methods focus on surface-level behavioral patterns while neglecting the deeper representational causes of malicious activations. This lack of mechanistic understanding forces defenses to depend on empirical heuristics, limiting their robustness, generality, and practical applicability in real-world LLM deployment.
  To bridge this gap, we introduce DeCNIP (Defense with Critical Neuron Isolation Pruning), which leverages representational analysis to identify and neutralize backdoors in a unified pipeline. Specifically, DeCNIP identifies trigger-like behaviors by optimizing a cross-entropy loss between harmful prompts with candidate tokens and benign inputs. This representational discovery exposes latent threats by uncovering mechanisms through which triggers hijack model weights. It then isolates Backdoor Critical Neurons (BCNs) and prunes them selectively to remove malicious influence while preserving model utility. Extensive evaluations on six open-source LLMs and two benchmark datasets demonstrate that DeCNIP achieves over 95% relative reduction in Attack Success Rate (ASR), outperforming seven state-of-the-art defenses with only 0.1% neuron intervention. Moreover, it maintains 97% of the model's performance on normal benchmarks, demonstrating its efficacy, robustness, and scalability.

AI.tldr: DeCNIP is a defense against backdoor attacks in LLMs that uses representational analysis to identify Backdoor Critical Neurons (BCNs) via cross-entropy optimization, then selectively prunes them. It achieves >95% ASR reduction with only 0.1% neuron intervention while preserving 97% of normal performance, outperforming seven SOTA defenses across six LLMs and two benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing backdoor defenses for LLMs suffer from two critical limitations: (1) they only address fine-tuning-based backdoors (e.g., PEFT) and miss model-editing attacks that bypass training pipelines; (2) they are designed for simple classification tasks and don't naturally extend to open-ended LLM generation. More fundamentally, these methods rely on surface-level behavioral heuristics without understanding the mechanistic/representational causes of malicious activations, limiting robustness and real-world applicability.
AI.method: DeCNIP operates via a unified pipeline: (1) Trigger-like behavior discovery through optimizing cross-entropy loss between harmful prompts (with candidate tokens) and benign inputs, enabling representational analysis that reveals how triggers hijack model weights; (2) Identification and isolation of Backdoor Critical Neurons (BCNs) — neurons causally responsible for malicious activations; (3) Selective pruning of BCNs to neutralize backdoor influence while preserving model utility.
AI.result: DeCNIP achieves over 95% relative reduction in Attack Success Rate (ASR) across six open-source LLMs and two benchmark datasets, outperforming seven state-of-the-art defenses. It requires only 0.1% neuron intervention and retains 97% of the model's normal benchmark performance.
AI.conclusion: DeCNIP demonstrates that a mechanistic, representation-level approach to backdoor defense — identifying and pruning backdoor-critical neurons — is both highly effective and minimally invasive, offering a robust, general, and scalable solution for real-world LLM deployment that surpasses existing heuristic-based defenses.

title: VizRAG: Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Hypergraph Visualization
summary: Hypergraph-based RAG systems surpass traditional graph-based approaches by organizing complex n-ary atomic facts among entities, rather than relying solely on binary relationships. Despite the advancements in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with enhanced visual capabilities, current hypergraph-based RAG frameworks predominantly restrict knowledge retrieval and reconstruction to a unimodal, text-centric paradigm. This limitation prevents them from fully leveraging the powerful visual perception capabilities of modern MLLMs. To address this gap, we systematically explore the integration of hypergraph awareness in RAG systems through visual cues. By incorporating visual representations of hypergraphs into the RAG pipeline, we introduce VizRAG, the first RAG system to support visual hypergraph structure awareness. Experimental results demonstrate that VizRAG significantly outperforms strong baselines, validating the promising potential of hypergraph visualization as a novel approach for RAG systems.

AI.tldr: VizRAG introduces visual hypergraph structure awareness into RAG systems, addressing the limitation of current hypergraph-based RAG frameworks that operate solely in text-centric paradigms. It is the first RAG system to leverage MLLMs' visual perception capabilities by incorporating visual representations of hypergraphs, significantly outperforming existing baselines.
AI.motivation: Current hypergraph-based RAG frameworks are limited to unimodal, text-centric knowledge retrieval, failing to exploit the powerful visual perception capabilities of modern multimodal large language models (MLLMs). This gap motivates the exploration of integrating hypergraph awareness through visual cues.
AI.method: VizRAG incorporates visual representations of hypergraphs directly into the RAG pipeline, enabling MLLMs to perceive hypergraph structures through visual cues rather than purely textual encoding of n-ary atomic facts.
AI.result: Experimental results show that VizRAG significantly outperforms strong baselines, validating hypergraph visualization as an effective approach for RAG systems.
AI.conclusion: Visual hypergraph structure awareness represents a promising novel direction for enhancing RAG systems, with VizRAG serving as the first system to demonstrate this capability by bridging hypergraph-based knowledge organization with MLLM visual perception.

title: Statistically Grounded Sparse-Feature Interventions for Activation-Space Control in Large Language Models
summary: Activation steering offers a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for behavioral control of large language models, but SAE-based steering methods often rely on learned steering objectives or single-criterion feature selection. We introduce a transparent SAE-feature steering pipeline that first applies a six-condition reliability filter, then ranks sparse features through an unweighted Borda consensus over three complementary statistics: $F$-test, KSG mutual information, and Cohen's $d$. The resulting steering direction is constructed as a Cohen's-$d$-weighted combination of SAE decoder rows, providing an optimization-free direction motivated by Fisher-LDA under approximate SAE-feature decorrelation. Across three Gemma-family models, four behavioral domains, and 356 layer-strength configurations, the method produces measurable domain-specific shifts while revealing a substantial gap between raw attribute movement and quality-preserving generation. In the strongest configuration, logical-correctness steering reaches a primary-score delta of $+1.16$ in Gemma~2 9B; however, our broader finding is that usable steering is highly localized by model, domain, layer, and strength. These results argue that activation-steering evaluations should report quality-conditioned success alongside raw behavioral shift. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/Oshayer-Siddique/LLM-Steering-Using-SAE.
