AI.tldr: A transparent SAE-based activation steering pipeline uses six-condition reliability filtering and Borda-ranked feature selection with Cohen's-d-weighted decoder rows, achieving domain-specific behavioral shifts across 356 configurations but revealing that usable steering is highly localized and must be evaluated by quality-conditioned success, not just raw score deltas.
AI.motivation: Existing SAE-based steering methods for LLM behavioral control rely on opaque learned objectives or simplistic single-criterion feature selection. The authors aim to introduce a fully transparent, principled pipeline and to highlight the underappreciated gap between measurable attribute shifts and actual quality-preserving generation, advocating for better evaluation standards.
AI.method: A pipeline with three stages: (1) a six-condition reliability filter applied to SAE features; (2) ranking surviving features via unweighted Borda consensus over F-test, KSG mutual information, and Cohen's d; (3) constructing a steering direction as a Cohen's-d-weighted combination of SAE decoder rows, motivated by Fisher-LDA under approximate feature decorrelation. Evaluated across three Gemma-family models, four behavioral domains, and 356 layer-strength configurations.
AI.result: The method produces measurable domain-specific shifts. The strongest result is a +1.16 primary-score delta on logical-correctness steering in Gemma 2 9B. However, the broader finding is that usable steering is highly localized by model, domain, layer, and strength, with a substantial gap between raw attribute movement and quality-preserving generation.
AI.conclusion: Activation steering evaluations must report quality-conditioned success alongside raw behavioral shift, as large raw deltas do not guarantee usable generation. The transparent, optimization-free pipeline demonstrates that effective steering exists but is narrow and configuration-dependent.

title: Decodable but Not Detectable: A Leakage Fingerprint for Near-OOD Benchmarks
summary: While auditing a perturbation-based OOD detector on a document benchmark, we recorded an AUROC of 0.326 -- well below the 0.5 chance level. The cause is a benchmark leak: the designated "OOD" class is one the model was trained on, so its examples sit inside the in-distribution fit set and the detector is penalized for correctly ranking them as familiar. Deleting the class and retraining 35 models across two domains raises the score to 0.911. We distill the contamination into a leak fingerprint -- near-perfect supervised decodability (AUROC approximately 1) coupled with unsupervised detection collapsed below 0.65 -- and validate it on a controlled battery of 52 settings (20 leaked, 32 clean) across ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 on CIFAR-10/100, achieving sensitivity 18/20 and specificity 31/32 in embedding space; the matched fit-set-exclusion controls are perfect at 20/20. An in-the-wild audit of 24 standard near/far OOD benchmark pairs fires on exactly one (the intrinsically hard CIFAR-100 vs CIFAR-10 pair) and on no far-OOD pair, confirming specificity and that standard cross-dataset construction is clean. Under the corrected protocol, perturbation signals are decodable but not detectable: a supervised reader recovers the OOD signal (AUROC 0.87-1.00) while no unsupervised detector does, and the perturbation method does not improve on plain Mahalanobis distance. We provide a theoretical account of why and, for transparency, retract an earlier circular correlation. The contributions are a corrected protocol and a validated leak diagnostic, not a new OOD method.

AI.tldr: The paper exposes a widespread benchmark leak in OOD detection evaluation where "OOD" samples belong to classes seen during training, causing detectors to be penalized for correctly recognizing them. The authors develop a leak fingerprint diagnostic, validate it across 52 controlled settings, audit standard benchmarks (finding them largely clean), and demonstrate that under corrected protocols, perturbation signals are decodable but not detectable by unsupervised methods.
AI.motivation: The authors discovered that a perturbation-based OOD detector scored below chance (AUROC 0.326) on a document benchmark due to a contamination leak: the supposed OOD class was in the model's training set. This motivated a systematic investigation into how prevalent such leaks are, how to detect them reliably, and what valid conclusions remain once leaks are controlled for.
AI.method: The paper proposes a two-pronged leak diagnostic called a "leak fingerprint": (1) near-perfect supervised decodability (AUROC ≈ 1) indicating the OOD signal is linearly separable in the representation space, combined with (2) unsupervised detection performance collapsed below 0.65. They validate this on a controlled battery of 52 settings (20 intentionally leaked, 32 clean) across ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 on CIFAR-10/100, using both embedding-space analysis and matched fit-set-exclusion controls. They then audit 24 standard near/far OOD benchmark pairs. Finally, they evaluate perturbation-based OOD methods under the corrected, leak-free protocol.
AI.result: The leak fingerprint achieves sensitivity 18/20 and specificity 31/32 in embedding space, with fit-set-exclusion controls reaching perfect 20/20. The in-the-wild audit of 24 standard benchmark pairs fires on only one pair (the intrinsically hard CIFAR-100 vs CIFAR-10) and on no far-OOD pairs, confirming that standard cross-dataset OOD benchmarks are generally clean. Under the corrected protocol, a supervised linear reader can recover the OOD signal (AUROC 0.87–1.00) while no unsupervised detector can, and the perturbation method does not outperform plain Mahalanobis distance.
AI.conclusion: The paper's contributions are methodological, not a new OOD detection technique: a corrected evaluation protocol and a validated leak diagnostic. Standard cross-dataset OOD benchmarks are clean; the previously reported perturbation-based OOD detection gains are artifacts of benchmark leakage. The authors retract an earlier circular correlation finding and provide a theoretical account of why perturbation signals are decodable but not detectable.

title: HijackKV: New Threat in Position-Independent KV Cache Reuse
summary:
Key-Value (KV) cache reduces inference latency in large language models (LLMs). Traditional prefix-based reuse has low cache hit rates across inference requests because it requires exact token and position matches. To improve efficiency, recent system optimizations introduce position-independent KV reuse, allowing KV cache to be reused whenever identical text chunks appear, regardless of their position in the sequence.
  We show this design introduces a new threat, KV Cache Hijacking. Since KV caches are retrieved by token match but encode the context in which they were originally computed, the KV tied to a benign-looking token chunk may encode an attacker-controlled prefix. When later reused in a victim query, this contaminated KV silently hijacks the model's behavior, even if no attacker-controlled text appears in the input.
  We introduce HIJACKKV, the first attack framework that systematically exploits this vulnerability, demonstrating its severity and practicality. HIJACKKV optimizes an attacker-controlled prefix, so that the KV computed for a subsequent common benign text encodes the attacker's goal, while the text remains unchanged for future cache hits. HIJACKKV achieves an average 94% success rate in a single attempt, remains effective under realistic constraints including low hit rates (10%) and frequent recomputation (50%), persists over multi-turn interactions, and transfers across models in black-box settings. We further provide design insights for building secure KV reuse systems.

AI.tldr: KV cache systems that allow position-independent reuse are vulnerable to a novel "KV Cache Hijacking" attack, where attacker-crafted prefixes contaminate cached key-value pairs for benign text, silently hijacking LLM behavior with 94% success rate even under realistic constraints.
AI.motivation: Recent LLM serving systems have moved beyond traditional prefix-based KV cache reuse to position-independent reuse, where KV cache is retrieved by token matching regardless of sequence position. This structural shift introduces a new, previously unidentified security vulnerability: KV cache entries encode the original context in which they were computed, but retrieval is based solely on token content, creating a mismatch that can be exploited.
AI.method: The authors propose HIJACKKV, an attack framework that optimizes an attacker-controlled prefix such that the KV cache subsequently computed for common benign text (e.g., "The quick brown fox") encodes the attacker's malicious goal. The attacker injects this contaminated KV into a shared cache; when a victim's query triggers a cache hit on the benign text, the retrieved KV silently steers model behavior toward the attacker's objective without any malicious tokens appearing in the victim's input. The framework evaluates under realistic conditions: low cache hit rates (10%), frequent recomputation (50%), multi-turn interactions, and black-box transfer across models.
AI.result: HIJACKKV achieves an average 94% attack success rate in a single attempt. It remains effective under low cache hit rates (10%) and with 50% recomputation frequency. The attack persists across multi-turn conversations and transfers successfully across different models in black-box settings.
AI.conclusion: Position-independent KV cache reuse introduces a serious security vulnerability that can be practically exploited. The authors provide design insights for building secure KV reuse systems to mitigate this threat.

title: D2VBench: Benchmarking Large Language Models with Value Dilemmas in Daily Scenarios
summary: With the wide application of large language models (LLMs) in real-world scenarios, the value implication of their outputs is crucial. However, existing evaluation benchmarks suffer from insufficient coverage of value dilemmas in daily scenarios involving multiple value conflicts and simplistic evaluation formalisms that fail to assess LLMs' value alignment. To address these issues, we propose D2VBench, a value alignment benchmark comprising 10,000 instances of real daily dilemma scenarios constructed through a multi-stage collaboration between LLMs and humans, grounded in 158 manually annotated fine-grained value concepts. For evaluation on the benchmark, we present a hybrid evaluation paradigm that integrates multiple-choice questions with open-ended questions. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on eight mainstream LLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that D2VBench exhibits high reliability and robustness, effectively reflecting the LLMs' alignment across different value categories and dimensions, and providing a more realistic and fine-grained tool for research on value alignment. The dataset is available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/D2VBench.

AI.tldr: D2VBench is a value alignment benchmark with 10,000 daily dilemma scenarios grounded in 158 fine-grained value concepts, evaluated via a hybrid multiple-choice/open-ended paradigm, revealing nuanced alignment behaviors across eight mainstream LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM value alignment benchmarks suffer from two key shortcomings: (1) insufficient coverage of real-world daily dilemmas involving multiple value conflicts, and (2) overly simplistic evaluation formalisms (e.g., multiple-choice only) that fail to capture the depth of LLMs' value reasoning and alignment.
AI.method: The authors construct D2VBench through a multi-stage human-LLM collaborative pipeline: first manually annotating 158 fine-grained value concepts, then generating 10,000 daily dilemma scenarios where these values conflict. For evaluation, they propose a hybrid paradigm combining multiple-choice questions with open-ended questions to assess both discriminative alignment and generative reasoning quality.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments on eight mainstream LLMs show D2VBench is reliable and robust. It effectively discriminates LLM alignment across different value categories and dimensions, providing finer-grained insights than prior benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: D2VBench offers a more realistic, fine-grained, and methodologically sound tool for value alignment research, addressing both coverage and evaluation depth limitations of existing benchmarks. The dataset is publicly released.

title: Logic-Guided Data Extraction with Answer Set Programming and Large Language Models
comment: 42nd International Conference on Logic Programming, to appear in Theory and Practice of Logic Programming (TPLP)
summary: When Large Language Models (LLMs) are used for semantic data extraction from unstructured text, producing candidate relational facts from natural language, they may remain unreliable for tasks requiring complex combinatorial reasoning and global consistency. This paper proposes a logic-guided data extraction framework combining LLM-based extraction with Answer Set Programming (ASP). The LLM produces candidate facts, whereas ASP performs validation, inference, consistency checking, and control. Unlike existing pipelines that query the LLM independently for all target predicates, the proposed approach uses ASP reasoning to identify which predicates are logically admissible at each stage and to guide extraction queries. By interleaving LLM calls with ASP derivation, the framework infers logically implied facts without further extraction and detects inconsistencies early. We formalize the pipeline and prove that, under mild assumptions, it is equivalent to the baseline approach with respect to the final extracted facts, while requiring fewer LLM calls. We also introduce a caching mechanism for logic-based control queries, exploiting monotonicity of conjunctive queries over incrementally constructed fact sets to reduce solver invocations. Experiments on ASP-derived benchmarks show that the framework reduces LLM calls and improves extraction quality by mitigating spurious outputs, demonstrating the value of non-monotonic logic programming for controlled semantic extraction.

AI.tldr: A logic-guided extraction framework that interleaves LLM-based fact extraction with Answer Set Programming (ASP) for validation, inference, and consistency checking, reducing LLM calls and improving extraction quality by filtering spurious outputs.
AI.motivation: LLMs are unreliable for semantic data extraction tasks requiring complex combinatorial reasoning and global consistency. Existing pipelines query LLMs independently for all target predicates, which is inefficient and prone to spurious outputs.
AI.method: The framework combines LLM-based candidate fact generation with ASP for validation, inference, consistency checking, and control. ASP reasoning identifies logically admissible predicates at each stage to guide extraction queries. It interleaves LLM calls with ASP derivation to infer logically implied facts and detect inconsistencies early. A caching mechanism exploiting monotonicity of conjunctive queries reduces solver invocations.
AI.result: The framework is proven equivalent to the baseline in final extracted facts (under mild assumptions) while requiring fewer LLM calls. Experiments on ASP-derived benchmarks show reduced LLM calls and improved extraction quality by mitigating spurious outputs.
AI.conclusion: Non-monotonic logic programming via ASP provides effective controlled semantic extraction, improving both efficiency and reliability over LLM-only baselines.

title: Cross-Subject Semantic Decoding with Shared-Space Alignment for Generalized Neural Representation Learning
summary: Generalizing across subjects remains challenging in invasive neural recordings because electrode configurations, anatomical structures, and neural signal patterns vary substantially across individuals. To investigate such inter-subject variability, we propose a cross-subject semantic decoding framework that aligns neural responses to speech perception from multiple subjects into a shared latent space and learns a mapping from the aligned neural representations to contextual embeddings. More specifically, using electrocorticography data collected during natural language comprehension, we estimate the shared space using the shared response model and train a decoder to predict contextual semantic embeddings from projected neural responses. For a held-out subject, we estimate a subject-specific projection into the predefined shared space, and directly apply the pretrained decoder without any retraining. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms baseline methods across evaluation settings and exhibits a reduced performance drop from source subject to held-out subject testing, indicating improved cross-subject generalization. These results suggest that aligning neural activity into a shared latent space, while decoding in a semantic embedding space, provides an effective strategy for improving cross-subject generalization by reducing subject-specific differences in neural responses while effectively capturing shared stimulus-related representations.

AI.tldr: Proposes a cross-subject semantic decoding framework using shared response modeling (SRM) to align ECoG neural responses into a shared latent space, then maps these to contextual semantic embeddings. The approach reduces subject-specific variability and enables zero-shot decoding on held-out subjects without retraining, outperforming baselines.
AI.motivation: Cross-subject generalization in invasive neural decoding is severely limited by inter-subject variability in electrode placement, anatomical differences, and idiosyncratic neural signal patterns. Existing decoders typically require per-subject training, which is impractical and data-inefficient. A method that learns shared neural representations across subjects and transfers to unseen individuals without retraining would substantially advance practical neural decoding applications.
AI.method: The framework has two stages: (1) Aligning neural responses across subjects using the Shared Response Model (SRM), which estimates a shared latent space and subject-specific projection matrices from ECoG data recorded during natural speech comprehension. (2) Training a decoder that maps from this aligned shared neural space to contextual semantic embeddings (e.g., from language models). For a held-out subject, only the subject-specific projection into the pre-established shared space is estimated; the pretrained decoder is then applied directly with no retraining.
AI.result: The proposed framework consistently outperformed baseline methods across multiple evaluation settings. Critically, it exhibited a reduced performance drop when testing on held-out subjects compared to within-subject performance, demonstrating improved cross-subject generalization. Zero-shot decoding on unseen subjects was feasible without any decoder retraining.
AI.conclusion: Aligning neural activity into a shared latent space via SRM, combined with decoding into a semantic embedding space, is an effective strategy for cross-subject generalization. It reduces subject-specific neural response differences while preserving shared stimulus-driven representations, enabling robust transfer to new subjects.

title: Taming the Security-Energy Paradox: A Green AI Approach to Optimized Android Malware Detection
summary: An increase in advanced Android malware requires the use of deep learning models, which can run on Android devices. But there is a trade-off between security and energy use, as strong detection models can drain the battery of devices fast. This work tests different Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) model configurations to balance malware detection performance and energy efficiency. In this work, we compared standard FP32 models with optimized INT8 quantized neural networks with different model depths using TUANDROMD and DREBIN datasets for both classification performance and energy consumption. The results show that INT8 quantization reduces model size by about 3.5 times with a decrease in energy consumption to 0.0189 mJ per inference, while maintaining more than 99.2\% detection accuracy. We found that shallow quantized architectures, such as 3-layer and 4-layer QNNs, reduce energy costs by improving throughput and shortening the time of CPU operating in a high-power state. This work shows that efficient malware protection can be achieved on resource-constrained smartphones and provides a foundation for Green AI in mobile security.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the trade-off between malware detection accuracy and energy consumption on Android devices by comparing standard FP32 MLPs with INT8 quantized neural networks, demonstrating that quantization reduces model size ~3.5× and energy to 0.0189 mJ/inference while maintaining >99.2% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Advanced Android malware demands deep learning-based detection that can run on-device, but there exists a critical trade-off between detection performance (security) and battery drain (energy consumption). The authors aim to find model configurations that achieve both high accuracy and energy efficiency for resource-constrained smartphones.
AI.method: The authors systematically compare standard FP32 (32-bit floating-point) Multi-Layer Perceptron models against INT8 (8-bit integer) quantized neural networks at various model depths. Experiments are conducted on two established Android malware datasets — TUANDROMD and DREBIN — evaluating both classification performance (accuracy) and energy consumption per inference.
AI.result: INT8 quantization achieves approximately 3.5× model size reduction, energy consumption as low as 0.0189 mJ per inference, and maintains over 99.2% detection accuracy. Shallow quantized architectures (3-layer and 4-layer QNNs) deliver the best energy efficiency by improving throughput and reducing the duration the CPU spends in high-power states.
AI.conclusion: Efficient on-device malware protection is feasible on resource-constrained smartphones through quantized shallow neural networks. The work establishes a foundation for Green AI principles in mobile security, demonstrating that quantization and architectural simplicity together resolve the security–energy trade-off.

title: Sentence Splitter: Uncovering Latent Factual Structure for Self-Supervised Learning
summary: This paper introduces Sentence Splitter, a self-supervised framework built upon a T5-based encoder--decoder architecture for uncovering the latent factual structure of natural language sentences. The proposed method identifies the semantic boundary between a descriptive prefix (head) and its factual completion (tail) by formulating sentence splitting as a discrete segmentation problem, where a sentence of length $N$ admits $N$ possible split points but only one recovers the intended head--tail structure. Rather than explicitly searching over all candidate boundaries, the model learns to recover the factual completion through probabilistic sequence generation. To eliminate the need for manual annotation, symbolic head--tail pairs are first verbalized into natural-language templates that provide supervision for training the Sentence Splitter. The trained splitter is then applied to raw text to extract aligned prefix--tail pairs, which are subsequently used to train a generative model that proposes additional plausible completions through a lightweight bootstrapping process. This unified pipeline provides a scalable and structure-aware approach to constructing self-supervised training data while bridging symbolic knowledge and natural language. Experiments on both structured and naturally occurring text demonstrate that the proposed splitter generalizes beyond synthetic templates and that the resulting structure-aware supervision consistently improves downstream performance on knowledge graph completion and commonsense question answering, highlighting the effectiveness of recovering latent factual structure for knowledge-centric NLP.

AI.tldr: Sentence Splitter is a self-supervised T5-based framework that segments sentences into descriptive prefixes and factual completions, generating aligned head–tail pairs without manual annotation, which are then used to train downstream models for improved knowledge graph completion and commonsense QA.
AI.motivation: Manually annotating the factual structure of sentences (head–tail pairs) is expensive and does not scale. The authors aim to automatically uncover latent factual structure in natural language to provide structure-aware supervision for knowledge-centric NLP tasks without human labeling.
AI.method: The method formulates sentence splitting as a discrete segmentation problem using a T5 encoder–decoder. Symbolic head–tail pairs are first verbalized into natural-language templates to provide supervision. The trained Sentence Splitter then extracts aligned prefix–tail pairs from raw text. A generative model proposes additional plausible completions via lightweight bootstrapping, creating a self-supervised pipeline.
AI.result: The splitter generalizes beyond synthetic templates to naturally occurring text. Structure-aware supervision from the pipeline consistently improves downstream performance on knowledge graph completion and commonsense question answering tasks.
AI.conclusion: Recovering latent factual structure through self-supervised sentence splitting provides effective, scalable, structure-aware supervision that bridges symbolic knowledge and natural language, yielding measurable gains on knowledge-centric NLP benchmarks.

title: Geometry-Guided Constraint Learning for LLM Safety Classification
summary: Safety as Polytope (SaP) learns linear half-space constraints in LLM hidden space but requires per-category tuning of the constraint count K. We show that sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature extraction resolves this: K=2 becomes optimal for 12/14 categories on Qwen3.5-9B, achieving 96-99% accuracy per category on our BeaverTails classification benchmark, largely eliminating the need for exhaustive sweeps (K=4-25 with random initialization). This convergence to two planes is consistent with the Linear Representation Hypothesis, providing suggestive evidence that safety boundaries in this setting admit a low-dimensional linear description in the SAE feature space. Building on this geometric perspective, we introduce a cone constraint whose learnable aperture adapts to each category's cluster concentration, stabilized by a three-phase training

AI.tldr: SaP (Safety as Polytope) previously required per-category tuning of constraint count K. Using SAE features, K=2 becomes near-universally optimal, achieving 96–99% accuracy on BeaverTails with Qwen3.5-9B, eliminating expensive hyperparameter sweeps. The authors further introduce an adaptive cone constraint with three-phase training for improved safety boundary modeling.
AI.motivation: Safety as Polytope (SaP) learns linear safety boundaries in LLM hidden space but suffers from needing per-category manual tuning of K (the number of half-space constraints), typically requiring exhaustive sweeps over K=4–25 with random initialization. This makes deployment impractical and computationally expensive. The authors aim to eliminate this tuning burden and provide a principled, geometry-grounded alternative.
AI.method: The core insight is that SAE (sparse autoencoder) feature extraction transforms the hidden representations such that safety boundaries become linearly separable with very few planes. Specifically: (1) SAE features are extracted from the LLM's hidden states; (2) a polytope classifier with K=2 half-space constraints is trained in this SAE feature space; (3) building on the finding that two planes suffice, the authors introduce a cone constraint — a learnable-aperture conic region that adapts to each category's cluster concentration — stabilized by a three-phase training procedure.
AI.result: K=2 is optimal for 12 out of 14 safety categories on Qwen3.5-9B when using SAE features, achieving 96–99% per-category accuracy on the BeaverTails classification benchmark. This largely eliminates the need for exhaustive K sweeps (previously K=4–25). The convergence to exactly two planes per category is consistent with the Linear Representation Hypothesis, suggesting safety boundaries admit a low-dimensional linear description in SAE feature space.
AI.conclusion: SAE feature extraction dramatically simplifies safety boundary modeling, reducing the required constraint count to K=2 for nearly all categories. This provides both practical efficiency (no hyperparameter sweeps) and theoretical support for the Linear Representation Hypothesis — safety concepts appear to be linearly separable in SAE space. The proposed cone constraint further refines this geometric approach by adapting to per-category cluster structure.

title: From Trajectories to Prefixes: Reusing Teacher Trajectories via Replayed Prefixes and Online Continuation
summary: Small language models are attractive backbones for interactive agents, but direct distillation from strong teacher trajectories often turns rich multi-turn behavior into one-shot imitation targets. This is inefficient in long-horizon environments, where early decisions shape later states and rewards. We propose Prefix-GRPO, a reinforcement learning framework that decomposes teacher trajectories into replay-aligned prefix queries and online continuations. Each prefix is replayed in the environment to recover a valid intermediate state, after which the student continues online interaction and receives task reward. Unlike response-only GRPO, Prefix-GRPO also applies clipped policy updates to historical assistant tokens inside the replayed prefix, using a policy-distilled SFT checkpoint to estimate their old log-probabilities. This unifies prefix learning and continuation learning within the same policy-optimization form. Experiments on TextCraft, BabyAI, and ALFWorld show that Prefix-GRPO improves small-model agents over distillation and standard RL baselines, while ablations show that replay alone is insufficient without explicit prefix-token optimization. The implementation and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/HappynessI/Prefix_GRPO.

AI.tldr: Prefix-GRPO is a reinforcement learning method that improves small language model agents by decomposing teacher trajectories into replay-aligned prefixes and online continuations, applying clipped policy updates to both prefix and continuation tokens. It outperforms distillation and standard RL baselines on TextCraft, BabyAI, and ALFWorld.
AI.motivation: Direct distillation from strong teacher trajectories in interactive agent settings collapses rich multi-turn behavior into one-shot imitation targets, which is inefficient in long-horizon environments where early decisions critically shape later states and rewards. Standard response-only GRPO fails to optimize historical tokens within the prefix.
AI.method: Prefix-GRPO decomposes teacher trajectories into (1) replay-aligned prefix queries that are replayed in the environment to recover valid intermediate states, and (2) online continuations where the student interacts and receives task rewards. Uniquely, it applies clipped policy updates to both continuation tokens and historical assistant tokens inside the replayed prefix, using a policy-distilled SFT checkpoint to estimate old log-probabilities for the prefix tokens.
AI.result: Prefix-GRPO improves small-model agent performance over distillation and standard RL baselines on TextCraft, BabyAI, and ALFWorld. Ablations demonstrate that replay alone, without explicit prefix-token optimization, is insufficient.
AI.conclusion: Prefix-GRPO offers an effective framework for training small interactive agents by unifying prefix learning and continuation learning under a single policy-optimization objective, addressing the inefficiency of naive distillation in multi-turn, long-horizon settings.

title: Small, Free, and Effective: Orchestrating Open-Weight Small Language Models to Outperform Single LLM for Malware Analysis
comment: To appear in Proceedings of the 29th International Symposium on Research in Attacks, Intrusions, and Defenses (RAID)
summary: Malware analysis demands rapid interpretation of complex detonation reports spanning filesystem, network, and process behaviours. While large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive capabilities for technical artifact interpretation, the opacity and escalating API costs of closed-weight frontier models motivate exploration of open-weight alternatives. However, many open-weight models are large, demanding significant compute resources and incurring non-trivial hosting costs that place them beyond reach for resource-constrained deployments. This paper investigates whether orchestrated ensembles of small language models (SLMs) can match or exceed single LLM performance on structured questions about malware detonation reports. We established baselines by testing eleven open-weight SLMs, three cyber security pre-trained models, and six frontier LLMs on Meta's CyberSecEval Malware Analysis benchmark. We then designed and evaluated four orchestration architectures: (i) a multi-agent pipeline that decomposes analysis into structured evidence-collection and reasoning stages, (ii) an adversarial debate framework in which two agents iteratively critique each other's reasoning, (iii) a hierarchical consultation system that pairs a general-purpose SLM with a cyber-specialised expert model, and (iv) a hybrid architecture that combines evidence-grounded pipelines with adversarial debate reasoning. The hybrid system (Qwen3-4B with Foundation-Sec-8B) achieved 35.30% overall accuracy, exceeding the strongest cyber-specialised baseline (22.54%) and the strongest ungrounded frontier baseline (34.77%); when given the same evidence pipeline, grounded Gemini remained the strongest configuration at 38.22%. These findings show that evidence-grounded orchestration can substantially improve the performance of collaborative SLMs for supporting interpretation of malware detonation reports.

AI.tldr: Investigates whether orchestrated ensembles of small language models (SLMs) can match or exceed single LLMs on malware detonation report analysis. A hybrid evidence-grounded + adversarial debate architecture (Qwen3-4B + Foundation-Sec-8B) achieved 35.30% accuracy, surpassing both cyber-specialised baselines (22.54%) and ungrounded frontier models (34.77%).
AI.motivation: Closed-weight frontier LLMs face opacity and escalating API costs, while many open-weight models are too large for resource-constrained deployments. The authors seek to determine whether collaborative, lightweight SLM ensembles can serve as viable, cost-effective alternatives for structured malware analysis tasks.
AI.method: Eleven open-weight SLMs, three cyber-security pre-trained models, and six frontier LLMs were baselined on Meta's CyberSecEval Malware Analysis benchmark. Four orchestration architectures were then evaluated: (1) a multi-agent pipeline decomposing analysis into evidence collection and reasoning stages, (2) an adversarial debate framework with iterative critique, (3) a hierarchical consultation pairing a general-purpose SLM with a cyber-specialised model, and (4) a hybrid combining evidence-grounded pipelines with adversarial debate.
AI.result: The hybrid system (Qwen3-4B with Foundation-Sec-8B) achieved 35.30% overall accuracy, outperforming the strongest cyber-specialised baseline (22.54%) and the strongest ungrounded frontier baseline (34.77%). Grounded Gemini with the same evidence pipeline remained the top configuration at 38.22%.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-grounded orchestration substantially improves collaborative SLM performance on malware detonation report interpretation, making SLM ensembles a practical, resource-efficient alternative to large single-model deployments for structured cybersecurity analysis tasks.

title: emb-diversity: A Tool for Embedding-Based Measurement of Data Diversity
summary: There is growing evidence that data diversity is crucial for developing fair and robust NLP models. However, current approaches to measure diversity remain inconsistent and fragmented: While there exist a number of tools for measuring the lexical diversity of texts, researchers lack standardized tools for quantifying diversity based on embeddings. Embedding-based diversity measures are highly flexible: They work with any embedding model and any data that can be embedded, and are thus applicable to many notions of diversity. With emb-diversity, we provide a comprehensive embedding-based diversity measurement tool, spanning a broad range of measures. We demonstrate its potential for several use cases: measuring the stylistic, semantic, language and speaker diversity of datasets. https://github.com/nlpsoc/emb-diversity/

AI.tldr: emb-diversity is a comprehensive tool for measuring data diversity using embeddings, offering a standardized, flexible framework applicable to stylistic, semantic, language, and speaker diversity across any embeddable data.
AI.motivation: Current NLP diversity measurement is fragmented: lexical diversity tools exist, but no standardized tools exist for embedding-based diversity, despite embeddings offering greater flexibility across data modalities and diversity notions.
AI.method: The authors present emb-diversity, a software tool that implements a broad range of embedding-based diversity measures, supporting any embedding model and embeddable data type, and applicable to multiple diversity dimensions.
AI.result: The tool successfully demonstrates utility across several use cases: measuring stylistic, semantic, language, and speaker diversity within datasets.
AI.conclusion: emb-diversity fills a critical gap by providing the first comprehensive, standardized tool for embedding-based diversity measurement in NLP, enabling more consistent fairness and robustness research.

title: Rethinking Uncertainty Evaluation in Large Language Models
summary: Calibration is the primary criterion for evaluating LLM confidence, but it is insufficient: it admits trivially incoherent estimators, depends on the evaluation distribution, and does not test the extent to which the estimation can be interpreted as a consistent, underlying probability function. What we actually need is for LLM confidence estimates to satisfy the conditions required of coherent probabilistic beliefs. We formalize these conditions along three axes (structural coherence, faithfulness, and usefulness) and operationalize them as the C1 metrics. Widely used estimators systematically violate these conditions despite appearing well-calibrated: models assign lower confidence to logically easier questions 31\% of the time, and common interventions reducing RMSCE leave structural violations unchanged, suggesting that calibration is orthogonal to probabilistic validity. RLHF and chain-of-thought improve usefulness metrics without restoring coherence. Our results show current LLM confidence estimates cannot be interpreted as coherent probabilities; our framework provides the tools to measure and close this gap.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that calibration alone is insufficient for evaluating LLM confidence; it proposes C1 metrics to measure structural coherence, faithfulness, and usefulness of confidence estimates, showing that well-calibrated models still exhibit systematic probabilistic incoherence.
AI.motivation: Calibration, the primary metric for LLM confidence evaluation, admits trivially incoherent estimators, depends on the evaluation distribution, and fails to test whether confidence estimates represent consistent underlying probability functions. The authors argue that LLM confidence should satisfy the conditions of coherent probabilistic beliefs — a stricter and more meaningful standard.
AI.method: The authors formalize three axes for coherent probabilistic beliefs: (1) structural coherence (e.g., monotonicity with respect to logical difficulty), (2) faithfulness (internal consistency of probability assignments), and (3) usefulness (downstream decision-making value). These are operationalized as the "C1 metrics," a suite of tests applied to widely used LLM confidence estimators, with interventions including RLHF and chain-of-thought prompting examined for their effects.
AI.result: Widely used estimators systematically violate coherence despite good calibration: models assign lower confidence to logically easier questions 31% of the time. Interventions that reduce RMSCE leave structural violations unchanged, indicating calibration and probabilistic validity are orthogonal. RLHF and chain-of-thought improve usefulness metrics but do not restore coherence.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM confidence estimates cannot be interpreted as coherent probabilities. The proposed C1 framework provides the diagnostic tools to measure this gap and guide efforts toward genuinely coherent uncertainty estimation in LLMs.

title: Memory Merge DQN: Sensitivity Weighted Target Updates for Stable Value Learning
summary: Deep Q-networks use target networks to stabilise bootstrapped value learning, but the standard hard copy update also introduces a tradeoff. Holding the target network fixed, improves short term stability, yet each hard update abruptly replaces the target parameters with the newest online network and discards recent parameter history. This can produce sudden changes in the bootstrap target and may remove value function structure that remains useful later in training. This paper introduces Memory Merge DQN, a target network update mechanism that maintains a short memory of recent historical online network copies and constructs the target network by merging network parameters based on the Q-value sensitivity rather than copying only the newest online network. Memory Merge gives greater influence to parameters that remain locally important for current Q-value behaviour, while using a recency prior to keep the merged target close to the latest online parameters. The method is inspired by Fisher Weight Model Merging, but uses Q-value sensitivity rather than Fisher information as the weighting signal. This paper evaluates Memory Merge DQN on Atari environments against DQN, Averaged DQN, DQN with layer normalisation, and PQN (with gradient clipping). The results show that Memory Merge DQN is highly competitive and it achieves the largest number of first place final performance results among the evaluated methods, beats DQN, Averaged DQN, and PQN (with gradient clipping), and produces substantial gains in several games where preserving useful value-function parameters appears beneficial. These findings suggest that selectively merging recent parameter weights and history can improve the stability and final performance of DQN agents, and that target network design is an important mechanism for preserving useful value function structure during long horizon value learning.

AI.tldr: Memory Merge DQN introduces a target network update mechanism that merges recent historical online network copies using Q-value sensitivity as a weighting signal, rather than performing hard copy updates. It achieves superior final performance on Atari benchmarks compared to DQN, Averaged DQN, DQN with layer normalisation, and PQN.
AI.motivation: Standard hard copy updates in DQNs introduce a tradeoff: they improve short-term stability by holding the target network fixed, but each abrupt replacement discards recent parameter history and can cause sudden changes in bootstrap targets, potentially removing useful value function structure. The authors aim to mitigate this by designing a more gradual, history-aware target network update.
AI.method: Memory Merge DQN maintains a short memory of recent online network copies and constructs the target network by merging parameters via weighted averaging. The weighting uses Q-value sensitivity (importance of parameters to current Q-value behavior) combined with a recency prior, inspired by Fisher Weight Model Merging but substituting Fisher information with Q-value sensitivity as the merging signal.
AI.result: Memory Merge DQN achieves the most first-place final performance results among all evaluated methods on Atari environments. It beats DQN, Averaged DQN, and PQN (with gradient clipping), with substantial gains in several games where preserving useful value-function parameters appears beneficial.
AI.conclusion: Selectively merging recent parameter history can improve DQN stability and final performance. Target network design is a crucial mechanism for preserving useful value function structure during long-horizon value learning.

title: The Ethics of Autonomous AI Agents for Offensive Security
summary: LLM-driven autonomous agents are reshaping offensive security. Unlike traditional penetration-testing tooling -- deterministic, narrowly scoped, and operated by trained practitioners -- agentic security tools exhibit \textit{indeterminacy} along three independent dimensions. First, their actions are drawn from a non-deterministic policy whose outputs resist both ex-ante and ex-post explanation, frustrating incident attribution and pre-deployment safety review. Second, their impact is open-ended due to the non-deterministic actions, agency of utilized models, and opaque LLM supply-chains. Third, their user population is indeterminate in both size and required skill: the operating skill floor for using or developing offensive capabilities has dropped sharply. These three properties are linked thematically, but are not derivable from one another. Combined with the structural cost asymmetry between offense and defense, they enable the industrialization of offensive capability. The net short-term effect favors attackers, even if the same technology may, in the long run, democratize access to defensive practice. Existing dual-use cybersecurity and AI-ethics frameworks were not designed for this combination. Our work analyzes how moral attribution becomes diffuse between users, tool-makers, and third parties when employing autonomous AI agents for offensive security. We also examine the stakeholder impact of this technology and provide stratified recommendations.

AI.tldr: LLM-driven autonomous agents introduce three forms of indeterminacy—action, impact, and user population—that reshape offensive security, favoring attackers in the short term and challenging existing dual-use and AI-ethics frameworks.
AI.motivation: Traditional penetration-testing tools are deterministic, narrowly scoped, and require skilled operators. The emergence of LLM-driven autonomous agents fundamentally alters this landscape by introducing non-determinism across multiple dimensions, yet existing cybersecurity dual-use frameworks and AI-ethics paradigms were not designed to address this new combination of properties, creating a regulatory and moral gap.
AI.method: The paper conducts a conceptual analysis identifying three independent but thematically linked dimensions of indeterminacy: (1) non-deterministic action policies resisting ex-ante and ex-post explanation, (2) open-ended impact stemming from non-deterministic actions, model agency, and opaque supply chains, and (3) indeterminate user population due to a collapsed skill floor. The authors then analyze how these properties interact with structural offense-defense cost asymmetry, examine the diffusion of moral attribution among users, tool-makers, and third parties, and assess stakeholder impact to produce stratified recommendations.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that the three indeterminacies collectively enable the industrialization of offensive capability, with a net short-term advantage for attackers. Moral attribution becomes irreducibly diffuse across users, developers, and third parties when autonomous AI agents are employed offensively. Existing dual-use and AI-ethics frameworks fail to adequately address this novel combination of properties.
AI.conclusion: The convergence of non-deterministic action, open-ended impact, and a drastically lowered skill barrier, combined with structural cost asymmetry favoring offense, produces a qualitatively new security landscape. While defensive applications may eventually benefit, the immediate imperative is to develop governance frameworks that account for diffuse moral attribution and the industrialized scale of AI-enabled offensive capability.

title: Overview of FinMMEval 2026 Task 1: Multilingual Financial Multiple-Choice Question Answering
comment: 9 pages. Task overview paper for CLEF 2026 Working Notes (CEUR Workshop Proceedings)
summary: FinMMEval 2026 Task 1 evaluates multilingual financial multiple-choice question answering in English, Chinese, Arabic, and Hindi. The task tests whether systems can select the correct answer to finance questions involving domain terminology, numerical interpretation, and conceptual financial reasoning across languages and scripts. The final-test set contains 800 questions, with 200 questions per language; gold answers were withheld during submission, and each language was ranked independently by accuracy. The final leaderboards contain 13 English, 11 Chinese, 11 Arabic, and 10 Hindi ranked submissions. Top accuracies range from 92.0% in Hindi to 97.5% in English and Arabic, with the same leading teams appearing near the top across all four languages. The documented systems used retrieval augmentation, direct answer-option scoring, language-specific prompting, selective self-consistency, confidence checks, and LLM-based review stages.

AI.tldr: FinMMEval 2026 Task 1 is a multilingual financial MCQ benchmark across English, Chinese, Arabic, and Hindi (800 questions total). Top systems achieved 92.0–97.5% accuracy using techniques like retrieval augmentation, answer-option scoring, and LLM-based review, with consistent leader performance across languages.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether systems can perform financial multiple-choice question answering across diverse languages and scripts, testing domain-specific terminology, numerical interpretation, and conceptual financial reasoning in a multilingual setting where each language is independently assessed.
AI.method: The shared task provides a final-test set of 800 questions (200 per language: English, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi) with withheld gold answers. Systems are ranked per language by accuracy. Participating approaches include retrieval-augmented generation, direct answer-option scoring, language-specific prompting, selective self-consistency, confidence checks, and LLM-based review stages.
AI.result: Top accuracies range from 92.0% (Hindi) to 97.5% (English and Arabic). The final leaderboards feature 13 English, 11 Chinese, 11 Arabic, and 10 Hindi ranked submissions, with leading teams consistently ranking near the top across all four languages.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual financial QA remains challenging, particularly for lower-resource languages like Hindi (lowest top accuracy). However, high English and Arabic scores and cross-language consistency among top teams suggest that retrieval augmentation and robust LLM-based strategies generalize well across languages and scripts in the financial domain.

title: Spectral-LSH: Sub-Quadratic Prompt Compression via Krylov-Projected Locality-Sensitive Hashing
summary:
Long-prompt inference remains expensive because prefill attention scales quadratically with sequence length. We propose Spectral-LSH, a training-free prompt compression method that operates before the prompt enters the language model. Spectral-LSH approximates the dominant components of an implicit attention-kernel operator using a Krylov subspace method together with random features, avoiding explicit $O(N^2)$ attention-kernel materialization. It then applies SimHash in the resulting attention eigenspace to group similar tokens and aggregate them into macro-tokens with causal positional assignments.
  We evaluate Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on C4. Our experiments reveal a compression-ratio phase transition. Below $ρ= 4 \times$, local token redundancy is low enough that lightweight chunking typically provides the best latency--quality trade-off. Above $ρ= 8 \times$, the spectral path preserves quality that chunking loses. At $ρ= 16 \times$, Qwen2.5-7B (adaptive) reduces the PPL ratio from 353.409 to 196.963, while Qwen2.5-14B (adaptive) reduces it from 9.533 to 3.427.
  On a small long-context structured stress test containing JSON-like, code-like, and table-like inputs, local LSH also improves every metric over chunking at $8 \times$. The adaptive backend captures both regimes by using the chunk path at low compression and spectral clustering at high compression, although chunking remains the fastest backend in total latency.

AI.tldr: Spectral-LSH is a training-free prompt compression method that uses Krylov subspace approximation with random features to avoid quadratic attention costs, then applies SimHash in attention eigenspace to group tokens into macro-tokens. It exhibits a phase transition: chunking is better below 4× compression, while the spectral approach preserves quality at 8×–16× compression, with an adaptive backend combining both regimes.
AI.motivation: Long-prompt inference is prohibitively expensive due to the quadratic scaling of prefill attention with sequence length. Existing prompt compression methods often degrade quality at high compression ratios, motivating a training-free method that can handle high compression without losing critical information.
AI.method: Spectral-LSH operates before the LM: (1) approximates dominant components of an implicit attention-kernel operator via a Krylov subspace method with random features, avoiding explicit O(N²) attention-kernel materialization; (2) applies SimHash in the resulting attention eigenspace to group semantically similar tokens; (3) aggregates grouped tokens into macro-tokens with causal positional assignments. An adaptive backend routes between lightweight chunking at low compression ratios and spectral clustering at high ratios.
AI.result: Evaluated on Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen2.5-14B using C4: a compression-ratio phase transition emerges — below 4×, chunking yields best latency-quality trade-off; above 8×, the spectral path preserves quality that chunking loses. At 16×, Qwen2.5-7B reduces PPL ratio from 353.41 to 196.96, and Qwen2.5-14B from 9.53 to 3.43. On structured stress tests (JSON/code/tables), local LSH improves all metrics over chunking at 8×. The adaptive backend captures both regimes effectively.
AI.conclusion: Spectral-LSH demonstrates that spectral approximation of attention structure enables effective prompt compression at high ratios (8×–16×) without training, while simple chunking suffices at low ratios. The phase transition motivates an adaptive dual-backend strategy, though chunking remains fastest overall in wall-clock latency.

title: Leveraging Offline Supervision for Efficient and Generalizable Reinforcement Learning in Large-Scale Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: It is commonly observed that online reinforcement learning (RL) produces better-performing strategies than offline methods across a broad range of performance measures. In particular, RL-trained policies exhibit stronger out-of-distribution (OOD) behavior, where models trained only with imitation learning approaches often struggle. A recent study introduced an OOD-focused benchmark and reported that RL-trained vision-language-action (VLA) policies achieve noticeably better OOD performance and slightly better in-distribution (IND) performance than their counterparts trained with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In this work, we investigate whether hybrid offline-online training can combine the advantages of both approaches. Specifically, we study RL methods regularized by offline supervision via either offline data or an offline-trained reference policy. We evaluate these approaches on the OOD benchmark and compare them with both offline-only training and standard RL. Our results show that although offline training achieves limited OOD performance by itself, incorporating offline supervision into RL preserves strong OOD capability while substantially improving training efficiency. In particular, the guided methods reach performance close to that of standard RL while requiring roughly half of the training budget. Rather than producing a trade-off between speed and OOD performance, the hybrid approach retains strong OOD capability while achieving this efficiency gain. Project page: https://alstar8.github.io/offline-supervision-vla-rl

AI.tldr: Hybrid offline-online training for VLA policies combines offline supervision with RL, maintaining strong OOD performance while halving the training budget compared to pure RL.
AI.motivation: Online RL produces better OOD performance than offline imitation learning for VLA policies, but pure RL is computationally expensive. The authors investigate whether hybrid offline-online training can combine the OOD robustness of RL with the efficiency benefits of offline supervision.
AI.method: The authors study RL methods regularized by offline supervision, using either offline data or an offline-trained reference policy. These guided RL approaches are evaluated on an existing OOD-focused benchmark and compared against offline-only (SFT) training and standard online RL baselines.
AI.result: Offline-only training achieves limited OOD performance. However, incorporating offline supervision into RL preserves strong OOD capability while substantially improving training efficiency. The guided methods reach performance close to standard RL while requiring roughly half the training budget, without trading off speed against OOD performance.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid offline-online training successfully combines the strengths of both paradigms: it retains the strong OOD generalization characteristic of RL while achieving significant efficiency gains through offline supervision, making it a practical alternative to pure online RL for training VLA policies.

title: Chained Attacks on Drone-Based Federated Learning: From Network Disruption to Device Impersonation
summary: Edge Intelligence (EI) has emerged as a transformative model for mission-critical unmanned platforms, such as drone swarms, by enabling collaborative model training at the network periphery. However, the security of FL deployments depends on both network availability and robust client authentication mechanisms. This paper investigates a chained attack against drone-based FL systems that combines network-layer denial-of-service with credential-based impersonation. We demonstrate that an adversary can: (1) force legitimate drones offline using 802.11 deauthentication attacks, and (2) subsequently impersonate the disconnected drone using extracted credentials. Through a systematic literature review and empirical validation using the Flower framework on two distinct testbeds of Raspberry Pi and Jetsons, we quantify the impact of availability disruptions under Independent and Identically Distributed (IID) and Non-Independently and Identically Distributed (Non-IID) data distributions, and confirm that single-factor authentication permits post-disconnect impersonation. Our findings reveal that even short-term wireless interruptions cascade into substantial training instability, particularly under non-IID conditions, while the authentication gap enables adversaries to seamlessly replace disconnected nodes. We discuss the compounded implications for mission-critical drone deployments and outline directions for future defenses addressing both availability and authentication vulnerabilities.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a chained attack against drone-based Federated Learning (FL) that combines 802.11 deauthentication attacks (network-layer DoS) with credential-based impersonation. Using Raspberry Pi and Jetson testbeds with the Flower framework, the authors demonstrate that short-term wireless disruptions cause cascading training instability — especially under Non-IID data — and that single-factor authentication allows adversaries to seamlessly replace disconnected nodes.
AI.motivation: Edge Intelligence and FL are critical for mission-critical unmanned platforms like drone swarms, but their security hinges on both network availability and robust client authentication. The authors identify a gap in existing research: no prior work has systematically studied the compounded effect of combining network-layer denial-of-service with post-disconnect impersonation in drone-based FL systems.
AI.method: The authors employ a two-pronged approach: (1) a systematic literature review to map the threat landscape, and (2) empirical validation using the Flower FL framework deployed across two distinct testbeds (Raspberry Pi and Jetson platforms). They simulate 802.11 deauthentication attacks to force legitimate drones offline, then impersonate disconnected drones using extracted credentials. Experiments are conducted under both IID and Non-IID data distributions to quantify the impact on training stability.
AI.result: Even short-term wireless interruptions cascade into substantial training instability, with significantly worse degradation under Non-IID conditions. Single-factor authentication is confirmed to be insufficient, as it permits adversaries to seamlessly replace disconnected nodes post-impersonation. The compounded availability + authentication attack creates a potent threat vector for mission-critical drone deployments.
AI.conclusion: The chained attack exposes a critical vulnerability in drone-based FL systems where availability and authentication weaknesses compound each other. The authors call for future defense mechanisms that simultaneously address both availability (network resilience) and authentication (multi-factor or continuous authentication) vulnerabilities to secure mission-critical edge intelligence deployments.

title: Overview of FinMMEval 2026 Task 2: Multilingual Financial Short-Answer Question Answering
comment: 9 pages. Task overview paper for CLEF 2026 Working Notes (CEUR Workshop Proceedings)
summary: FinMMEval 2026 Task 2 evaluates short-answer financial question answering over multilingual evidence. Each final-test item pairs an English question with financial statements and news in English, Chinese, Japanese, Spanish, and Greek. Participating systems submit one concise answer per item in JSONL format. The final-test set contains 256 items, split evenly between easy and expert tiers; each tier contains four question templates instantiated over 32 company-report groups. Gold answers were withheld during submission, and systems were ranked by macro-averaged item-level ROUGE-1 F1 against organizer-held reference answers. The final leaderboard includes 12 ranked submissions. The strongest systems are closely clustered, with the top four separated by less than one percentage point in ROUGE-1 F1. The submitted system papers document retrieval-augmented generation, cross-lingual evidence handling, structured prompting, answer compression, and validation strategies.

AI.tldr: FinMMEval 2026 Task 2 evaluates multilingual short-answer financial QA using English questions paired with evidence in five languages. Twelve systems are ranked on 256 items (easy/expert tiers) via macro-averaged ROUGE-1 F1, with top systems within 1% of each other.
AI.motivation: Financial question answering requires handling multilingual evidence sources (financial statements, news) across diverse languages, yet most QA benchmarks are monolingual. This task aims to spur development of systems that can retrieve and synthesize cross-lingual financial information to produce accurate short answers.
AI.method: The task provides English questions paired with financial statements and news in English, Chinese, Japanese, Spanish, and Greek. The test set contains 256 items divided into easy and expert tiers, each with four question templates instantiated over 32 company-report groups. Systems submit one concise answer per item in JSONL format. Ranking uses macro-averaged item-level ROUGE-1 F1 against hidden gold answers.
AI.result: Twelve systems were ranked on the final leaderboard. The top four systems are separated by less than one percentage point in ROUGE-1 F1. Submitted system papers document approaches including retrieval-augmented generation, cross-lingual evidence handling, structured prompting, answer compression, and validation strategies.
AI.conclusion: The close clustering of top-performing systems suggests that current approaches converge on effective strategies for multilingual financial QA, while the diversity of documented methods (RAG, structured prompting, answer compression) indicates multiple viable paths to strong performance. The task successfully benchmarks cross-lingual financial reasoning at scale.

title: Beyond Tracking or Shortcut: Composition-Bounded Predictive States in Poker Autoregressive Models
summary: Hidden-state probes often recover latent labels in imperfect-information sequence models, but this alone does not establish that a model maintains a posterior belief distribution over hidden states. This paper studies this ambiguity in a no-range Limit Hold'em autoregressive model trained only on action and value targets, not on an opponent's hand or range. Opponent-range probes are positive after action/value controls in two of three seeds, and the behavior head predicts held-out actions about five percentage points above a baseline using only observable public history. However, visible public betting composition explains more opponent-range signal than residual hidden states, suggesting that most recoverable information comes from betting summaries. Action/value+composition baselines reach 16.5-16.7% top-10 accuracy while composition-residual hidden probes fall to 11.4-12.2%, and matched-composition comparisons are negative in every seed. We call this evidence pattern composition-bounded predictive support: hidden states remain behavior-predictive and opponent-range correlated, but most recoverable range information is explained by visible betting composition rather than residual hidden-state structure. This is a case-study claim about opponent-range representational evidence, not exact Bayesian posterior tracking or a causal belief mechanism. Synthetic control and oracle validations show that the same diagnostics accept posterior-sensitive states and reject raw composition states under matched controls. Thus positive belief probes should be interpreted through targeted alternatives before being treated as evidence of belief tracking.

AI.tldr: Hidden-state probes in a poker model recover opponent-range information, but most of this signal is explained by visible betting composition rather than residual hidden states, challenging the interpretation that the model maintains posterior belief distributions over hidden states.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether positive hidden-state probes in imperfect-information sequence models genuinely indicate posterior belief tracking, or whether recoverable information merely reflects visible betting composition — addressing an ambiguity in interpreting probe results as evidence of belief representations.
AI.method: Train a no-range Limit Hold'em autoregressive model on action/value targets only. Probe hidden states for opponent-range information, controlling for action/value and betting composition. Compare full hidden-state probes against composition-residual probes. Validate diagnostics with synthetic controls that accept posterior-sensitive states and reject raw composition states under matched conditions.
AI.result: Opponent-range probes are positive in 2/3 seeds after action/value controls. Composition-residual probes drop from 16.5–16.7% to 11.4–12.2% top-10 accuracy, and matched-composition comparisons are negative in all seeds. Synthetic controls confirm the diagnostics discriminate posterior-sensitive from raw-composition states.
AI.conclusion: The evidence pattern — termed "composition-bounded predictive support" — shows hidden states remain behavior-predictive and opponent-range correlated, but most recoverable range information comes from visible betting composition. Positive belief probes should be evaluated against targeted alternatives before being interpreted as evidence of belief tracking.

title: Predictive single cell foundation model for gene regulation and aging with privacy-preserving tabular learning
comment: 98 pages, 4 main figures, and 15 supplementary figures
summary: Pre-trained foundation models (FMs) have begun transforming single-cell genomics, but scaling them raises privacy concerns. Moreover, unlike text data, single-cell data is unordered and exhibits a unique tabular structure that current single-cell FMs overlook. We introduce Tabula, a privacy-preserving FM designed with federated learning (FL) that explicitly models the tabular structure of single-cell data. To deploy Tabula, we further developed Chiron, a decentralized AI agent-enabled platform for collaborative training across institutions without sharing raw data. Beyond strong performance across downstream benchmarks, Tabula reveals combinatorial regulatory logic across diverse biological systems, including hematopoiesis, pancreatic endogenesis, neurogenesis, and cardiogenesis. Using a new scRNA-seq dataset of paired young and aged human fibroblasts, Tabula nominates rejuvenation factors through age- and identity score-guided in silico prioritization, outperforming conventional approaches. Thus, Tabula represents an important advance in single-cell foundation modeling by integrating tabular learning with FL, paving the way toward privacy-preserving virtual cells for human health.

AI.tldr: Tabula is a privacy-preserving single-cell foundation model that combines tabular structure-aware learning with federated learning, enabling collaborative training across institutions without sharing raw data, and demonstrates strong performance in regulatory logic discovery and rejuvenation factor nomination.
AI.motivation: Existing foundation models for single-cell genomics raise privacy concerns when scaled, and they overlook the unique unordered tabular structure of single-cell data (unlike text). There is a need for privacy-preserving collaborative training that respects this data structure.
AI.method: Tabula explicitly models the tabular structure of single-cell data using a privacy-preserving architecture trained via federated learning (FL). Deployment is facilitated by Chiron, a decentralized AI agent-enabled platform that enables cross-institutional collaborative training without raw data sharing. The model is evaluated on downstream benchmarks and applied to regulatory logic discovery across biological systems, as well as in silico prioritization of rejuvenation factors using age- and identity score guidance.
AI.result: Tabula achieves strong performance across downstream benchmarks. It reveals combinatorial regulatory logic in hematopoiesis, pancreatic endogenesis, neurogenesis, and cardiogenesis. Using a new paired young/aged human fibroblast scRNA-seq dataset, Tabula nominates rejuvenation factors via in silico prioritization and outperforms conventional approaches.
AI.conclusion: Tabula represents a significant advance in single-cell foundation modeling by integrating tabular learning with federated learning, enabling privacy-preserving collaborative training and paving the way toward virtual cells for human health applications.

title: Constant-time decoding of Gabidulin codes and their generalizations with application to RQC
summary: Gabidulin codes are a rank metric analog of Reed-Solomon codes. Although these codes are used in different very efficient rank-based cryptosystems like the RQC cryptosystem or the Loidreau cryptosystem, there was no constant-time implementation of Gabidulin codes, when having a constant-time implementation is crucial for real-life development of cryptosystems. In this paper, we propose the first constant-time decoding algorithm of Augmented Gabidulin (AG) codes, a simple variation on Gabidulin codes where one adds zero columns to Gabidulin codes, and which contains the case of Gabidulin codes. These AG codes are used in practice in the most efficient variations of the RQC cryptosystem. We prove that AG code decoding can be achieved with quadratic complexity. We further present a constant-time algorithm for the left division of $q$-polynomials along with a complete description of the AG code decoding procedure. These algorithms are integrated into the RQC-Block-MS-AG scheme, and we evaluate the performance of our implementation through benchmarks. Our results show that our implementation outperforms the original RQC, though it remains approximately four times slower than HQC. However, it achieves ciphertexts and key sizes about four times smaller, highlighting an appealing trade-off between performance and compactness.

AI.tldr: First constant-time decoding algorithm for Augmented Gabidulin (AG) codes, achieving quadratic complexity and enabling secure, efficient implementations for the RQC cryptosystem with significant size-performance trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Gabidulin codes are widely used in rank-based cryptosystems (e.g., RQC, Loidreau), yet no constant-time implementation existed. Constant-time implementations are crucial to prevent timing side-channel attacks in real-world cryptographic deployments.
AI.method: The authors design a constant-time decoding algorithm for Augmented Gabidulin (AG) codes — Gabidulin codes with added zero columns — which subsume standard Gabidulin codes. They develop a constant-time left division algorithm for q-polynomials and provide a full decoding procedure. The approach is integrated into the RQC-Block-MS-AG scheme and benchmarked.
AI.result: The decoding algorithm achieves quadratic complexity. Benchmarks show the implementation outperforms the original RQC scheme. Compared to HQC, it is ~4× slower but yields ciphertexts and key sizes ~4× smaller, demonstrating a favorable compactness-performance trade-off.
AI.conclusion: The proposed constant-time AG code decoding fills a critical gap in rank-based cryptography, enabling practical, side-channel-resistant deployments. The work highlights that AG-code-based schemes offer an appealing balance between performance and communication overhead.

title: Efficient Chain-of-Modality Reasoning via Progressive Compression for Spoken Language Models
summary: Spoken language models (SLMs) enable natural human-computer interaction, but their reasoning ability still lags behind that of text-based large language models, especially on spoken mathematical question answering tasks. One important reason is that SLMs reason over purely verbalized mathematical expressions, which are harder to interpret than symbolic text. However, directly transferring text-based reasoning to SLMs is nontrivial due to architectural constraints and the additional computational requirements. To address this challenge, we propose Efficient Chain-of-Modality Reasoning (ECoM Reasoning), the first framework to introduce compressed reasoning into SLMs. By compressing the textual component so that it jointly serves as speech guidance and reasoning representation, ECoM Reasoning improves reasoning accuracy while using a smaller token budget than the standard Chain-of-Modality (CoM) architecture, which generates intermediate text before speech. To train this capability, we further propose Progressive Compression, a curriculum-based strategy that gradually trains the model from full-form reasoning to compressed reasoning. Experiments on spoken mathematical question answering benchmarks show that ECoM Reasoning improves accuracy by 21% over standard CoM without explicit reasoning, and by 3% over CoM with full reasoning traces while using only 40% of the text tokens, demonstrating that it enhances SLM reasoning while remaining inference-efficient.

AI.tldr: ECoM Reasoning introduces compressed textual reasoning into spoken language models (SLMs), improving reasoning accuracy on spoken math QA tasks by 3% over full Chain-of-Modality while using only 40% of the text tokens.
AI.motivation: Spoken language models struggle with mathematical reasoning because they operate over verbalized expressions that are harder to interpret than symbolic text. Directly transferring text-based reasoning to SLMs is challenging due to architectural constraints and computational overhead.
AI.method: The authors propose Efficient Chain-of-Modality (ECoM) Reasoning, which compresses the textual reasoning component so it jointly serves as speech guidance and reasoning representation, reducing token budget. They also introduce Progressive Compression, a curriculum-based training strategy that gradually transitions the model from full-form reasoning to compressed reasoning.
AI.result: ECoM Reasoning achieves a 21% accuracy improvement over standard CoM without explicit reasoning, and a 3% improvement over CoM with full reasoning traces, while using only 40% of the text tokens.
AI.conclusion: ECoM Reasoning effectively enhances SLM reasoning capabilities in an inference-efficient manner, demonstrating that compressed reasoning representations can match or surpass full-text reasoning traces on spoken mathematical QA benchmarks.

title: Mitigating Scaffolding Collapse in Socratic Tutors via Representation Alignment
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based Socratic tutors increasingly guide students through multi-turn questioning, but they can suffer from scaffolding collapse: under sustained student pressure, a tutor gradually abandons guided inquiry and reveals solutions directly. Prior defenses primarily constrain observable responses through prompting, preference optimization, or filtering, leaving the internal representation drift that precedes trajectory-level collapse largely unaddressed. We propose Scaffold-Preserving Representation Alignment, a two-stage framework that first warms up a Socratic tutor with supervised fine-tuning, then combines trajectory-weighted direct preference optimization with a margin-preserving representation loss anchored to frozen reference states. Our method is designed to maintain separation between scaffold-preserving and collapse-inducing hidden states across dialogue turns. We evaluate our method across five STEM disciplines and five red-teaming attack strategies. On Qwen3-8B, our method lowers Collapse Rate to 32%, delays average collapse onset beyond nine turns, and keeps over-refusal low, suggesting that representation-level alignment can improve the robustness of long-horizon Socratic tutoring under our red-teaming protocol.

AI.tldr: To prevent LLM Socratic tutors from prematurely revealing answers under student pressure, the authors propose a two-stage framework that combines representation-level alignment with trajectory-weighted preference optimization, achieving lower collapse rates and delayed collapse onset across multiple STEM disciplines and attack strategies.
AI.motivation: LLM-based Socratic tutors suffer from "scaffolding collapse," where sustained student pressure causes the tutor to abandon guided inquiry and directly reveal solutions. Prior defenses (prompting, preference optimization, filtering) only constrain observable outputs, leaving internal representation drift unaddressed. The authors aim to tackle this representation-level vulnerability.
