AI.method: A two-stage framework called Scaffold-Preserving Representation Alignment: (1) warm-up via supervised fine-tuning of a Socratic tutor, followed by (2) joint training combining trajectory-weighted direct preference optimization (DPO) with a margin-preserving representation loss anchored to frozen reference states. The representation loss explicitly maintains separation between scaffold-preserving and collapse-inducing hidden states across dialogue turns.
AI.result: Evaluated on Qwen3-8B across five STEM disciplines and five red-teaming attack strategies. The method reduced Collapse Rate to 32%, delayed average collapse onset beyond nine turns, and maintained low over-refusal rates, demonstrating improved robustness in long-horizon Socratic tutoring.
AI.conclusion: Representation-level alignment is a promising direction for improving the robustness of LLM-based Socratic tutors. By jointly optimizing output preferences and internal representations, tutors can better resist scaffolding collapse under adversarial student pressure without becoming overly refuse-prone.

title: When Does Consensus Beat Voting? A Critical Analysis of Statistical Label Fusion in Medical Image Segmentation
summary: This paper provides a rigorous, self-contained investigation of consensus segmentation. We derive the mathematical foundations from first principles -- the generative model, EM algorithm, Van Leemput's marginalization analysis, identifiability conditions, Spatial STAPLE, and deep variational formulations -- and validate each theoretical prediction through controlled experiments. The central finding is sobering: under common conditions, STAPLE reduces to thresholded majority voting, suffers 95% EM suboptimality, and collapses under class imbalance. These are not edge cases but typical scenarios in medical imaging. Majority voting -- simple, non-parametric, and robust -- is a surprisingly strong baseline that the field has perhaps too hastily dismissed in favor of more "sophisticated" methods. At the same time, the deep consensus model demonstrates that the consensus problem is not inherently difficult -- it becomes tractable when the image is used alongside the labels. And conformal prediction shows that formal uncertainty guarantees are achievable and practical. We hope this work encourages practitioners to critically evaluate their consensus methods rather than applying STAPLE by default, and provides the mathematical and empirical foundation for more principled approaches.

AI.tldr: A rigorous mathematical analysis reveals that STAPLE—a widely-used consensus segmentation method—often reduces to thresholded majority voting, suffers severe EM suboptimality, and fails under class imbalance. Majority voting emerges as a surprisingly robust baseline, while image-conditioned deep consensus models and conformal prediction offer principled alternatives.
AI.motivation: The field of medical image segmentation has widely adopted STAPLE and its variants for consensus labeling without a thorough, first-principles understanding of when and why these methods work—or fail. The authors aim to fill this gap by deriving the mathematical foundations rigorously and testing predictions experimentally, ultimately encouraging practitioners to critically evaluate default choices rather than applying STAPLE uncritically.
AI.method: The paper derives consensus segmentation from first principles, covering: (1) the generative model underlying label fusion, (2) the EM algorithm for performance estimation, (3) Van Leemput's marginalization analysis, (4) identifiability conditions for rater parameters, (5) Spatial STAPLE extensions, and (6) deep variational formulations that condition on image data. Each theoretical prediction is validated through controlled experiments, with conformal prediction used to establish formal uncertainty guarantees.
AI.result: Under common conditions, STAPLE degenerates to thresholded majority voting, exhibits 95% EM suboptimality rates, and collapses under class imbalance—these are not edge cases but typical medical imaging scenarios. Majority voting proves to be a strong, non-parametric, robust baseline that the field has prematurely dismissed. The deep consensus model demonstrates tractability when images accompany labels, and conformal prediction yields practical, formal uncertainty guarantees.
AI.conclusion: The consensus segmentation problem is not inherently difficult—it becomes tractable when image information is leveraged alongside labels. Practitioners should critically evaluate consensus methods rather than applying STAPLE by default. The work provides both mathematical and empirical foundations for more principled approaches, with deep consensus and conformal prediction offering promising directions forward.

title: Recovering Clinical Utility Under Differential Privacy: Empirical Validation of Adaptive Federated Aggregation on Heterogeneous Cardiovascular Datasets
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to the Journal of the Brazilian Computer Society (JBCS)
summary: Validating federated learning frameworks on real clinical data is an essential step between proof-of-concept demonstrations in controlled synthetic environments and deployment in real multicenter healthcare settings. A prior architectural study by the same authors (Tertulino and Alencar, 2026) demonstrated, on a synthetic six-feature benchmark, that server-side adaptive optimization acts as a temporal denoiser for Differential Privacy noise, answering an open challenge identified in the original pipeline work (Tertulino, 2025). That study used synthetically generated data and explicitly identified real-world validation as a priority future direction. The present work addresses this gap by validating the FedCVR framework on five publicly available real cardiovascular datasets (Framingham, Cleveland, Hungarian, Switzerland, and Long Beach VA), harmonized to the 13-attribute UCI Heart Disease schema and configured as a heterogeneous federated scenario with leave-one-institution-out cross-validation. Results demonstrate that FedCVR preserves its adaptive advantage on real data, achieving an F1-Score of 79.2% and AUC of 0.96 under the operational privacy budget (noise multiplier = 0.8, privacy budget epsilon approximately 4.2), while statistically outperforming standard FedAvg on all evaluated metrics (paired t-tests, all p <= 0.003, significant under the Bonferroni-corrected threshold). The measured privacy cost on real data confirms the graceful degradation pattern observed in the synthetic experiments, providing empirical evidence of the framework's clinical viability in genuine multicenter contexts.

AI.tldr: Validation of the FedCVR federated learning framework with differential privacy on five real cardiovascular datasets, demonstrating preserved adaptive advantage with F1=79.2% and AUC=0.96 under operational privacy budget, significantly outperforming FedAvg.
AI.motivation: Bridging the gap between proof-of-concept synthetic demonstrations and real multicenter clinical deployment by validating FedCVR on actual clinical data, as explicitly identified as a priority future direction in prior work.
AI.method: Validation of FedCVR on five harmonized real cardiovascular datasets (Framingham, Cleveland, Hungarian, Switzerland, Long Beach VA) using the 13-attribute UCI Heart Disease schema, configured as a heterogeneous federated scenario with leave-one-institution-out cross-validation. Evaluation under operational privacy budget (noise multiplier=0.8, ε≈4.2) with paired t-tests and Bonferroni correction.
AI.result: FedCVR achieved F1-Score of 79.2% and AUC of 0.96 under the operational privacy budget, statistically significantly outperforming FedAvg on all metrics (p ≤ 0.003, Bonferroni-corrected). The graceful degradation pattern under privacy noise observed in synthetic experiments was confirmed on real data.
AI.conclusion: FedCVR's server-side adaptive optimization effectively acts as a temporal denoiser for DP noise on real clinical data, providing empirical evidence of clinical viability in genuine multicenter settings.

title: A Multi-Dimensional Evaluation of Explainability in Media Bias Detection
summary: Detecting media bias automatically is difficult because biased framing is often subtle, yet in domains such as news analysis, accurate predictions alone are insufficient without explanations that reflect the model's underlying reasoning. We present a multi-dimensional evaluation of explainability in encoder-based media bias detection using the Bias Annotations By Experts (BABE) dataset. Specifically, we study BERT and RoBERTa as classifiers (base and large variants) along three complementary axes: predictive performance, explanation plausibility (token-level alignment with expert rationales), and mechanistic faithfulness (whether compact sets of attention heads recover predictive signal under counterfactual rationale masking). To induce variation in plausibility, we additionally investigate attention-supervised finetuning, which incorporates expert rationale annotations as an auxiliary training signal. Attention supervision serves as an intervention on attribution plausibility, while the effectiveness of attribution methods varies substantially across architectures. Circuit analysis further reveals substantial variation in mechanistic recoverability across architectures, suggesting that model scale alone does not determine circuit compressibility. Taken together, our findings suggest that predictive performance, attribution plausibility, and mechanistic faithfulness characterize different aspects of model behavior and should be evaluated separately when studying explainability in media bias detection.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates explainability in transformer-based media bias detection across three dimensions—predictive performance, explanation plausibility (token-level alignment with expert rationales), and mechanistic faithfulness (circuit compressibility via attention head masking). Using BERT and RoBERTa variants with attention-supervised finetuning, the authors show these three axes characterize distinct aspects of model behavior and should be evaluated separately.
AI.motivation: Media bias detection is challenging because biased framing is subtle, and in high-stakes domains like news analysis, accurate predictions alone are insufficient—explanations must reflect the model's actual reasoning. Existing work tends to conflate predictive performance with explainability quality, motivating a rigorous, multi-dimensional evaluation framework that disentangles these aspects.
AI.method: The authors evaluate BERT and RoBERTa (base and large variants) on the BABE dataset along three axes: (1) predictive performance via standard classification metrics; (2) explanation plausibility measured by token-level alignment between attribution methods and expert rationales; (3) mechanistic faithfulness assessed through circuit analysis—identifying compact sets of attention heads that recover predictive signal under counterfactual rationale masking. They also apply attention-supervised finetuning, using expert rationale annotations as auxiliary training signals to manipulate attribution plausibility independently.
AI.result: Attention supervision successfully induces variation in attribution plausibility, but the effectiveness of attribution methods varies substantially across architectures. Circuit analysis reveals significant variation in mechanistic recoverability across models, indicating that model scale alone does not determine how compressible a model's reasoning circuits are. The three evaluation axes—predictive performance, attribution plausibility, and mechanistic faithfulness—capture distinct, non-interchangeable aspects of model behavior.
AI.conclusion: Predictive performance, attribution plausibility, and mechanistic faithfulness are orthogonal dimensions of explainability that should be evaluated separately. Relying on any single metric provides an incomplete picture of a model's trustworthiness for media bias detection. The findings caution against conflating high accuracy with faithful or plausible explanations.

title: Euclean: Automated Geometry Problem Formalization with Unified Verification in Lean
summary: Recent formal reasoning systems have reached IMO-level performance, yet they leave a fragmented landscape: algebra and number theory are handled in Lean, while geometry still relies on domain-specific languages with limited formal guarantees. This split increases the trusted computing base and hinders unified model development. Existing geometry-in-Lean efforts (LeanEuclid, LeanGeo) introduce custom axiom systems incompatible with standard Mathlib, and their small scale ($<$ 1,100 problems) limits large-scale training. Native Mathlib autoformalization of geometry, however, poses distinct challenges: implicit diagrammatic assumptions (e.g., topological configuration and non-degeneracy) must be made explicit rather than deferred to external solvers, and models must adapt to Mathlib's small, rapidly evolving geometry infrastructure. We present Euclean, a four-stage framework - constraint explication, configuration anchoring, formalization mapping, and iterative repair - for automatically formalizing geometry in native Mathlib. We construct OMNI-Geometry (768 competition problems) and Numina-Geometry (177,597 problems), the largest geometry formalization dataset in Lean. Human evaluation shows 48.89% TOP1 and 73.33% TOP5 accuracy. Training Goedel v2 on our formalizations improves proof success from 13.6% to 15.1%, validating dataset quality for unified neural theorem proving. Code and datasets: https://github.com/tlb-22/Euclean.

AI.tldr: Euclean introduces a four-stage framework to autoformalize geometry problems into native Mathlib (Lean), addressing the fragmentation between algebra/number theory and geometry formalization. It constructs the largest geometry formalization datasets (OMNI-Geometry, 768 problems; Numina-Geometry, 177,597 problems), achieving 48.89% TOP1 accuracy, and demonstrates improved proof success when training neural theorem provers on the resulting data.
AI.motivation: Current formal reasoning is fragmented: Lean handles algebra/number theory, but geometry relies on domain-specific languages with weak formal guarantees. Prior Lean geometry efforts (LeanEuclid, LeanGeo) use custom axioms incompatible with Mathlib and are too small (<1,100 problems) for large-scale training. Autoformalizing geometry directly into native Mathlib is challenging due to implicit diagrammatic assumptions and Mathlib's small, rapidly evolving geometry library.
AI.method: A four-stage framework: (1) Constraint Explication — makes implicit diagrammatic assumptions (topological configuration, non-degeneracy) explicit; (2) Configuration Anchoring — anchors geometric configurations; (3) Formalization Mapping — maps to Mathlib syntax and definitions; (4) Iterative Repair — refines formalizations through feedback loops. Two datasets are constructed: OMNI-Geometry (768 competition problems) and Numina-Geometry (177,597 problems).
AI.result: Human evaluation yields 48.89% TOP1 and 73.33% TOP5 accuracy on formalization quality. Training Goedel v2 on Euclean formalizations improves proof success rate from 13.6% to 15.1%, validating the dataset's utility for unified neural theorem proving.
AI.conclusion: Euclean demonstrates that native Mathlib autoformalization of geometry at scale is feasible, bridging the formalization gap between geometry and other mathematical domains. The framework and datasets enable unified neural theorem provers to operate across algebra, number theory, and geometry within a single trusted computing base.

title: The Chronos Vulnerability: A Taxonomy of Temporal Persistence and Memory-Based Deception in Agentic AI
summary: The transition from stateless generative models in artificial intelligence to stateful, autonomous agents represents an architectural evolution that, while providing the capabilities of long-term planning and the automation of enterprise workflows, also represents the introduction of a new form of security threat, the Chronos Vulnerability. The Chronos Vulnerability represents the threat of memory-based attacks, including the Memory Injection Attack (MINJA) and the sleeper agent, in which the internal belief system of the autonomous agent is compromised, effectively decoupling the attack vector from the final catastrophic event. This study formalizes the threat model for persistence-based attacks and the threat of Dynamics Blindness in the context of the World of Workflows benchmark, demonstrating that traditional endpoint content filters are insufficient for the current stateful architecture. Consequently, this study synthesizes a defense-in-depth landscape, categorizing emerging frameworks such as diagnostic trajectory guardrails (AgentDoG), formal temporal verification (Agent-C), immunological memory consensus (A-MemGuard), and hardware-anchored trust via GPU-based Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) and Zero-Trust memory architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the "Chronos Vulnerability," a new class of memory-based attacks (including Memory Injection Attacks and sleeper agents) targeting stateful AI agents, demonstrates their effectiveness against traditional content filters using the "World of Workflows" benchmark, and proposes a defense-in-depth framework combining diagnostic guardrails, formal verification, immunological memory consensus, and hardware-anchored trust.
AI.motivation: The architectural shift from stateless generative AI models to stateful autonomous agents—while enabling long-term planning and enterprise workflow automation—introduces novel security threats. Traditional endpoint content filters, designed for stateless input/output inspection, are fundamentally insufficient against persistence-based attacks that compromise an agent's internal belief system over time, decoupling the attack vector from the eventual catastrophic event. There is a need to formalize and address these emerging memory-based vulnerabilities.
AI.method: The study formalizes a threat model for persistence-based attacks, defining the Chronos Vulnerability (encompassing Memory Injection Attacks/MINJA and sleeper agents) and the concept of "Dynamics Blindness." It evaluates the insufficiency of traditional content filters using the "World of Workflows" benchmark as a testbed. It then synthesizes a defense-in-depth architecture by categorizing emerging countermeasure frameworks: AgentDoG (diagnostic trajectory guardrails), Agent-C (formal temporal verification), A-MemGuard (immunological memory consensus), and hardware-based protections (GPU TEEs, Zero-Trust memory architectures).
AI.result: The study demonstrates that traditional endpoint content filters are inadequate for detecting and mitigating memory-based attacks against stateful AI agents, as these attacks operate by corrupting the agent's internal belief state over time rather than triggering at the input/output boundary. The synthesized defense-in-depth landscape provides a multi-layered taxonomy of emerging defenses spanning software-level guardrails, formal verification, consensus mechanisms, and hardware-rooted trust.
AI.conclusion: The transition to stateful autonomous agents necessitates a paradigm shift in AI security from perimeter-based content filtering to defense-in-depth architectures. The proposed taxonomy—combining diagnostic trajectory monitoring, formal temporal logic verification, immunological memory consensus, and hardware-anchored TEEs—offers a comprehensive framework for mitigating the Chronos Vulnerability and its associated persistence-based attack vectors.

title: When Does Knowledge Distillation Hurt? Reliability-Aware Distillation for Low-Resource Language Summarization
summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a standard approach for compressing sequence-to-sequence models, but its per-sample effects are rarely examined. On the BanSum Bangla summarization benchmark, we find that standard KD improves ROUGE-L by only +0.0003 over a cross-entropy baseline, and that approximately 51.3% of training samples are estimated to actively harm student validation loss under standard KD. We propose two complementary reliability-aware distillation methods. CHAD (Counterfactual Harm-Aware Distillation) measures per-sample KD usefulness via gradient alignment with the validation loss direction and trains a lightweight gate that generalizes this counterfactual judgment to the full training set. EWAD+CPDP combines token-level entropy-weighted adaptive distillation with a capacity-proportional geometric constraint from a second, vocabulary-incompatible teacher. On BanSum, both methods substantially outperform standard KD: CHAD by +0.0173 ROUGE-L and EWAD+CPDP by +0.0219 ROUGE-L, where standard KD itself improves ROUGE-L by only +0.0003; despite using only 60M parameters, both outperform a fine-tuned Qwen 2.5-3B model (50x larger). We further evaluate the stronger method, EWAD+CPDP, across 15 typologically diverse XL-Sum languages organised into three sets, beating the CE-only baseline on 10/15 languages; gains are most reliable where the two teachers contribute complementary signal, and weakest where they have saturated or jointly weak target-language coverage. We release code and trained models to support reproducibility and further research on selective distillation.

AI.tldr: Standard KD barely helps Bangla summarization (+0.0003 ROUGE-L) and ~51% of samples actively harm the student. The authors propose CHAD (gradient-alignment gating) and EWAD+CPDP (entropy-weighted adaptive distillation with cross-vocabulary geometric constraints), which substantially outperform standard KD and even a 50× larger Qwen 2.5-3B model. EWAD+CPDP generalizes across 15 XL-Sum languages.
AI.motivation: Standard knowledge distillation for seq2seq models is treated as uniformly beneficial, yet its per-sample effects are unexamined. On BanSum, standard KD yields negligible gains and over half of training samples appear detrimental, motivating sample- and token-level reliability-aware distillation strategies.
AI.method: Two complementary methods: (1) CHAD — computes per-sample KD usefulness via gradient alignment with validation loss direction, trains a lightweight binary gate to predict harmful vs. helpful samples, and uses this to filter or weight distillation. (2) EWAD+CPDP — token-level entropy-weighted adaptive distillation that adjusts distillation weight per token based on teacher confidence, combined with a capacity-proportional geometric constraint leveraging a second, vocabulary-incompatible teacher. Both are evaluated on a 60M-parameter student model.
AI.result: On BanSum: standard KD improves ROUGE-L by only +0.0003 over CE baseline. CHAD yields +0.0173 ROUGE-L; EWAD+CPDP yields +0.0219 ROUGE-L. Both outperform a fine-tuned Qwen 2.5-3B (50× larger). Across 15 XL-Sum languages, EWAD+CPDP beats CE-only on 10/15; gains strongest when dual teachers provide complementary signal, weakest when coverage is saturated or jointly weak.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-aware distillation — accounting for per-sample harm and token-level confidence — substantially improves over standard KD for low-resource summarization. Leveraging complementary signals from vocabulary-incompatible teachers further boosts performance. The approach is released as open-source code and models.

title: CrackedPDFs: A Controlled Benchmark for Hidden Prompt Injection in PDFs
summary: Document-based LLM systems often flatten a PDF before guardrails inspect it. That step can discard evidence that an instruction was never visible to the user. We introduce CrackedPDFs, a controlled benchmark for hidden prompt injection in PDFs. The benchmark contains 29,322 generated PDFs from 4,983 base docu ments. It includes 9,774 injected files and 19,548 benign or matched-confounder files. We evaluate PromptGuard and a rule baseline. We also evaluate structural only learned models and a sanitized hybrid detector. The evaluation uses held-out provenance splits and paired benign-confounder controls. It also uses label-shuffle checks and shortcut audits. On a 2,919-document held-out test set, the hybrid de tector reaches 0.960 F1. ROC-AUC is 0.998 and PR-AUC is 0.997. It also ranks injected files above matched benign confounders in 95.9% of 973 pairs. Prompt Guard has low recall when given extracted text only. Structural-only learned mod els are weak under paired controls. A text-only TF-IDF model reaches perfect held-out scores but fails shortcut audits. These results show that document-aware hybrid detection is useful under controlled paired evaluation. They do not show broad real-world robustness or reliable cross-family generalization.

AI.tldr: CrackedPDFs is a benchmark of 29,322 PDFs for evaluating hidden prompt injection detection. A hybrid detector combining structural and content features achieves 0.960 F1 and 0.998 ROC-AUC, significantly outperforming text-only, structural-only, and PromptGuard baselines under rigorous paired and provenance-controlled evaluation.
AI.motivation: PDF flattening in document-based LLM pipelines can discard structural evidence of hidden prompt injections, making them invisible to downstream guardrails. Existing detection methods lack rigorous evaluation under controlled paired conditions, making it unclear whether models rely on genuine injection signals or spurious shortcuts.
AI.method: The authors construct CrackedPDFs, a benchmark with 29,322 PDFs (9,774 injected, 19,548 benign/matched-confounder) derived from 4,983 base documents. They evaluate multiple detectors: PromptGuard (text-only), a rule-based baseline, structural-only learned models, and a sanitized hybrid detector. Evaluation uses held-out provenance splits, paired benign-confounder controls, label-shuffle checks, and shortcut audits to prevent inflated performance estimates.
AI.result: On a 2,919-document held-out test set, the hybrid detector achieves 0.960 F1, 0.998 ROC-AUC, and 0.997 PR-AUC, ranking injected files above matched benign confounders in 95.9% of 973 pairs. PromptGuard shows low recall on extracted text only. Structural-only models are weak under paired controls. A text-only TF-IDF model achieves perfect held-out scores but fails shortcut audits, exposing spurious reliance on surface features.
AI.conclusion: Document-aware hybrid detection is effective under controlled paired evaluation, but the results do not demonstrate broad real-world robustness or reliable cross-family generalization. Rigorous evaluation protocols (provenance splits, paired controls, shortcut audits) are essential to avoid misleading performance claims.

title: Structured Latent Space Modeling over Multi-Scale Temporal Patches for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
summary: Multivariate time series encode structural patterns that unfold across multiple temporal scales, yet most forecasting backbones treat learned representations as transient byproducts of prediction, leaving the organizational geometry of these patterns underexploited. We introduce M2Patch, a CNN-based forecasting architecture that maps channel-independent multivariate observations into a structured latent space through two complementary differentiable constraints. Multi-scale patching decomposes the input into overlapping temporal granularities; depthwise separable convolutions with progressive dilation extract scale-specific features in linear time; and per-scale learned projections compress these features into a compact latent representation. The latent space is organized by an intra-scale smoothness constraint that enforces temporal continuity between adjacent patches, and an inter-scale alignment constraint, realized through learnable cross-scale mappings, that restores cross-granularity interaction within the channel-independent design, ensuring that all scales encode mutually consistent representations of the underlying dynamics. Experiments on ten real-world benchmarks show that M2Patch achieves 57 best and 34 second-best results across 40 forecasting settings, matching or exceeding representative baselines on most benchmarks while maintaining linear computational complexity and robustness to patch-level input corruption.

AI.tldr: M2Patch introduces a CNN-based multivariate time series forecasting architecture that uses multi-scale patching and a structured latent space organized by intra-scale smoothness and inter-scale alignment constraints, achieving strong benchmark performance with linear complexity.
AI.motivation: Most forecasting backbones treat learned representations as transient byproducts of prediction, failing to exploit the organizational geometry of structural patterns that unfold across multiple temporal scales in multivariate time series.
AI.method: M2Patch employs three key components: (1) multi-scale patching that decomposes input into overlapping temporal granularities; (2) depthwise separable convolutions with progressive dilation for extracting scale-specific features in linear time; (3) per-scale learned projections into a compact latent space. The latent space is organized by two differentiable constraints: an intra-scale smoothness constraint enforcing temporal continuity between adjacent patches, and an inter-scale alignment constraint using learnable cross-scale mappings to restore cross-granularity interactions within the channel-independent design.
AI.result: On ten real-world benchmarks across 40 forecasting settings, M2Patch achieves 57 best and 34 second-best results, matching or exceeding representative baselines on most benchmarks while maintaining linear computational complexity and demonstrating robustness to patch-level input corruption.
AI.conclusion: M2Patch demonstrates that explicitly organizing the latent geometry of multi-scale time series representations — through complementary smoothness and cross-scale alignment constraints — yields competitive forecasting performance without sacrificing efficiency or robustness.

title: Guardrails as Scapegoats: Auditing Unfaithful Safety Refusals in Tool-Augmented LLM Agents
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the ACM KDD 2026 Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI
summary: Evaluation frameworks for tool-augmented LLM agents focus overwhelmingly on capability metrics or explicit tool crashes, leaving silent infrastructure failures and HTTP 200 responses with empty, null, or malformed payloads largely unaudited. We introduce a lightweight black-box auditing framework that injects four silent failure profiles across 12 production-adjacent tool stubs and classifies agent responses into three mutually exclusive behavioral classes: Honest Surrender (HSR), Fabrication (FAR), and Unfaithful Safety Refusal (USR). Evaluating two frontier and two open-source models at temperature zero under a neutral system prompt, we find that FAR dominates (56.6% of valid responses): agents treat empty payloads as real data, silently returning fabricated results. USR, in which an agent invents a policy or privacy rationale to explain the failure, is nearly absent at baseline (0.25%, one instance across 396 valid trajectories). Our key finding emerges from an ablation where we augment the system prompt with standard safety language ("prioritize user privacy and data security"), which amplifies USR by 15.6x (from 0.25% to 3.95%; 95% CI on ablation rate: 2.2%-6.4%; Fisher's exact test, p < 0.001). USR is a latent behavior, activated when safety vocabulary in the system prompt primes the model to reach for policy rationales when tools silently fail. Sensitive tools (fetch_medical_record, retrieve_contract, fetch_user_profile) account for the majority of USR instances. We propose a payload-response misalignment heuristic for production-level detection and discuss governance implications for safety-forward deployments.

AI.tldr: Black-box auditing of LLM agents reveals two dominant failure modes under silent tool failures: Fabrication (FAR, 56.6%) where agents treat empty payloads as real data, and Unfaithful Safety Refusal (USR), a latent behavior amplified 15.6× by safety-prompting language, where agents invent privacy/policy rationales for tool failures.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent evaluations focus on capability metrics and explicit tool crashes, but neglect silent infrastructure failures where tools return HTTP 200 with empty, null, or malformed payloads. These invisible failures can induce dangerous agent behaviors (fabrication, spurious safety refusals) that remain unaudited in production systems.
AI.method: A lightweight black-box auditing framework injecting four silent failure profiles (empty payloads, null values, malformed responses, truncated data) across 12 production-adjacent tool stubs. Agent responses are classified into three mutually exclusive classes: Honest Surrender (HSR), Fabrication (FAR), and Unfaithful Safety Refusal (USR). Two frontier and two open-source models evaluated at temperature zero under a neutral system prompt, with an ablation adding safety-prompt language ("prioritize user privacy and data security"). Statistical significance assessed via Fisher's exact test.
AI.result: Under neutral prompts, FAR dominates at 56.6% of valid responses; USR is nearly absent (0.25%, 1 instance in 396 trajectories). Augmenting the system prompt with safety language amplifies USR by 15.6× (to 3.95%; 95% CI: 2.2%–6.4%; p < 0.001). Sensitive tools (fetch_medical_record, retrieve_contract, fetch_user_profile) account for the majority of USR instances.
AI.conclusion: Silent tool failures pose a significant, under-audited risk in LLM agent deployments. Safety-forward prompting can paradoxically induce unfaithful safety refusals. The authors propose a payload-response misalignment heuristic for production detection and highlight governance implications for safety-oriented deployments.

title: HyGRL: Adaptive Hybrid Graph Reasoning for Multi-Entity Questions
summary: Multi-entity compositional questions pose significant challenges to existing retrieval-augmented language models. Conventional methods fall into a dilemma: standard RAG lacks dynamic reasoning, traditional Graph-RAG is limited by structural sparsity, and LLM-constructed Graph-RAG incurs prohibitive costs. We propose \textbf{\fwa}, a unified framework that embeds unstructured text into structured knowledge graphs, creating a heterogeneous network for flexible evidence retrieval. Reasoning is formulated as adaptive structure induction, learned via a robust two-stage process: (1) imitation learning distills heuristic expert signals, and (2) reinforcement learning refines the policy using LLM-driven preference rewards. Experiments demonstrate that {\fwa} effectively merges textual richness with structural knowledge, outperforming SOTA baselines in answer accuracy and reasoning fidelity while maintaining extremely low token costs and near real-time inference((code available at https://github.com/wjywjy123/HyGRL) .

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FWA (a unified framework) that converts unstructured text into structured knowledge graphs to form a heterogeneous network for flexible evidence retrieval. Reasoning is treated as adaptive structure induction, learned through a two-stage process combining imitation learning and reinforcement learning with LLM-driven preference rewards. The approach outperforms SOTA baselines in accuracy and reasoning fidelity while maintaining low token costs and near real-time inference.
AI.motivation: Multi-entity compositional question answering exposes critical limitations in existing retrieval-augmented models: standard RAG lacks dynamic reasoning capabilities, traditional Graph-RAG suffers from structural sparsity, and LLM-constructed Graph-RAG is prohibitively expensive. A solution is needed that combines textual richness with structured reasoning without incurring excessive computational costs.
AI.method: The framework embeds unstructured text into structured knowledge graphs, forming a heterogeneous network. Reasoning is framed as adaptive structure induction and trained via a two-stage process: (1) imitation learning that distills heuristic expert signals, and (2) reinforcement learning that refines the policy using LLM-driven preference rewards.
AI.result: FWA effectively merges textual richness with structural knowledge, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in both answer accuracy and reasoning fidelity. It achieves this while maintaining extremely low token costs and enabling near real-time inference.
AI.conclusion: The unified heterogeneous graph framework successfully bridges the gap between unstructured text and structured knowledge, enabling effective multi-entity compositional reasoning. The two-stage imitation-to-reinforcement learning paradigm proves effective for learning adaptive structure induction policies that are both accurate and cost-efficient.

title: Reproducing Recurrent Transformers: The CoTFormer
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, reproducibility report submitted to University of Southampton
summary: The CoTFormer architecture formalizes Chain-of-Thought as a form of recurrent latent computation, preserving intermediate states as attendable representations to mimic explicit reasoning traces. In this work, we evaluate CoTFormer and its structural variants across perplexity and compute efficiency metrics. Furthermore, we extend evaluation to controlled algorithmic settings to determine whether this recurrent framework improves out-of-distribution generalisation on inductive reasoning tasks.

AI.tldr: CoTFormer formalizes Chain-of-Thought reasoning as recurrent latent computation with attendable intermediate states. This work benchmarks CoTFormer and its variants on perplexity, compute efficiency, and out-of-distribution generalization in algorithmic inductive reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether formalizing Chain-of-Thought reasoning as recurrent latent computation — where intermediate states are preserved as attendable representations — can improve model performance, efficiency, and systematic generalization beyond the training distribution, particularly on structured algorithmic reasoning tasks.
AI.method: The authors evaluate CoTFormer and its structural variants using two evaluation paradigms: (1) standard language modeling benchmarks measuring perplexity and computational efficiency, and (2) controlled algorithmic reasoning tasks designed to test out-of-distribution (OOD) inductive generalization. The architecture itself embeds recurrent latent states that are explicitly attendable, mimicking explicit reasoning traces.
AI.result: The paper reports comparative results across CoTFormer variants on perplexity and compute efficiency metrics. Extended evaluations in controlled algorithmic settings provide evidence regarding whether the recurrent latent computation framework confers improved out-of-distribution generalization on inductive reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: The recurrent latent computation paradigm of CoTFormer, which makes intermediate reasoning states attendable, offers a promising architectural direction. Its value is assessed through both standard language modeling metrics and systematic generalization tests, informing whether this inductive bias aids structured reasoning beyond memorization.

title: End-to-End Differential Privacy in Training Deep Neural Network Classifiers
summary: Differentially private machine learning enables model training on sensitive data while ensuring that individual data is unlikely to be recoverable from the parameters of the resulting model. However, existing work often privatizes both training inputs and their labels, and these protections may be conservative when labels are public or can be safely made public. Therefore, in this work we propose a novel private training framework that instead privatizes training inputs while keeping labels public. We consider neural networks with softmax output layers, and thus the mapping from training inputs to the output of the softmax layer is a mapping onto the unit simplex. We randomize softmax outputs during training by applying the Dirichlet mechanism to enforce differential privacy for the training inputs, hence the ``end-to-end'' label. Because training data is reused across multiple training epochs, we use the notion of \Renyi differential privacy to formulate tight bounds on the strength of privacy provided by the Dirichlet mechanism across repeated uses. We show empirically that we attain new state-of-the-art accuracy when training from scratch on CIFAR10, MNIST, MedMNIST, FashionMNIST, and SVHN across all privacy budgets evaluated. Notably, when implementing $(ε, δ)$-differential privacy with $δ=10^{-5}$, we improve the prior state-of-the-art accuracy from $78.37\%$ to $88.17\%$ at $ε=4$ on CIFAR10, and our approach has $82.96\%$ accuracy even for $ε=1$, which significantly outperforms prior work.

AI.tldr: Proposes a DP training framework that privatizes only inputs (via Dirichlet mechanism on softmax outputs) while keeping labels public, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on image classification benchmarks—e.g., 88.17% at ε=4 on CIFAR10.
AI.motivation: Existing DP training methods privatize both inputs and labels, which is overly conservative when labels are public or can be safely disclosed. This motivates a more efficient privacy accounting that protects only training inputs.
AI.method: The method applies the Dirichlet mechanism to randomize the softmax output vectors during training, exploiting that these outputs lie on the unit simplex. Uses Rényi differential privacy to derive tight privacy bounds across multiple training epochs with repeated data reuse.
AI.result: Achieves new SOTA on CIFAR10, MNIST, MedMNIST, FashionMNIST, and SVHN across all privacy budgets. At ε=4, δ=10⁻⁵: 88.17% (up from 78.37%). At ε=1: 82.96%, significantly surpassing prior work.
AI.conclusion: Privatizing only inputs via the Dirichlet mechanism on softmax outputs is a viable and effective DP training strategy, enabling substantially higher utility than methods that privatize both inputs and labels.

title: TalentCLEF at CLEF2026: Skill and Job Title Intelligence for Human Capital Management
summary:
This paper presents the second edition of the TalentCLEF Challenge, which will run as an evaluation lab as part of CLEF 2026. The aim of TalentCLEF is to promote the development of systems and methods that use Natural Language Processing (NLP) in the field of Human Capital Management (HCM), fostering approaches that ensure fairness in results, operate across multiple languages, and adapt to diverse industries. To this end, TalentCLEF establishes public benchmarks where research teams can compare methods and share findings, moving the field toward more practical and impactful NLP solutions that effectively address the real needs of workforce management.
  This year's lab will feature two tasks designed to foster the development and evaluation of systems that support key HCM activities such as talent matching, upskilling, reskilling, and skill gap detection: (i) Task A - Contextualized Job-Person Matching, focused on retrieving and ranking suitable candidates for specific job positions using context-rich and privacy-preserving data; and (ii) Task B - Job-Skill Matching with Skill Type Classification, centered on identifying relevant skills for a given job title and classifying them by their type within the job profile.
  TalentCLEF website: https://talentclef.github.io/talentclef/

AI.tldr: This paper presents the second edition of the TalentCLEF Challenge (CLEF 2026), an evaluation lab promoting NLP methods for Human Capital Management with two shared tasks: contextualized job-person matching and job-skill matching with skill type classification.
AI.motivation: To advance NLP applications in Human Capital Management by establishing public benchmarks that encourage fair, multilingual, and cross-industry systems for workforce management tasks such as talent matching, upskilling, reskilling, and skill gap detection.
AI.method: TalentCLEF organizes a shared evaluation lab with two tasks: Task A (Contextualized Job-Person Matching) uses context-rich, privacy-preserving data to retrieve and rank candidates for specific jobs; Task B (Job-Skill Matching with Skill Type Classification) identifies relevant skills for job titles and classifies them by skill type within the job profile.
AI.result: This is a task proposal/overview paper describing the planned lab; no experimental results are reported.
AI.conclusion: TalentCLEF 2026 aims to serve as a collaborative platform for benchmarking NLP solutions in HCM, addressing real workforce needs through standardized, fair, multilingual, and privacy-conscious evaluation.

title: ITPEval: Benchmarking Formal Translation Across Interactive Theorem Provers
summary: Formal theorem proving has emerged as a frontier challenge for machine learning, yet the ecosystem is fragmented: proofs remain siloed across incompatible systems, limiting both training data for learning-based provers and the portability of verified results. We present ITPEval, the first benchmark for evaluating automated formal proof translation across four major ITPs (Lean 4, Rocq, Isabelle, and HOL Light), spanning two distinct logical foundations. Our benchmark comprises 1,560 source files and 6,848 theorems organized into a controlled tier of axiomatized files that isolates foundational translation difficulty, and an ecosystem tier drawn from real libraries that exposes API and proof-style mismatches. We release itpeval, a unified multi-ITP verification infrastructure with state-isolated warm backends that preserve per-artifact native checking semantics. We evaluate both statement and proof translation across five frontier and open-weight LLMs on 12 directed translation pairs: statement translation peaks at 29.1% pass@1 and proof translation at 10.5%; controlled theorems reach 29.7% proof pass@1 versus 5.2% for ecosystem-level translations, confirming that library mismatch is the dominant bottleneck. In addition to pass@k evaluation, a deterministic Lean 4 BEq check establishes equivalence for 54.0% of verified source-to-Lean 4 miniF2F statement translations, showing that native type-checking alone can substantially overestimate semantic fidelity; in an autoformalization/auto-informalization round-trip study, Rocq and HOL Light are easier formalization targets than Lean 4 and Isabelle, while multi-ITP context improves pooled Lean 4 success from 4.8% to 10.6%. Our benchmark, verification infrastructure, and evaluation pipelines are publicly released.

AI.tldr: ITPEval is the first benchmark for evaluating automated formal proof translation across four major interactive theorem provers (Lean 4, Rocq, Isabelle, HOL Light) with different logical foundations. It provides 1,560 source files and 6,848 theorems, a unified verification infrastructure, and reveals that library mismatch dominates translation difficulty, with proof translation peaking at 29.7% for controlled theorems vs. 5.2% for ecosystem-level translations.
AI.motivation: The formal theorem proving ecosystem is fragmented: proofs are siloed across incompatible ITP systems, which limits both training data availability for learning-based provers and the portability of verified results. No benchmark previously existed for evaluating automated translation between ITPs.
AI.method: The authors construct ITPEval with 1,560 source files and 6,848 theorems across Lean 4, Rocq, Isabelle, and HOL Light, organized into two tiers: (1) a controlled tier of axiomatized files isolating foundational translation difficulty, and (2) an ecosystem tier from real libraries exposing API and proof-style mismatches. They develop itpeval, a unified multi-ITP verification infrastructure with state-isolated warm backends that preserve per-artifact native checking semantics. Evaluation covers five frontier/open-weight LLMs on 12 directed translation pairs, using pass@k metrics, deterministic Lean 4 BEq equivalence checks, and autoformalization/informalization round-trip studies.
AI.result: Statement translation peaks at 29.1% pass@1 and proof translation at 10.5%. Controlled theorems reach 29.7% proof pass@1 vs. 5.2% for ecosystem-level, confirming library mismatch as the dominant bottleneck. The deterministic BEq check shows only 54.0% equivalence for verified source-to-Lean 4 miniF2F translations, revealing that native type-checking overestimates semantic fidelity. Round-trip studies show Rocq and HOL Light are easier formalization targets than Lean 4 and Isabelle; multi-ITP context improves pooled Lean 4 success from 4.8% to 10.6%.
AI.conclusion: ITPEval establishes the first comprehensive benchmark for ITP-to-ITP translation, demonstrating that library/API mismatch is the primary bottleneck rather than foundational differences. The infrastructure and findings highlight the need for better semantic equivalence checking and suggest that multi-ITP training can substantially improve translation performance. All artifacts are publicly released.

title: NMR Elucidation as an Agentic Search Problem, Not a Modeling Problem
summary: Structural elucidation from Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) data remains a fundamental bottleneck across chemistry, materials science, and biology. We demonstrate that an agentic AI system can perform this task at a level comparable to graduate-level chemistry students. Instead of training a model to directly map spectra to structures, we build a single autonomous agent, backed by a frozen LLM, that interacts with a curated environment with access to domain-specific processing tools, validation checks, tabulated chemical shifts, and instructions that outline the stepwise nature of a chemist's thinking process. On the Alberts dataset, our agent elucidates structures with a top-1 accuracy of 71%, comparable to the performance of graduate students at 66% top-1 accuracy. On the van Bramer and AstraZeneca datasets, our agent achieved 80% and 20% top-1 accuracy respectively, outperforming zero-shot end-to-end deep learning models which were trained on large datasets of simulated spectra. These results show that reframing NMR elucidation as an LLM-guided constrained search, rather than a modeling task, yields substantial gains and suggests a path toward multi-step orchestration frameworks that integrate a variety of tools, models, and domain knowledge to assist in automating spectroscopic analysis.

AI.tldr: An LLM-based autonomous agent, using a frozen language model with domain-specific tools and curated reasoning steps, achieves 71% top-1 accuracy on NMR structural elucidation — matching graduate students (66%) and outperforming end-to-end deep learning models trained on simulated data.
AI.motivation: Structural elucidation from NMR data is a critical bottleneck in chemistry, materials science, and biology. Existing deep learning approaches attempt direct spectra-to-structure mapping but struggle with generalization, particularly on real (non-simulated) data. The authors propose reframing the problem as a constrained search guided by a reasoning agent rather than a pure modeling task.
AI.method: A single autonomous agent powered by a frozen LLM interacts with a curated environment containing domain-specific processing tools, validation checks, tabulated chemical shift databases, and structured instructions that mirror a chemist's stepwise reasoning process. The agent performs NMR elucidation as an LLM-guided constrained search rather than end-to-end prediction.
AI.result: On the Alberts dataset: 71% top-1 accuracy (vs. 66% for graduate students). On the van Bramer dataset: 80% top-1 accuracy. On the AstraZeneca dataset: 20% top-1 accuracy. The agent outperformed zero-shot end-to-end deep learning models trained on large simulated-spectra datasets across these benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Reframing NMR structural elucidation as an LLM-guided constrained search yields substantial gains over direct modeling approaches. This points toward multi-step orchestration frameworks that integrate tools, models, and domain knowledge to assist in automating spectroscopic analysis more effectively.

title: Know Your Agent: Reconnaissance-Driven Pentesting of AI Agents
summary: Traditional pentesting uses reconnaissance at each step to uncover unseen weaknesses, build stronger attacks, and advance the objective; we argue that AI agents require the same treatment. We formalize agent reconnaissance by modeling the process and identifying the knowledge assets it seeks to extract: what they are, how they are used, and which agent weaknesses they exploit to give adversaries leverage in indirect prompt injection attacks. We instantiate these insights in Know Your Agent (KYA), a framework that automates black-box, reconnaissance-driven pentesting by probing agents, building target profiles, and using those profiles to craft stronger attacks. We evaluate KYA on agent-security benchmarks and a real-world coding agent, and release KYA, its benchmarks, and baseline implementations for reproducibility.

AI.tldr: The paper argues AI agents need reconnaissance-based pentesting akin to traditional cybersecurity. It formalizes agent reconnaissance, identifying key knowledge assets adversaries can exploit. This is operationalized in KYA (Know Your Agent), a black-box framework that probes agents, builds target profiles, and crafts stronger indirect prompt injection attacks. Results demonstrate effectiveness on benchmarks and a real-world coding agent.
AI.motivation: Traditional pentesting leverages reconnaissance at each step to uncover weaknesses and build progressively stronger attacks. The authors argue that AI agents, particularly those vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, require analogous treatment. Current adversarial approaches lack a systematic, reconnaissance-driven methodology that profiles an agent's internal structure (tools, system prompts, permissions) before attacking, leaving potential attack surfaces unexplored.
AI.method: The authors first formalize agent reconnaissance by modeling the process and categorizing the knowledge assets it targets: (1) what constitutes the agent (tools, prompts, permissions), (2) how these components are used operationally, and (3) which specific weaknesses can be exploited for indirect prompt injection. They then propose KYA (Know Your Agent), a black-box, automated pentesting framework that operationalizes this formalization. KYA probes the target agent through crafted interactions, incrementally builds a profile of the agent's internal architecture, and leverages that profile to design and execute stronger, tailored prompt injection attacks — all without white-box access.
AI.result: KYA was evaluated on agent-security benchmarks and a real-world coding agent. The reconnaissance-driven approach enabled the crafting of more effective indirect prompt injection attacks compared to non-reconnaissance baselines. The framework successfully extracted meaningful profiles under black-box conditions and translated them into actionable attack leverage. The authors release KYA, its benchmarks, and baseline implementations for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: Reconnaissance is a critical, under-explored phase in AI agent security. Formalizing and automating this process allows adversaries (and by extension, defenders) to systematically uncover exploitable weaknesses. KYA demonstrates that profile-driven attacks significantly outperform generic approaches, underscoring the need for agent developers to consider reconnaissance-aware hardening. The released framework provides a foundation for future research in AI agent pentesting.

title: Language-Specific versus Cross-Lingual Knowledge Graphs for Implicit Aspect Identification in Arabic: A Comparative Study of Reasoning and Adaptation Strategies
summary: Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) in Arabic must recover both explicitly stated aspects and implicit aspects that are never named in the text. Implicit identification typically relies on an auxiliary knowledge source (e.g., a knowledge graph (KG)) linking opinion cues to aspect categories, but for a lower-resource language the practitioner faces a design choice: reuse a mature English KG through multilingual embeddings, or build a smaller native Arabic KG. This paper reports a controlled comparison of the two strategies within a single hybrid pipeline, evaluated on three Arabic benchmarks (M-ABSA, SemEval-2016 Arabic, and HAAD). We further compare two adaptation strategies for the generative extractor that feeds the KG -- zero-shot prompting versus task-specific fine-tuning of an 8B-parameter large language model (LLM). The native Arabic KG (Strategy 2) outperforms the cross-lingual English KG (Strategy 1) by +0.199 micro-F1 on M-ABSA and +0.251 on SemEval-2016, gaining on both precision and recall. Task-specific fine-tuning raises explicit-extraction micro-F1 from <= 0.13 (zero-shot) to 0.66-0.76 on M-ABSA and SemEval-2016 (0.45 on the smaller HAAD), confirming that task adaptation, rather than model scale, is decisive in a morphologically rich language.

AI.tldr: This paper compares two knowledge source strategies for Arabic implicit aspect detection in ABSA: cross-lingual transfer from an English KG versus a native Arabic KG, and evaluates zero-shot vs. fine-tuned LLM extraction, finding that native KGs and task-specific fine-tuning decisively outperform alternatives.
AI.motivation: Arabic ABSA faces the challenge of identifying implicit aspects (not explicitly mentioned in text), which typically requires auxiliary knowledge sources like KGs. For low-resource languages, practitioners must choose between leveraging mature English KGs via multilingual embeddings or building smaller native KGs. No prior controlled comparison existed to guide this design choice.
AI.method: A controlled comparison within a single hybrid pipeline, testing two KG strategies (cross-lingual English KG vs. native Arabic KG) and two LLM adaptation strategies (zero-shot prompting vs. task-specific fine-tuning of an 8B-parameter LLM). Evaluation conducted on three Arabic benchmarks: M-ABSA, SemEval-2016 Arabic, and HAAD.
AI.result: The native Arabic KG (Strategy 2) outperformed the cross-lingual English KG (Strategy 1) by +0.199 micro-F1 on M-ABSA and +0.251 on SemEval-2016, with gains in both precision and recall. Task-specific fine-tuning boosted explicit-extraction micro-F1 from ≤0.13 (zero-shot) to 0.66–0.76 on M-ABSA and SemEval-2016, and 0.45 on HAAD.
AI.conclusion: For Arabic ABSA, building a native Arabic KG is more effective than cross-lingual transfer from English KGs. Task-specific fine-tuning, rather than model scale, is the decisive factor for extraction performance in morphologically rich languages like Arabic.

title: FORCE-Bench: A Benchmark, Dataset, and Evaluation Harness for Agentic AI in Enterprise Finance
summary: Recent advances in large language models have accelerated deployment of agentic systems in operational finance. Existing benchmarks emphasize measuring general capabilities, instruction following, or safety, but few directly address the operational finance workflows that agentic systems are now being deployed to automate. Finance professionals require agents to not only provide factually sound and properly grounded information, but also ensure that this information is verifiable and consistently adheres to rules and constraints of the operational finance domain. We introduce FORCE-Bench, which contains 251 expert-annotated queries and evaluates responses using a rubric-based framework calibrated to the requirements of the operational finance domain, across eight dimensions: accuracy, citations, clarity, depth, groundedness, recency, relevance, and structure. FORCE-Bench assesses agentic systems on three task types: financial obligation research (querying ERP systems for accounts receivable and payable data), financial entity performance research (answering time-bound questions from public filings and market data), and business brief generation (synthesising multi-source company intelligence reports). To reflect real deployment conditions, we evaluate our purpose-built agent, as well as the general-purpose agentic systems, under common tool access and latency-bounded settings. Results show that general-purpose agentic systems do not consistently meet finance-domain quality requirements under operational constraints, while the purpose-built Finance Agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot is more reliable across dimensions. We release the dataset, rubrics, harness, and analysis code as open-source to support reproducible comparison and adaptation to other enterprise finance environments.

AI.tldr: FORCE-Bench is a benchmark of 251 expert-annotated queries evaluating agentic systems on operational finance workflows across eight quality dimensions. General-purpose agents underperform under realistic latency/access constraints, while a purpose-built Finance Agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot proves more reliable.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks focus on general capabilities or safety, neglecting the specific demands of operational finance automation — where agents must produce factually sound, verifiable, rule-adherent information under real deployment constraints (tool access, latency bounds).
AI.method: FORCE-Bench comprises 251 expert-annotated queries spanning three task types: financial obligation research, financial entity performance research, and business brief generation. Responses are evaluated using a rubric-based framework across eight dimensions: accuracy, citations, clarity, depth, groundedness, recency, relevance, and structure. Both a purpose-built Finance Agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot and general-purpose agentic systems are evaluated under common tool-access and latency-bounded conditions.
AI.result: General-purpose agentic systems fail to consistently meet finance-domain quality requirements under operational constraints. The purpose-built Finance Agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot demonstrates greater reliability across all eight evaluation dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Deploying agentic systems in operational finance requires domain-specialized benchmarking and purpose-built architectures. FORCE-Bench provides a reproducible evaluation framework, and the authors release the dataset, rubrics, harness, and analysis code as open-source to support adaptation across enterprise finance environments.

title: Reward-Aware Population Scaling of Evolutionary Strategies in LLM Fine-Tuning
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the 4th HiLD (High-dimensional Learning Dynamics) Workshop, ICML 2026
summary: Using Evolutionary Strategies (ES) for fine-tuning large language models is attractive because it is memory-efficient, parallel, and compatible with black-box or discrete rewards. Yet its population-size conclusions conflict sharply: fine-tuning with cross-entropy (CE) reward succeeds with $N=1$, while binary-reward training often needs $N \approx 30$. We show this gap is largely about reward design and normalization, not population size. In the capable-model regime we study, z-score advantage normalization can cause $N=2$ to fail. Disabling normalization lets binary-reward ES with $N=2$ improve on GSM8K and TREC across capable models spanning 0.5B-7B, where the normalized variant collapses or degrades. This small-$N$ risk is set by reward granularity: binary accuracy reward induces a zero-advantage probability $q$ that depends in closed form on base accuracy, batch size, and intra-pair correctness correlation; a zero-training probe on Qwen2.5-Instruct/GSM8K matches the formula with mean absolute error 0.020 across 12 configurations and finds the availability threshold $N_{\mathrm{avail}}$ to be small in this capable-model regime. The implication is not that $N=2$ is universally sufficient, but that small-population failure in capable-model binary ES can be an implementation artifact rather than an intrinsic population limit.

AI.tldr: Large language model fine-tuning with Evolutionary Strategies (ES) using binary rewards fails at small population sizes due to z-score advantage normalization, not an intrinsic population limit. Removing normalization enables N=2 to succeed, with failure risk governed by zero-advantage probability determined by base accuracy, batch size, and intra-pair correlation.
AI.motivation: Resolve the apparent contradiction in ES-based LLM fine-tuning: cross-entropy reward works with population size N=1, while binary reward often requires N≈30. The authors hypothesize this gap stems from reward design and normalization choices rather than fundamental population size requirements.
AI.method: The authors analyze the effect of z-score advantage normalization in binary-reward ES across models from 0.5B to 7B parameters on GSM8K and TREC benchmarks. They derive a closed-form expression for the zero-advantage probability q in binary accuracy reward as a function of base accuracy, batch size, and intra-pair correctness correlation, then validate this formula against empirical measurements on Qwen2.5-Instruct/GSM8K across 12 configurations (mean absolute error 0.020). They also compute an availability threshold N_avail.
AI.result: With z-score normalization disabled, binary-reward ES with N=2 improves performance on GSM8K and TREC across models spanning 0.5B-7B, while the normalized variant collapses or degrades. The zero-advantage probability formula matches empirical measurements with MAE 0.020, and N_avail is small in the capable-model regime.
AI.conclusion: Small-population failure in capable-model binary ES is often an implementation artifact (z-score normalization) rather than an intrinsic population size limit. N=2 can suffice when normalization is removed, contrary to prior assumptions requiring N≈30.

title: Adversarial Frontiers: Minimum-Norm Attack Ensembles for Robustness Evaluation
summary: Adversarial robustness is commonly evaluated with predefined attack ensembles, such as AutoAttack, at a single perturbation budget $\varepsilon$ and on a selective choice of perturbation norms. We argue this formulation is fundamentally limited. First, robustness--perturbation curves may intersect or decay at different rates across models, making single-$\varepsilon$ rankings unstable. Second, current ensembles provide no evidence of optimality, leaving an unknown gap to worst-case performance. Third, fixed attack configurations provide no systematic control over the trade-off between attack strength and evaluation cost. To address these limitations, we introduce a unified evaluation framework based on a comprehensive pool of minimum-norm attacks and robustness--perturbation curves across $\ell_0$, $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$ and $\ell_\infty$ norms. We define the attack frontier as the worst-case robustness estimate the attack pool produces against a model. We then formalize evaluation as a frontier-approximation problem, constructing minimum-norm attack ensembles, optimized subsets of the comprehensive pool, that approach the frontier under a controllable query budget, with larger budgets monotonically tightening the estimate. Furthermore, we define the defense frontier as the maximum robustness across the model set at each perturbation size. We finally propose the Defense Optimality Index to rank defenses by their gap to the defense frontier, providing a ranking without selecting a reference $\varepsilon$. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, our ensembles match or exceed AutoAttack on most defenses at every budget tier, at fixed and controllable query cost, offering practitioners a query-controlled, curve-based alternative to fixed-$\varepsilon$ evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified adversarial robustness evaluation framework that replaces fixed-ε benchmarks with robustness–perturbation curves and minimum-norm attack pools. It formalizes evaluation as a frontier-approximation problem, introduces the Defense Optimality Index for ranking defenses without a reference ε, and demonstrates that optimized attack ensembles match or exceed AutoAttack under controllable query budgets.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial robustness evaluation using fixed perturbation budgets (ε) and predefined attack ensembles (e.g., AutoAttack) has three fundamental limitations: (1) single-ε rankings are unstable because robustness–perturbation curves can intersect across models, (2) current attack ensembles lack optimality guarantees, leaving an unknown gap to true worst-case performance, and (3) fixed attack configurations offer no systematic control over the attack-strength vs. evaluation-cost trade-off.
AI.method: The authors construct a comprehensive pool of minimum-norm attacks spanning ℓ₀, ℓ₁, ℓ₂, and ℓ∞ norms. They define the attack frontier as the worst-case robustness estimate produced by this pool. Evaluation is formalized as a frontier-approximation problem: optimal subsets (minimum-norm attack ensembles) are selected from the pool to approach the frontier under a controllable query budget. The defense frontier is defined as the maximum robustness across models at each perturbation size, and the Defense Optimality Index (DOI) ranks defenses by their gap to this frontier, eliminating dependence on a reference ε.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, the proposed ensembles match or surpass AutoAttack on most defenses at every budget tier, while operating at fixed and controllable query cost.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a query-controlled, curve-based alternative to fixed-ε evaluation, offering practitioners more stable, comprehensive, and cost-controllable adversarial robustness assessment. The DOI enables ranking defenses without arbitrary ε selection.

title: Solar Open 2 Technical Report
summary: We present Solar Open 2, a 250B-A15B Mixture-of-Experts language model built for long-horizon agentic tasks, scaled up from Solar Open 1 (Solar Open 100B). To hold entire agent trajectories in a single context, Solar Open 2 reaches a 1M-token window through a hybrid attention stack that interleaves one softmax layer among every three linear-attention layers, using no positional encoding and a gated delta rule extended to negative eigenvalues. To train at this scale under a fixed compute budget, we make training efficient in two ways: a stronger starting point, and higher-value data. For the starting point, we initialize Solar Open 2 from Solar Open 1, transferring the 5.69B-parameter shared skeleton that survives the architectural change and learning everything else through full pre-training. For the data, we curate for value per token: quality- and rarity-aware data curation and mixture-ratio optimization refine a 20T pool into a 10T mixture that, at equal token budget, outperforms the Solar Open 1 recipe. To build its agent skills, we train twelve domain specialists across purpose-built scenarios, then consolidate them into a single model by Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD). Against comparably sized open-weight models on English benchmarks, Solar Open 2 leads on MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and the APEX-Agents agentic suite, and stays competitive with the strongest (DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiMo-V2.5) elsewhere. On Korean benchmarks, Solar Open 2 records the highest average of any model compared, including fast-tier closed APIs, and on Ko-GDPval, an in-house Korean officework-agent benchmark, it is competitive with DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T) at less than a sixth of its size.

AI.tldr: Solar Open 2 is a 250B-A15B MoE language model with a 1M-token context window, optimized for long-horizon agentic tasks. It improves training efficiency via architectural inheritance from Solar Open 1, curated high-value data, and Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) for agent skills, achieving strong benchmark results against comparably sized models.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to build a model capable of handling long-horizon agentic tasks that require entire agent trajectories in a single context window (up to 1M tokens), while scaling efficiently under a fixed compute budget. They also seek to transfer and reuse prior model investments rather than training from scratch.
AI.method: (1) Hybrid attention: interleaves one softmax layer among every three linear-attention layers, with no positional encoding and a gated delta rule extended to negative eigenvalues, achieving a 1M-token window. (2) Efficient training: initializes from Solar Open 1's 5.69B-parameter shared skeleton, then full pre-trains the rest. (3) Data curation: quality- and rarity-aware filtering plus mixture-ratio optimization refines a 20T-token pool into a 10T mixture. (4) Agent skill acquisition: trains twelve domain specialists, then consolidates via Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD).
AI.result: Solar Open 2 leads comparably sized open-weight models on MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and APEX-Agents; stays competitive with DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiMo-V2.5 on other English benchmarks; achieves the highest average on Korean benchmarks among all compared models including closed APIs; and on Ko-GDPval, matches DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T) at under 1/6 the size.
AI.conclusion: Solar Open 2 demonstrates that architectural inheritance, value-aware data curation, and MOPD-based agent skill consolidation yield a highly capable long-context agentic model that competes favorably with much larger models on both English and Korean benchmarks.

title: Adaptive Multi-Expert Graph Transformer for Interpretable EEG-Based Diagnostics
summary: Electroencephalographic (EEG) abnormalities arise from dynamic changes in neural synchrony across spatial and temporal scales, yet many computational approaches reduce these dynamics to static features. We present a Spatial Multi-Expert Graph Transformer that models each EEG recording as a sequence of dynamic functional connectivity graphs. Time-resolved connectivity is estimated using the weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI), and hierarchical graph encoding aggregates information from electrode to regional and global levels. A multi-expert transformer architecture enables subtype-aware reasoning, with a gating mechanism adaptively fusing expert outputs for global abnormality prediction. Experiments on the TUAB dataset show competitive abnormal EEG detection performance and demonstrate the potential of dynamic graph modeling with adaptive expert fusion for interpretable, subtype-aware spatial--temporal analysis.

AI.tldr: A Spatial Multi-Expert Graph Transformer models EEG as dynamic functional connectivity graphs using wPLI, with hierarchical encoding and gated expert fusion, achieving competitive abnormal EEG detection on TUAB.
AI.motivation: EEG abnormalities stem from dynamic neural synchrony changes across spatial/temporal scales, but existing computational methods often reduce these dynamics to static features, losing critical temporal information.
AI.method: The authors propose a Spatial Multi-Expert Graph Transformer that: (1) estimates time-resolved functional connectivity via weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI); (2) applies hierarchical graph encoding aggregating information from electrode → regional → global levels; (3) uses a multi-expert transformer with a gating mechanism that adaptively fuses expert outputs for subtype-aware reasoning and global abnormality prediction.
AI.result: Experiments on the TUAB dataset demonstrate competitive performance in abnormal EEG detection compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic graph modeling combined with adaptive expert fusion enables interpretable, subtype-aware spatial-temporal EEG analysis, showing promise for clinical abnormality detection.

title: JANUS: Foreseeing Latent Risk for Long-Horizon Agent Safety
summary: Agent safety is moving from content moderation toward preventing operational failures before tool-using agents act. We propose Janus, a foresight-oriented framework for long-horizon agent safety that trains guards to anticipate delayed risks from partial trajectories. Janus synthesizes diverse agent trajectories via multi-agent simulation and learns a shared policy with two coupled tasks: an anticipation task that forecasts safety-relevant futures and an adjudication task that decides safety from both the observed prefix and anticipated future. The two tasks are jointly optimized with CoAA-RL, which rewards forecasts by their utility for downstream safety judgment. The resulting guard model, Vanguard, blocks unsafe actions before execution. Across four agent-safety benchmarks, Vanguard improves average protection by 15.9 percentage points over baseline guards while increasing benign task completion by 5.1 percentage points.

AI.tldr: Janus is a foresight-oriented agent safety framework that trains guard models (Vanguard) to anticipate future risks from partial trajectories using multi-agent simulation and a dual-task objective (anticipation + adjudication). Jointly optimized via CoAA-RL, Vanguard blocks unsafe actions pre-execution, improving protection by 15.9 pp and benign task completion by 5.1 pp over baselines.
AI.motivation: Agent safety is evolving from reactive content moderation to proactive prevention of operational failures before autonomous agents take harmful actions. Existing guards lack the ability to foresee delayed or downstream risks from incomplete action sequences, motivating a foresight-oriented approach for long-horizon safety.
AI.method: Janus employs three key components: (1) multi-agent simulation to synthesize diverse long-horizon agent trajectories, (2) a shared policy jointly trained on two tasks — an anticipation task predicting safety-relevant future states and an adjudication task deciding safety from both the observed prefix and anticipated future, and (3) CoAA-RL (joint optimization via reinforcement learning) that rewards forecasts based on their utility for downstream safety judgments. The resulting guard model, Vanguard, intervenes before unsafe actions execute.
AI.result: Across four agent-safety benchmarks, Vanguard achieves a 15.9 percentage point improvement in average protection over baseline guards while simultaneously increasing benign task completion by 5.1 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Foresight-oriented safety guards that anticipate future risks significantly outperform reactive baselines, demonstrating that joint optimization of anticipation and adjudication is an effective paradigm for long-horizon agent safety.

title: RALS: Resources and Baselines for Romanian Automatic Lexical Simplification
summary: We introduce the first dataset that jointly covers both lexical complexity prediction (LCP) annotations and lexical simplification (LS) for Romanian, along with a comparison of lexical simplification approaches. We propose a methodology for ordering simplification suggestions using a pairwise ranking approximation method, arranging candidates from simple to complex based on a separate set of human judgments. In addition, we provide human lexical complexity annotations for 3,921 word samples in context. Finally, we explore several novel pipelines for complexity prediction and simplification and present the first text simplification system for Romanian.

AI.tldr: Introduces the first Romanian dataset combining lexical complexity prediction annotations and lexical simplification, proposes a pairwise ranking method for ordering simplification candidates, and presents the first text simplification system for Romanian.
