By focusing generation strictly on the evolving storm structure, GeoDES synthesizes physically consistent, high-fidelity weather events suitable for stress-testing forecast models and expanding meteorological datasets. Evaluations demonstrate that GeoDES outperforms prior methods on key metrics, achieving $52\%$ lower Peak Vorticity Error and $8\%$ higher Anomaly Correlation Coefficient than the next strongest methods on the North Atlantic test set.

AI.tldr: GeoDES is a diffusion-based image-to-video model that generates high-fidelity, physically consistent cyclonic storm evolutions, outperforming prior methods with 52% lower Peak Vorticity Error and 8% higher Anomaly Correlation Coefficient on North Atlantic test data.
AI.motivation: Machine learning weather models struggle to capture fine-grained storm structure: regional models lack sufficient historical data within fixed boundaries, while global models are computationally expensive and too coarse-resolution. A method is needed to synthesize detailed, evolving storm events for stress-testing forecasts and augmenting meteorological datasets.
AI.method: GeoDES (Geospatial Diffusion-based Evolution Synthesis) is a custom image-to-video diffusion model that focuses generation strictly on the evolving structure of cyclonic storms, producing physically consistent storm event sequences.
AI.result: GeoDES achieved 52% lower Peak Vorticity Error and 8% higher Anomaly Correlation Coefficient than the next strongest methods on the North Atlantic test set.
AI.conclusion: GeoDES effectively bridges the gap between regional and global weather models by synthesizing high-fidelity storm evolution sequences, enabling improved stress-testing of forecast models and expansion of meteorological training datasets.

title: HalluTruthQA: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Hallucination Detection, Localization, and Explanation in Arabic Question Answering
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent Arabic answers, yet factual errors remain difficult to detect, localize, explain, and verify. Existing hallucination benchmarks often provide response-level labels, with limited support for identifying the exact erroneous content, explaining why it is incorrect, or selecting the correct factual answer. We introduce \textsc{HalluTruthQA}, a fine-grained benchmark for hallucination evaluation in Arabic question answering. The benchmark contains 2,400 expert-curated examples across four knowledge-intensive domains: Islamic knowledge, history, science, and geography. Each example pairs an Arabic question and a model-generated answer with a verified reference answer, a binary hallucination label, six candidate answers for factual verification, and, for hallucinated answers, character-level erroneous spans, human-written explanations, and macro and micro hallucination types.
  We evaluate four open-source LLMs, \textsc{Allam}, \textsc{Falcon-H1}, \textsc{Qwen32}, and \textsc{Silma}, in a zero-shot setting across hallucination detection, span-level localization, factual verification, and explanation evaluation. Results show that these tasks capture different abilities: no single model achieves the strongest performance across all tasks, with best scores of 0.880 Macro-F1 for detection, 0.516 F1-Sp for localization, 0.852 LO-Score for factual verification, and 0.644 final score for explanation evaluation. Our taxonomy shows that hallucination evaluation should move beyond detection toward localizing, verifying, and explaining factual errors. The code, dataset, prompts, and evaluation scripts are available at https://gitlab.com/nlpresearcher/HalluTruthQA.

AI.tldr: HalluTruthQA is a fine-grained Arabic QA benchmark with 2,400 expert-curated examples spanning four domains, enabling hallucination evaluation beyond detection to include span localization, factual verification, and explanation. Evaluation of four LLMs reveals task-specific strengths, with no model excelling across all dimensions.
AI.motivation: Existing hallucination benchmarks for Arabic LLMs provide only coarse response-level labels and lack support for pinpointing exact erroneous spans, explaining why content is wrong, or selecting correct answers. There is a need for fine-grained, multi-dimensional hallucination evaluation in Arabic QA.
AI.method: The authors construct HalluTruthQA, comprising 2,400 expert-curated examples across Islamic knowledge, history, science, and geography. Each example includes a question, model-generated answer, verified reference answer, binary hallucination label, six candidate answers for verification, and for hallucinated cases: character-level erroneous spans, human-written explanations, and macro/micro hallucination types. Four open-source LLMs (Allam, Falcon-H1, Qwen32, Silma) are evaluated zero-shot on four tasks: hallucination detection, span localization, factual verification, and explanation evaluation.
AI.result: No single model dominates all tasks. Best scores per task: detection 0.880 Macro-F1, localization 0.516 F1-Sp, factual verification 0.852 LO-Score, explanation evaluation 0.644 final score. Results demonstrate that these tasks capture distinct capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Hallucination evaluation should progress beyond binary detection to encompass localization, verification, and explanation of factual errors. HalluTruthQA provides a standardized resource for this multi-faceted assessment in Arabic QA.

title: MOF-Sleuth: Tool-Grounded Reward Alignment for Explainable Fine-Grained MOF CIF Auditing
summary: Large metal-organic framework (MOF) databases support simulation, screening, and machine learning through crystallographic information files (CIFs). Subtle chemical and structural errors in these inputs can compromise downstream results and hinder manual inspection. LLM advances in computational chemistry offer paths beyond predictive screening toward fine-grained diagnosis with evidence-grounded explanations. However, two challenges remain: (i) limited fine-grained attribution: MOF-specific validators and machine-learning models scale detection but provide fixed checks, readiness scores, or coarse labels rather than evidence-grounded explanations; and (ii) unreliable CIF reasoning: direct LLM auditing is costly and unreliable because chemical evidence is implicit across atom-site records and requires geometric, connectivity, occupancy, and charge calculations. Both stem from weak coupling between chemical evidence and language-model explanation. We introduce MOF-Sleuth, a reinforcement-guided CIF auditing agent with two modules: a deterministic Forensic Lab and a Sleuth reasoning engine. The Lab derives composition, geometry, connectivity, occupancy, coordination, and charge evidence, and Sleuth uses this evidence to produce an evidence-grounded explanation, error types, and a binary decision. Reward-guided reinforcement learning (RL) turns tool measurements into chemical explanation-level supervision, rewarding not only the final answer but also cited chemical evidence and evidence-supported diagnoses. We introduce Chemically Grounded Diagnosis (Chem-GD), a metric that assesses whether a correct diagnosis is explained by factual, relevant CIF-derived evidence. Across four benchmarks, MOF-Sleuth establishes state-of-the-art performance among LLM-based approaches and MOF-specific machine-learning methods, demonstrating gains in detection, attribution, and grounded explanation quality.

AI.tldr: MOF-Sleuth is a reinforcement-guided AI agent that audits MOF crystallographic files (CIFs) by combining a deterministic "Forensic Lab" that extracts chemical evidence (composition, geometry, connectivity, etc.) with an LLM reasoning engine, using RL to reward evidence-grounded explanations. It introduces Chem-GD, a metric for evaluating whether correct diagnoses are backed by factual CIF-derived evidence, and achieves SOTA on four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Large MOF databases are vulnerable to subtle chemical/structural errors in CIFs that compromise downstream simulation and screening. Existing validators and ML models scale detection but only provide fixed checks, readiness scores, or coarse labels—not evidence-grounded explanations. Direct LLM auditing is unreliable because chemical evidence is implicit across atom-site records requiring complex geometric, connectivity, occupancy, and charge calculations. The core problem is the weak coupling between chemical evidence and language-model explanation.
AI.method: MOF-Sleuth comprises: (1) a deterministic Forensic Lab that derives composition, geometry, connectivity, occupancy, coordination, and charge evidence from CIFs; and (2) a Sleuth reasoning engine (LLM) that consumes this evidence to produce explanations, error types, and binary decisions. Reward-guided reinforcement learning converts tool measurements into chemical explanation-level supervision, rewarding correct final answers as well as cited chemical evidence and evidence-supported diagnoses. A new metric, Chemically Grounded Diagnosis (Chem-GD), evaluates whether correct diagnoses are explained by factual, relevant CIF-derived evidence.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks, MOF-Sleuth achieves state-of-the-art performance among both LLM-based approaches and MOF-specific machine-learning methods, with gains in detection accuracy, error attribution, and grounded explanation quality.
AI.conclusion: Coupling deterministic chemical evidence extraction with LLM reasoning via reinforcement learning enables reliable, evidence-grounded CIF auditing that surpasses both traditional validators and direct LLM approaches. The Chem-GD metric provides a principled way to evaluate explanation quality beyond mere prediction accuracy.

title: SynPre-FL: Synthetic data-driven pretraining integrated Federated Learning training framework
summary: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to privacy-preserving clinical risk prediction, but its deployment remains limited by restricted data sharing, client heterogeneity, class imbalance, and the lack of realistic tabular electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks. Synthetic data generation may alleviate data scarcity, yet its integration with federated optimisation has received limited systematic study. We propose SynPre-FL, a unified framework combining high-fidelity synthetic EHR generation with synthetic-pretrained FL for robust prediction under non-IID conditions. A latent autoencoder-diffusion model generates privacy-preserving synthetic cohorts, which are used to warm-start federated training. This pretraining is followed by heterogeneity-aware optimisation using class-balanced local objectives, proximal regularisation, and adaptive server aggregation. Post-hoc calibration and federated-safe explainability support reliable and interpretable risk estimates. Experiments show that the synthetic generator preserves univariate, bivariate, and multivariate structure while protecting against membership-inference and reconstruction attacks. The generated data achieve strong downstream utility under TSTR, TRTS, and model-based evaluations. Across federated settings with 5, 10, and 15 heterogeneous clients, SynPre-FL consistently improves robustness and scalability over baseline methods, especially under severe non-IID fragmentation. Calibration improves probability reliability, while SHAP analysis produces stable and clinically coherent feature attributions across federation sizes. SynPre-FL therefore provides a practical and reproducible framework for combining synthetic data with FL to enable privacy-aware, interpretable, and robust clinical prediction from distributed tabular EHR data.

AI.tldr: SynPre-FL is a unified framework that combines diffusion-based synthetic EHR generation with synthetic-pretrained federated learning, incorporating class-balanced objectives, proximal regularization, and adaptive aggregation to achieve robust, privacy-preserving, and interpretable clinical risk prediction under non-IID conditions.
AI.motivation: Federated learning for clinical risk prediction is hindered by restricted data sharing, client heterogeneity, class imbalance, and a lack of realistic tabular EHR benchmarks. While synthetic data could alleviate data scarcity, its systematic integration with federated optimization remains underexplored.
AI.method: SynPre-FL comprises: (1) a latent autoencoder-diffusion model for privacy-preserving synthetic EHR generation; (2) warm-starting federated training with synthetic data; (3) heterogeneity-aware optimization using class-balanced local objectives, proximal regularization, and adaptive server aggregation; and (4) post-hoc calibration with federated-safe SHAP-based explainability.
AI.result: The synthetic generator preserves univariate, bivariate, and multivariate structure while resisting membership-inference and reconstruction attacks. Synthetic data demonstrates strong utility under TSTR, TRTS, and model-based evaluations. In federated settings with 5–15 heterogeneous clients, SynPre-FL consistently outperforms baselines in robustness and scalability, particularly under severe non-IID fragmentation. Calibration improves probability reliability, and SHAP produces stable, clinically coherent attributions.
AI.conclusion: SynPre-FL offers a practical, reproducible framework that unifies synthetic data generation with federated learning, enabling privacy-aware, interpretable, and robust clinical prediction from distributed tabular EHR data.

title: On the Systematic Challenges of Culturally Loaded Machine Translation: Dream of the Red Chamber as the Cultural Lens
summary: Culturally loaded translation poses unique challenges for machine translation (MT), as meanings are deeply embedded in socio-cultural contexts beyond surface linguistic forms. Although large language models (LLMs) have enabled MT systems to achieve human-like quality in many scenarios, their ability to handle culturally loaded expressions remains underexplored. In this study, we systematically investigate the challenges posed by culturally loaded translation in LLM-based MT systems. We construct a Chinese-Japanese bilingual dataset from the culturally representative corpus Dream of the Red Chamber, containing 500 segments across diverse cultural categories. Using a comprehensive evaluation protocol, we reveal three main challenges: (1) task challenges, where frontier LLMs exhibit notable performance gaps and struggle with culturally loaded content; (2) human evaluation challenges, where evaluator backgrounds lead to substantial disagreement in translation judgments; and (3) automatic evaluation challenges, where widely used metrics fail to reliably assess translation quality for this task. These findings may offer valuable insights for culture-oriented translation research in both computational science and linguistics.

AI.tldr: This study systematically investigates LLM-based MT performance on culturally loaded translation using a Chinese-Japanese dataset from Dream of the Red Chamber, revealing three key challenges: LLM performance gaps, evaluator disagreement due to background differences, and unreliable automatic metrics for culturally embedded content.
AI.motivation: While LLMs achieve near-human MT quality in general domains, their capacity to handle culturally loaded expressions — where meaning is deeply embedded in socio-cultural contexts — remains underexplored, motivating a systematic investigation of this gap.
AI.method: The authors construct a Chinese-Japanese bilingual dataset of 500 segments drawn from Dream of the Red Chamber (a culturally representative literary corpus), covering diverse cultural categories. They then apply a comprehensive evaluation protocol encompassing task performance assessment of frontier LLMs, human evaluation with diverse evaluator backgrounds, and automatic metric evaluation.
AI.result: Three main challenges are identified: (1) frontier LLMs exhibit notable performance gaps and struggle with culturally loaded content; (2) human evaluators' backgrounds cause substantial inter-evaluator disagreement; (3) widely used automatic metrics fail to reliably assess translation quality for culturally loaded tasks.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight critical limitations in LLM-based MT for culturally embedded translation and offer insights for advancing culture-oriented translation research in both computational science and linguistics.

title: SenWorld: A Digital-Twin Simulation for Generating Context-Rich Evaluation Data
summary: Smartphone personal assistants reason over longitudinal personal data, yet evaluating them requires context-rich evaluation data whose correct answers are known, and real device traces are too privacy-sensitive to share. To address this challenge, we present SenWorld, a physically grounded, deterministic, event-sourced digital-twin simulation that generates such data with ground truth fixed by construction. In SenWorld, personas live through a full day in a world built from real map, weather, holiday, and network data; every observable signal is archived in full-system snapshots; and each evaluation case is labeled by a pointer to an existing record rather than by post-hoc annotation or a large language model (LLM) judge. We evaluate this method with 16 personas in Beijing. The generated data closely matches the held-out real-user benchmark in category distribution (Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) 0.070) and in the daily rhythm of communication records (JSD below 0.1), though generated records remain shorter than real ones. Without scripted interaction, personas form a fully reciprocated dialogue subgraph and differentiated behavioral repertoires. Projected into 717 evaluation cases, the generated data exposes 78 failures in a production smartphone assistant, concentrating on call and Short Message Service (SMS) records while contacts, schedules, and alarms never fail. The snapshot pointer confirms each failure as an assistant-side retrieval error, with no LLM judge involved. Overall, SenWorld offers a privacy-safe, reproducible, and distribution-checked path to evaluation data whose labels are fixed by construction.

AI.tldr: SenWorld is a deterministic digital-twin simulation that generates privacy-safe, physically grounded evaluation data for smartphone personal assistants, with ground-truth labels fixed by construction through snapshot pointers rather than LLM judges or post-hoc annotation.
AI.motivation: Evaluating smartphone personal assistants requires context-rich longitudinal personal data with known correct answers, but real device traces are too privacy-sensitive to share. Existing approaches rely on post-hoc annotation or LLM judges, which introduce ambiguity and error.
AI.method: SenWorld uses an event-sourced digital-twin simulation where personas live through a full day in a world built from real map, weather, holiday, and network data. Every observable signal is archived in full-system snapshots, and each evaluation case is labeled by a pointer to an existing record rather than by annotation or LLM judgment. The method was tested with 16 personas in Beijing.
AI.result: Generated data closely matched held-out real-user benchmarks: JSD of 0.070 for category distribution and below 0.1 for daily communication rhythms, though generated records were shorter. Personas formed fully reciprocated dialogue subgraphs with differentiated behavioral repertoires without scripting. When projected into 717 evaluation cases, the data exposed 78 failures in a production smartphone assistant, concentrated on call and SMS records; contacts, schedules, and alarms never failed. Snapshot pointers confirmed all failures as assistant-side retrieval errors.
AI.conclusion: SenWorld provides a privacy-safe, reproducible, and distribution-checked method for generating smartphone assistant evaluation data with labels fixed by construction, eliminating reliance on LLM judges while maintaining fidelity to real-world behavioral patterns.

title: The C-index illusion: discrimination without calibration in published survival models
summary: "Stop Chasing the C-index when Evaluating Survival Analysis Models" (ICML 2026, Spotlight) argued normatively, on synthetic data, that evaluating survival models by discrimination alone, i.e. the concordance index, produces systematically misleading model comparisons, because the metric ignores calibration and time-dependent accuracy. Whether this matters for real, published, non-clinical models has not been tested. We reproduce three published survival-ML models across three structurally distinct domains (hard-drive failure, peer-to-peer credit default, and user disengagement on digital platforms), validate our evaluation instrument against the anchor paper's own synthetic experiment, and test five pre-registered hypotheses under a Holm-corrected family-wise error rate. Three of five reject. A model that reproduces the published discrimination almost exactly (C = 0.9595 vs. 0.958 reported) fails a formal calibration test at p = 2.6e-136; a broad feature-ablation search finds no single attribute responsible for this discrimination, so the calibration failure is not an artifact of a trivial shortcut. A lender's estimated default risk is biased upward by roughly two percentage points, growing to nearly four points in the riskiest segment, when loan prepayment is treated as non-informative censoring rather than as a competing risk. A platform's churn model shows probability estimates that degrade with the prediction horizon even as its global discrimination stays within the pre-registered C-index band. A direct test of whether metric choice inverts which model is preferred does not reject, though with limited power given only two to three models per domain; the failure mode we document is better characterized as misplaced confidence in a chosen model than as choice of the wrong one. We release a reusable, pre-registered evaluation harness with full code and a single annotated notebook.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically validates, across three real-world non-clinical domains, the claim that evaluating survival models solely by the C-index (discrimination) is misleading. The authors reproduce three published survival-ML models and find systematic calibration failures and time-dependent accuracy degradation even when C-index values are faithfully reproduced, demonstrating that metric choice masks critical weaknesses in model reliability.
AI.motivation: Prior work argued normatively and on synthetic data that the C-index alone is insufficient for evaluating survival models because it ignores calibration and time-dependent accuracy. However, whether this critique matters for real, published, non-clinical survival-ML models had never been empirically tested. The authors seek to bridge this gap by reproducing published models and subjecting them to rigorous, pre-registered hypothesis tests.
AI.method: The authors reproduce three published survival-ML models across three domains (hard-drive failure prediction, P2P credit default, and user disengagement on digital platforms). They validate their evaluation instrument against the anchor paper's synthetic experiment, then test five pre-registered hypotheses under a Holm-corrected family-wise error rate. Methods include formal calibration tests, feature-ablation searches to rule out trivial shortcuts, competing-risk analysis for loan prepayment, and tracking probability estimate degradation over prediction horizons while monitoring C-index stability.
AI.result: Three of five hypotheses reject. Key findings: (1) a model with near-identical C-index (0.9595 vs. 0.958 reported) fails calibration at p=2.6e-136, with no single feature responsible; (2) treating loan prepayment as non-informative censoring biases default risk estimates upward by ~2 percentage points (~4 in the riskiest segment); (3) a churn model's probability estimates degrade with prediction horizon while C-index remains stable; (4) the direct test of metric-driven model preference inversion does not reject, suggesting the failure mode is misplaced confidence rather than selecting the wrong model.
AI.conclusion: The C-index systematically masks calibration failures and time-dependent degradation in real published models, validating concerns previously shown only on synthetic data. The failure mode is better characterized as overconfidence in a chosen model rather than selecting the wrong model. The authors release a reusable, pre-registered evaluation harness to facilitate broader adoption of rigorous survival model evaluation practices.

title: Exposure is Optional: Learning Unlike Coordination in Language Models
comment: 13 pages, 6 tables, 2 figures, to submit to TACL
summary: Coordination, a fundamental linguistic structure, remains a subject of intense debate, and its exact nature continues to elude theoretical linguistics. A common view holds that only same-category constituents can be conjoined, which has been challenged by the many grammatical unlike coordinations found in natural language. Treating language models as a computational testbed, we investigate whether the acquisition of unlike coordination requires direct exposure in the training data, or whether it can emerge organically from general compositional abilities. Using Filtered-Corpus Training (FiCT), we train GPT-2 models on corpora from which all instances of unlike coordination have been removed. We find that direct exposure is not necessary: models trained on filtered data successfully generalize to unlike coordination, achieving perplexity and grammaticality judgments comparable to models trained on unfiltered text. Furthermore, our analyses of internal representations indicate that language models process unlike coordination by treating the conjoined elements as belonging to similar structural categories or through a mechanism akin to deletion, both of which appear learnable from exposure to alike coordination alone. This work contributes to the growing understanding of how language models internally represent linguistic structures, while also adding to the broader debate on coordination by showing how models generalize and process unlike coordination without direct exposure.

AI.tldr: Using Filtered-Corpus Training, the authors show that GPT-2 models generalize to unlike coordination (e.g., conjoining different syntactic categories) without direct exposure, suggesting that such generalization emerges from compositional abilities learned from alike coordination alone. Internal representations reveal models handle unlike coordination via similar-category treatment or deletion-like mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Resolve a longstanding debate in theoretical linguistics: whether the ability to process unlike coordination (conjoining constituents of different syntactic categories) requires direct empirical exposure, or whether it can emerge from general compositional mechanisms. This tests whether unlike coordination is learned from surface patterns or reflects deeper grammatical principles.
AI.method: Filtered-Corpus Training (FiCT): GPT-2 models were trained on corpora with all instances of unlike coordination removed, then tested on held-out unlike coordination examples. Evaluation used perplexity scores, grammaticality judgments, and analysis of internal representations to probe how models process these structures.
AI.result: Models trained on filtered data successfully generalized to unlike coordination, achieving perplexity and grammaticality judgments on par with models trained on unfiltered text. Internal representation analysis showed models treat conjoined elements as belonging to similar structural categories or employ a deletion-like mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Direct exposure to unlike coordination is not necessary for its acquisition; the phenomenon can emerge from alike coordination exposure alone. This supports the view that coordination generalization reflects deeper compositional abilities, and contributes both to debates in theoretical linguistics and to understanding how language models internally represent linguistic structures.

title: EvoThink: Evolving Thinking in Large Reasoning Models via Self-Pruning and Aha-Moment Preference Optimization
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) often suffer from overthinking due to redundant verification steps. Existing approaches for mitigating overthinking, such as fast-slow thinking switching and reasoning trajectory compression, fail to make a fine-grained distinction between beneficial and redundant steps within the LRM's reasoning process, and may thus impair reasoning capability in their pursuit of efficiency. To simultaneously improve reasoning efficiency and capability, we propose EvoThink, a framework that reduces redundant verification and encourages the exploration of new reasoning paths. EvoThink comprises two key components: Self-Pruning Training (SPT), an unsupervised method that iteratively prunes redundant reasoning steps and self-trains on the concise trajectories; and Aha-Moment Preference Optimization (AMPO), which, inspired by genetic algorithms, identifies valuable failed reasoning attempts, synthesizes from-wrong-to-right aha-moment data, and optimizes the model to internalize this reasoning pattern. Extensive evaluations across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks demonstrate that EvoThink not only substantially reduces inference-time token usage but also improves the reasoning capability of LRMs.

AI.tldr: EvoThink is a framework that tackles overthinking in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) by combining Self-Pruning Training (SPT) to remove redundant verification steps and Aha-Moment Preference Optimization (AMPO) to repurpose failed reasoning attempts into useful training data. It simultaneously improves reasoning efficiency and capability, reducing token usage while boosting benchmark performance in math and code generation.
AI.motivation: LRMs waste computation on redundant verification steps (overthinking). Existing remedies — fast-slow thinking switching and trajectory compression — operate at too coarse a granularity, failing to distinguish beneficial from redundant reasoning steps, which can degrade reasoning capability in the pursuit of efficiency.
AI.method: EvoThink has two components: (1) Self-Pruning Training (SPT), an unsupervised method that iteratively prunes redundant reasoning steps and self-trains the model on the resulting concise trajectories; (2) Aha-Moment Preference Optimization (AMPO), which uses a genetic-algorithm-inspired approach to identify valuable failed reasoning attempts, synthesizes from-wrong-to-right "aha-moment" data, and optimizes the model to internalize this corrective reasoning pattern.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks show that EvoThink substantially reduces inference-time token usage while also improving the reasoning capability of LRMs.
AI.conclusion: EvoThink demonstrates that fine-grained pruning of redundant steps combined with learning from failed attempts can solve the overthinking problem in LRMs without sacrificing — and indeed improving — reasoning performance.

title: Trustworthy Privacy-Preserving Multimodal Federated Learning for Personalised Breast Cancer Prediction
summary: Federated learning has emerged as a potential solution to privacy concerns associated with using sensitive health data for training predictive models, particularly in personalised cancer care. This research investigates whether federated learning can support the development of robust models for predicting tumour progression in breast cancer patients while addressing four critical deployment pillars: transparency, scalability, security, and fairness. This study evaluates a federated learning framework using multimodal data, including clinical information, tumour characteristics, biomarker data, and patient demographics, alongside medical imaging data such as MRI scans, to model changes in tumour characteristics over time. The performance of the federated approach was compared with that of a centralised model trained on aggregated data. The report then further examines strategies to enhance secure model updates, maintain performance across patient subgroups, and support scalability across institutions. The findings assess whether federated learning can achieve predictive performance comparable to centralised learning while preserving data locality. These results contribute to understanding the feasibility of privacy-preserving, multimodal predictive modelling and support future applications such as digital twins to assist clinicians and patients in personalised treatment planning.

AI.tldr: This study investigates federated learning with multimodal health data (clinical, biomarker, MRI) for predicting breast cancer tumour progression, evaluating its performance against centralized models across four pillars: transparency, scalability, security, and fairness.
AI.motivation: Privacy concerns surrounding sensitive health data limit centralized training of predictive models. The authors aim to determine whether federated learning can match centralized performance while addressing transparency, scalability, security, and fairness in personalised cancer care.
AI.method: A federated learning framework is evaluated using multimodal data — clinical information, tumour characteristics, biomarkers, patient demographics, and MRI scans — to model tumour characteristic changes over time. Performance is benchmarked against a centralized model trained on aggregated data. Strategies for secure model updates, subgroup fairness, and cross-institutional scalability are also examined.
AI.result: The findings assess whether federated learning achieves predictive performance comparable to centralized learning while preserving data locality. (Specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.)
AI.conclusion: The research contributes to understanding the feasibility of privacy-preserving multimodal predictive modelling and supports future digital twin applications for personalised treatment planning, contingent on achieving parity with centralized performance.

title: The Maskability Index: Predicting Task-Objective Alignment in Pretrained Language Models
summary: Large-scale pretrained language models such as T5 and BERT have demonstrated strong capabilities for generating structured knowledge. However, their performance depends on how closely the prompting strategy matches the objectives used during pretraining. We introduce the Maskability Index (MI), a quantitative metric that estimates whether a knowledge relation is better suited to masked-style prompting or prefix-style prompting in few-shot generation. MI is computed from differences in DepthRank scores between masked and unmasked templates, providing a principled measure of objective-template alignment. We evaluate MI on a diverse set of relations from the ATOMIC2020 knowledge base completion benchmark and show that it is positively correlated with downstream generation performance. These results indicate that MI can help select appropriate prompting templates and adaptation strategies for extracting relational knowledge from pretrained language models, especially in low-resource settings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Maskability Index (MI), a quantitative metric that predicts whether a knowledge relation is better extracted via masked-style or prefix-style prompting in few-shot settings, and validates it on the ATOMIC2020 benchmark.
AI.motivation: Pretrained language models (T5, BERT) can generate structured knowledge, but performance varies significantly based on whether the prompting strategy aligns with the model's pretraining objective. There is no principled, quantitative method to determine which prompting style (masked vs. prefix) is optimal for a given knowledge relation, especially in low-resource few-shot settings.
AI.method: The authors propose the Maskability Index (MI), computed from the difference in DepthRank scores between masked and unmasked templates. DepthRank quantifies how well a template aligns with a model's pretraining objective. MI thus provides a principled measure of objective-template alignment, indicating whether a relation favors masked-style or prefix-style prompting.
AI.result: MI is positively correlated with downstream few-shot generation performance across a diverse set of relations from the ATOMIC2020 knowledge base completion benchmark, demonstrating its predictive validity for selecting appropriate prompting strategies.
AI.conclusion: MI serves as an effective tool for selecting prompting templates and adaptation strategies when extracting relational knowledge from pretrained LMs, particularly beneficial in low-resource settings where exhaustive prompt engineering is infeasible.

title: The Giant Hippocampus: From Structural Monoculture to a System of Systems
summary: AI researchers describe state-of-the-art models as one thing repeated at scale: the Transformer, wired identically for text, pixels, or speech. Neuroscientists describe the cortex as a mosaic - dense Layer 4 in visual cortex for spatial encoding, thick Layers 5/6 in motion cortex for temporal integration - different jobs solved by different structures. This paper argues the gap is a structural error, not a stylistic one, and is measurable. A century of cytoarchitecture, from Brodmann to single-cell Patch-seq, shows distinct cognitive functions are implemented by qualitatively different structures, not by rescaling one template. The convolutional neural network is the field's own proof: local receptive fields and hierarchical depth encoded this prior directly, reaching strong image recognition on far less data than later architectures needed. The paper traces how this lesson was discarded: the "Hardware Lottery" made the Transformer the path of least resistance, not the principled choice, and Mixture-of-Experts, often cited as diversity, in fact partitions parameters among identical experts. A functionalist analysis shows the Transformer is best understood as a functional analog of the hippocampal formation, not a general-purpose cortex - the same mistake as treating cortex as one giant Broca's area, except the field has now standardized on a giant hippocampus, applied to tasks it was never built for: audition, executive gating, working memory. The paper closes with an alternative: a Heterogeneous Topological Network, a System of Systems in which distinct modules keep the inductive bias their computation demands and communicate through standardized interfaces. This is a design discipline for AI architects, not cognitive science: specify modularity before training, using structural evidence as a design input rather than reverse-engineering architecture from a trained model's behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI's reliance on a uniform Transformer architecture for all modalities is a structural error, contrasting it with the cortex's heterogeneous, task-specialized cytoarchitecture. It traces how the "Hardware Lottery" led to Transformer dominance over architectures like CNNs that encoded stronger inductive biases, and proposes instead a Heterogeneous Topological Network — a modular System of Systems where distinct computational modules with appropriate inductive biases communicate through standardized interfaces.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to expose a measurable structural gap between how AI and neuroscience conceptualize architecture: AI homogenizes around the Transformer for text, vision, and audio, while neuroscience reveals the cortex as a mosaic of qualitatively different structures optimized for distinct cognitive functions. The authors argue this is not a stylistic difference but a fundamental error that limits computational efficiency and biological plausibility.
AI.method: The paper employs a multi-pronged analytical method: (1) a century-scale review of cytoarchitectonic evidence from Brodmann to single-cell Patch-seq demonstrating structure-function correspondence in cortex; (2) a historical analysis of how the "Hardware Lottery" — GPU-optimized matrix multiplication — made Transformers the path of least resistance, displacing CNNs; (3) a functionalist critique reinterpreting the Transformer as a hippocampal analog rather than a general-purpose cortex; and (4) a proposal for Heterogeneous Topological Networks as an alternative architectural paradigm, treating modularity as a pre-training design discipline informed by structural evidence.
AI.result: Key analytical findings include: CNNs, with their local receptive fields and hierarchical depth, achieved strong image recognition with far less data than Transformers — demonstrating that encoded inductive bias reduces sample complexity. Mixture-of-Experts, often cited as architectural diversity, merely partitions parameters among structurally identical experts. The Transformer functionally resembles the hippocampal formation (specialized for relational memory and sequence encoding) rather than a general-purpose cortex, yet it is misapplied to audition, executive gating, and working memory tasks for which the hippocampus is ill-suited.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that AI needs a design discipline where modularity and inductive biases are specified before training — using structural evidence from neuroscience and task analysis as design inputs — rather than reverse-engineering architecture from post-hoc behavioral analysis. The Heterogeneous Topological Network is proposed as a System of Systems approach, retaining distinct computational modules with appropriate biases, connected through standardized interfaces, to better mirror the cortex's functional specialization.

title: Agent-Centric Animal Pose Forecasting
summary: Understanding animal behavior at an algorithmic level -- what animals attend to, how they form internal models and plans, and how this maps to action -- remains a central challenge in neuroscience and ethology. Data-driven generative models offer a path toward this understanding. We introduce a framework for training agent-centric autoregressive models of animal behavior from tracked pose, applicable to single animals and to groups in which each agent senses and responds to its conspecifics. Our models input egocentric sensory observations and output egocentric movements, mirroring the biological constraint that animals observe and act on the world from their own reference frame. Social behavior emerges from agents independently sensing and responding to one another. This agent-centric formulation requires managing many parallel representations of the same data, along with ML-specific transformations like discretization. We release a general-purpose library focused on the composable sequences of operations that translate between these representations. We show that trained models capture the distribution of social behavior in groups of courting Drosophila, and our library includes quantitative tools for measuring fit. We demonstrate how the library supports systematic comparison across input and output representations and that it adapts straightforwardly to a new domain.

AI.tldr: A framework for training agent-centric autoregressive models of animal behavior from pose data, with a library for managing egocentric representations, demonstrated on social behavior in courting Drosophila.
AI.motivation: Understanding animal behavior at an algorithmic level — what animals attend to, how they form internal models and plans, and how action emerges — remains a central challenge. The authors argue that data-driven generative models offer a path toward this understanding, but existing approaches lack an agent-centric formulation that respects the biological constraint that animals perceive and act from their own egocentric reference frame.
AI.method: The authors introduce a framework for training agent-centric autoregressive models from tracked pose data. The models take egocentric sensory observations as input and produce egocentric movements as output. Social behavior emerges from multiple agents independently sensing and responding to conspecifics. The framework handles the complexity of maintaining parallel egocentric representations and ML-specific transformations (e.g., discretization). They release a general-purpose library for composable sequences of operations that translate between these representations, with quantitative tools for measuring model fit.
AI.result: Trained models successfully capture the distribution of social behavior in groups of courting Drosophila. The library enables systematic comparison across different input and output representations and adapts straightforwardly to new domains beyond the initial demonstration.
AI.conclusion: Agent-centric autoregressive modeling is a viable and principled approach for data-driven understanding of animal behavior, particularly social behavior. The released library facilitates broader adoption by abstracting the representational complexities inherent in egocentric, multi-agent behavioral modeling.

title: Which Values Do LLMs Confuse? A Schwartz-Based Recognition Study
summary: Large language models are increasingly evaluated through the values they endorse, but such evaluations presuppose that models can identify the value expressed in a concrete situation. We study this prerequisite as controlled top-1 recognition over Schwartz's ten basic values. Our evaluation set contains 1,000 Russian situational texts, balanced across the ten values and independently labeled by two human annotators per item. We evaluate 21 instruction-tuned LLM runs under a fixed ranked-response protocol; 20 runs with reliable outputs form the semantic panel. Pooled Acc@1 is 0.683 and Acc@3 is 0.892, showing that models often locate the correct motivational region while ranking close alternatives unstably. Adjacent values account for 50.9% of semantic errors, compared with 24.4% under a checkpoint-specific null. Eight directed confusions recur across checkpoints and human-confirmed subsets. Several are strongly asymmetric, including Universalism to Benevolence, Tradition to Conformity, and Security to Power, whereas Stimulation-Hedonism forms a bidirectional boundary. Their severity is checkpoint-specific and can bias higher-order value profiles. The results motivate value-recognition evaluation that combines exact accuracy, ranked recovery, and directed error analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether LLMs can recognize Schwartz's ten basic values in situational texts. Using 1,000 Russian texts with dual human annotations, 21 instruction-tuned LLM runs achieve pooled Acc@1 of 0.683 and Acc@3 of 0.892. Adjacent values account for 50.9% of errors, with eight recurring directed confusions identified — several strongly asymmetric. Results argue for value-recognition evaluation combining exact accuracy, ranked recovery, and directed error analysis.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly evaluated on the values they endorse, but such evaluations presuppose that models can first identify which value is expressed in a concrete situation. This prerequisite — value recognition — has not been systematically studied, creating a gap in the validity of downstream value-alignment assessments.
AI.method: The authors construct a balanced evaluation set of 1,000 Russian situational texts spanning Schwartz's ten basic values, each independently labeled by two human annotators. They evaluate 21 instruction-tuned LLM runs using a fixed ranked-response protocol where models rank all ten values per item. From these, 20 runs with reliable outputs form a "semantic panel." Analysis covers exact accuracy (Acc@1), ranked recovery (Acc@3), and directed error analysis comparing observed confusions against a checkpoint-specific null model and human-confirmed subsets.
AI.result: Pooled Acc@1 is 0.683 and Acc@3 is 0.892, indicating models often locate the correct motivational region but struggle to rank close alternatives stably. Adjacent values account for 50.9% of semantic errors versus 24.4% under the null. Eight directed confusions recur across checkpoints, several strongly asymmetric: Universalism→Benevolence, Tradition→Conformity, Security→Power; Stimulation–Hedonism forms a bidirectional boundary. Confusion severity is checkpoint-specific and can bias higher-order value profiles.
AI.conclusion: Value recognition in LLMs is non-trivial and error-prone in structured ways. The authors recommend that value-recognition evaluation should incorporate three components: exact accuracy (Acc@1), ranked recovery (Acc@k), and directed error analysis to uncover systematic asymmetric confusions that can propagate bias into downstream value profiles.

title: Coordinating from Memory: Graph-Structured Experience Reuse for Multi-Agent Adaptation in Dynamic Manufacturing
summary: Dynamic manufacturing environments require multi-agent systems to coordinate effectively under frequent operational disturbances such as machine failures, urgent job arrivals, and processing time variations. Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches treat each disturbance episode independently, discarding valuable coordination experience that could accelerate future adaptation. In this paper, we propose a Graph-Structured Experiential Memory (GSEM) framework for multi-agent coordination in dynamic manufacturing. The framework encodes historical coordination episodes as heterogeneous relational graphs that capture task dependencies, machine states, and inter-agent collaboration patterns. When a new disturbance occurs, a graph neural network-based retrieval mechanism identifies structurally similar past episodes, enabling experience-guided policy adaptation rather than learning from scratch. Experiments on dynamic flexible job-shop scheduling benchmarks with three disturbance types show that GSEM reduces makespan by 4.1%-10.0% and adaptation time by 33%-38% compared to the strongest memory-augmented baseline, with the advantage increasing under higher disturbance frequency. Ablation studies and cross-disturbance transfer experiments further validate the necessity of graph-structured encoding and similarity-based retrieval and demonstrate the cross-disturbance generalizability of learned coordination patterns.

AI.tldr: GSEM encodes historical coordination episodes as heterogeneous relational graphs and uses GNN-based similarity retrieval to accelerate multi-agent policy adaptation under disturbances, achieving 4-10% makespan reduction and 33-38% faster adaptation.
AI.motivation: Existing MARL methods treat each disturbance episode independently, wasting reusable coordination experience. The authors aim to leverage past coordination patterns to accelerate adaptation to new disturbances in dynamic manufacturing.
AI.method: The Graph-Structured Experiential Memory (GSEM) framework encodes past coordination episodes as heterogeneous relational graphs capturing task dependencies, machine states, and inter-agent collaboration. A GNN-based retrieval mechanism identifies structurally similar past episodes to guide policy adaptation when new disturbances arise.
AI.result: On dynamic flexible job-shop scheduling benchmarks with three disturbance types, GSEM achieves 4.1%-10.0% makespan reduction and 33%-38% adaptation time reduction over the strongest memory-augmented baseline, with gains increasing under higher disturbance frequency.
AI.conclusion: Graph-structured encoding and similarity-based retrieval are both essential; learned coordination patterns exhibit cross-disturbance generalizability, validating the framework's design.

title: Sound Probabilistic Safety Bounds for Large Language Models
comment: The Initial version of this manuscript has been available on OpenReview, see https://openreview.net/forum?id=papImkPLf5
summary: We propose a novel framework for computing rigorous bounds on the probability that a large language model (LLM) generates harmful output to a given prompt. We study a new application of the Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals to obtain probably approximately correct (PAC) bounds for this problem. As our main technical contribution, we propose an algorithm that leverages features in the latent space to prioritize exploring branches in the auto-regressive generation tree that are more likely to produce harmful outputs. Our approach in particular enables the efficient computation of useful lower bounds, even in scenarios where the true harm probability is extremely small, and crucially, the obtained lower bounds are sound, i.e., formally proven to be less than the actual harmfulness probability: our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by computing non-trivial lower bounds on state-of-the-art LLMs. This study newly enables the evaluation and statistical certification of LLMs.

AI.tldr: A framework using Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals and latent-space-guided tree search to compute rigorous, sound lower bounds on the probability an LLM generates harmful outputs, enabling statistical certification even for extremely rare harm events.
AI.motivation: Existing methods lack the ability to provide formal statistical guarantees about LLM harmfulness. There is a need for rigorous, probably approximately correct (PAC) bounds on harm probability, especially when true harm rates are extremely small, to enable trustworthy evaluation and certification of LLMs.
AI.method: The authors apply Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals to obtain PAC bounds and propose an algorithm that uses latent-space features to prioritize exploration of branches in the autoregressive generation tree that are more likely to yield harmful outputs. This guided search efficiently produces sound lower bounds on harm probability.
AI.result: The method successfully computes non-trivial lower bounds on state-of-the-art LLMs, even when the true harm probability is extremely small, and the obtained bounds are formally proven to be lower than the actual harmfulness probability.
AI.conclusion: The framework newly enables rigorous statistical evaluation and certification of LLMs with respect to harmful output generation, filling a critical gap in AI safety and reliability assessment.

title: CLARK: Closed-loop Learning for Adaptive Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs
comment: 18 pages, 3 Figures, 1 algorithm, 3 tables, submitted to The International Semantic Web Conference'26
summary: Machine Learning models are widely used for automating classification tasks by extracting statistical patterns from data. However, their performance deteriorates if the data distribution changes, making them ill-suited to handle uncertain and evolving information. Moreover, they provide limited support for integrating prior knowledge. To address these limitations, we present CLARK (Closed-loop Learning for Adaptive Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs), a framework that integrates knowledge graphs, symbolic rule mining, and probabilistic reasoning under the Logic Programs with Markov Logic Networks (LP$^{\text{MLN}}$) formalism. Starting from CACTUS-derived KGs, CLARK translates graph structure into an LP$^{\text{MLN}}$ program and iteratively enriches it with candidate rules proposed by symbolic learners. These rules are calibrated through probabilistic weight learning, enabling reasoning under uncertainty and refinement of the underlying graph structure. We evaluate CLARK on two medical datasets, analysing both rule quality and downstream classification performance. Results demonstrate that CLARK leads to improved classification performance and more generalisable inference. Overall, CLARK provides a principled approach to constructing adaptive, interpretable, knowledge-driven models for classification.

AI.tldr: CLARK is a framework that integrates knowledge graphs, symbolic rule mining, and probabilistic reasoning (LP^MLN) to create adaptive, interpretable classifiers robust to distribution shifts. It iteratively enriches CACTUS-derived KGs with learned symbolic rules, calibrates them via weight learning, and demonstrates improved classification and generalizability on medical datasets.
AI.motivation: Machine learning classifiers degrade under data distribution shifts and offer limited support for integrating prior knowledge. There is a need for models that combine statistical learning with structured knowledge to handle uncertainty and evolving information robustly.
AI.method: CLARK operates under the LP^MLN formalism. Starting from CACTUS-derived knowledge graphs, it translates graph structure into an LP^MLN program, then iteratively enriches it with candidate rules from symbolic learners. These rules undergo probabilistic weight learning for calibration, enabling reasoning under uncertainty and refinement of the underlying graph.
AI.result: Evaluated on two medical datasets, CLARK shows improved downstream classification performance and more generalizable inference compared to baselines. Rule quality analysis confirms the viability of the mined symbolic rules.
AI.conclusion: CLARK offers a principled, adaptive, interpretable, knowledge-driven framework for classification that effectively combines knowledge graphs, symbolic rule mining, and probabilistic reasoning to handle distributional shifts.

title: The Mechanism Matters: When Knowledge Graphs Help Reinforcement Learning
summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are widely used to inject prior knowledge into reinforcement learning (RL), yet the literature is dominated by single-domain, positive-result method papers, so we lack a systematic account of when KG structure helps an agent, when it is neutral, and when it hurts. We conduct a controlled study that independently varies the RL task, the injection mechanism (state features, action masking, or potential-based reward shaping), and KG quality. Using a synthetic, fully controllable KG over MiniGrid environments, we report three findings. First, on compositional sparse-reward tasks structured KG guidance improves sample efficiency and solve reliability (70% to 97% of seeds), and a shuffle control that permutes the KG's edges while preserving their count collapses the benefit toward baseline (masking p=0.0001; shaping p=0.006), so the gain is structural rather than generic regularization. Second, KG value scales with the amount of task-relevant knowledge the graph contains. Third, and most consequential, safety depends on the mechanism: soft, optimality-preserving injection benefits from correct knowledge and harmlessly ignores incorrect knowledge, whereas hard masking is brittle, forbidding essential actions when the KG is incomplete or corrupted and making a wrong KG worse than none. A UMLS-derived clinical case study on sepsis management under offline RL is a careful null, underscoring that benefits require task structure the chosen mechanism can exploit. Our results give practitioners concrete guidance on how, and how much, to trust a KG when using it to guide RL.

AI.tldr: A controlled study investigating when and how knowledge graph (KG) structure benefits reinforcement learning agents reveals that KG-guided RL improves sample efficiency on compositional sparse-reward tasks due to structural knowledge (not generic regularization), that value scales with task-relevant knowledge, and that soft injection mechanisms (reward shaping) are robust to incorrect knowledge while hard masking is brittle and can make a wrong KG worse than none.
AI.motivation: The literature on KG-guided RL is dominated by single-domain positive-result papers with no systematic understanding of when KG structure helps, is neutral, or hurts agent performance. Practitioners lack principled guidance on how and how much to trust KGs for RL.
AI.method: A controlled factorial study independently varying three factors: (1) the RL task (compositional sparse-reward MiniGrid environments), (2) the KG injection mechanism (state features, action masking, or potential-based reward shaping), and (3) KG quality (including a shuffle control that permutes edges while preserving count, plus variations in completeness and corruption). A UMLS-derived clinical case study on sepsis management under offline RL serves as a null-result validation.
AI.result: Three main findings: (1) Structured KG guidance improves sample efficiency and solve reliability (70%→97%) on compositional sparse-reward tasks; the shuffle control collapses this benefit (masking p=0.0001; shaping p=0.006), confirming the gain is structural. (2) KG value scales with task-relevant knowledge quantity. (3) Soft injection (reward shaping) is robust to incorrect knowledge, harmlessly ignoring it, while hard action masking is brittle—forbidding essential actions when the KG is incomplete/corrupted, making a wrong KG worse than none. The clinical case study yields a null result, showing benefits require exploitable task structure.
AI.conclusion: KG injection into RL is not universally beneficial. Practitioners should (1) ensure task structure aligns with the KG, (2) prefer soft, optimality-preserving mechanisms like reward shaping for safety under uncertainty, (3) avoid hard masking unless KG quality is guaranteed high, and (4) recognize that the benefit is structural rather than merely a regularizing effect of additional information.

title: PyroDash: Cost-Efficient Token-Level Small-Large Language Model Collaborative Inference
summary: Large language models (LLMs) provide strong reasoning capabilities but are expensive to serve at scale, whereas small language models (SLMs) are cheaper but less reliable on difficult problems. We introduce PyroDash, a cost-aware framework for token-level SLM-LLM collaborative inference. During generation, the SLM decides whether to request assistance by emitting a control token. A Collaborate Engine then sends the query and partial reasoning trace to a frozen LLM for completion through a single handoff. The policy is internalized in the SLM, requiring neither a separate router, LLM retraining, nor access to LLM logits. PyroDash trains the SLM in three stages: control-token embedding learning, offloading-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and cost-aware alignment with Group Relative Policy Optimization. Its reward balances answer accuracy against inference cost normalized by LLM-only inference. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, PyroDash supports different accuracy-cost operating points. With $λ=0.05$, it achieves 64.04 percent average accuracy, 6.36 percentage points above the LLM-only baseline, while reducing cost by 20.4 percent. With $λ=0.6$, it achieves 54.55 percent accuracy with a 1.90 percent LLM token ratio and 0.012 LLM calls per example, reducing total cost from USD 49.36 to USD 1.78. These results show that learned token-level handoffs can reduce LLM use while preserving strong reasoning performance.

AI.tldr: PyroDash is a cost-aware framework enabling token-level collaboration between SLMs and LLMs. The SLM learns to emit control tokens to request LLM assistance during generation, trained via a three-stage process. It achieves higher accuracy than LLM-only baselines while significantly reducing inference costs, demonstrating that learned token-level handoffs effectively balance reasoning performance and cost.
AI.motivation: LLMs offer strong reasoning but are expensive to serve at scale; SLMs are cheaper but unreliable on hard problems. Existing collaborative approaches require separate routers, LLM retraining, or LLM logit access. The authors aim for a simpler, cost-aware solution where the SLM internalizes the routing decision at the token level.
AI.method: PyroDash trains an SLM with three stages: (1) control-token embedding learning, (2) offloading-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and (3) cost-aware alignment using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). During inference, the SLM emits a control token to request LLM help; a Collaborate Engine handles a single handoff, sending the query and partial trace to a frozen LLM. The reward function balances answer accuracy against inference cost, normalized by LLM-only cost, governed by a tunable λ parameter.
AI.result: On five mathematical reasoning benchmarks: With λ=0.05, PyroDash achieves 64.04% average accuracy (+6.36pp over LLM-only) while reducing cost by 20.4%. With λ=0.6, it achieves 54.55% accuracy using only 1.90% LLM token ratio and 0.012 LLM calls per example, reducing total cost from $49.36 to $1.78.
AI.conclusion: Learned token-level handoffs effectively reduce LLM reliance while preserving strong reasoning performance. The framework supports flexible accuracy-cost operating points via the λ parameter, making it practical for diverse deployment scenarios.

title: Safe Remediation as Risk-Constrained Intervention Decision in Microservice Systems
summary: In modern IT operations (IT-Ops), the cost of an incorrect repair often exceeds the cost of no action at all. Yet existing automated remediation systems are designed to generate actions rather than to decide whether intervention is warranted, leaving safety as an afterthought enforced by manual approval. This paper makes three contributions to close this gap: (i) we reformulate safe remediation as a risk-constrained intervention decision problem and cast it as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP), in which the agent maximizes repair success subject to a bounded false remediation rate (FRR); (ii) we introduce a three-dimensional risk decomposition comprising blast radius, reversibility, and epistemic uncertainty, providing operators with an interpretable per-action safety interface; and (iii) we design a context-adaptive human-in-the-loop (HITL) gate that turns escalation from a binary failsafe into a bandwidth-aware control layer responsive to on-call load and business criticality. The full policy is learned offline from historical incident logs, enabling explicit control of the expected FRR. Experiments on the Train Ticket microservice benchmark with Chaos Mesh fault injection and an RCAEval-aligned fault taxonomy show that our framework reduces FRR by 39% while improving repair success by 2.5 points over a strong runbook baseline, and reduces on-call escalation load by 17% relative to a fixed-threshold variant.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates safe automated remediation in IT operations as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) that maximizes repair success under a bounded false remediation rate. It introduces a 3D risk decomposition (blast radius, reversibility, epistemic uncertainty) and a bandwidth-aware human-in-the-loop gating mechanism, achieving a 39% reduction in false remediation rate and 17% lower on-call escalation load.
AI.motivation: In IT-Ops, incorrect automated repairs are often more costly than taking no action, yet existing remediation systems prioritize action generation over intervention safety, relying on manual approval as a crude safeguard. There is a gap in principled, risk-aware decision-making for automated remediation.
AI.method: The authors (i) cast safe remediation as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) where the agent maximizes repair success subject to a bounded false remediation rate (FRR); (ii) propose a three-dimensional risk decomposition—blast radius, reversibility, and epistemic uncertainty—for interpretable per-action safety; (iii) design a context-adaptive HITL gate that modulates escalation based on on-call load and business criticality. The policy is learned offline from historical incident logs.
AI.result: On the Train Ticket microservice benchmark with Chaos Mesh fault injection and RCAEval-aligned fault taxonomy, the framework reduces FRR by 39%, improves repair success by 2.5 points over a runbook baseline, and cuts on-call escalation load by 17% relative to a fixed-threshold HITL variant.
AI.conclusion: Risk-constrained CMDP formulation combined with interpretable 3D risk decomposition and adaptive HITL gating provides a principled, safer, and operationally practical approach to automated remediation, significantly reducing false interventions while maintaining high repair success.

title: SCPP: A Unified Python Library for Soft Clustering
summary: In this paper, we present SCPP (Soft Clustering Python Package), an open-source Python framework for soft clustering. SCPP establishes a canonical, scikit-learn-compatible estimator interface that standardizes model training, prediction, membership representation, evaluation, and benchmarking across heterogeneous soft clustering methods, including fuzzy, probabilistic, graph-based, matrix factorization, and deep learning methods. The framework currently integrates 40 representative algorithms together with a comprehensive benchmarking comprising datasets, clustering quality metrics, and standardized runtime, memory, and scalability evaluation. SCPP further provides extensive documentation, practical examples, automated testing, and seamless integration with the scientific Python ecosystem, enabling reproducible experimentation and straightforward extension with new algorithms. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/soft-clustering/soft-clustering.

AI.tldr: SCPP is an open-source Python framework that standardizes soft clustering with a scikit-learn-compatible interface, integrating 40 algorithms across multiple paradigms along with comprehensive benchmarking tools.
AI.motivation: The lack of a unified, standardized interface for the diverse landscape of soft clustering methods (fuzzy, probabilistic, graph-based, matrix factorization, deep learning) hinders reproducible experimentation, fair comparison, and ease of use.
AI.method: SCPP provides a canonical estimator API compatible with scikit-learn, unifying training, prediction, membership representation, and evaluation. It integrates 40 representative algorithms, curated datasets, clustering quality metrics, and standardized runtime/memory/scalability benchmarks, all supported by documentation, automated testing, and scientific Python ecosystem integration.
AI.result: The framework enables reproducible experimentation across heterogeneous soft clustering methods, offers standardized benchmarking of 40 algorithms, and provides seamless extensibility for new methods.
AI.conclusion: SCPP fills a critical gap in the soft clustering ecosystem by providing a unified, well-documented, and extensible open-source platform that lowers the barrier to entry for both practitioners and researchers.

title: Generative AI floods and dilutes the market for books
summary: Generative AI can produce book-length works of fiction at near-zero cost. These books are often dismissed as low-quality ``slop'' that buyers will ignore, and are assumed to carry little commercial weight. We test that assumption with full-text AI detection across 14,419 self-published genre-fiction books sold on Amazon from 2023 to 2026, matched to daily sales records through June 2026. None of these books disclose whether or not they contain AI-produced content. We find that books for which we detected substantial AI text ($>$ 25\%) make up a large share of the catalog but a smaller share of sales. Even so, they reach commercial scale, winning a growing share of sales over time and taking more of the scarce top-rank positions once held by books with no detected AI text. Over this period, the number of books with observed sales in a quarter grew 19.2-fold, while quarterly revenue grew only 8.9-fold. The market therefore added selling books faster than it added revenue, and revenue per selling book fell across most genres. Books with no AI text lose the most ground in genres with high AI diffusion, and most of all where Kindle Unlimited availability is high. Among top-selling books, those with substantial AI text draw on more distinctive language from existing books than do books with no AI text; for these books overlap rises with revenue, a gradient we do not detect for books with no AI text. Generative AI can thus reshape a creative market through scale rather than quality. Our results bear directly on the market-effect question at the center of the fair use defense to copyright infringement.

AI.tldr: An empirical study of 14,419 self-published Amazon books (2023–2026) finds that AI-generated fiction, though commercially discounted, captures a growing share of sales and top-rank positions, reshaping the market through sheer scale rather than quality, with implications for copyright fair use.
AI.motivation: To test the prevailing assumption that AI-generated books are low-quality "slop" with negligible commercial impact, and to provide evidence directly relevant to the market-effect question central to the fair use defense in copyright law.
AI.method: Full-text AI detection applied to 14,419 self-published genre-fiction books sold on Amazon from 2023 through June 2026, matched to daily sales records. Books were categorized by AI text proportion (>25% threshold). Market analysis examined catalog share, sales share, revenue trends, genre-level diffusion, Kindle Unlimited effects, and linguistic distinctiveness via overlap with existing books.
AI.result: Books with substantial AI text (>25%) constitute a large share of the catalog but a smaller share of sales, yet achieve commercial scale with growing sales share and increasing occupation of scarce top-rank positions. Over the period, the number of selling books grew 19.2-fold while revenue grew only 8.9-fold, depressing per-book revenue across most genres. Books without AI text lose the most ground in high-AI-diffusion genres, especially where Kindle Unlimited is prevalent. Among top sellers, AI-heavy books exhibit higher linguistic overlap with existing books, and that overlap increases with revenue—a gradient absent in non-AI books.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI reshapes a creative market through scale rather than quality, displacing human-authored books from top-rank positions and compressing per-book revenue. These findings directly inform the market-effect analysis required for fair use determinations in copyright infringement cases.

title: EvoDRC: A Self-Evolving Agentic Framework for Automated DRC Violation Repair
summary: Design rule check (DRC) closure remains a major bottleneck in advanced-node physical design. Although detailed routers are rule-aware, residual design rule violations (DRVs) often require manual engineering change order iterations. Automating this process is challenging because repairs must account for complex geometric interactions, preserve circuit connectivity, and avoid introducing new violations. We present EvoDRC, a skill-evolution framework for agentic block-level DRC repair. EvoDRC initializes layer-specific repair skills using knowledge distilled from an unrelated reference design and continuously evolves these skills using traceable repair experience collected from the target design. EvoDRC decomposes the layout into bounded repair regions and assigns an LLM repair agent to each region. Local DRC analysis, connectivity-checking, and impact-preview tools provide feedback on proposed modifications. Repair operations and their resulting DRV changes are stored in a knowledge database and used to evolve the repair skills. Experiments on seven block-level designs from the DAC26 DRC Benchmark show that EvoDRC achieves a 73.5\% overall reduction compared to the reported baseline.

AI.tldr: EvoDRC is an agentic framework that uses LLM agents with continuously evolving repair skills to automatically fix design rule violations in chip physical design, achieving 73.5% DRV reduction on benchmark designs.
AI.motivation: DRC closure is a major bottleneck in advanced-node physical design. Manual ECO iterations are time-consuming, and automation is hard due to complex geometric interactions, connectivity preservation requirements, and the risk of introducing new violations.
AI.method: EvoDRC initializes layer-specific repair skills via knowledge distillation from an unrelated reference design, then evolves them using traceable repair experience from the target design. The layout is decomposed into bounded repair regions, each assigned an LLM repair agent. Local DRC analysis, connectivity-checking, and impact-preview tools provide closed-loop feedback. Repair operations and DRV outcomes are stored in a knowledge database to continuously evolve the skills.
AI.result: Evaluated on seven block-level designs from the DAC26 DRC Benchmark, EvoDRC achieves a 73.5% overall DRV reduction compared to the reported baseline.
AI.conclusion: EvoDRC demonstrates that skill-evolution with LLM agents, guided by structured feedback tools and a growing experience database, can effectively automate DRC repair in block-level physical design, significantly reducing manual effort.

title: HypEMBER: Hypernetwork-based Ensemble for Robust Policy Learning of Parametrized Dynamical Systems
summary: In this work we investigate reinforcement learning (RL) as a framework for the robust control of parametrized dynamical systems in presence of measurements and model uncertainties. High-dimensional state spaces, expensive numerical solvers, the partial knowledge of the governing equations, and the dependence on physical parameters that may be uncertain or difficult to estimate accurately, make the use of standard RL approaches computationally unfeasible. Indeed, lack of robustness and poor generalization across parameter variations are further amplified in presence of noisy or incomplete measurements, ultimately hampering control performance. To address these challenges, we introduce HypEMBER, a novel RL framework based on the combination of hypernetworks and ensemble learning. In the proposed approach, both the policy and value functions are represented through hypernetworks that generate the weights of the underlying models conditioned on the physical parameters of the system, thereby enabling parametric generalization across different dynamical regimes. In addition, an ensemble of policy and value approximators is employed to quantify epistemic uncertainty, leading to improved exploration strategies and enhanced robustness during and after training. The performance of the proposed framework is assessed on two representative parametrized control problems: (i) the one-dimensional Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation and (ii) a particle-navigation task in a two-dimensional time-dependent gyre flow, focusing on robustness with respect to measurement noise and parameter misspecification. Numerical results demonstrate that HypEMBER consistently improves training stability and sample efficiency, while achieving superior robustness to uncertainties affecting both the system dynamics and the available observations, in comparison with state-of-the-art RL methods.

AI.tldr: HypEMBER combines hypernetworks with ensemble learning in RL to achieve parametric generalization and uncertainty-aware robust control for parametrized dynamical systems under noisy measurements and model uncertainties.
AI.motivation: Standard RL struggles with parametrized dynamical systems due to high-dimensional state spaces, expensive solvers, partial knowledge of governing equations, and uncertain physical parameters. These challenges are exacerbated by noisy/incomplete measurements, leading to poor generalization across parameter variations and lack of robustness.
AI.method: HypEMBER uses hypernetworks to generate policy and value function weights conditioned on physical parameters, enabling parametric generalization. An ensemble of policy and value approximators quantifies epistemic uncertainty, improving exploration and robustness during and after training.
