AI.result: HypEMBER demonstrated improved training stability, sample efficiency, and superior robustness to measurement noise and parameter misspecification compared to state-of-the-art RL methods on two test problems: the 1D Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation and a particle-navigation task in 2D time-dependent gyre flow.
AI.conclusion: HypEMBER is an effective RL framework for robust control of parametrized dynamical systems under uncertainty, consistently outperforming existing methods in stability, efficiency, and robustness.

title: Notes to Self: Can LLMs Benefit from Experiential Abstractions?
summary: Humans distill experience into reusable abstractions, e.g., strategies and cautionary reminders, and apply them to gradually solve problems more effectively. We study whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can similarly benefit from such experiential abstractions. From LLMs' solution traces on the MATH training set, a stronger teacher or the LLMs themselves extract natural-language abstractions into a retrievable library. We explore two usage modes: (1) inference-time retrieval and (2) reinforcement learning (RL) with abstraction-augmented training prompts. Experiential abstractions improve LLM performance on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks. Self-extracted abstractions match teacher-extracted ones, and our abstraction usage framework can transfer to other datasets and models. These findings suggest LLMs can extract and apply experiential abstractions much as humans leverage distilled experience.

AI.tldr: LLMs can extract reusable natural-language abstractions from their own problem-solving traces, store them in a retrievable library, and apply them via inference-time retrieval or RL training—improving math/logical reasoning performance, with self-extracted abstractions matching teacher-extracted ones.
AI.motivation: Humans learn by distilling experience into reusable abstractions (strategies, reminders) that improve future problem-solving. This paper investigates whether LLMs can similarly benefit from such experiential abstractions, moving beyond single-instance reasoning to cumulative learning from past solution traces.
AI.method: Starting from LLM solution traces on the MATH training set, a stronger teacher model or the LLM itself extracts natural-language abstractions (e.g., strategies, common pitfalls) into a retrievable library. Two usage modes are explored: (1) retrieval-augmented inference, where relevant abstractions are fetched at test time; (2) reinforcement learning with abstraction-augmented training prompts. The framework is tested on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks, with transfer experiments across datasets and models.
AI.result: Experiential abstractions consistently improve LLM performance on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks. Self-extracted abstractions perform on par with those extracted by a stronger teacher model. The abstraction usage framework successfully transfers across different datasets and models, demonstrating generality.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can extract and apply experiential abstractions in a manner analogous to human use of distilled experience. This capability suggests a path toward more cumulative, experience-driven learning in language models, bridging individual reasoning episodes into reusable knowledge.

title: Global Difference Constraint Propagation for Constraint Programming
summary: Difference constraints of the form $x - y \leq d$ are well studied, with efficient algorithms for satisfaction and implication, because of their connection to shortest paths. Finite domain propagation algorithms, however, typically do not make use of these algorithms, and treat each difference constraint as a separate propagator. Propagation does guarantee completeness of solving, but can be needlessly slow. In this paper we describe how to build a (bounds consistent) global propagator for difference constraints that treats them all simultaneously. SAT modulo theory solvers have included theory solvers for difference constraints for some time. While a theory solver for difference constraints gives the basis of a global difference constraint propagator, we show how the requirements on the propagator are quite different. Crucially, we show how to explain propagations by a global difference constraint propagator, in order to use it within a lazy clause generation solver. We give experiments showing that treating difference constraints globally can substantially improve on the standard propagation approach.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a global, bounds-consistent propagator for difference constraints (x - y ≤ d) that treats all constraints simultaneously, rather than as separate propagators. It adapts SAT modulo theory (SMT) difference constraint solving for use within a lazy clause generation (LCG) solver, crucially adding explanation generation for propagations, and demonstrates substantial performance improvements over per-constraint propagation.
AI.motivation: Difference constraints are typically handled in finite domain propagation by treating each constraint as an independent propagator. While this guarantees completeness, it is unnecessarily slow because it fails to exploit the global structure and efficient graph-based algorithms (shortest paths) available for difference constraints. SMT solvers have long included theory solvers for difference constraints, but these do not directly translate into constraint programming propagators, particularly because they lack mechanisms for explaining propagations — a requirement for lazy clause generation solvers.
AI.method: The authors construct a bounds-consistent global propagator for difference constraints by adapting SMT theory solver techniques (specifically, shortest-path-based algorithms on the constraint graph). The key innovation is integrating this global propagator into a lazy clause generation (LCG) framework by developing a method for explaining the propagations it makes — i.e., providing a clause that logically justifies each bound update. This involves tracking which constraints contribute to each inferred bound and generating explanations from the shortest-path derivations.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that the global difference constraint propagator substantially outperforms the standard per-constraint propagation approach. The performance improvements are attributed to the global propagation's ability to reason about all difference constraints simultaneously, reducing the number of propagation steps and solver iterations required.
AI.conclusion: Treating difference constraints globally within a lazy clause generation solver, with proper explanation generation, yields significant performance gains over conventional per-constraint propagation. The work bridges the gap between SMT difference constraint solving and CP propagation by addressing the critical requirement of explanation generation.

title: Anatomy of a Sound Neural Reasoner: One-Shot Amortization, First-Pass Poisoning, and Search Inertness in Clue-Rich Completion
summary: Neural solvers are built to deduce, branch, and revise intermediate states. The Lattice Deduction Transformer (LDT) appears to do exactly that. In clue-rich Sudoku, it does not: one forward pass commits essentially the entire grid (every blank cell on standard 6x6, 94-96% on augmented 9x9), turning the iterative solver into a one-shot predictor wrapped in an exact verifier. All hard-slice failures are decided before search begins, when the first pass confidently deletes a value required by the true solution. We call this first-pass poisoning. Adding learned branching, MRV, backtracking, value exclusion, and shared nogoods (CoLT) does not change which Sudoku instances are solved; it cuts repeated invalid derivations 1,497-fold. At the frozen training budget, constraint-graph attention alone matches full-CoLT accuracy, while positional tables recover only under substantially longer training, indicating an optimization and sample-efficiency advantage rather than an absolute capacity difference. The diagnosis predicts two effective interventions. Digit-permutation augmentation raises 9x9 accuracy from below 1% to 96.5 +/- 0.3 across three training seeds on a symmetry-disjoint split. Test-time union over symmetry-transformed passes raises all three hard-slice checkpoints from 72.8-78.9% to 100% without retraining. On from-scratch graph coloring, one-shot behavior disappears and search changes accuracy. In clue-rich completion, LDT-like systems are one-shot amortized predictors rather than learned search procedures: accuracy is determined by calibration and symmetry, while search primarily removes computational waste.

AI.tldr: LDT-based neural solvers for clue-rich Sudoku behave as one-shot amortized predictors rather than learned search procedures. First-pass poisoning determines all failures before search begins. Search reduces computational waste but does not change which instances are solved. Symmetry augmentation and test-time symmetry ensembling dramatically improve accuracy, achieving up to 100% on hard slices.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether neural solvers like the Lattice Deduction Transformer (LDT) genuinely perform iterative reasoning (deduce, branch, revise) in constraint satisfaction problems, or whether their apparent search behavior masks a fundamentally one-shot prediction mechanism.
AI.method: The authors analyze LDT on Sudoku (6x6, 9x9) and graph coloring. They measure grid commitment rates in the first forward pass, identify first-pass poisoning (confident early deletion of required values), and test whether adding search components (MRV, backtracking, value exclusion, nogoods via CoLT) changes the set of solved instances. Interventions include digit-permutation augmentation and test-time symmetry ensembling.
AI.result: First pass commits 94-96% of blank cells on 9x9 Sudoku. First-pass poisoning determines all hard-slice failures before search. Adding CoLT search components does not change which instances are solved, only cuts redundant derivations 1,497-fold. Constraint-graph attention matches full-CoLT accuracy at the same training budget. Digit-permutation augmentation raises 9x9 accuracy from <1% to 96.5±0.3%. Test-time symmetry ensembling lifts hard-slice accuracy from 72.8-78.9% to 100%. On graph coloring, one-shot behavior disappears and search affects accuracy.
AI.conclusion: In clue-rich completion tasks, LDT-like systems function as one-shot amortized predictors whose accuracy is determined by calibration and symmetry, while search serves only to eliminate computational waste. True learned search behavior is task-dependent, emerging in graph coloring but not in clue-rich Sudoku.

title: LKValues: Aligning Large Language Models with Sri Lankan Societal Values
comment: 37 pages, 10 figures, and 15 tables. Includes appendices. Datasets are available at the project repository
summary: Value alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) has been shown to be culturally biased toward Western norms. This results in the mishandling of local values in multilingual societies such as Sri Lanka that have their unique cultural dynamics. Existing benchmarks overlook Sri Lankan-contextualized values in its official language Sinhala, hindering culturally sensitive evaluation and fine-tuning. To bridge this gap, we propose LKValues, the first survey-grounded resource suite for Sri Lankan value alignment. From a trilingual survey of 205 respondents, blending adapted global frameworks and LLM-elicited local constructs, we derive 40 majority-endorsed societal values. Using these values, we construct LKvaluesIT, a Sinhala-English news-derived instruction corpus containing 150k scenario-based instances, and LKvaluesBench, a value-sensitive evaluation benchmark of 1,000 instances. We evaluate a set of proprietary and open-weight LLMs with LKvaluesBench. We fine-tune three open-weight base models (Qwen3.5-4B-Base, Qwen3.5-9B-Base, and Aya-Expanse-8B-Base). Our experiments show that newer and larger LLMs still exhibit low-resource and cultural value-alignment gaps. LKValues fine-tuning improves Qwen-family models in English and Sinhala, reducing invalid outputs and cross-lingual disparities, though gains remain model-family dependent. These highlight LKValues efficacy in embedding Sri Lankan values, offering a replicable pipeline for low-resource, country-specific pluralist value alignment. The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/NextME14/LKValues.

AI.tldr: LKValues introduces a survey-grounded resource suite for aligning LLMs with Sri Lankan societal values, comprising a 150k-instance Sinhala-English instruction corpus and a 1,000-instance benchmark. Fine-tuning on LKValues reduces cultural alignment gaps but reveals model-family-dependent improvements and persistent low-resource disparities.
AI.motivation: LLM value alignment is culturally biased toward Western norms, and existing benchmarks overlook Sri Lanka's unique cultural dynamics and its official language Sinhala. This hinders culturally sensitive evaluation and fine-tuning for multilingual, non-Western societies.
AI.method: The authors conducted a trilingual survey of 205 respondents, blending adapted global value frameworks with LLM-elicited local constructs to derive 40 majority-endorsed societal values. From these, they built (1) LKvaluesIT, a Sinhala-English news-derived instruction corpus with 150k scenario-based instances, and (2) LKvaluesBench, a 1,000-instance value-sensitive evaluation benchmark. They evaluated proprietary and open-weight LLMs on LKvaluesBench and fine-tuned three base models (Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B, Aya-Expanse-8B) to assess alignment improvements.
AI.result: Newer and larger LLMs still exhibit low-resource and cultural value-alignment gaps. Fine-tuning with LKValues improves Qwen-family models in both English and Sinhala, reducing invalid outputs and cross-lingual disparities, though gains are model-family dependent (Aya-Expanse benefits less).
AI.conclusion: LKValues demonstrates efficacy in embedding Sri Lankan values into LLMs and offers a replicable pipeline for low-resource, country-specific pluralist value alignment. The dataset is publicly released to facilitate further research.

title: Reading and Steering Representations of Materials-Science Mechanisms in an Open-Weight Language Model
summary: Large language models can answer scientific questions, yet a correct output does not reveal whether the model represents or uses the governing physics. Here we show that materials science mechanism information in the open-weight google/gemma-4-E4B-it model has three experimentally separable forms: concepts are readable in individual hidden states, constitutive orientation is carried by controlled transformations between states, and selected internal representations causally control engineering answers. We combine matched direct and Jacobian vocabulary readouts, option-free state geometry, a 60-law counterfactual benchmark and causal interventions. In 50 held-out materials descriptions, three independently fitted Jacobian lenses reproduced concept ranks, and target-free word sets from both readouts enabled blinded identification of 9 of 10 mechanism families. A separate 72-prompt benchmark produced mechanism-specific hidden-state neighborhoods, but an exact graph audit showed that this apparent physical organization was equally explained by numerical comparison. We therefore compared otherwise identical prompts in which only the direction of the physical input was reversed, asking whether the resulting hidden-state movement followed the supplied constitutive law. These state transformations ordered direct, physically neutral and inverse laws across 60 frozen relations and correctly oriented 39 of 40 directional laws, whereas lexical controls were near chance. Bidirectional interventions shifted answer probabilities toward or away from the physically appropriate outcome across all 12 matched cases, while counterfactual state patches transferred opposing decision signals across mechanisms and answer formats. Physical relationships were therefore more visible in controlled state changes than in absolute states alone.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether the open-weight Gemma model internally represents materials science physics, finding that physical mechanisms are encoded in three separable forms: readable concepts in hidden states, directional constitutive relations in state transformations, and causally active internal representations. Notably, physical relationships are more visible in controlled state changes than in absolute states.
AI.motivation: To determine whether LLMs that correctly answer scientific questions actually represent and use the governing physics internally, rather than merely producing superficially correct outputs through pattern matching or memorization.
AI.method: The authors probe the google/gemma-4-E4B-it model using: (1) matched direct and Jacobian vocabulary readouts for concept decoding, (2) option-free state geometry analysis, (3) a 60-law counterfactual benchmark, (4) causal interventions including bidirectional interventions and counterfactual state patches, (5) directional reversal experiments comparing hidden-state movement under direct vs. reversed physical inputs, and (6) exact graph audits to distinguish physical organization from numerical comparison artifacts.
AI.result: Three independently fitted Jacobian lenses reproduced concept ranks on 50 held-out descriptions. Target-free word sets enabled blinded identification of 9/10 mechanism families. However, mechanism-specific hidden-state neighborhoods were equally explained by numerical comparison. State transformations correctly ordered direct, physically neutral, and inverse laws across 60 frozen relations and correctly oriented 39/40 directional laws (lexical controls near chance). Bidirectional causal interventions shifted answer probabilities appropriately across all 12 matched cases, while counterfactual state patches transferred opposing decision signals across mechanisms and formats.
AI.conclusion: Physical relationships in LLMs are more faithfully revealed by controlled state transformations than by absolute hidden states alone. The model possesses separable representations for materials science concepts, constitutive orientations, and causally active engineering knowledge, demonstrating genuine internal use of physical principles rather than shallow pattern matching.

title: Expert-Guided Forecast Editing for Time-Series Foundation Models
summary: Time-series foundation models can forecast across heterogeneous domains without task-specific training, but their forecasts are fixed once produced and cannot directly incorporate task-specific expert feedback. We study expert-guided forecast editing: a frozen foundation model generates candidate future trajectories, and an expensive expert evaluator scores them to guide forecast revision. Under a tight query budget, two natural strategies sit at opposite ends: best-of-$N$ purely exploits the foundation model's predictive distribution, while optimization approaches mostly explore the forecast horizon as an unstructured high-dimensional vector. Each extreme is individually sub-optimal. We introduce \textbf{DEFT}, an expert-guided forecast editing framework that balances the two by first exploiting the foundation model's predictive samples in a decomposed trend--seasonal space, then exploring around them via component-wise refinement. DEFT queries the expert only on complete trajectories, then reuses scores for the trend and seasonal components that appeared in the queried recombinations. This lets each expert query provide structured component-level feedback while keeping the foundation model frozen. We compare DEFT against direct search approaches, including best-of-$N$, cross-entropy methods, and Bayesian optimization, under matched expert-query budgets. Across two forecasting benchmarks consisting of 78 datasets, three time-series foundation models, four feedback types, and seven query budgets, DEFT consistently improves the effectiveness of expert guidance. A molecular-dynamics case study further suggests that the same principle extends to more physically grounded feedback, supporting the hypothesis that sparse test-time guidance should be spent balancing prior exploitation with structured exploration.

AI.tldr: DEFT is an expert-guided forecast editing framework that balances exploitation of a frozen time-series foundation model's predictive distribution with structured exploration via decomposed trend-seasonal component-wise refinement, achieving consistent improvements over best-of-N, cross-entropy, and Bayesian optimization across extensive benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Time-series foundation models produce fixed forecasts without the ability to incorporate task-specific expert feedback. Under a tight query budget, existing approaches fall into two extremes: best-of-N purely exploits the model's prior, while optimization methods treat the forecast horizon as an unstructured high-dimensional vector, leading to inefficient exploration. Both extremes are sub-optimal, motivating a method that balances exploitation and structured exploration.
AI.method: DEFT decomposes candidate forecast trajectories from a frozen foundation model into trend and seasonal components. It first exploits the model's predictive samples in this decomposed space, then performs component-wise refinement for structured exploration. Expert queries are made only on complete trajectories, and scores are reused for the trend and seasonal components that appeared in queried recombinations, providing structured component-level feedback per query without modifying the foundation model.
AI.result: Across 78 datasets, three time-series foundation models, four feedback types, and seven query budgets, DEFT consistently outperforms best-of-N, cross-entropy methods, and Bayesian optimization under matched expert-query budgets. A molecular-dynamics case study further validates the approach with physically grounded feedback.
AI.conclusion: Sparse test-time guidance is most effective when balanced between exploiting the foundation model's prior and structured exploration in a decomposed component space. DEFT operationalizes this principle and demonstrates robust, cross-domain improvements, suggesting broader applicability beyond forecasting to settings with physically grounded feedback.

title: PRO-LONG: Programmatic Memory Enables Long-Horizon Reasoning
summary: Long-horizon tasks require sustained perception, reasoning, and exploration, and are a persistent challenge for large language model (LLM) agents. This gap is reflected in their limited performance on continual learning benchmarks such as ARC-AGI-3, especially when models are evaluated out of the box. Various agent harnesses have been proposed to close this gap, and each commits to a strategy for handling long sequences of observations, i.e., what information to save from the environment and how to load it into model context, a choice we argue is particularly consequential. Existing methods for context management face a significant tradeoff, as preserving more information makes retrieving relevant details less tractable. We propose PRO-LONG, a minimal context management framework built around programmatic memory for LLM agents in long-horizon, exploratory settings. PRO-LONG addresses the tradeoff by keeping a complete, structured interaction log and capitalizing on recent progress in coding agents to search this history efficiently. On the full ARC-AGI-3 public game set, PRO-LONG improves over a base coding agent by an average of 18.0 percentage points across frontier models, and matches or exceeds state-of-the-art specialized harnesses (up to 76.1% pass@1) while using 4.2-5.8x fewer tokens. With Fable 5, PRO-LONG achieves 97.4% best@2 at a total cost of \$1,750. Relevant code and logs are available at https://github.com/alexisfox7/PRO-LONG.

AI.tldr: PRO-LONG is a context management framework for LLM agents that uses programmatic memory—a complete, structured interaction log searched via coding agents—to handle long-horizon tasks. It improves pass rates on ARC-AGI-3 by 18 pp over base agents, matches SOTA specialized harnesses with 4.2–5.8× fewer tokens, and achieves 97.4% best@2 on Fable 5.
AI.motivation: LLM agents struggle with long-horizon tasks requiring sustained perception, reasoning, and exploration because existing context management methods face a fundamental tradeoff: preserving more information from the environment makes retrieving relevant details less tractable. This limits out-of-the-box performance on continual learning benchmarks like ARC-AGI-3.
AI.method: PRO-LONG introduces programmatic memory: it maintains a complete, structured interaction log of all observations and actions, then leverages recent advances in coding agents to efficiently search and retrieve relevant information from this history via code-based queries, avoiding the context-vs-retrieval tradeoff.
AI.result: On the full ARC-AGI-3 public game set, PRO-LONG improves over a base coding agent by 18.0 percentage points on average across frontier models, matches or exceeds specialized harnesses (up to 76.1% pass@1) while using 4.2–5.8× fewer tokens, and achieves 97.4% best@2 on Fable 5 at a total cost of $1,750.
AI.conclusion: Programmatic memory via coding agents is an effective, minimal, and token-efficient strategy for context management in long-horizon, exploratory LLM agent tasks, closing the gap with specialized harnesses while dramatically reducing token usage.

title: Efficient Clustering with Provable Guardrails for LLM Inference at Scale
comment: Accepted for presentation at ICML HiLD workshop 2026 (non-archival)
summary: Scaling LLM-based applications to millions of users is bottlenecked by the inference cost and latency of modern foundation models. A natural fix is to cluster the inputs and call the LLM only on cluster representatives, letting other members inherit the output -- but this is only safe if each member is measurably close to its representative. Existing clustering methods do not offer such per-sample quality control at scale: none jointly guarantee a minimal within-cluster similarity, exact matching of categorical attributes, and scalability to tens of millions of samples. We propose a two-stage algorithm that generates initial clusters with Mini-batch K-Means, then greedily selects representatives within each initial cluster -- a step equivalent to the Johnson-Chvatal heuristic for Set Cover over alpha-balls in embedding space. The algorithm enforces the similarity and attribute guardrails exactly by construction, and runs in $O(nd + n^2 d/K)$ time and $O(nd + n^2/K^2)$ memory for $n$ samples, feature dimension $d$, and $K$ initial clusters -- linear in $n$ when $K$ grows proportionally with $n$. We provide benchmarks against common clustering methods on internal and public datasets: our method not only delivers per-sample guardrails but also runs 10-1000x faster and scales to data sizes where most standard methods become intractable. Deployed on 38 million customers for a persona-based recommender, the clustering method cut downstream cost and latency by 50-fold while preserving personalization and unblocked the production launch.

AI.tldr: A two-stage clustering algorithm (Mini-batch K-Means + greedy representative selection via Set Cover) that provides per-sample similarity guarantees, exact categorical matching, and linear scalability, reducing LLM inference cost and latency by 50x in production.
AI.motivation: Scaling LLM applications to millions of users is constrained by inference cost and latency. Clustering inputs and querying only cluster representatives is a natural solution, but existing methods fail to simultaneously provide: (1) per-sample minimal within-cluster similarity guarantees, (2) exact matching of categorical attributes, and (3) scalability to tens of millions of samples.
AI.method: A two-stage algorithm: Stage 1 generates initial clusters using Mini-batch K-Means. Stage 2 greedily selects representatives within each initial cluster, which is equivalent to applying the Johnson-Chvatal heuristic for Set Cover over α-balls in embedding space. The algorithm enforces similarity and attribute guardrails exactly by construction, with time complexity O(nd + n²d/K) and memory O(nd + n²/K²) — linear in n when K grows proportionally with n.
AI.result: On internal and public datasets, the method runs 10–1000× faster than common clustering baselines and scales to data sizes where standard methods fail. Deployed on 38 million customers for a persona-based recommender, it reduced downstream cost and latency by 50-fold while preserving personalization quality and unblocked the production launch.
AI.conclusion: The proposed algorithm is the first to jointly deliver per-sample quality control, exact categorical guardrails, and linear scalability, making LLM-based applications economically viable at massive scale.

title: TRUST-ESD: A Risk-Calibrated and Governance-Aware AI Framework for Enterprise Strategic Decision Support Under Uncertainty
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to APWeb-WAIM 2026, Danang, Vietnam, September 7-9, 2026
summary: Enterprise strategic decision support requires AI systems that are not only accurate, but also uncertainty-aware, risk-calibrated, explainable, and governance-compliant. This paper proposes TRUST-ESD, a risk-calibrated and governance-aware framework for enterprise decision support under uncertainty. TRUST-ESD evaluates feasible counterfactual strategies through predictive utility estimation, conformal uncertainty calibration, CVaR-based downside-risk scoring, risk-memory retrieval, policy-as-code governance, explainability, and human oversight. Unlike prediction-only methods that select actions by maximum expected utility, TRUST-ESD recommends strategies that balance value, reliability, risk exposure, and compliance. Experimental results show that TRUST-ESD improves risk-adjusted utility by 7.95%, reduces risk exposure by 23.22%, reduces CVaR by 23.78%, lowers calibration error by 13.89%, improves explanation fidelity by 10.90%, and increases governance compliance by 9.76% compared with strong uncertainty-aware baselines, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy. Ablation and case-study analyses further confirm that uncertainty calibration, downside-risk scoring, risk memory, explainability, and governance validation jointly improve trustworthy enterprise decision-making.

AI.tldr: TRUST-ESD is a governance-aware decision support framework that integrates conformal uncertainty calibration, CVaR downside-risk scoring, risk memory, explainability, and policy-as-code governance to recommend enterprise strategies that balance value, reliability, risk, and compliance—outperforming baselines across risk-adjusted utility, risk exposure, calibration error, explanation fidelity, and governance compliance.
AI.motivation: Enterprise strategic decision support demands AI systems that go beyond predictive accuracy to incorporate uncertainty awareness, risk calibration, explainability, and governance compliance. Existing prediction-only methods that maximize expected utility fail to account for downside risk, reliability, and regulatory constraints, motivating the need for a holistic trustworthy framework.
AI.method: TRUST-ESD evaluates counterfactual strategies through seven integrated components: (1) predictive utility estimation, (2) conformal uncertainty calibration, (3) CVaR-based downside-risk scoring, (4) risk-memory retrieval for historical context, (5) policy-as-code governance validation, (6) explainability generation, and (7) human oversight integration. Strategies are recommended by balancing value, reliability, risk exposure, and compliance rather than solely maximizing expected utility.
AI.result: Compared with strong uncertainty-aware baselines, TRUST-ESD achieves: +7.95% risk-adjusted utility, -23.22% risk exposure, -23.78% CVaR, -13.89% calibration error, +10.90% explanation fidelity, and +9.76% governance compliance, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy. Ablation and case-study analyses confirm each component's contribution to trustworthy decision-making.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty calibration, downside-risk scoring, risk memory, explainability, and governance validation jointly and significantly improve trustworthy enterprise decision-making. TRUST-ESD provides a comprehensive, production-ready alternative to utility-maximization-only approaches.

authors: Venkata Naga Sai Vishnu Rohit Pulipaka
title: How Fast Can Reward Models Score? A Systems Study of C++ and PyTorch Inference Runtimes for RLHF
summary: In RLHF pipelines, reward scoring blocks policy updates. Slow scoring bottlenecks the entire loop, since no update runs until every rollout gets a score. And yet most setups just default to PyTorch eager mode or torch.compile, no one checks if that's actually fastest. Scoring itself is small. Rollout generation eats far more of a typical RLHF step. But scoring and generation fight over the same CPU and GPU resources, so a faster scoring engine doesn't shrink step time on its own. It mainly frees up capacity generation can use instead. We built a native C++ inference engine on ONNX Runtime. First step: confirm correctness. Output matched the PyTorch reference to 5.7 x 10^-6 on CPU and 4.2 x 10^-3 on GPU, close enough to trust. Then we tested it against PyTorch eager mode, torch.compile, and FastAPI, on both CPU and GPU. CPU was decisive. Our engine beat every baseline, confidence intervals didn't even overlap. GPU gave a different view: we beat PyTorch and FastAPI, but torch.compile came out ahead. Further testing traced the speedup to ONNX Runtime itself, not C++ as a language. And batching strategy mattered more than either the language or the runtime choice, more than we expected. The results are from repeated, independent runs, since single runs just aren't reliable enough to trust.

AI.tldr: In RLHF pipelines, reward scoring is a bottleneck that blocks policy updates. The authors built a C++ inference engine on ONNX Runtime to accelerate scoring. On CPU, their engine decisively beat PyTorch eager, torch.compile, and FastAPI. On GPU, torch.compile was superior. The key finding: ONNX Runtime (not C++) drove the speedup, and batching strategy mattered more than language or runtime choice.
AI.motivation: In standard RLHF pipelines, reward model scoring blocks policy updates — no gradient step occurs until every rollout receives a score. Despite this bottleneck, practitioners default to PyTorch eager mode or torch.compile without benchmarking alternatives. Scoring is computationally small relative to rollout generation, but both compete for shared CPU/GPU resources. A faster scoring engine may not directly shrink wall-clock step time; rather, it frees capacity that generation can exploit, making the overall pipeline more efficient.
AI.method: The authors built a native C++ inference engine targeting ONNX Runtime for reward model scoring. They first validated correctness against a PyTorch reference, achieving agreement within 5.7×10⁻⁶ on CPU and 4.2×10⁻³ on GPU. They then benchmarked their engine against PyTorch eager mode, torch.compile, and FastAPI serving, on both CPU and GPU hardware, using repeated independent runs to ensure statistical reliability (non-overlapping confidence intervals). They also performed ablation analysis to isolate whether gains stemmed from C++ as a language or ONNX Runtime as the execution backend, and systematically varied batching strategies.
AI.result: On CPU, the ONNX Runtime C++ engine decisively outperformed all baselines, with non-overlapping confidence intervals. On GPU, it beat PyTorch eager and FastAPI but was surpassed by torch.compile. Ablation revealed that ONNX Runtime (not C++ language) was the primary source of speedup. Most critically, batching strategy exerted a larger influence on throughput than either the programming language or the runtime backend — a finding the authors describe as unexpected in magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that reward scoring in RLHF can be meaningfully accelerated, but the optimal backend depends on hardware: ONNX Runtime excels on CPU, while torch.compile leads on GPU. More importantly, practitioners should prioritize tuning batching strategy over language or runtime choices, as it dominates performance. The work also underscores the value of statistically rigorous, repeated-measurement benchmarking rather than relying on single runs.

title: CUSUM-Shaped Inference-Time Monitoring and Targeted Re-Decoding for Quantized Small Language Model Reasoning
summary: Quantized small autoregressive reasoning models can enter long, repetitive, or unproductive trajectories, yet inference-time compute is usually allocated without observing how a trajectory develops. Building on an earlier token-level e-CUSUM controller, we develop MGT-B (Monitoring-Guided Test-time Backtracking), a revised external controller that maps overlapping windows of pre-sampling uncertainty and degeneration features to position-conditional empirical tail probabilities, accumulates mixture betting factors with a CUSUM-shaped reset, and responds to an alarm by estimating a rollback point, restoring token and key-value-cache state, and performing constrained re-decoding. To audit whether the effect persists on problem identities first observed after the manual choice of log threshold h = 10, we retrospectively exclude 260 IDs present in pre-threshold artifacts and retain the chronologically first post-threshold pair for each remaining ID, yielding a 240-pair chronology-audit set. On this set, accuracy changes from 82/240 to 88/240 (+2.50 percentage points; 13 corrections, 7 regressions; exact McNemar p = 0.2632; paired bootstrap 95% interval [-1.25, +6.25]). A broader 467-pair historical-coverage set of seed-matched pairs changes accuracy from 146/467 to 167/467 (+4.50 points; McNemar p = 0.000753), but includes 200 seed-1 IDs available before or during threshold selection and is reported only as an exploratory estimate. All 316 no-alarm outputs in the 467-pair set are identical to vanilla, while the 151 alarmed trajectories contain 29 corrections and 8 regressions. Neither analysis is confirmatory, and the empirical factors are not established as a valid e-process or e-detector. The results support a selective monitoring-and-repair mechanism for the studied MATH-500 setting, rather than a general or theoretically certified reasoning improvement.

AI.tldr: MGT-B is an external controller that monitors autoregressive reasoning model trajectories for degeneration using windowed uncertainty features and mixture betting factors, triggering backtracking and constrained re-decoding upon alarm. Evaluated on MATH-500, it shows modest accuracy improvements, with the primary chronology-audit analysis (+2.50 pp) not reaching statistical significance, while broader exploratory analysis shows larger gains. The mechanism is presented as selective monitoring-and-repair, not a certified reasoning improvement.
AI.motivation: Quantized small autoregressive reasoning models often produce long, repetitive, or unproductive trajectories, yet standard inference-time compute allocation does not dynamically observe or respond to trajectory quality. The authors aim to develop a monitoring mechanism that detects degenerate behavior and intervenes via backtracking, rather than blindly allocating compute.
AI.method: MGT-B (Monitoring-Guided Test-time Backtracking) extends a token-level e-CUSUM controller by: (1) mapping overlapping windows of pre-sampling uncertainty and degeneration features to position-conditional empirical tail probabilities; (2) accumulating mixture betting factors with a CUSUM-shaped reset; (3) upon alarm, estimating a rollback point, restoring token and KV-cache state, and performing constrained re-decoding. A chronology-audit methodology was employed to control for threshold selection bias: retrospectively excluding 260 IDs present in pre-threshold artifacts, retaining chronologically first post-threshold pairs for each remaining ID (240-pair set). A broader 467-pair historical-coverage set is also reported exploratorily.
AI.result: On the primary 240-pair chronology-audit set: accuracy improved from 82/240 to 88/240 (+2.50 pp; 13 corrections, 7 regressions; exact McNemar p = 0.2632, not significant; bootstrap 95% CI [-1.25, +6.25]). On the exploratory 467-pair set: accuracy improved from 146/467 to 167/467 (+4.50 pp; McNemar p = 0.000753). Among 467 pairs, all 316 no-alarm outputs were identical to vanilla; the 151 alarmed trajectories contained 29 corrections and 8 regressions.
AI.conclusion: The results support a selective monitoring-and-repair mechanism for the studied MATH-500 setting but do not constitute a general or theoretically certified reasoning improvement. The empirical factors are not established as a valid e-process or e-detector, and neither analysis is confirmatory. The chronology-audit methodology provides a more rigorous evaluation by mitigating threshold selection bias.

title: Koopman Dreamer: Spectrally Constrained Latent Dynamics for Stable World-Model Imagination
summary: Latent world models improve sample efficiency in continuous control by optimizing policies over imagined latent trajectories, but common neural transitions offer limited direct control over modal persistence and error accumulation in long rollouts. We propose Koopman Dreamer, a Dreamer-style world model with a spectrally constrained deterministic latent dynamics core. Its Koopman-inspired backbone uses two-dimensional rotation--scaling blocks with bounded radii to represent damping, rotation, and near-periodic modes. Linear and low-rank bilinear action terms capture global and state-dependent control effects, while stochastic-state modulation supplies local correction information. To reduce the mismatch between posterior-conditioned training and prior-only imagination, the model combines posterior-conditioned EMA teacher targets with one-step consistency, multi-step rollout, and open-loop observation-prediction objectives. We further derive a multi-step rollout-error bound that separates amplification by the spectral backbone and bilinear interaction from the additive effects of stochastic-state mismatch and modeling residuals, clarifying the trade-off between error attenuation and long-term information retention. Experimental results on proprioceptive continuous-control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite and UAV-LiDAR autonomous navigation demonstrate that Koopman Dreamer improves the stability of long-horizon latent rollouts and achieves stronger closed-loop control performance on tasks that rely on high-quality multi-step imagination.

AI.tldr: Koopman Dreamer integrates a spectrally constrained Koopman-inspired dynamics core into Dreamer-style world models, using bounded rotation-scaling blocks, linear/bilinear action terms, and stochastic modulation. It combines EMA teacher targets with consistency and rollout objectives to reduce posterior-prior mismatch, and derives a rollout-error bound clarifying error amplification versus attenuation trade-offs. Results show improved long-horizon latent rollout stability and stronger control on proprioceptive and UAV navigation tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard neural transition models in Dreamer-style world models lack direct control over modal persistence and suffer from error accumulation during long latent rollouts. The authors aim to address this by imposing spectral structure on the latent dynamics to explicitly manage damping, rotation, and periodic modes, thereby improving long-horizon imagination stability and sample-efficient control.
AI.method: Koopman Dreamer replaces the standard MLP-based recurrent state-space model with a Koopman-inspired deterministic core: (1) 2D rotation-scaling blocks with bounded radii for damping/rotation/near-periodic modes; (2) linear and low-rank bilinear action terms for global and state-dependent control; (3) stochastic-state modulation for local corrections. Training uses posterior-conditioned EMA teacher targets combined with one-step consistency, multi-step rollout, and open-loop observation-prediction objectives to reduce posterior-prior mismatch. A derived multi-step rollout-error bound analytically separates spectral amplification and bilinear interaction effects from stochastic mismatch and modeling residuals.
AI.result: On proprioceptive continuous-control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite and a UAV-LiDAR autonomous navigation task, Koopman Dreamer demonstrates improved stability in long-horizon latent rollouts and achieves superior closed-loop control performance, particularly on tasks requiring high-quality multi-step imagination.
AI.conclusion: Imposing spectrally constrained Koopman dynamics within a Dreamer-style world model effectively mitigates error accumulation in long latent rollouts while preserving sufficient expressiveness for control. The approach clarifies the trade-off between error attenuation and long-term information retention, and shows practical gains in both standard continuous-control benchmarks and real-world robotic navigation scenarios.

title: PoTRE: Test-Time Reasoning inspired by Cognitive Heterogeneity
comment: Accepted at Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR 2026)
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at many tasks, they frequently struggle with complex reasoning that requires long-horizon planning and iterative error correction. Furthermore, standard single-stream prompting proves brittle when models encounter novel abstractions or rigorous domain constraints. We introduce PoTRE (Poly-Topological Reasoning Ensembles), a heterogeneous framework that decouples inference into four agents: (1) Adversarial Refinement Agent, (2) Hierarchical strategic Planning Agent, (3) Spectrum Search Agent, and (4) Direct Chain Agent. A final Task-Adaptive Aggregation Layer dynamically reconciles these perspectives -- via final candidate selection, semantic synthesis, or neuro-symbolic verification -- to produce a robust global solution. We evaluate PoTRE on three frontier benchmarks: ARC-AGI-2, Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), and PRBench Finance. PoTRE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy of 49.92% on HLE, surpassing the previous best official score. We demonstrate that this architectural heterogeneity achieves improved reasoning performance using similar or fewer inference tokens compared to heavily scaled homogeneous baselines.

AI.tldr: PoTRE is a heterogeneous multi-agent reasoning framework that decomposes LLM inference into four specialized agents (Adversarial Refinement, Hierarchical Planning, Spectrum Search, and Direct Chain), combined via a Task-Adaptive Aggregation Layer. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on HLE (49.92%) with token efficiency comparable to or better than scaled homogeneous baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with complex reasoning tasks requiring long-horizon planning and iterative error correction. Standard single-stream prompting is brittle when facing novel abstractions or strict domain constraints. The authors aim to overcome these limitations through architectural heterogeneity rather than simply scaling homogeneous inference.
AI.method: PoTRE employs a four-agent ensemble: (1) Adversarial Refinement Agent — critiques and refines outputs; (2) Hierarchical Strategic Planning Agent — decomposes tasks into sub-goals; (3) Spectrum Search Agent — explores diverse solution paths; (4) Direct Chain Agent — produces straightforward chain-of-thought reasoning. A Task-Adaptive Aggregation Layer dynamically reconciles these outputs via candidate selection, semantic synthesis, or neuro-symbolic verification to produce the final solution.
AI.result: PoTRE achieves 49.92% accuracy on Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), a new state-of-the-art surpassing the previous best official score. It also demonstrates strong performance on ARC-AGI-2 and PRBench Finance, while using similar or fewer inference tokens compared to heavily scaled homogeneous baselines.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous multi-agent reasoning architectures like PoTRE offer a more effective and token-efficient path to robust complex reasoning than scaling homogeneous single-stream approaches, as evidenced by SOTA results on challenging benchmarks.

title: Analytic Distribution of Classifier-Free Guidance for Schedule Design
summary: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is the default mechanism for conditional generation in diffusion models, but the distribution sampled by its deterministic guided dynamics is not captured by the usual product-distribution heuristic $p_0^ωq_0^{1-ω}$. We analyze CFG through the probability flow ODE and derive exact analytic path-integral representations of the induced distributions for both constant and time-dependent guidance. The resulting formulas show that CFG modifies $p_{t_0}$ by an exponential path-integral correction, and that a time-dependent schedule enters this correction through the weight $ω(t)-1$. This characterization explains how score discrepancies accumulate along sampling trajectories and motivates Distribution-Guided CFG (DG-CFG), a schedule that balances timestep contributions while accounting for signal strength and low-noise score-error amplification. A toy model with analytic scores closely verifies the predicted distributions. On Stable Diffusion~1.5, DG-CFG improves generation and yields a stronger diversity--fidelity trade-off across guidance strengths, with especially clear gains when strong guidance causes saturation and quality degradation in constant and heuristic schedules. Across NFE budgets, DG-CFG reaches fixed image-quality targets with fewer sampling steps, reducing the sampling cost needed to achieve target metrics.

AI.tldr: This paper provides an exact analytic characterization of classifier-free guidance (CFG) via path-integral representations of the probability flow ODE, revealing that CFG induces an exponential path-integral correction to the base distribution. Based on this analysis, the authors propose Distribution-Guided CFG (DG-CFG), a time-dependent guidance schedule that balances timestep contributions while accounting for signal strength and low-noise score-error amplification, demonstrating improved quality and diversity-fidelity trade-offs on Stable Diffusion.
AI.motivation: The standard heuristic for CFG — that it samples from a product distribution p₀^ω q₀^(1−ω) — does not accurately describe the distribution actually produced by deterministic guided dynamics. The authors aim to rigorously characterize what distribution CFG truly samples from and leverage this understanding to design better guidance schedules.
AI.method: The authors analyze CFG through the probability flow ODE framework and derive exact analytic path-integral representations of the induced distributions for both constant and time-dependent guidance. They show that CFG modifies the marginal distribution at time t₀ by an exponential path-integral correction, where the time-dependent schedule enters through the weight ω(t)−1. This motivates DG-CFG, a schedule that balances contributions across timesteps while accounting for signal strength and low-noise score-error amplification. Validation is performed on a toy model with analytic scores and on Stable Diffusion 1.5.
AI.result: A toy model with analytic scores closely verifies the predicted distributions. On Stable Diffusion 1.5, DG-CFG improves generation quality and yields a stronger diversity-fidelity trade-off across guidance strengths, with especially clear gains when strong guidance causes saturation and quality degradation under constant and heuristic schedules. DG-CFG reaches fixed image-quality targets with fewer sampling steps (lower NFE budgets), reducing the sampling cost required to achieve target metrics.
AI.conclusion: CFG's induced distribution is exactly characterized by an exponential path-integral correction, not the naive product-distribution heuristic. The DG-CFG schedule, derived from this theoretical understanding, consistently outperforms constant and heuristic schedules, particularly under strong guidance and low NFE budgets, offering both better quality and computational efficiency.

title: Train the Model, Not the Reader: Decodability Supervision for Verifiable Activation Explanations
summary: Natural-language autoencoders score explanations of hidden activations by reconstruction: an explanation is deemed faithful if the activation can be regenerated from it. The test is structurally insensitive to individual false claims: if flipping a claim does not change the reconstruction, the claim is never penalized. We show the test is passed in two ways, neither faithful. On a released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer, explanations reconstruct well above chance while ~2% of specific claims are reconstruction-dependent, so the score tracks gist, not specific facts. Under exact synthetic ground truth, the standard recipe develops co-adapted private codes (false wording the reconstruction depends on) in 5/5 runs, and fixes that leave the target model unchanged do not help. We contribute two audit protocols, the grounded-vs-true cross and the evaluator swap, and RECAP (Readable Encodings via Co-trained Auxiliary Predictors): linear heads trained alongside the target model to keep designated content decodable. On RECAP-trained sandbox models, fresh verbalizers state the designated content truly and the codes vanish, at a +0.001-nat cost. This replicates on a pretrained Pythia-160M: the content becomes reliably probe-decodable, though a fresh verbalizer conveys it only in part (truth 0.44-0.46 vs a near-zero control). For interpretability, high reconstruction does not certify individual claims. For AI safety, RECAP makes designated internal content independently checkable against probes rather than asserted by prose a model can game: an independent probe scores the verbalizer's true claims above its false ones (AUC 0.96, vs 0.82 without RECAP). Against an adversary that edits an explanation to maximize the reconstruction score while lying (suppressing ~87% of its lie penalty), the RECAP probe still flags the lies (AUC 0.95) while the control probe collapses to chance (0.51).

AI.tldr: Autoencoder-based faithfulness tests for neural network explanations can be gamed through two failure modes: (1) reconstruction scores mainly track gist rather than specific factual claims, and (2) models develop co-adapted private codes that make false claims reconstruction-dependent. The authors propose RECAP, which trains linear probes alongside the target model to keep designated content decodable, and two audit protocols to detect unfaithful explanations.
AI.motivation: Current methods for scoring faithfulness of natural-language explanations of hidden activations rely on reconstruction-based autoencoder tests. The authors demonstrate this test is structurally blind to individual false claims — if flipping a claim doesn't change reconstruction quality, the falsehood goes unpenalized. This raises serious concerns for interpretability and AI safety, where faithful explanations are critical.
AI.method: The paper contributes: (1) two audit protocols — the grounded-vs-true cross and the evaluator swap — to detect unfaithful explanations; (2) empirical demonstration on Qwen-2.5-7B showing reconstruction tracks gist (~2% of claims are reconstruction-dependent); (3) synthetic ground-truth experiments revealing co-adapted private codes emerge in 5/5 runs; (4) RECAP (Readable Encodings via Co-trained Auxiliary Predictors), which trains linear heads alongside the target model during training to keep designated content probe-decodable, preventing private codes at a cost of +0.001 nats; (5) replication on pretrained Pythia-160M; and (6) adversarial evaluation where a RECAP-trained probe maintains lie detection (AUC 0.95) against an adversary that edits explanations to maximize reconstruction while lying.
AI.result: On Qwen-2.5-7B, explanations reconstruct well above chance but only ~2% of specific claims are reconstruction-dependent. Under synthetic ground truth, co-adapted private codes emerge in 5/5 runs. RECAP-trained sandbox models yield truthful verbalizations with codes vanishing at +0.001 nat cost. On Pythia-160M, designated content becomes probe-decodable (truth 0.44-0.46 vs near-zero control). Against a lying adversary (suppressing ~87% of lie penalty), the RECAP probe detects lies at AUC 0.95 while the control probe collapses to chance (0.51). The independent probe scores true claims above false ones at AUC 0.96 vs 0.82 without RECAP.
AI.conclusion: High reconstruction does not certify individual claim faithfulness in neural network explanations. RECAP provides a practical fix by making internal content independently checkable via probes rather than relying solely on model-generated prose, which can be gamed. This has significant implications for both interpretability research and AI safety, where verifiable internal representations are essential.

title: The World Model Remembers, the Actor Forgets: Dream Rehearsal for Continual Model-Based RL
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures. Code, pre-registration trail, and run data: https://github.com/gurpnijjer/dream-rehearsal
summary: Model-based reinforcement-learning agents of the DreamerV3 family forget catastrophically when trained on task sequences, even when an unbounded replay buffer preserves every earlier experience. We ask a question the continual-RL literature has assumed an answer to but never measured: which component forgets? Under never-clear replay, pre-registered component-level probes (n=3 seeds throughout) show that the world model retains essentially everything measurable about old tasks -- reward discrimination (retention ratio ~1.0), value estimates, and termination structure -- while the actor's behavior collapses. Forgetting in this regime is a channel problem, not a memory problem. We demonstrate this by intervention: with the world model frozen and identical imagined rollouts, reinforcement learning in imagination fails to recover a lost skill (0/3 seeds), while supervised self-imitation on the world model's own graded dreams recovers it on 3/3 seeds with zero environment interaction. Interleaved during training, this graded dream rehearsal yields a task-label-free, parameter-constant continual learner: 3/3 four-task chains retained where plain replay passes 0/3, 3/3 eight-task chains, and consistent gains over matched real-episode cloning (paired difference +0.13, bootstrap 95% CI [0.07, 0.24], complete seed separation). The dream-grading step is load-bearing: we characterize two scoring failure modes, provide an offline selection gauge that caught both before they contaminated results, and give a realized-first grading rule that closes them. All experiments were pre-registered with committed protocols; every refuted hypothesis is reported.

AI.tldr: DreamerV3 agents forget catastrophically on task sequences due to actor (policy) collapse, not world model degradation. The authors demonstrate that frozen world models retain full task knowledge, and propose "graded dream rehearsal" — supervised self-imitation on the world model's own imagined rollouts — which enables task-label-free, parameter-constant continual learning across up to eight tasks where plain replay fails completely.
AI.motivation: The continual RL literature has broadly assumed that catastrophic forgetting in model-based agents stems from degradation of the world model (memory). The authors challenge this untested assumption, seeking to precisely identify which component — the world model or the actor — is responsible for forgetting when an unbounded replay buffer is used.
AI.method: 1) **Component-level probing**: Pre-registered probes (3 seeds) measure retention of reward discrimination, value estimates, and termination structure in the world model vs. actor behavior across task sequences under never-clear replay. 2) **Intervention experiments**: With world model frozen, compare RL-in-imagination vs. supervised self-imitation ("graded dream rehearsal") for skill recovery. 3) **Graded dream rehearsal**: During training, the actor performs supervised imitation on the world model's own generated rollouts, filtered through a grading mechanism that scores dream quality. Two failure modes of grading are characterized, with an offline selection gauge and a "realized-first" grading rule proposed as remedies. 4) **Continual learning evaluation**: Tested on four-task and eight-task chains, compared against plain replay and real-episode cloning. All experiments pre-registered with committed protocols.
AI.result: Under never-clear replay, the world model retains essentially all measurable task knowledge (reward discrimination retention ratio ~1.0), while the actor's behavior collapses completely. With frozen world model: RL-in-imagination recovers lost skills on 0/3 seeds; supervised self-imitation succeeds on 3/3 seeds with zero environment interaction. Graded dream rehearsal achieves 3/3 four-task chains retained (vs. 0/3 for plain replay), 3/3 eight-task chains, and consistent gains over real-episode cloning (paired difference +0.13, bootstrap 95% CI [0.07, 0.24], complete seed separation). Two dream-grading failure modes were identified and addressed.
AI.conclusion: Forgetting in DreamerV3 under unbounded replay is a channel problem (actor collapse) rather than a memory problem (world model degradation). Graded dream rehearsal provides an effective, task-label-free, parameter-constant solution for continual RL, with the dream-grading mechanism being essential to success. The work establishes a new methodological standard through pre-registration and comprehensive reporting of refuted hypotheses.

title: SoftReason: A Fully Differentiable Neuro-Soft-Symbolic Deductive Reasoning Architecture over High-Dimensional Perceptual Data
summary: In many reasoning problems, the premises are not observed as discrete symbols, but must be inferred from high-dimensional inputs. Further, the predicate vocabulary, argument structure, and trusted evidence are supplied by a Knowledge Graph (KG), or rule definitions. Classical neuro-symbolic pipelines have a discrete interface between perception and deduction. We present a neuro-soft-symbolic architecture for differentiable deductive reasoning over latent perceptual facts and knowledge-provided predicates. SoftReason removes the gradient gap by representing the deductive state as a local soft interpretation tensor over candidate constants and predicates. Perception proposes probabilistic base facts, KG triples enter as high-confidence soft evidence, and every query anchor, predicate choice, and closure update remains differentiable. Our core innovation is a learned differentiable lift of the immediate-consequence operator. It uses predicate-definition embeddings and latent composition channels to form soft body-predicate mixtures, aggregate over all possible witnesses, propose query-conditioned head facts, and update the interpretation through a monotone probabilistic OR. We instantiate the framework on Knowledge-aware Visual Question Answering (KVQA), and demonstrates how SoftReason supports end-to-end perceptual grounding, KG evidence injection, and differentiable deductive closure in one trainable architecture.

AI.tldr: SoftReason is a neuro-soft-symbolic architecture that enables differentiable deductive reasoning over latent perceptual facts and knowledge graph predicates. It introduces a learned differentiable lift of the immediate-consequence operator, allowing end-to-end training for tasks like Knowledge-aware Visual Question Answering (KVQA) by removing the gradient gap between perception and deduction.
AI.motivation: Traditional neuro-symbolic systems suffer from a discrete (non-differentiable) interface between perceptual modules and deductive reasoning engines. When premises are not observed as discrete symbols but must be inferred from high-dimensional inputs (e.g., images), and when predicate vocabulary and argument structure come from a Knowledge Graph, the gradient cannot flow end-to-end. SoftReason addresses this by making the entire pipeline — perception, KG evidence injection, and deductive closure — fully differentiable.
AI.method: SoftReason represents the deductive state as a local soft interpretation tensor over candidate constants and predicates. Perception proposes probabilistic base facts; KG triples are injected as high-confidence soft evidence. The core innovation is a learned differentiable lift of the immediate-consequence operator, employing: (1) predicate-definition embeddings and latent composition channels to form soft body-predicate mixtures, (2) aggregation over all possible witnesses, (3) proposal of query-conditioned head facts, and (4) monotone probabilistic OR-based interpretation updates. This eliminates the gradient gap while preserving deductive semantics.
AI.result: The framework is instantiated on Knowledge-aware Visual Question Answering (KVQA), demonstrating that SoftReason successfully supports end-to-end perceptual grounding, KG evidence injection, and differentiable deductive closure within a single trainable architecture.
AI.conclusion: SoftReason demonstrates that differentiable deductive reasoning can be achieved by softening the immediate-consequence operator, enabling neuro-symbolic systems to be trained end-to-end without sacrificing the structured reasoning capabilities provided by knowledge graphs and predicate definitions.

title: Convergence-Latency-Aware Adaptive Modulation and Resource Allocation in RIS-Assisted Wireless Federated Learning
summary: Federated learning (FL) over wireless networks suffers from significant training latency and degraded convergence due to unreliable wireless transmission, especially under blocked propagation environments. Although reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) can improve communication reliability, existing wireless FL studies rarely characterize the trade-off between learning convergence and communication delay under modulation-dependent transmission errors. In this paper, we consider a wireless FL system operating under RIS-assisted blocked-link propagation scenarios, and focus on adaptive modulation and sub-channel allocation for convergence-latency aware communication design. By characterizing the effect of symbol errors on uploaded local gradients, we derive a convergence-related upper bound that reveals the impact of symbol error rate (SER) on FL loss decay. Based on this result, we formulate a joint convergence-latency optimization problem, which is cast as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem, and solve it using a low-complexity hybrid alternating optimization framework. Extensive experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Speech Commands show that the proposed scheme consistently achieves faster convergence and higher test accuracy than existing adaptive communication schemes, especially in complex tasks and challenging wireless scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the convergence-latency trade-off in federated learning (FL) over wireless networks with blocked links, leveraging RIS-assisted communication. The authors derive a convergence bound incorporating symbol error rate (SER) effects, formulate a joint adaptive modulation and sub-channel allocation problem (MINLP), and solve it via a hybrid alternating optimization framework, demonstrating faster convergence and higher accuracy on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Speech Commands.
AI.motivation: Wireless FL suffers from training latency and degraded convergence due to unreliable transmission, especially under blocked propagation. While RISs can improve reliability, existing studies lack characterization of the convergence-latency trade-off under modulation-dependent transmission errors. The authors aim to bridge this gap by jointly optimizing adaptive modulation and sub-channel allocation.
AI.method: The authors first derive a convergence upper bound that explicitly captures how symbol error rate (SER) affects FL loss decay. They then formulate a joint convergence-latency optimization problem as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP). The problem is solved using a low-complexity hybrid alternating optimization framework that jointly optimizes adaptive modulation and sub-channel allocation in RIS-assisted blocked-link scenarios.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Speech Commands demonstrate that the proposed scheme consistently achieves faster convergence and higher test accuracy than existing adaptive communication schemes, particularly in complex tasks and challenging wireless conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed convergence-latency aware communication design, incorporating RIS assistance and adaptive modulation/sub-channel allocation, effectively mitigates the impact of unreliable wireless links on FL performance. The derived SER-aware convergence bound and the hybrid alternating optimization approach provide a principled framework for improving FL in blocked propagation environments.

title: AlphaRoute: Large Language Models as Semantic Optimizers for Multi-Objective Routing
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in the IEEE International Conference on LLM-Aided Design, 2026, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA. Code available at https://github.com/Kcbir/AlphaRoute
summary: Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) global routing is an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem requiring signal net assignment across capacity-constrained 3D grids while minimizing congestion, wirelength, and via transitions. Because traditional heuristics rely on static penalty schedules that fail on complex congestion topologies, we present AlphaRoute: a multi-objective adaptive search framework reformulating rip-up and reroute (R&R) into a dynamic optimization system. We introduce SHAP-based overflow decomposition to isolate per-net congestion, driving targeted subgraph extraction via 3D Dijkstra maze routing and an adaptive PathFinder policy. Crucially, AlphaRoute employs Large Language Models (LLMs) as semantic policy optimizers. Bounded by a deterministic knowledge graph, the LLMs interpret congestion metrics to dynamically adjust penalty parameters. Evaluated on ISPD 2025 benchmarks, AlphaRoute reduces overflow by 98.6% on MEMPOOL. On the constrained ARIANE design, we achieve an overflow of 146,109 (a 29.8x reduction in overflow over the state of the art), yielding a penalized score of S_orig = 0.0538 versus the State-of-the-art (SOTA) 1.780. These results demonstrate that superior algorithmic search geometry can overcome the latency of interpreted Python implementations.

AI.tldr: AlphaRoute reformulates VLSI global routing rip-up and reroute as a dynamic optimization system using SHAP-based congestion decomposition, adaptive PathFinder policies, and LLMs as semantic policy optimizers bounded by a deterministic knowledge graph, achieving 98.6% overflow reduction on MEMPOOL and a 29.8x reduction over SOTA on the ARIANE design (S_orig = 0.0538 vs. 1.780).
AI.motivation: Traditional VLSI global routing heuristics rely on static penalty schedules that fail on complex congestion topologies. There is a need for a multi-objective adaptive search framework capable of dynamically responding to congestion patterns without being bottlenecked by hand-tuned parameter regimes.
AI.method: AlphaRoute reformulates rip-up and reroute (R&R) as a dynamic optimization system. It introduces: (1) SHAP-based overflow decomposition to isolate per-net congestion contributions; (2) targeted subgraph extraction via 3D Dijkstra maze routing; (3) an adaptive PathFinder negotiation-based policy; and (4) LLMs acting as semantic policy optimizers, bounded by a deterministic knowledge graph, that interpret congestion metrics to dynamically adjust penalty parameters. Evaluated on ISPD 2025 benchmarks.
AI.result: On ISPD 2025 benchmarks, AlphaRoute reduces overflow by 98.6% on MEMPOOL. On the constrained ARIANE design, it achieves an overflow of 146,109 (a 29.8x reduction over SOTA), yielding a penalized score of S_orig = 0.0538 versus the SOTA's 1.780.
AI.conclusion: Superior algorithmic search geometry — enabled by SHAP-driven congestion attribution, adaptive PathFinder policies, and LLM-based semantic optimization — can overcome the latency overhead of interpreted Python implementations, producing state-of-the-art VLSI global routing results.

title: An Isotropy-Preserving Spectral Cap for Muon: Theory and Three Case Studies
comment: Preliminary Report; Larger scale experiments ongoing; Comments are welcome
summary: Muon and related matrix-sign optimizers are increasingly used to pre-train large language models, but their effect on the internal geometry of individual weight matrices is not well understood. This preliminary report proposes a unified framework built on a single idealizing assumption -- exact scale invariance of the loss under weight rescaling, which holds approximately in normalization-heavy networks. Under this assumption, plain SGD carries a built-in 1/||W|| brake on its update size, whereas Muon's matrix-sign step removes that brake, so both the Frobenius and spectral norms drift outward faster (t^{1/2} versus t^{1/4}). We further observe that the spectral-norm perturbation has a non-negative second-order term. This implies that a lightweight "spectral cap" -- which projects out only the first-order growth of the single top singular direction from each update -- can control the output covariance W K_X W^T without freezing training: the weight keeps learning through non-top directions, top-direction rotation, and top switching. We relate this cap to the min-entropy (H-infinity) of the singular-value spectrum. We then study three systems trained with Muon: a nanoGPT feed-forward projection, a 64-expert mixture-of-experts router, and the query/key projections of a bf16 FlashAttention block. In each case the cap increases isotropy and, at the margins -- a router collapsing to a single expert, and the near-divergence of one attention head -- prevents a concrete failure, while leaving validation loss essentially unchanged. We emphasize that the scale-invariance assumption is strong and that these small-scale results are preliminary; comments are welcome.

AI.tldr: Under a scale-invariance assumption, Muon optimizer removes the natural brake that SGD imposes on weight norm growth, causing Frobenius and spectral norms to grow faster (t^{1/2} vs t^{1/4}). A lightweight "spectral cap" that suppresses first-order growth of the top singular direction can prevent failure modes (router collapse, attention head divergence) without hurting loss.
AI.motivation: Muon and matrix-sign optimizers are increasingly popular for LLM pre-training, but their impact on the internal geometry of weight matrices is poorly understood. The authors aim to explain and control undesirable norm growth dynamics induced by these optimizers.
AI.method: The analysis builds on the idealized assumption of exact scale invariance (loss unchanged under W → cW), which holds approximately in normalization-heavy networks. Under this, they analytically compare SGD (which has a built-in 1/||W|| brake) to Muon (which lacks it), derive growth rates for Frobenius and spectral norms, and identify a non-negative second-order spectral perturbation term. They propose a "spectral cap" that projects out first-order growth of only the top singular direction and test it on three systems: a nanoGPT feed-forward projection, a 64-expert MoE router, and FlashAttention Q/K projections.
AI.result: Under scale invariance, SGD yields ||W|| ~ t^{1/4} while Muon yields ~ t^{1/2}. The spectral cap increases isotropy and prevents concrete failure modes — router collapsing to a single expert and attention head near-divergence — while leaving validation loss essentially unchanged. The cap relates to min-entropy (H∞) of the singular value spectrum.
AI.conclusion: The spectral cap is a lightweight, targeted intervention that controls Muon's excessive norm growth without impeding learning. The authors caution that the scale-invariance assumption is strong and results are preliminary given small-scale experiments; they invite community feedback.

title: OPIUM: Mitigating Steering Externalities and Over-Refusal via Dual Objective Latent Optimization
comment: Accepted to the Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Activation steering provides a lightweight mechanism for controlling large language models at inference time, but steering vectors can have unintended externalities: utility vectors may weaken safety behavior, while refusal vectors may induce over-refusal on benign prompts. We introduce OPIUM (Optimizing Protected Injections via Utility Manifolds), a training-free method for sanitizing steering vectors through representation matching. Given reference behaviors on two prompt sets, OPIUM optimizes a new steering vector that preserves the downstream representations induced by the desired intervention while matching a safer reference behavior on prompts where the original vector fails. Across steering-externality and over-refusal settings, OPIUM improves the safety--utility tradeoff relative to vanilla steering and directional ablation, suggesting that harmful side effects of activation steering can often be mitigated directly in activation space.

AI.tldr: OPIUM is a training-free method that sanitizes activation steering vectors by optimizing for representation matching, improving the safety-utility tradeoff in LLM inference-time control.
AI.motivation: Activation steering vectors, while lightweight, exhibit harmful side effects: utility-enhancing vectors can degrade safety guardrails, and refusal vectors can cause over-refusal on benign prompts. A method is needed to mitigate these externalities directly in activation space without retraining.
AI.method: OPIUM optimizes a new steering vector that (1) preserves downstream representations induced by the desired intervention on its intended prompt set, and (2) matches a safer reference behavior on prompts where the original vector produces undesirable side effects. This is framed as a representation-matching optimization problem solved directly in activation space, requiring no additional training.
AI.result: Across steering-externality and over-refusal benchmarks, OPIUM consistently improves the safety-utility tradeoff compared to vanilla steering and directional ablation baselines.
AI.conclusion: Harmful side effects of activation steering can often be mitigated directly in activation space through representation matching, without requiring retraining or architectural changes.

title: Auto-Fill: Learning to Predict Missing Values Accurately with Specialist Language Models
summary:
Predicting missing cell values in tabular data is a fundamental problem in data cleaning. While state-of-the-art reasoning models show great promise in predicting missing values in tables, by reasoning holistically across rows and columns, they are costly to deploy at scale and tend to be overconfident, often generating hallucinated or false-positive predictions.
