  In this paper, we observe that achieving high-precision missing-value prediction in tables requires a distinct combination of three capabilities: (1) world knowledge, (2) text-based reasoning, and (3) code-based reasoning. We systematically explore design choices for combining these capabilities, and propose an Auto-Fill approach that post-trains three specialist small language models (SLMs), each optimized for one capability. We develop a calibrated ensemble mechanism that either dynamically selects the most confident specialist or abstains, ensuring high accuracy.
  Extensive experiments on 11 benchmarks with 2200 real tables drawn from diverse domains show that Auto-Fill achieves superior accuracy compared to state-of-the-art reasoning models (e.g., o3-pro, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek R1), while operating at a fraction (less than 1%) of the cost of these frontier models. Our results highlight the effectiveness of specialization and calibrated abstention in the important domain of tabular data. Auto-Fill is publicly available at https://github.com/lyrain2001/auto-fill.

AI.tldr: Auto-Fill uses three specialized small language models (world knowledge, text reasoning, code reasoning) with a calibrated ensemble mechanism to predict missing tabular cell values, achieving superior accuracy to frontier models at <1% of the cost.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art reasoning models are effective at predicting missing table values but are costly to deploy at scale and suffer from overconfidence, producing hallucinated predictions. High-precision imputation requires a targeted combination of world knowledge, text reasoning, and code reasoning capabilities not optimally served by a single large model.
AI.method: Post-train three specialist SLMs, each optimized for one capability (world knowledge, text-based reasoning, code-based reasoning). A calibrated ensemble mechanism dynamically selects the most confident specialist or abstains from predicting to maintain high precision.
AI.result: Auto-Fill outperforms frontier reasoning models (o3-pro, Gemini 3 Pro, DeepSeek R1) on 11 benchmarks covering 2,200 real tables from diverse domains, while operating at less than 1% of their cost.
AI.conclusion: Specialization and calibrated abstention are highly effective strategies for tabular missing-value prediction, enabling small models to surpass large reasoning models in both accuracy and cost-efficiency.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Regret for Reinforcement Learning without Horizon Dependence
summary:
We study horizon-free regret minimization for finite-horizon time-homogeneous tabular Markov decision processes with $S$ states, $A$ actions, horizon $H$, and per-trajectory total reward bounded by $1$.
  We propose a new algorithm and prove a regret upper bound \[\tilde O(\sqrt{SAK}+S^8A^3)\] with failure probability $δ$, where $K$ is the number of episodes and $\tilde O(\cdot)$ hides $\mathsf{poly}\log(S,A,K,1/δ)$.
  Thus, the regret is $H$-free and asymptotically optimal, matching the contextual-bandit lower bound $Ω(\sqrt{SAK})$ up to logarithmic factors. This completely removes the $\log H$ dependence from the previous $\tilde O(\sqrt{SAK\log H}+S^2A\log H)$ guarantee of Zhang et al. (2021), and drastically improves the prior best horizon-free regret $\tilde O(\sqrt{S^9A^3K})$ of Zhang et al. (2022) asymptotically.
  The main technical difficulty is that the optimal value functions $\{V_h^*\}_{h=1}^H$ are time-inhomogeneous even though the transition kernel is time-homogeneous. A direct union bound over all value functions typically incurs an additional $\min\{\log H,S\}$ factor. We avoid this factor by (i) exploiting the monotonicity of $V_h^*$ in $h$ and (ii) non-trivially projecting the value functions onto an $S$-dimensional grid.
  Our analysis relies on three additional ingredients. First, we introduce a horizon-truncation argument that enables reward-based exploration and removes the cost of a separate reward-free exploration phase. Second, we design a cutting bonus that preserves both optimism and the monotonicity needed for planning. Third, we prove a new bound on total deviation for time-homogeneous MDPs, which controls the clipped variance terms in the cutting bonus with adjustable polynomial dependence on $S$ and without any dependence on $H$. Together, these tools yield an asymptotically optimal horizon-free regret guarantee.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a new algorithm for finite-horizon tabular MDPs that achieves a horizon-free regret bound of Õ(√(SAK) + S⁸A³), asymptotically matching the Ω(√(SAK)) lower bound and eliminating the log H dependence present in prior work.
AI.motivation: Prior horizon-free regret bounds either contained a log H factor (Zhang et al., 2021) or scaled as Õ(√(S⁹A³K)) (Zhang et al., 2022). The goal is to achieve a truly horizon-free, asymptotically optimal regret bound of Õ(√(SAK)) without any dependence on H, even logarithmic.
AI.method: The algorithm combines three key techniques: (1) a horizon-truncation argument enabling reward-based exploration without a separate reward-free phase; (2) a cutting bonus that preserves optimism and monotonicity for planning; (3) a new bound on total deviation for time-homogeneous MDPs controlling clipped variance terms with polynomial S-dependence and zero H-dependence. Crucially, to avoid the log H factor from union-bounding over time-inhomogeneous optimal value functions V*_h, the authors exploit the monotonicity of V*_h in h and non-trivially project value functions onto an S-dimensional grid.
AI.result: The proposed algorithm achieves regret Õ(√(SAK) + S⁸A³) with failure probability δ, completely removing the log H dependence from prior work and drastically improving upon the previous best horizon-free regret of Õ(√(S⁹A³K)).
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes the first asymptotically optimal horizon-free regret bound for finite-horizon time-homogeneous tabular MDPs, matching the contextual-bandit lower bound Ω(√(SAK)) up to logarithmic factors. The additive S⁸A³ term, while large, is independent of K and thus vanishes asymptotically.

title: Local Causal Structure Learning in the Presence of Latent Variables and Selection Bias
summary: Discovering the direct causes and effects of a target variable from observational data is a fundamental problem in causal discovery, with broad applications in domains such as gene regulatory analysis and biomedical research. Existing causal discovery methods either learn a global causal structure, which incurs substantial computational cost, or assume the absence of latent variables and selection bias, assumptions that are often violated in real-world settings. Motivated by these challenges, we study local causal structure learning in the presence of latent variables and selection bias. Specifically, we first characterize a local region that enables target-specific causal discovery without recovering the entire global structure. We then establish a theoretical bridge between causal information learned from the observed distribution induced on this local region and the corresponding information in the global causal structure. Building on these foundations, we propose LoCaLS, a local causal structure learning algorithm that is sound and complete under standard assumptions and identifies the same direct causes and effects of a target variable as those identifiable by global causal discovery methods, while allowing for latent variables and selection bias. Extensive experiments on random and real-world structures demonstrate that the proposed method consistently achieves higher structural accuracy than existing local methods while requiring substantially less computational effort than state-of-the-art global methods. Furthermore, applications to two real-world gene expression datasets reveal biologically plausible target-specific causal structures, demonstrating its practical applicability in large-scale biological data analysis.

AI.tldr: LoCaLS is a local causal structure learning algorithm that identifies direct causes and effects of a target variable in the presence of latent variables and selection bias, without learning the entire global causal graph. It achieves higher accuracy than existing local methods and requires less computation than global methods, with demonstrated effectiveness on real-world gene expression data.
AI.motivation: Existing causal discovery methods face a critical trade-off: global methods incur substantial computational cost, while local methods typically assume no latent variables or selection bias — assumptions frequently violated in real-world settings such as gene regulatory analysis and biomedical research. The authors aim to bridge this gap by enabling local causal discovery that is robust to latent confounders and selection bias.
AI.method: The authors first characterize a local region around a target variable that suffices for target-specific causal discovery without full global structure recovery. They establish a theoretical bridge linking causal information from the observed distribution on this local region to the global causal structure. Building on this, they propose LoCaLS, a sound and complete local causal structure learning algorithm operating under standard assumptions (presumably faithfulness and causal Markov), capable of handling latent variables and selection bias.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on both synthetic (random) and real-world causal structures show that LoCaLS consistently achieves higher structural accuracy compared to existing local methods. It also requires substantially less computational effort than state-of-the-art global methods. Applications to two real-world gene expression datasets yield biologically plausible target-specific causal structures, validating practical utility in large-scale biological data analysis.
AI.conclusion: LoCaLS effectively addresses the gap between local and global causal discovery by enabling accurate, computationally efficient identification of direct causes and effects for a target variable, even in the presence of latent variables and selection bias. Its strong empirical performance and successful application to gene expression data underscore its promise for large-scale, real-world causal discovery tasks.

title: Nonlinear Bias-Compensated Adaptive Filter and Its Application for Time-Series Prediction
summary: Most existing nonlinear adaptive filtering algorithms only account for output noise, neglecting the fact that input noise is also prevalent in practice. Although the recently proposed bias-compensated kernel least mean square (BCKLMS) algorithm addresses input noise in the nonlinear errors-in-variables (EIV) model, it still suffers from two major limitations. First, the use of a fixed-size dictionary restricts network growth but also prevents it from fully capturing the characteristics of the input signal. Second, as an least mean square (LMS) based algorithm, it exhibits poor robustness in the presence of non-Gaussian noise in the output signal. To overcome these issues, this paper proposes the random Fourier bias-compensated filter under general adaptive function (RFFBCGA) algorithm. Within the random Fourier feature based bias-compensated (RFFBC) framework, the proposed algorithm not only maintains a fixed network structure and effectively mitigates input noise interference through the BC term, but also achieves improved characterization of the input signal. Moreover, by leveraging the flexible form of the general adaptive (GA) function, the algorithm's robustness across various noise scenarios is further enhanced. Extensive simulations, including real-world time series prediction tasks, demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the RFFBCGA algorithm, which addresses input noise via bias compensation within a random Fourier feature framework and enhances robustness against non-Gaussian output noise through a general adaptive function, outperforming existing methods like BCKLMS.
AI.motivation: Existing nonlinear adaptive filters (e.g., BCKLMS) suffer from two limitations: (1) a fixed-size dictionary restricts full capture of input signal characteristics, and (2) LMS-based updates exhibit poor robustness under non-Gaussian output noise. Both input and output noise are prevalent in practical EIV scenarios, necessitating a more flexible and robust solution.
AI.method: The authors propose the Random Fourier Bias-Compensated filter under General Adaptive function (RFFBCGA). It operates within the RFFBC framework, using random Fourier features to maintain a fixed network structure while a bias-compensation term mitigates input noise. The general adaptive (GA) function replaces the standard LMS cost, providing flexible error criteria (e.g., correntropy, Geman-McClure) to improve robustness against diverse non-Gaussian output noise distributions.
AI.result: Extensive simulations, including real-world time series prediction, demonstrate that RFFBCGA achieves superior performance compared to existing nonlinear adaptive filtering algorithms in EIV scenarios with both input noise and non-Gaussian output noise.
AI.conclusion: The RFFBCGA algorithm successfully overcomes the limitations of BCKLMS by combining random Fourier features for better input characterization with a GA function for enhanced noise robustness, offering a practical and superior solution for nonlinear EIV modeling.

title: Time Series Network Utilization KPI Forecasting Using Advanced AI/ML Models
summary: The rapid proliferation of data-intensive applications, cloud infrastructure, and IoT ecosystems has made proactive resource provisioning critical for maintaining optimal network performance. However, network administrators face a constant battle against capacity constraints, where traditional reactive approaches fail to accurately anticipate traffic fluctuations. This inability to foresee demand leads to costly over-provisioning, unexpected downtime, and degraded quality of service directly impacting operational budgets and business continuity. To achieve efficient capacity planning, accurate forecasting of bandwidth utilization is essential. This study addresses the challenge by evaluating a diverse spectrum of models including seasonal decomposition, Prophet, Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Regression, and advanced deep learning architectures like bidirectional and Convolutional LSTMs - using a common interface dataset benchmarked across MAPE, NRMSE, and R-square metrics. Ultimately, this research delivers actionable insights into the trade-offs between model accuracy and computational efficiency, empowering engineers, operators, and business owners to select the optimal forecasting model for their specific infrastructure needs.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates a range of forecasting models—from classical statistical methods to advanced deep learning architectures—for bandwidth utilization prediction, benchmarking them on standardized metrics to guide practical model selection for network capacity planning.
AI.motivation: Traditional reactive approaches to network resource provisioning fail to anticipate traffic fluctuations, leading to costly over-provisioning, unexpected downtime, and degraded QoS. Proactive, accurate bandwidth forecasting is essential to address these capacity planning challenges in data-intensive, cloud, and IoT environments.
AI.method: The authors benchmark a diverse set of forecasting models—seasonal decomposition, Prophet, Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Regression (SVR), bidirectional LSTMs, and Convolutional LSTMs—using a common interface dataset. Performance is evaluated across three metrics: MAPE, NRMSE, and R².
AI.result: The study provides a comparative analysis revealing the trade-offs between prediction accuracy and computational cost across all evaluated models, offering actionable guidance for selecting the optimal forecasting approach based on specific infrastructure requirements.
AI.conclusion: No single model universally dominates; the optimal choice depends on the practitioner's priority—accuracy versus computational efficiency. The findings equip network engineers, operators, and business stakeholders with evidence-based insights for informed forecasting model selection in real-world capacity planning scenarios.

title: Good Practice Guide for quantifying uncertainties for machine learning models applied to photoplethysmography signals
summary: This Good Practice Guide presents work done in the QUMPHY project (Uncertainty quantification for machine learning models applied to photoplethysmography signals) that considered both machine learning and uncertainty quantification for problems which used photoplethysmography (PPG) signals from wearable devices as input. It provides high-level guidance on what types of machine learning model might be used and how different models compare when applied to both regression and classification tasks. It provides guidance on the implementation of different methods for uncertainty quantification, covering both model-dependent and model-independent techniques, and on the validation of the results provided by those methods. It also describes six benchmark problems together with pointers to different benchmark datasets for each problem. Software is described that can assist practitioners in implementing the methods described herein and there is a brief consideration of ethical issues. It concludes with a summary and recommendations.

AI.tldr: A good practice guide from the QUMPHY project providing guidance on machine learning models and uncertainty quantification methods for PPG signal analysis from wearables, including benchmark problems, datasets, software, and ethical considerations.
AI.motivation: The increasing use of wearable photoplethysmography (PPG) signals in health applications demands reliable machine learning models with robust uncertainty quantification. However, practitioners lack standardized guidance on model selection, UQ implementation, and validation — motivating the QUMPHY project to produce a comprehensive good practice guide.
AI.method: The guide systematically compares machine learning models (for both regression and classification tasks) applied to PPG signals, covering both model-dependent and model-independent uncertainty quantification techniques. It establishes six benchmark problems with associated datasets, describes supporting software tools, and addresses validation strategies for UQ results alongside ethical considerations.
AI.result: The deliverable is a practical guide synthesizing comparative evaluations of ML models, implementation recipes for various UQ methods, six curated benchmark problems with dataset pointers, and accompanying software to assist practitioners.
AI.conclusion: The guide concludes with a summary of findings and actionable recommendations for practitioners seeking to apply machine learning with rigorous uncertainty quantification to PPG-based applications from wearable devices.

title: Post-Training in Time Series Foundation Models: A Unifying Framework
summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have emerged as general-purpose models for time series analysis, but pretraining alone is often insufficient for reliable downstream deployment. Bridging this gap requires further intervention to handle domain shift, task heterogeneity, limited supervision, and computational constraints, which motivates post-training as a broad class of methods to adapt, augment, compose, calibrate, or specialize pretrained TSFMs for downstream tasks. In this work, we analyze TSFM post-training methods based on their locus of intervention in the prediction pipeline, yielding five categories: parameter adaptation, context augmentation, model composition, output processing and uncertainty control, and compression and specialization. Within each category, we study main representative methods and discuss their current limitations. We further identify future directions toward controlled adaptation, reliable context construction, uncertainty-aware model composition, calibrated output processing, and deployment-aware specialization. Overall, by providing a unifying framework for the emerging TSFM post-training landscape, this work aims to support future research to navigate the design space between a pretrained TSFM and its reliable downstream deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a structured taxonomy of post-training methods for time series foundation models (TSFMs), categorizing them into five intervention types (parameter adaptation, context augmentation, model composition, output processing/uncertainty control, and compression/specialization), analyzes their limitations, and outlines future directions for bridging the gap between pretrained TSFMs and reliable downstream deployment.
AI.motivation: Pretrained TSFMs alone are insufficient for reliable real-world deployment due to domain shift, task heterogeneity, limited supervision, and computational constraints. There is a need for a systematic understanding of post-training methods that adapt, augment, compose, calibrate, or specialize TSFMs, yet the field lacks a unifying organizational framework.
AI.method: The authors conduct a literature survey and taxonomic analysis, organizing TSFM post-training methods according to their "locus of intervention" in the prediction pipeline. This yields five categories: (1) parameter adaptation, (2) context augmentation, (3) model composition, (4) output processing and uncertainty control, and (5) compression and specialization. Representative methods within each category are examined and their limitations discussed.
AI.result: The work provides a comprehensive conceptual framework mapping the emerging TSFM post-training landscape, identifies current limitations within each of the five categories, and proposes future research directions: controlled adaptation, reliable context construction, uncertainty-aware model composition, calibrated output processing, and deployment-aware specialization.
AI.conclusion: By establishing a unifying taxonomy, this survey aims to guide future research in navigating the design space between pretrained TSFMs and their dependable downstream deployment, facilitating more principled development of post-training strategies.

title: The Blessing of Dimensionality: How Near-Orthogonality in High-Dimensional Spaces Explains Temporal Portability
summary: Fine-tuning has been widely used to adapt large language models (LLMs) for domain-specific tasks. Parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) are frequently used to reduce computational costs. PortLLM is a training-free and data-free scheme used to adapt LLMs after continual pretraining. Although the initial PortLLM results show that LoRA patches exhibit short-term temporal portability, the long-term performance of PortLLM across several updates of continual pretraining remains underexplored. Furthermore, the intriguing effectiveness of PortLLM is not well understood from a theoretical standpoint. We address these two open questions by (1) performing an extensive empirical study of the long-term temporal portability of PortLLM patches across 10 continual pretraining steps using base models Mistral, Gemma, and Qwen; and (2) offering two theoretical analyses to explain our observation that the simple PortLLM method achieves competitive performance. We find empirically that the portability persists across longer time duration, indicating that repeated fine-tuning is not required when the base model is periodically updated. We find theoretically that near-orthogonality of high-dimensional vectors is a key justification for temporal portability. Our analyses also demonstrate a geometric perspective of the loss landscape in facilitating the theoretical comparison of different adaptation options.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the long-term temporal portability of PortLLM—a training-free, data-free PEFT scheme—across 10 continual pretraining steps, and provides theoretical explanations for its effectiveness rooted in near-orthogonality of high-dimensional vectors and geometric properties of the loss landscape.
AI.motivation: Prior work (PortLLM) showed that LoRA patches exhibit short-term temporal portability, but two open questions remain: (1) whether this portability holds over longer continual pretraining horizons, and (2) why the simple PortLLM approach works so effectively from a theoretical standpoint.
AI.method: The authors conduct an extensive empirical study evaluating PortLLM patch portability across 10 sequential continual pretraining steps using three base models (Mistral, Gemma, Qwen). They complement this with two theoretical analyses: one leveraging near-orthogonality of high-dimensional vectors to explain temporal portability, and another using a geometric perspective of the loss landscape to compare different adaptation strategies.
AI.result: Empirically, PortLLM patches maintain competitive performance over extended time durations (10 continual pretraining updates), eliminating the need for repeated fine-tuning when the base model is periodically updated. Theoretically, near-orthogonality in high-dimensional spaces serves as a key justification for why portability persists, and the geometric loss-landscape analysis enables principled comparison of adaptation methods.
AI.conclusion: PortLLM's temporal portability is robust over long continual pretraining horizons, and its efficacy is theoretically grounded in high-dimensional geometry—specifically near-orthogonality—and the structure of the loss landscape, providing both practical and theoretical insights for PEFT-based model adaptation.

title: Generalized Kalman filter based temporal difference reinforcement learning
summary: In this paper, we present a generalized temporal-difference (TD) reinforcement learning framework based on the theory of conditional expectations. The value and action-value (Q-value) functions are treated as uncertain quantities, and their estimation is formulated as a stochastic inference problem. Unlike classical Kalman-based temporal-difference learning, which relies on linear-Gaussian assumptions, the proposed formulation is derived directly from the conditional expectation framework and naturally extends to nonlinear models and non-Gaussian probability distributions. The proposed method recursively estimates not only the conditional expectation of the value function but also its second probabilistic moment, thereby quantifying the uncertainty associated with the learned value function throughout the learning process. To obtain a computationally tractable algorithm, the stochastic problem is discretized using either polynomial chaos expansions or ensemble-based approximations, providing efficient representations of the underlying random variables. The proposed framework is demonstrated on two optimal control problems: a linear mass--spring--damper system and a nonlinear heat conduction problem in a closed cavity. The numerical examples illustrate the capability of the proposed method to accurately estimate both the value function and its associated uncertainty, while extending classical Kalman-based temporal-difference learning to a broader class of stochastic systems.

AI.tldr: A generalized TD learning framework based on conditional expectation theory is proposed that treats value/Q-value functions as uncertain quantities, extending Kalman-based TD methods beyond linear-Gaussian assumptions to nonlinear, non-Gaussian settings while quantifying uncertainty via second-moment estimation using polynomial chaos or ensemble-based approximations.
AI.motivation: Classical Kalman-based temporal-difference learning is limited by its reliance on linear-Gaussian assumptions, which restricts applicability to more complex real-world stochastic systems. There is a need for a principled framework that handles nonlinear models and non-Gaussian distributions while also quantifying the uncertainty of the learned value function.
AI.method: The value and action-value functions are reformulated as uncertain quantities within a stochastic inference problem grounded in conditional expectation theory. The method recursively estimates both the conditional expectation (first moment) and the second probabilistic moment of the value function, enabling uncertainty quantification. Computational tractability is achieved through discretization via polynomial chaos expansions or ensemble-based approximations of the underlying random variables.
AI.result: The framework was demonstrated on a linear mass-spring-damper system and a nonlinear heat conduction problem in a closed cavity. Results show accurate estimation of both the value function and its associated uncertainty, successfully extending classical Kalman-based TD learning to a broader class of stochastic systems.
AI.conclusion: The proposed conditional-expectation-based TD framework generalizes Kalman-based TD learning to nonlinear and non-Gaussian settings, provides principled uncertainty quantification through second-moment estimation, and offers a computationally tractable pathway via polynomial chaos or ensemble discretizations.

title: Zero-Shot Heart Rate Variability Forecasting from Consumer Wearables Using Time Series Foundation Models
comment: Accepted to Computing in Cardiology (CinC) 2026. 4 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables
summary: Short-term Heart Rate Variability (HRV) forecasting could provide clinicians with actionable lead time for detecting autonomic dysfunction and adverse cardiac events. Consumer wearable devices generate fragmented, artifact-rich HRV signals that challenge conventional forecasting approaches. In this study, we evaluated the forecasting ability of three Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), TimesFM, Chronos, and MOIRAI, against traditional baselines (Mean, Exponential Smoothing, and Exponentially Weighted Moving Average) on real-world wearable data collected from 49 healthy individuals. To address data fragmentation, we introduce a variability-preserving imputation method that augments linear interpolation with locally adaptive stochastic noise, retaining physiological dynamics essential for accurate forecasting. The results show that TSFMs outperformed all baselines without fine-tuning, achieving average Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE) between 0.81 and 0.87 across TSFMs and both context lengths (32 and 64 time steps), with Chronos and TimesFM as the top models, though MOIRAI showed limited gains over baselines. With up to a 2-hour forecast horizon, the results establish a baseline for TSFMs' performance on a real-world dataset, highlighting domain-specific fine-tuning as a promising direction for clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: Evaluated three Time Series Foundation Models (TimesFM, Chronos, MOIRAI) against traditional baselines for short-term HRV forecasting on fragmented wearable data from 49 healthy subjects, using a novel variability-preserving imputation method. TSFMs achieved MASE 0.81–0.87, outperforming baselines without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Short-term HRV forecasting can provide clinicians lead time for detecting autonomic dysfunction and adverse cardiac events. However, consumer wearable devices produce fragmented, artifact-rich HRV signals that challenge conventional forecasting methods. There is a need to evaluate whether modern Time Series Foundation Models can effectively forecast on such real-world, noisy wearable data.
AI.method: HRV data were collected from 49 healthy individuals via consumer wearables. To handle data fragmentation, the authors introduce a variability-preserving imputation method that combines linear interpolation with locally adaptive stochastic noise. Three TSFMs (TimesFM, Chronos, MOIRAI) and three traditional baselines (Mean, Exponential Smoothing, Exponentially Weighted Moving Average) were evaluated using context lengths of 32 and 64 time steps, with forecast horizons up to 2 hours, assessed via Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE).
AI.result: TSFMs outperformed all traditional baselines without any fine-tuning. Average MASE ranged from 0.81 to 0.87 across TSFMs and both context lengths. Chronos and TimesFM were the top-performing models, while MOIRAI showed only limited improvement over baselines. The variability-preserving imputation successfully retained physiological dynamics essential for accurate forecasting.
AI.conclusion: TSFMs demonstrate strong zero-shot HRV forecasting capability on real-world wearable data, establishing a performance baseline. Domain-specific fine-tuning is identified as a promising direction for future clinical deployment.

title: Evaluating and Mitigating Gender Bias in Pre-trained Embeddings for ML-based Recruitment
comment: Accepted for presentation at the TRUST-AI 2026 Workshop, held in conjunction with IJCAI/ECAI 2026, Bremen, Germany
summary: AI-based recruitment systems that rely on machine learning models trained on historical CV data, risk perpetuating and amplifying social biases. A key challenge arises in unstructured CV text, where pre-trained language model embeddings may infer sensitive attributes such as gender even after explicit indicators are removed. In this paper, we evaluate nine pre-trained embedding models on the synthetic FairCVdb dataset, analyzing the informativeness of their embeddings for applicant scoring and their susceptibility to gender leakage, on both original and gender-scrubbed biographies. We further use a multi-task adversarial learning framework with gradient reversal to predict applicant suitability while suppressing gender information from learned representations. Finally, we use a multi-objective Pareto-front-based model selection to balance predictive utility and fairness. Our experimental results show that explicit gender scrubbing substantially reduces but does not eliminate gender leakage, while adversarial learning improves fairness mainly on original biographies and acts as a complementary strategy rather than a substitute for text-level debiasing.

AI.tldr: Evaluates nine pre-trained embedding models on synthetic CV data for gender bias leakage, finding explicit scrubbing reduces but doesn't eliminate bias, while adversarial debiasing serves as a complementary strategy. A Pareto-front approach balances utility and fairness in model selection.
AI.motivation: AI recruitment systems trained on historical CV data risk perpetuating social biases, particularly because pre-trained language model embeddings may inadvertently encode sensitive attributes like gender from unstructured text, even after removing explicit gender indicators.
AI.method: Nine pre-trained embedding models are evaluated on the synthetic FairCVdb dataset. Embedding informativeness for applicant scoring and gender leakage susceptibility are measured on both original and gender-scrubbed biographies. A multi-task adversarial learning framework with gradient reversal is employed to predict suitability while suppressing gender. Multi-objective Pareto-front-based model selection is used to balance predictive utility and fairness.
AI.result: Explicit gender scrubbing substantially reduces but does not eliminate gender leakage. Adversarial learning improves fairness primarily on original (unscrubbed) biographies and functions as a complementary strategy rather than a replacement for text-level debiasing.
AI.conclusion: Text-level gender scrubbing and adversarial debiasing should be combined for fairer AI recruitment systems. Neither approach alone suffices to fully mitigate gender bias encoded in pre-trained embeddings.

title: Co-Evolving LLM Evaluators and Policies via DynamicRubric
summary: Post-training with evaluator feedback on policy-induced samples serves as a major mechanism for improving large language models. As policies improve, these sampled responses become close in quality. These close candidates create a bottleneck for policy optimization: collapsed relative evaluator score gaps yield weak or misleading policy supervision. We theoretically characterize why these gaps matter through a probability allocation view, showing that the directional gain of shifting probability mass from one response to another is exactly the evaluator score gap between them. This identifies relative score gaps as the policy optimization signals that guide updates. Motivated by this view, we propose DynamicRubric, a response-set-conditioned evaluator--policy co-evolution framework that generates weighted binary rubric items for each candidate set and aggregates the resulting judgments into response-level scores. In our experiments with 8B backbones, DynamicRubric improves evaluator performance and provides stronger policy supervision than baselines using a 70B reward model or a 235B static rubric generator. DynamicRubric-optimized policies also show gains on verifiable reasoning and coding tasks. A DynamicRubric-optimized model is fully deployed in WeChat Search's AI answering scenario, where it serves all online traffic across tens of millions of requests per day and improves key online metrics. These results suggest a principle for evaluator-guided post-training: evaluators should evolve with the policies they supervise.

AI.tldr: DynamicRubric addresses the bottleneck in LLM post-training where improving policies produce near-equal-quality responses, causing collapsed evaluator score gaps that weaken optimization signals. The authors theoretically show that relative score gaps between candidate responses directly determine policy gradient strength. They propose a co-evolution framework where the evaluator generates per-candidate-set weighted binary rubrics, yielding richer score differentiation. Experiments with 8B models show stronger supervision than 70B reward models or 235B static rubric generators, with gains on reasoning and coding. The system is deployed in WeChat Search, handling tens of millions of daily requests.
AI.motivation: As LLM policies improve during post-training, sampled responses become increasingly similar in quality, leading to collapsed relative score gaps from evaluators. These small gaps provide weak or misleading supervision signals for policy optimization. The authors identify that the directional gradient for shifting probability between two responses is exactly proportional to their evaluator score gap, making gap collapse a fundamental bottleneck.
AI.method: DynamicRubric is a response-set-conditioned evaluator-policy co-evolution framework. For each candidate response set, it dynamically generates weighted binary rubric items (rather than static criteria), then aggregates the resulting judgments into fine-grained response-level scores. The evaluator and policy evolve together: as the policy improves, the evaluator adapts its rubric generation to maintain discriminative score gaps, providing stronger optimization signals.
AI.result: Using 8B backbone models, DynamicRubric outperforms baselines using a 70B reward model and a 235B static rubric generator in both evaluator accuracy and policy optimization signal quality. DynamicRubric-optimized policies achieve gains on verifiable reasoning and coding benchmarks. In production, the model is fully deployed in WeChat Search's AI answering scenario, serving all online traffic (tens of millions of requests/day) and improving key online metrics.
AI.conclusion: Effective evaluator-guided post-training requires evaluators that co-evolve with the policies they supervise. DynamicRubric demonstrates this principle practically by generating set-conditioned rubrics that maintain informative score gaps, leading to better policy optimization and real-world deployment success.

title: CURED: Creating, Understanding, and Repairing Errors Demonstrator
summary: Detecting and cleaning errors in tabular data is a prerequisite for data intense software applications. Recent research at the intersection of Machine Learning (ML) and Database Management Systems (DBMS) highlights the potential of statistical learning algorithms for error detection and cleaning. This paper combines our recent work on ML-based data cleaning and error models in a unified demonstrator. The web application allows users to upload tabular data, perturb the data with realistic data dependent errors and use modern ML methods to clean and understand error mechanisms in data. Our demonstrator helps to bridge the gap between theoretical advancements and intuitive practical insights in the context of error models and data cleaning algorithms for tabular data. The demonstrator is available at https://cured.demo.calgo-lab.de/

AI.tldr: A web-based demonstrator that integrates ML-based error detection and data cleaning for tabular data, allowing users to upload data, inject realistic errors, and apply modern ML methods to clean and understand error mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between theoretical advancements in ML-based data cleaning and practical, intuitive understanding by providing an accessible, unified tool that showcases error models and cleaning algorithms for tabular data.
AI.method: A unified web application combining prior work on ML-based data cleaning and error modeling. Users upload tabular data, perturb it with data-dependent realistic errors, and apply statistical learning algorithms for error detection and correction.
AI.result: A publicly available demonstrator deployed at https://cured.demo.calgo-lab.de/ that enables hands-on experimentation with error injection and ML-driven data cleaning pipelines.
AI.conclusion: The demonstrator effectively translates ML-based data cleaning research into an interactive tool, facilitating both understanding of error mechanisms and practical application of error detection and cleaning algorithms.

title: Active Inference as a Convex Markov Decision Process
summary: Active Inference (AIF) frames adaptive behavior as the minimization of expected free energy (EFE), combining epistemic and pragmatic objectives within a single variational principle. We frame AIF as policy optimization and show that, for closed-loop control policies, EFE minimization can be formulated as a convex Markov decision process (MDP). In this formulation, the pragmatic terms are linear in the predictive state marginals and therefore equivalent to reward maximization in a latent MDP, while the epistemic value introduces a nonlinear component that distinguishes EFE minimization from standard reinforcement learning. This perspective further reveals the epistemic drive of active inference as a policy-dependent (performative) reward. We analyze finite-horizon, discounted, and average-reward formulations of EFE and derive a mirror descent (MD) algorithm that locally linearizes the objective around the current state marginals, yielding a policy-dependent reward that is compatible with actor-critic methods and dynamic programming. Finally, we argue that coupling world-model learning with policy optimization gives active inference the structure of performative reinforcement learning, providing a route toward grounding active inference within modern reinforcement learning and optimization theory, including convergence analysis and principled policy improvement guarantees.

AI.tldr: Active Inference is reformulated as policy optimization in a convex MDP, where epistemic value becomes a performative, policy-dependent reward. A mirror descent algorithm is derived, bridging EFE minimization with actor-critic methods and performative reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: To bridge Active Inference with modern reinforcement learning and optimization theory by reformulating Expected Free Energy minimization within a convex MDP framework, thereby enabling convergence analysis and principled policy improvement guarantees.
AI.method: The authors frame AIF as policy optimization, casting EFE minimization as a convex MDP where pragmatic terms are linear in predictive state marginals (equivalent to reward maximization) and epistemic value is a nonlinear, policy-dependent (performative) reward. They derive a mirror descent algorithm that locally linearizes the objective around current state marginals, yielding a reward compatible with actor-critic methods and dynamic programming. Finite-horizon, discounted, and average-reward formulations are analyzed.
AI.result: EFE minimization is shown to be equivalent to a convex MDP with performative rewards. The derived mirror descent algorithm produces a linearized, policy-dependent reward signal that integrates with standard actor-critic architectures and dynamic programming.
AI.conclusion: Coupling world-model learning with policy optimization gives Active Inference the structure of performative reinforcement learning, grounding it within established RL and optimization frameworks and opening the door to formal convergence guarantees.

title: Local Stability and Gaussian Smoothing of Quantized Neural Networks
comment: Accepted at the 23rd IFAC World Congress (IFAC WC 2026), Busan, Republic of Korea, 2026; 6 pages, 2 figures
summary: We study Gaussian averaging as a smooth surrogate for quantized neural models. Under bounded local oscillation, we derive a local dimension-dependent bound on |f-g|, linking Gaussian smoothing to the stability analysis of discontinuous networks. We compute closed-form Gaussian averages of the rectified linear unit (ReLU) and sign activation functions, and illustrate the mechanism on a high-dimensional binary perceptron, where layer-preactivation aggregation under an explicit quantization-noise surrogate yields the Gaussian envelope used in inference-side smoothing and training-side smooth surrogate gradients.

AI.tldr: The paper studies Gaussian averaging as a smooth surrogate for quantized neural networks, derives dimension-dependent bounds linking Gaussian smoothing to stability of discontinuous models, provides closed-form averages for ReLU and sign activations, and demonstrates the mechanism via a high-dimensional binary perceptron.
AI.motivation: Quantized neural networks employ discontinuous activation functions (e.g., sign), which pose challenges for gradient-based training and stability analysis. The authors seek to establish Gaussian smoothing as a principled framework for obtaining smooth surrogates that enable both inference-side smoothing and training-side smooth surrogate gradients.
AI.method: The authors analyze Gaussian averaging as a smooth surrogate, deriving a local dimension-dependent bound on |f-g| under a bounded local oscillation condition. They compute closed-form Gaussian averages for ReLU and sign activations. The mechanism is illustrated on a high-dimensional binary perceptron, where layer-preactivation aggregation under an explicit quantization-noise surrogate yields the Gaussian envelope.
AI.result: A local dimension-dependent bound on the difference between the original function and its Gaussian-smoothed surrogate is derived under bounded local oscillation. Closed-form expressions for Gaussian-averaged ReLU and sign activations are obtained. The binary perceptron example demonstrates how quantization-noise modeling leads to the Gaussian envelope used for both inference smoothing and surrogate gradient training.
AI.conclusion: Gaussian averaging provides a mathematically principled bridge between quantized/discontinuous neural models and their smooth approximations, with the dimension-dependent bound offering theoretical grounding for stability analysis. The closed-form activation averages and the perceptron illustration validate the framework's practical applicability to both inference and training.

title: Self-organizing Architecture of Receptron Units: a Hardware-Aware Framework for Edge Intelligence
comment: This work has been submitted to NeuroPHY 2026
summary: The growing demand for intelligent processing at the edge of IoT networks is constrained by the severe computational and memory limitations of microcontroller units, which render impractical conventional deep learning approaches. We propose a neuromorphicinspired classifier based on the Receptron model, a single-unit architecture capable of implementing non-linearly separable decision boundaries, without resorting to multi-layer networks. The model is designed for direct deployment on mid-range MCUs, while supporting continuous on-device adaptation. Experimental evaluation on basic dataset benchmarks yields cross-validated accuracies compatible with standard machine learning method baselines. These results position the Receptron as a viable and interpretable alternative for resource-constrained neuromorphic edge systems operating in dynamic, non-stationary environments.

AI.tldr: A neuromorphic classifier called the Receptron — a single-unit architecture capable of non-linearly separable decision boundaries — is proposed for direct deployment on resource-constrained MCUs, achieving accuracy comparable to standard ML baselines while supporting continuous on-device adaptation.
AI.motivation: Conventional deep learning is impractical for edge IoT due to severe computational and memory constraints of microcontroller units (MCUs). There is a need for lightweight, interpretable classifiers that can learn non-linear decision boundaries without multi-layer networks and adapt continuously on-device in dynamic, non-stationary environments.
AI.method: The authors propose a neuromorphic-inspired classifier based on the Receptron model — a single-unit architecture that implements non-linearly separable decision boundaries without requiring multi-layer networks. The model is designed for direct deployment on mid-range MCUs and supports continuous on-device adaptation. Experimental validation uses basic dataset benchmarks with cross-validation.
AI.result: Cross-validated accuracies on basic dataset benchmarks are compatible with standard machine learning method baselines.
AI.conclusion: The Receptron is a viable and interpretable alternative for resource-constrained neuromorphic edge systems operating in dynamic, non-stationary environments.

title: Instance Hardness-Based Relevance for Imbalanced Regression
summary: Imbalanced regression problems arise when the target variable has an asymmetric distribution, resulting in underrepresented value ranges in the dataset. Traditional approaches for identifying rare instances rely on a relevance function that assigns higher importance to specific regions of the target distribution. However, the effectiveness of imbalance-aware learning methods depends strongly on how relevance is defined. In more complex scenarios, such as bimodal distributions, traditional relevance functions struggle to capture rarity, as they assign fixed relevance values based solely on target values, thereby compromising the distinction between truly rare and normal instances. To address these limitations, this study proposes an Instance Hardness-based relevance function (InHaR) for identifying rare instances in regression problems. Unlike traditional relevance functions, the proposed approach incorporates learning difficulty, allowing rarity to be inferred not only from the target distribution but also from the difficulty of instances for the learning algorithm. This property is particularly important in bimodal scenarios, where rarity cannot be accurately inferred from target values alone. Experimental results demonstrate that the InHaR correctly identifies rare regions under bimodal distributions and, when used to guide resampling strategies such as Random Oversampling (RO) and Gaussian Noise (GN), leads to significant improvements in predictive performance compared to traditional relevance-based approaches. The code, dataset, and further details about the proposed method are publicly available at https://github.com/VitorLeitao/instance-hardness-Imbalanced-regression.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes InHaR, an Instance Hardness-based relevance function for identifying rare instances in imbalanced regression. Unlike traditional relevance functions that rely solely on target values, InHaR incorporates learning difficulty, enabling accurate rarity identification even in complex scenarios like bimodal distributions. When combined with resampling strategies (Random Oversampling, Gaussian Noise), InHaR significantly improves predictive performance over traditional approaches.
AI.motivation: Traditional relevance functions for imbalanced regression assign fixed relevance based solely on target values, which fails in complex scenarios like bimodal distributions where rarity cannot be accurately inferred from the target distribution alone. This compromises the distinction between truly rare and normal instances, motivating the need for a relevance function that also accounts for learning difficulty.
AI.method: The authors propose InHaR (Instance Hardness-based relevance), a relevance function that incorporates learning difficulty to identify rare instances. Unlike traditional approaches that define rarity purely from the target distribution, InHaR infers rarity from both the target distribution and the difficulty of instances for the learning algorithm. The method evaluates instance hardness to assign relevance, and is used to guide resampling strategies such as Random Oversampling (RO) and Gaussian Noise (GN).
AI.result: Experimental results show that InHaR correctly identifies rare regions under bimodal distributions. When used to guide RO and GN resampling strategies, InHaR leads to significant improvements in predictive performance compared to traditional relevance-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: InHaR effectively addresses the limitations of traditional relevance functions by incorporating instance hardness, enabling robust rare instance identification across diverse target distributions—particularly bimodal ones—and enhancing downstream regression performance when paired with resampling strategies. Code and datasets are publicly available.

title: On Optimization Complexity of Second-Order Certified Unlearning
summary: We study machine unlearning: the removal of memorized training data from a trained model. Specifically, we investigate the algorithmic complexity of certified unlearning from an optimization perspective. We formalize the goal of an unlearning algorithm as simultaneously achieving certified unlearning and optimization accuracy. Utilizing the notion of uniformly convex regularizers, we prove new bounds on the distance between initial and unlearned models using a novel substitute for generalization error. Thus we theoretically demonstrate that if the removed data is well-predicted by the unlearned model, the corresponding optimization problem is simple. Furthermore, we develop a new second-order unlearning algorithm with an anisotropic Gaussian mechanism and state-of-the-art global convergence. We prove fast rates for our method in achieving certified unlearning for linear models with quasi-self-concordant losses. As a direct application, our theory covers unlearning for logistic and exponential regressions and shows a provable benefit of utilizing second-order information compared to first-order unlearning methods.

AI.tldr: This paper studies certified machine unlearning from an optimization perspective, proving that when removed data is well-predicted by the unlearned model, the problem is simpler. It introduces a second-order unlearning algorithm with an anisotropic Gaussian mechanism that achieves state-of-the-art global convergence and fast rates for linear models with quasi-self-concordant losses (e.g., logistic/exponential regression).
AI.motivation: Existing machine unlearning methods lack rigorous understanding of the algorithmic complexity involved in achieving certified unlearning while maintaining optimization accuracy. The authors aim to bridge this gap by formalizing unlearning as an optimization problem and providing theoretical guarantees.
AI.method: The authors formalize certified unlearning with optimization accuracy as a dual objective. They leverage uniformly convex regularizers to derive novel bounds on the distance between initial and unlearned models via a generalization error substitute. They then develop a second-order unlearning algorithm employing an anisotropic Gaussian mechanism, and prove global convergence with fast rates for linear models under quasi-self-concordant losses.
AI.result: The theory shows that unlearning is simpler when removed data is well-predicted. The proposed second-order method achieves certified unlearning with fast rates, provably outperforming first-order methods for logistic and exponential regression.
AI.conclusion: Certified unlearning can be achieved efficiently using second-order optimization, with theoretical advantages over first-order approaches. The framework provides a principled understanding of when unlearning is computationally easy.

title: OLEDLM: A Unified Language Model for OLED Molecular Design
summary: The development of organic light-emitting diode (OLED) materials faces the compounded challenges of an astronomically large chemical space, stringent quantum-chemical constraints, and a scarcity of labeled data. Although the question of OLED generation is important, few models have been trained effectively for this specific domain. We propose an inverse molecular design framework based on causal language models: given target optoelectronic properties (e.g., excitation energy, oscillator strength), our model directly generates OLED SMILES sequences satisfying the specified constraints. We employ a multi-stage strategy: first, we establish a foundational chemical language model using a LLaMA-style transformer architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first successful adaptation of LLMs specifically for the OLED domain, bridging the gap between generic molecular generation and the stringent structural requirements of optoelectronic materials. Second, we fine-tune property predictors based on a BERT model pre-trained on our large-scale OLED dataset. Then, we perform Reinforcement Learning on our fine-tuned model, leveraging our property predictor, for better SMILES generation. Finally, through DFT verification, we demonstrate that our framework can efficiently navigate the OLED chemical space, generating novel candidates with high structural validity and optimized optoelectronic properties.

AI.tldr: A causal language model framework using LLaMA-style transformers generates OLED SMILES sequences with desired optoelectronic properties, combining multi-stage pre-training, BERT-based property prediction, and reinforcement learning fine-tuning, with DFT verification confirming structural validity and optimized properties.
AI.motivation: OLED materials discovery is hindered by an enormous chemical search space, strict quantum-chemical constraints, and limited labeled data. Existing generative models are poorly adapted to the OLED domain, creating a gap between generic molecular generation and the specific structural requirements of optoelectronic materials.
AI.method: A three-stage inverse molecular design framework: (1) A LLaMA-style causal language model is trained from scratch on OLED chemical data to establish a domain-specific foundation model — reportedly the first LLM adaptation for OLEDs. (2) A BERT-based property predictor is fine-tuned on a large-scale OLED dataset to map SMILES to optoelectronic properties (excitation energy, oscillator strength). (3) Reinforcement learning fine-tunes the generative model using the property predictor as a reward signal to steer SMILES generation toward target properties. Final candidates undergo DFT verification.
AI.result: The framework successfully generates novel OLED molecular candidates with high structural validity. DFT verification confirms that the generated molecules satisfy target optoelectronic constraints, demonstrating efficient navigation of the OLED chemical space.
AI.conclusion: Causal language models, when augmented with domain-specific pre-training, property predictors, and RL-based optimization, offer a viable and effective approach for inverse molecular design in OLED materials discovery, bridging the gap between general-purpose molecular generation and the stringent demands of optoelectronic applications.

title: The Quadrilateral Loss: Additivity as a Measurable Behavior of Dense Neural Networks
summary: Additive models buy interpretability by forbidding feature interactions, a constraint that neural instantiations enforce architecturally. We introduce the quadrilateral loss, a differentiable penalty that treats additivity as a measurable behavior instead: a second-order mixed difference on pairs of training points swapping one coordinate, which vanishes if and only if the coordinate carries no interaction, remains informative for piecewise-linear networks, and equals in expectation the per-coordinate interaction mass of the interventional Shapley-GAM. The loss turns additivity into a dial - most learned interactions prove removable almost for free, and on small datasets a moderate penalty improves accuracy and additivity simultaneously - and into an online observable: its per-feature surrender curves show, across seeds and datasets, that pre-regularization interaction magnitude barely predicts what a regularized model retains, undermining post-hoc interaction rankings. Against this instrument we compare routes to exact additivity, spanning structural masks, behavioral penalties (optionally crystallized into exact structure), weight decay, backfitting, the shared-section model, and bagged boosted stumps: constraining behavior before structure dominates weight-space constraints, rankings reverse between data regimes, and converging routes agree on the shape functions themselves. Three silent failure modes we document share one anatomy: guarantees imported into settings that quietly void their preconditions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the quadrilateral loss, a differentiable penalty that quantifies feature interaction through second-order mixed differences on training point pairs. It enables additivity as a tunable dial, reveals that pre-regularization interaction magnitude poorly predicts post-regularization retention, and compares multiple routes to exact additivity, finding behavioral constraints dominate weight-space constraints while documenting three failure modes from mismatched theoretical guarantees.
AI.motivation: Additive models achieve interpretability by forbidding feature interactions, but neural instantiations enforce this architecturally rather than behaviorally. The authors argue additivity should be treated as a measurable, differentiable behavior, enabling it to be tuned rather than hard-coded, and seek to understand how different routes to additivity compare and where they fail.
AI.method: The core method is the quadrilateral loss: a second-order mixed difference computed on pairs of training points that swap one coordinate. It vanishes iff the coordinate carries no interaction, applies to piecewise-linear networks, and equals in expectation the per-coordinate interaction mass of the interventional Shapley-GAM. The authors use this as both a penalty (turning additivity into a dial) and an observable (per-feature surrender curves). They systematically compare structural masks, behavioral penalties (optionally crystallized into exact structure), weight decay, backfitting, the shared-section model, and bagged boosted stumps as routes to exact additivity.
AI.result: Most learned interactions prove removable almost for free. On small datasets, moderate penalty improves both accuracy and additivity. Pre-regularization interaction magnitude barely predicts what a regularized model retains, undermining post-hoc interaction rankings. Behavioral constraints dominate weight-space constraints. Rankings between routes reverse across data regimes. Converging routes agree on shape functions. Three failure modes are documented where theoretical guarantees are imported into settings that void their preconditions.
AI.conclusion: Additivity is better treated as a tunable behavioral property than a hard architectural constraint. The quadrilateral loss provides both a practical tool for controlling interactions and a diagnostic instrument revealing that interaction importance rankings are unstable across regularization regimes. Researchers should verify that guarantees' preconditions hold when importing additive modeling techniques across contexts.

title: ELSAA: Efficient Low-Rank and Sparse Attention Approximation for Training Transformers
summary: The quadratic $N\times N$ attention score matrix remains a central obstacle to extending Transformers to longer input lengths. Existing efficient attention methods usually reduce this bottleneck by either imposing sparsity, so that each query attends to only a small subset of keys, or by using low-rank/kernel sketches, so that global interactions are compressed into a lower-dimensional representation. We propose \emph{ELSAA}, an efficient low-rank and sparse approximation of attention. Importantly, ELSAA does \emph{not} decompose the learned projection or output matrices of the Transformer into sparse and low-rank factors. Instead, after dense projections produce $Q,K,V$, ELSAA approximates the induced attention score operator itself: a sparse branch captures selected high-similarity interactions, while a low-rank branch summarizes diffuse global interactions. Since the two branches can be normalized over supports with very different denominator mass, ELSAA introduces a denominator-aware fusion term that scales the sparse branch according to its estimated attention mass relative to the low-rank branch. This gives a practical framework for constructing low-rank and sparse attention outputs without materializing the full quadratic score matrix, aiming to enable longer-context training while preserving both sharp token-level interactions and broad contextual mixing.

AI.tldr: ELSAA proposes an efficient attention mechanism that combines sparse and low-rank approximations directly on the attention score operator (not on projection matrices), with a novel denominator-aware fusion term to properly normalize the two branches, enabling longer-context Transformers without materializing the full N×N attention matrix.
AI.motivation: The quadratic O(N²) complexity of the attention score matrix fundamentally limits Transformers from scaling to longer sequences. Existing solutions either enforce sparsity (sacrificing global context) or use low-rank sketches (blurring fine-grained token interactions). Neither approach alone captures both sharp local interactions and diffuse global mixing simultaneously.
AI.method: ELSAA decomposes the attention score operator into two parallel branches after dense Q, K, V projections: (1) a sparse branch that captures high-similarity token pairs via a selection mechanism, and (2) a low-rank branch that summarizes global, diffuse interactions via dimensionality compression. Critically, ELSAA introduces a denominator-aware fusion term that scales the sparse branch's contribution based on its estimated attention mass relative to the low-rank branch, since the two branches operate over supports with substantially different denominator (softmax normalization) masses. This avoids materializing the full N×N score matrix.
AI.result: The paper presents a practical framework demonstrating that the combined low-rank and sparse approximation, with denominator-aware fusion, enables longer-context training while preserving both sharp token-level interactions and broad contextual mixing.
AI.conclusion: ELSAA provides an effective and principled approach to scaling Transformers to longer sequences by jointly leveraging sparsity and low-rank structure in the attention score operator itself, with proper normalization handling via the denominator-aware fusion mechanism.

title: User-Centric Modeling of Transactional Sequences with Explainable State Space Models
summary: We propose a hybrid approach for user-centric modeling of transactional event sequences that combines contrastive representation learning (CoLES) with State Space Models (SSMs). While contrastive methods yield high-quality compressed user representations, existing encoders -- RNNs and Transformers -- suffer from vanishing gradients or quadratic complexity, respectively. Mamba, a selective SSM, efficiently handles long-range dependencies but remains underexplored for personalized user analysis. We investigate two integration strategies: (1)~initializing the Mamba hidden state with a CoLES embedding, and (2)~prepending the projected CoLES embedding as a prefix token to the input sequence. Both approaches supply the model with an informative user prior from the first step. Experiments on three public datasets -- Age (multiclass age-group prediction), MBD (multi-label product acquisition), and Taobao (binary purchase prediction) -- demonstrate consistent improvements over standalone Mamba and CoLES with a linear classifier, with the hybrid models converging 2--3$\times$ faster than the plain SSM baseline. Explainability analysis via discretization-step maps and Integrated Gradients reveals selective event filtering on behavior-rich datasets and identifies the most informative transaction features.

AI.tldr: A hybrid approach combining contrastive representation learning (CoLES) with Mamba state space models for user-centric transactional sequence modeling, achieving 2-3× faster convergence and consistent performance gains over standalone baselines on three public datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing encoders for contrastive user representation learning (RNNs suffer from vanishing gradients; Transformers incur quadratic complexity) are suboptimal for long transactional sequences. Mamba, a selective SSM, efficiently handles long-range dependencies but remains unexplored for personalized user modeling. The authors aim to bridge this gap by integrating CoLES embeddings with Mamba.
AI.method: Two integration strategies are investigated: (1) initializing the Mamba hidden state with a CoLES-derived user embedding, and (2) prepending a projected CoLES embedding as a prefix token to the input event sequence. Both supply the model with an informative user prior from the first step. Evaluation uses three public datasets spanning multiclass age prediction (Age), multi-label product acquisition (MBD), and binary purchase prediction (Taobao).
AI.result: Hybrid models consistently outperform standalone Mamba and CoLES + linear classifier baselines across all three datasets. The hybrid approaches converge 2-3× faster than the plain SSM baseline. Explainability analysis via discretization-step maps and Integrated Gradients shows selective event filtering on behavior-rich datasets and identifies the most informative transaction features.
AI.conclusion: Injecting contrastively learned user representations into Mamba, either via hidden state initialization or prefix token prepending, is an effective strategy for user-centric event sequence modeling, yielding faster convergence, improved performance, and interpretable behavior filtering.

title: PIER: Physics-Informed Environmental Retrieval for Time-Series Modeling
summary: Accurate modeling of environmental systems is fundamental to scientific understanding and decision-making, yet remains challenging because observations are limited and physical dynamics vary across systems. Retrieval-augmented approaches offer a natural path to transfer knowledge across systems, but standard embedding-based retrieval does not guarantee consistency of underlying physical processes, since scenarios with similar embeddings may arise from different underlying mechanisms. We propose Physics-Informed Environmental Retrieval (PIER), a model-agnostic framework that augments embedding-based retrieval with a physics-aware stream that scores candidates by flux-response consistency with the target, using local verifiers trained on physics-derived flux features. A weight adjustment mechanism then learns per-scenario weights that adaptively balance the two retrieval streams based on diagnostic features summarizing physics-stream reliability. Experiments on 356 lakes across the Midwestern United States spanning 41 years show that PIER consistently outperforms baselines for water temperature and dissolved oxygen prediction, and serves as a general augmentation strategy across diverse backbones.

AI.tldr: PIER enhances environmental retrieval by adding a physics-aware stream that scores candidates by flux-response consistency, adaptively balancing it with embedding-based retrieval via learned per-scenario weights. Tested on 356 lakes over 41 years, it consistently improves water temperature and dissolved oxygen predictions across diverse model backbones.
AI.motivation: Standard retrieval-augmented approaches for environmental modeling rely on embedding similarity, which does not guarantee physical consistency — similar embeddings can arise from different underlying physical mechanisms. There is a need for retrieval that respects physical dynamics to enable robust knowledge transfer across systems.
AI.method: PIER is a model-agnostic framework with two retrieval streams: (1) standard embedding-based retrieval, and (2) a physics-aware stream that scores candidates by flux-response consistency using local verifiers trained on physics-derived flux features. A weight adjustment mechanism learns per-scenario weights that adaptively balance both streams based on diagnostic features summarizing physics-stream reliability.
AI.result: PIER consistently outperforms baselines on water temperature and dissolved oxygen prediction across 356 Midwestern US lakes spanning 41 years, and generalizes effectively as an augmentation strategy across diverse backbone architectures.
AI.conclusion: PIER demonstrates that injecting physics-derived consistency checks into retrieval-augmented environmental modeling yields robust performance gains, offering a general-purpose strategy for improving predictions in data-scarce, physically heterogeneous systems.

title: PhaseAware: Interpretable Human-in-the-Loop Rehabilitation Scoring with Boundary Monitoring
comment: 22 pages, 4 main figures, 3 tables, and 17 supplementary figures. Supplementary Information is included in the same PDF
summary: Rehabilitation scoring systems are most useful when their outputs can be reviewed and interpreted within clinical workflows. This study presents PhaseAware, a compact framework for continuous rehabilitation quality assessment that combines a temporal backbone with phase- and body-group descriptors through a backbone-conditioned gated residual pathway. The model was evaluated on the UI-PRMD deep-squat protocol and further tested on the KIMORE squatting subset. On UI-PRMD, PhaseAware achieved an RMSE of 0.0230, corresponding to an 88.9% reduction relative to the accepted baseline. It also maintained favorable performance on KIMORE, suggesting that the phase-aware design transfers across related squatting protocols. In addition to score prediction, PhaseAware generates structured review cues based on phase- and body-level sensitivity, highlighting the movement stages and body regions most relevant to each prediction. The architecture employs a backbone-conditioned gated residual mechanism to stabilize feature representation, supporting use in resource-constrained settings. These cues are intended to support clinician review, boundary-case monitoring, and human-in-the-loop triage rather than autonomous decision-making. Overall, PhaseAware offers a practical and interpretable approach to rehabilitation scoring that may help integrate automated assessment into information systems while preserving clinician oversight.

AI.tldr: PhaseAware is a compact, interpretable framework for continuous rehabilitation quality assessment that uses a temporal backbone with phase- and body-group descriptors via a backbone-conditioned gated residual pathway, achieving an 88.9% RMSE reduction on UI-PRMD while generating clinician-reviewable cues.
AI.motivation: Rehabilitation scoring systems need outputs that are interpretable and integrable into clinical workflows, yet existing automated approaches often lack transparency. There is a need for a practical framework that not only predicts scores accurately but also provides structured, interpretable cues to support clinician oversight, boundary-case monitoring, and human-in-the-loop triage.
AI.method: PhaseAware employs a temporal backbone network combined with phase-specific and body-group-specific descriptors. A backbone-conditioned gated residual pathway stabilizes feature representation and conditions predictions. The model generates structured review cues by analyzing phase- and body-level sensitivity, highlighting which movement stages and body regions most influence each prediction. Evaluation used the UI-PRMD deep-squat protocol and the KIMORE squatting subset.
AI.result: On UI-PRMD, PhaseAware achieved an RMSE of 0.0230, representing an 88.9% reduction relative to the accepted baseline. Favorable performance was maintained on KIMORE, suggesting cross-protocol transferability of the phase-aware design.
AI.conclusion: PhaseAware offers a practical, interpretable approach to rehabilitation scoring that integrates automated assessment into clinical information systems while preserving clinician oversight. The framework is suitable for resource-constrained settings and supports — but does not replace — clinician decision-making.

title: Breaking the $T^{3/4}$ Barrier for Regret Minimization With Bi-Dimensional CDFs
summary: We study regret minimization for learning CDF-related objectives of the form \[ g(x)\cdot\mathbb{P}_{X\sim\mathcal{D}}(X\le x), \] over $[0,1]^2$, where $g$ is a known Lipschitz function and $\mathcal{D}$ is an unknown distribution. At each round $t$, the learner selects a point $x_t$ and observes the binary feedback $\mathbb{I}(X_t\le x_t)$, where $X_t\sim\mathcal{D}$. We design an algorithm achieving regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{7/10})$, improving over the previous best-known bound of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{3/4})$ and showing that the curse of dimensionality can be at least partially lifted for this class of objectives, though a gap remains with the $Ω(T^{2/3})$ lower bound. As an application, our techniques yield the same $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{7/10})$ regret bound for profit maximization in repeated bilateral trade with fixed prices.

AI.tldr: The paper studies regret minimization for learning CDF-related objectives over the unit square, achieving a regret bound of Õ(T^(7/10)), improving prior Õ(T^(3/4)) results, with applications to bilateral trade profit maximization.
AI.motivation: Previous work achieved only Õ(T^(3/4)) regret for learning CDF-related objectives in two dimensions, and there exists a Ω(T^(2/3)) lower bound. The gap between upper and lower bounds motivates finding tighter regret bounds and understanding whether the curse of dimensionality can be partially lifted for this class of problems.
AI.method: The learner selects points x_t in [0,1]^2 sequentially and receives binary feedback indicating whether a random draw X_t ~ D lies below x_t. The objective is g(x) · P(X ≤ x), with known Lipschitz g and unknown distribution D. The authors design a new algorithm that exploits structural properties of the CDF-based objective to achieve improved regret.
AI.result: The proposed algorithm achieves regret Õ(T^(7/10)), improving over the previous best-known bound of Õ(T^(3/4)). This demonstrates that the curse of dimensionality can be at least partially lifted.
