The same techniques yield Õ(T^(7/10)) regret for profit maximization in repeated bilateral trade with fixed prices.
AI.conclusion: The improved regret bound of Õ(T^(7/10)) narrows the gap to the Ω(T^(2/3)) lower bound, though a gap remains. The results suggest that further improvements may be possible and that the techniques have broader applicability, as demonstrated by the bilateral trade application.

title: Interpretable Fuzzy Rule-Based Regression Extension for Ex-Fuzzy Library
summary: Machine learning models achieve high predictive accuracy in regression tasks, but their deployment in safety-critical and regulated domains requires interpretability. While fuzzy rule-based systems offer transparent, linguistically explicit interpretable models, Mamdani-style fuzzy regression remains underrepresented in modern machine learning software libraries. This paper presents an interpretable regression extension for the Ex-Fuzzy library, enabling Mamdani fuzzy inference with scalar consequents learned directly from data. For this, a target-aware partition initialisation strategy based on Fuzzy C-Means clustering is introduced, in which linguistic variables are derived from an augmented input-output space to emphasise output-relevant regions of the feature space. The proposed extension is evaluated on ten regression datasets from the KEEL repository, comparing Gaussian and trapezoidal partition strategies against standard baselines including linear regression, multilayer perceptron, and random forests. Experimental results show that Gaussian partitions consistently outperform uniform trapezoidal partitions, achieving a mean coefficient of determination of approximately 0.86 while producing compact rule bases of 10-15 human-readable rules. The proposed implementation provides a transparent and competitive alternative to black-box regression models, supporting practical interpretability with competitive predictive performance.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Ex-Fuzzy library with Mamdani-style fuzzy regression using scalar consequents learned from data. A novel target-aware Fuzzy C-Means clustering initialisation partitions the input-output space to emphasise output-relevant regions. Evaluated on 10 KEEL datasets, Gaussian partitions achieve a mean R² of ~0.86 with 10–15 compact rules, offering a transparent, competitive alternative to black-box models.
AI.motivation: Machine learning regression models achieve high accuracy but lack interpretability, which is essential for safety-critical and regulated domains. Mamdani fuzzy rule-based systems provide linguistically explicit, transparent models, yet remain underrepresented in modern ML libraries. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing an interpretable regression framework that combines competitive predictive performance with human-readable rule bases.
AI.method: The authors extend the Ex-Fuzzy library to support Mamdani fuzzy inference with scalar consequents. A target-aware partition initialisation strategy is introduced, using Fuzzy C-Means clustering on an augmented input-output space to derive linguistic variables that emphasise output-relevant feature regions. Two partition strategies — Gaussian and trapezoidal — are compared. The approach is benchmarked against linear regression, multilayer perceptron, and random forests across 10 KEEL regression datasets.
AI.result: Gaussian partitions consistently outperform uniform trapezoidal partitions. The method achieves a mean coefficient of determination (R²) of approximately 0.86 while generating compact rule bases of 10–15 human-readable rules, balancing interpretability with competitive predictive performance against standard black-box baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Mamdani fuzzy regression extension provides a transparent, interpretable, and practically competitive alternative to black-box regression models. Gaussian fuzzy partitions with target-aware initialisation yield strong predictive accuracy with compact, linguistically meaningful rule bases, advancing the usability of fuzzy systems in modern, interpretability-sensitive applications.

title: Classical Hardware Acceleration of Quantum Autoencoders for Real-Time Anomaly Detection in Collider Experiments
summary: Quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms in high energy physics (HEP) can efficiently represent and leverage long-range, high-order correlations in high-dimensional collider data, potentially with fewer parameters and favorable scaling relative to classical models. Deployment of QML in real-time collider applications such as trigger systems requires the ability to emulate and compile quantum circuits classically, then synthesize the resulting quantum gates onto low-latency hardware accelerators, namely field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). We present a study of variational quantum autoencoder models for real-time anomaly detection triggers in modern collider experiments. The models achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art classical approaches and, after FPGA synthesis, satisfy resource usage and timing constraints consistent with trigger applications in future colliders. This work provides one of the first FPGA implementations of QML models for HEP triggers, enabling higher-capability models in today's classical data acquisition pipelines while advancing quantum readiness of collider experiment infrastructure.

AI.tldr: This paper presents FPGA-synthesized variational quantum autoencoders for real-time anomaly detection triggers in collider experiments, achieving performance comparable to classical state-of-the-art while meeting hardware resource and latency constraints.
AI.motivation: QML models can capture high-order correlations in collider data with fewer parameters, but real-time trigger deployment demands classical emulation, compilation, and synthesis onto low-latency FPGA hardware — a pipeline not previously demonstrated for HEP trigger systems.
AI.method: Variational quantum autoencoder models are trained for anomaly detection, then classically emulated and compiled into quantum gates, which are subsequently synthesized onto FPGA accelerators for real-time inference in the trigger data acquisition pipeline.
AI.result: The QML models achieve anomaly detection performance comparable to state-of-the-art classical methods and, after FPGA synthesis, meet both resource utilization and timing constraints required for future collider trigger applications.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates one of the first FPGA implementations of QML for HEP triggers, enabling deployment of higher-capability quantum-inspired models within classical data acquisition pipelines and advancing quantum readiness of collider infrastructure.

title: Multi-modal transformer for signal classification in nanopore blockade experiments
summary: Nanopore devices have emerged as powerful tools for single-molecule sensing, with potential for rapid, portable diagnostics. They detect changes in ionic current as analytes enter nanometer-scale pores, providing a means of identifying diverse biomarkers from their characteristic signal patterns. However, these signals are highly complex, and reliably assigning them to specific molecules remains a major challenge. Here, we address this by introducing a multi-modal deep learning architecture that jointly processes multiple signal representations, including raw time-series data, wavelet-based images, and static feature vectors. Our approach surpasses existing methods by more than 10 percentage points on a 42-peptide benchmark and transfers to a 20-amino-acid dataset with near-perfect accuracy. The model integrates complementary information from these representations, with attention analysis showing that the time-series and wavelet-image inputs emphasize different features of the same event. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of machine learning to enable robust, high-accuracy molecular identification with nanopore sensors.

AI.tldr: A multi-modal deep learning architecture combining raw time-series, wavelet-based images, and static feature vectors achieves >10% improvement on a 42-peptide benchmark and near-perfect accuracy on a 20-amino-acid dataset for nanopore molecular identification.
AI.motivation: Nanopore sensors produce highly complex ionic current signals, and reliably assigning these signals to specific molecules remains a major bottleneck, limiting practical portable diagnostics applications.
AI.method: A multi-modal deep learning architecture that jointly processes three complementary signal representations: raw time-series data, wavelet-transformed images, and static feature vectors. Attention mechanisms are used to analyze how different modalities contribute to classification decisions.
AI.result: The model surpasses existing methods by over 10 percentage points on a 42-peptide benchmark. On a 20-amino-acid dataset, it achieves near-perfect accuracy. Attention analysis reveals that time-series and wavelet-image inputs emphasize distinct features of the same translocation event.
AI.conclusion: Multi-modal deep learning, by integrating complementary signal representations, enables robust and high-accuracy molecular identification with nanopore sensors, demonstrating strong potential for real-world diagnostic applications.

title: Interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks (iPANN and fPANN) for uncertainty quantification and propagation in constitutive modeling
summary: Constitutive modeling under uncertainty remains a central challenge for reliable mechanics simulations, particularly when the available stress-deformation data are sparse, noisy, or heterogeneous. We propose interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks (iPANNs and fPANNs) for uncertainty-aware hyperelastic constitutive modeling. iPANNs learn sparse lower, mean, and upper free energy density branches whose stresses, obtained by automatic differentiation, ultimately enclose noisy stress observations. In contrast to this deterministic interval description, fPANNs embed the learned iPANN branches into a fuzzy-set representation through alpha-cut interpolation, yielding a nested family of admissible responses. iPANNs and fPANNs encode mechanistic constraints - preserving objectivity, consistency and promoting polyconvexity - and smoothed L0 regularization promotes interpretable energy representations. The bound models are trained through a two-stage transfer-learning procedure in which a sparse mean constitutive response is learned first and then fine-tuned into lower and upper energy branches. We evaluate the framework on synthetic isotropic hyperelastic data with heteroscedastic noise, varying random realizations, shifted noise means, and varying noise magnitudes. The results show that the learned bounds enclose noisy stress observations while generalizing to the test set. Further, we examine the propagation of uncertainty through the mean, upper and lower bound predictions of the learned iPANN models in a finite element setting. The proposed framework provides a compact, physics-consistent route for distribution-free aleatoric uncertainty quantification in hyperelastic constitutive modeling, and propagation in downstream finite element simulations.

AI.tldr: Proposes interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks (iPANNs and fPANNs) for uncertainty-aware hyperelastic constitutive modeling. iPANNs learn sparse lower, mean, and upper free energy branches that bound noisy stress data, while fPANNs embed these into fuzzy sets via alpha-cut interpolation. The framework enforces polyconvexity, objectivity, and consistency, uses smoothed L0 regularization for interpretability, and employs two-stage transfer learning. Demonstrated on synthetic data with heteroscedastic noise and in FEM uncertainty propagation.
AI.motivation: Constitutive modeling under uncertainty is challenging with sparse, noisy, or heterogeneous stress-deformation data. Existing approaches lack a compact, physics-consistent, distribution-free method for aleatoric uncertainty quantification in hyperelasticity that can propagate uncertainty to downstream finite element simulations.
AI.method: iPANNs learn sparse lower, mean, and upper free energy density branches via automatic differentiation, enclosing noisy stress observations. fPANNs embed these branches into fuzzy sets through alpha-cut interpolation. Both enforce objectivity, consistency, and polyconvexity constraints, with smoothed L0 regularization. A two-stage transfer-learning procedure learns the mean response first, then fine-tunes into bound branches. Uncertainty propagation is tested in finite element simulations.
AI.result: Learned bounds successfully enclose noisy stress observations across heteroscedastic noise, varying random realizations, shifted noise means, and varying noise magnitudes, while generalizing to unseen test data. The framework effectively propagates uncertainty through mean, upper, and lower bound predictions in finite element analyses.
AI.conclusion: The iPANN/fPANN framework provides a compact, physics-consistent, distribution-free approach for aleatoric uncertainty quantification in hyperelastic constitutive modeling with demonstrated utility in downstream FEM uncertainty propagation.

title: Variance-reduced Domain Adaptation using Paired Sampling
summary: Correlation alignment and the maximum mean discrepancy are two widely used distribution-matching frameworks for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). However, high variance in these losses has been shown to undermine their effectiveness in minibatch optimisation settings. Furthermore, the losses lack finite-sum structure, which renders them incompatible with classical stochastic variance reduction (SVR) methods. This paper proposes Paired Sampling for Domain Adaptation (PSDA), a novel SVR technique tailored to such objectives. PSDA pairs observations both within and across domains, to form quadruplets that are always sampled together during training. The pairings are designed to minimise expected gradient variance, and reduce to solving a set of linear assignment problems. Our simulations demonstrate reduced variance compared to related methods, and experiments on three domain shift datasets show improved target domain accuracy.

AI.tldr: PSDA proposes a stochastic variance reduction method for UDA that pairs samples within and across domains into quadruplets, minimizing gradient variance via linear assignment problems, improving target accuracy over existing distribution-matching losses.
AI.motivation: Existing distribution-matching losses for UDA (CORAL, MMD) suffer from high variance in minibatch settings and lack finite-sum structure, making them incompatible with classical SVR methods. This motivates a tailored variance reduction approach.
AI.method: PSDA forms quadruplets by pairing observations within each domain and across domains, sampling them together during training. Pairings are optimized to minimize expected gradient variance, formulated as solving a set of linear assignment problems.
AI.result: Simulations show reduced gradient variance compared to related methods. Experiments on three domain shift datasets demonstrate improved target domain classification accuracy.
AI.conclusion: PSDA effectively reduces variance in distribution-matching UDA objectives, enabling more stable minibatch optimization and yielding better target domain performance.

title: Online Variance Reduction for Domain Adaptation on Streaming Data
summary: This paper studies the problem of stochastic variance reduction (SVR) for the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) and correlation alignment (CORAL) loss functions. Although various offline SVR algorithms for these losses have been proposed, these are incompatible with online, distributed, or incremental learning settings. This paper presents Adaptive vaRiance Reduction via Online reWeighting (ARROW), the first online SVR algorithm for the MMD and CORAL for streamed data. The method maintains moving average references of the alignment statistics, and adaptively reweights incoming minibatches so that the minibatch and reference statistics are aligned. Further, we propose a relaxed reweighting scheme so that the ensuing weight-optimisation problem is tractable. In experiments and simulations, we show that ARROW performs competitively with offline algorithms in terms of runtime, degree of variance reduction achieved, and target domain accuracy.

AI.tldr: ARROW is the first online stochastic variance reduction algorithm for MMD and CORAL losses, using moving average reference statistics and adaptive minibatch reweighting to align streaming data statistics, achieving competitive performance with offline methods.
AI.motivation: Existing stochastic variance reduction (SVR) algorithms for MMD and CORAL loss functions are offline only, making them unsuitable for online, distributed, or incremental learning settings where data arrives as a stream.
AI.method: ARROW maintains moving average references of alignment statistics (for MMD and CORAL), then adaptively reweights incoming minibatches so that the weighted minibatch statistics align with the reference statistics. A relaxed reweighting scheme is introduced to make the resulting weight-optimization problem computationally tractable.
AI.result: ARROW performs competitively with offline SVR algorithms on metrics of runtime, degree of variance reduction, and target domain accuracy.
AI.conclusion: ARROW enables effective online SVR for domain adaptation losses (MMD, CORAL), bridging the gap between offline variance reduction and streaming data scenarios, with practical tractability and strong empirical performance.

title: PG-KINN: A Physics-Informed Petrov-Galerkin Kolmogorov-Arnold Network for Solving Forward and Inverse PDEs
summary: Physics-informed learning of partial differential equations (PDEs) has been dominated by multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), whose spectral bias and dense parameterization limit both accuracy and interpretability. Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KANs) mitigate these limitations because their learnable spline activations are structurally aligned with the piecewise-polynomial bases of classical discretizations. However, the way a PDE is cast into a loss functional is as decisive as the choice of approximator: strong-form residual minimization requires high-order derivatives and heavily weighted losses, the energy (Bubnov-Galerkin) form is restricted to self-adjoint operators and, as we show, collapses to a trivial solution for parameter-identification problems, and boundary integral forms require a known fundamental solution. We propose PG-KINN, a physics-informed KAN built on a Petrov-Galerkin formulation in which the trial space is a KAN and the test space is an independent, compactly supported, piecewise-polynomial space evaluated with Gauss-Legendre quadrature. Integration by parts lowers the differentiation order while retaining applicability to general non-self-adjoint, nonlinear, and inverse problems; the localized test functions turn the global residual into a set of element-wise weak residuals with favorable conditioning. On a suite of benchmarks spanning crack singularities, stress concentration, Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity, inverse parameter identification in heterogeneous media, and complex geometries, PG-KINN consistently outperforms legacy MLP baselines and state-of-the-art KAN-based strong/energy/inverse formulations (PIKAN). These results position the Petrov-Galerkin coupling of KAN trial spaces and polynomial test spaces as a robust and accurate route for AI-based computational mechanics.

AI.tldr: PG-KINN combines Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with a Petrov-Galerkin weak formulation to solve PDEs, using KANs as trial functions and compactly supported polynomial test functions. This approach overcomes limitations of MLP-based physics-informed methods (spectral bias, poor interpretability) and existing KAN formulations (strong-form derivative issues, energy-form restrictions, boundary-integral prerequisites), demonstrating superior performance across diverse computational mechanics benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing physics-informed PDE learning is dominated by MLPs, which suffer from spectral bias and dense, uninterpretable parameterization. While KANs offer structural alignment with classical piecewise-polynomial discretizations, current PDE loss formulations each have critical flaws: strong-form residual minimization demands high-order derivatives; energy (Bubnov-Galerkin) forms are limited to self-adjoint operators and collapse for parameter identification; boundary integral forms require known fundamental solutions. A formulation is needed that combines KAN's advantages with broad PDE applicability.
AI.method: PG-KINN employs a Petrov-Galerkin framework where the trial space uses a KAN (with learnable spline activations) and the test space uses an independent, compactly supported, piecewise-polynomial basis. Integration by parts reduces differentiation order via Gauss-Legendre quadrature. The localized test functions decompose the global residual into element-wise weak residuals, yielding better conditioning. This formulation handles non-self-adjoint, nonlinear, and inverse problems without requiring fundamental solutions.
AI.result: On benchmarks including crack singularities, stress concentration, Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity, inverse parameter identification in heterogeneous media, and complex geometries, PG-KINN consistently outperforms both legacy MLP-based baselines and state-of-the-art KAN-based formulations (PIKAN, including strong, energy, and inverse variants).
AI.conclusion: The Petrov-Galerkin coupling of KAN trial spaces with polynomial test spaces provides a robust and accurate framework for AI-driven computational mechanics, combining the structural advantages of KANs with the flexibility and conditioning benefits of weak-form residual evaluation.
